The juneau-bean-jsonapi module provides Java beans for the JSONAPI standardises a document shape, resource objects, relationships, errors, and link semantics so clients and servers can interoperate without ad-hoc per-API conventions.

The juneau-bean-jsonpatch module provides Java beans for JSON Patch (RFC 6902), the canonical patch document format used by application/json-patch+json. A JSON Patch document is a JSON array of operation objects describing changes (add, remove, replace, move, copy, test) to apply to a target JSON document.

The juneau-bean-jsonrpc module provides Java beans modelling the revision-neutral JSON-RPC 2.0 envelope: request/response/error framing plus a runtime exception for handler-side error propagation. It carries no protocol-specific knowledge and depends only on juneau-marshall, making it the shared framing layer beneath protocol-specific bean modules such as juneau-bean-mcp-v20250618.
The juneau-bean-jsonschema module provides Java beans for working with JSON Schema documents following the JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 specification.

The juneau-bean-mcp-v20250618 module provides Java beans modelling the Model Context Protocol (MCP) 2025-06-18 wire format. It's paired with a separate, revision-neutral module, juneau-bean-jsonrpc, which carries the underlying JSON-RPC 2.0 envelope, and with a 2026-07-28 sibling, juneau-bean-mcp-v20260728. See Choosing your MCP setup for why the two revisions are separate adapter modules and why they're maintained differently going forward.
The juneau-bean-openapi-v3 module provides Java beans for working with OpenAPI 3.0 documents and user interfaces.
The juneau-bean-rfc7807 module provides Java beans for RFC 7807 — Problem Details for HTTP APIs, the canonical machine-readable error format used by application/problem+json.
The juneau-bean-swagger-v2 module provides Java beans for working with Swagger 2.0 documents and user interfaces.
The juneau-commons module is the foundational layer of the Juneau ecosystem.

The org.apache.juneau.commons.beanquery package is a protocol-agnostic API for searching, sorting, projecting and paging rows of beans. The same query runs over an in-memory collection or, through the juneau-beanquery-sql module, a database table.

The org.apache.juneau.commons.bean package provides Juneau's bean-modeling layer — the annotations and introspection engine that describe how Java beans are recognized, read, written, and mapped, independently of any particular marshalling format. The marshalling modules build on this layer through a small set of SPI seams so the bean model stays decoupled from serialization concerns.

The org.apache.juneau.commons.collections package provides enhanced collection utilities that extend the standard Java Collections Framework with fluent APIs, specialized collection types, and caching capabilities.
The org.apache.juneau.commons.concurrent package provides small concurrency helpers that make locks and atomic references work cleanly with try-with-resources and Optional-style APIs.
The org.apache.juneau.commons.conversion package provides a lightweight, pluggable type-conversion engine for converting objects between types without requiring a full marshalling context or session.

The org.apache.juneau.commons.function package extends the standard java.util.function toolkit with higher-arity functional interfaces, checked-exception–friendly variants, small immutable tuples, and lazy/nullable suppliers used throughout the framework.

The org.apache.juneau.commons.http package provides lightweight, dependency-free primitives for parsing and modeling HTTP header values — media types, content-negotiation ranges, and name/value parameters — as defined by RFC 2616.

The org.apache.juneau.commons.httppart package provides the shared enumerations and exception used to describe HTTP "parts" (query parameters, path variables, headers, form data, and request/response bodies) for OpenAPI-schema-based serialization and parsing.
The org.apache.juneau.commons.io package provides file and stream utilities, console support, MIME type detection, and path builders for working with files and I/O operations.

The org.apache.juneau.commons.inject package provides Juneau's lightweight injection model. The framework is JSR-330–aligned (jakarta.inject / javax.inject) and layers a small set of Spring-flavored conveniences (@Bean, @Configuration, @Primary, @Order, @Conditional) on top — all under Juneau-owned annotations, and without a compile-time dependency on jakarta.inject-api or jakarta.annotation-api.
The org.apache.juneau.commons.lang package provides language utilities including value wrappers, version management, string formatting, state enums, and other common language constructs.

The org.apache.juneau.commons.logging package now centers on RichLogger, a JUL-compatible logger wrapper with configurable message rendering, hierarchical capture propagation, and deterministic test-capture ergonomics.

The org.apache.juneau.commons.reflect package provides comprehensive reflection utilities for working with classes, methods, fields, constructors, and annotations in a more convenient and type-safe way than the standard Java reflection APIs.
The org.apache.juneau.commons.runtime package provides lean accessors for two common runtime inputs: command-line arguments and JAR manifest files.

The org.apache.juneau.commons.settings package provides a thread-safe way to access system properties with support for global and per-thread overrides, making it useful for unit tests and configuration management.
The org.apache.juneau.commons.time package provides a precision-aware date/time type for granular time operations.

The org.apache.juneau.commons.utils package provides general-purpose utility classes for common operations including string manipulation, collection operations, class utilities, file operations, and more. It contains the most frequently used utility classes in the codebase — most notably Shorts (a terse one-import alias facade) and StringUtils, which are imported statically across the Juneau ecosystem.

Get startedDocumentation // Once, at startup. static final InMemoryBeanQueryContext<Person> PEOPLE = InMemoryBeanQueryContext .create(Person.class) .exclude("passwordHash") // Never searchable, sortable or viewable. .guard(p -> ! p.isDeleted()) // Server-only filter a request cannot remove. .defaultLimit(50) .maxLimit(500) .build(); // Per request — binding straight from raw request parameters. try (InMemoryBeanQuerySession<Person> session = PEOPLE.getSession(people)) { BeanQuery query = new BeanQuery() .setSearch("age=$gt(21),name=$prefix(Al)") .setSort("name,age-") .setLimit(20) .setOpts("counts=both"); Page<Person> page = session.find(query); page.rows().forEach(this::render); page.total().ifPresent(total -> renderFooter(page.matched().orElse(0) + " of " + total)); } One protocol-agnostic query (search, view, sort, position and limit) over a collection or a SQL table. Each guide does one task end to end: what you need first, the complete code, how to run it, and where to go next. New to Juneau? Work through Getting Started first; the guides assume you have. Build a REST API on Spring Boot: a JSON pet API on Spring Boot's Tomcat, with a Spring bean injected into the resource. About 15 minutes. Secure an endpoint with JWT and OAuth: require a bearer token, accept JWTs and opaque OAuth tokens, and check scopes. About 20 minutes. Test an endpoint with MockRestClient: unit-test a REST resource in-process, with no server or port. About 10 minutes. Call an existing REST API with a typed proxy: describe an API as a Java interface and call it through the next-generation client. About 15 minutes. Serialize a type Juneau doesn't know: write a swap so a class you can't change round-trips through JSON. About 10 minutes. Externalize config with INI/YAML and variables: move settings into an INI or YAML file and fill them from system properties and the environment. About 15 minutes. Teach Juneau to write and read a class that isn't a bean and that you can't change, by giving it a swap: a small class that converts the type to a simpler one and back.
documents.s: Serialize a type Juneau doesn't know

documents.t: An Invoice bean whose fields use a third-party-style Money type. Without help, Juneau writes Money through its toString() and can't parse it back. You'll add a MoneySwap that turns Money into a string such as "12.50 EUR" and back again, register it two ways, and round-trip an invoice through JSON. The finished program prints: with swap: {"number":"INV-1001","payments":["10.00 EUR","2.50 EUR"],"total":"12.50 EUR"} round trip: Money(amount=12.50, currency=EUR), equal=true

Java 17 or later and Maven 3. org.apache.juneau:juneau-marshall:10.0.0-SNAPSHOT, shown in the POM in step 1. About 10 minutes. 10.0.0-SNAPSHOT is not on Maven Central, so the POM adds the Apache snapshots repository. See the note in the MCP Quickstart and Install Juneau.
Put each class in src/main/java/com/example/ and start each file with package com.example;. Any package works if you use it everywhere.

Create an empty directory with this pom.xml: <project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"> <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion> <groupId>com.example</groupId> <artifactId>customswaps</artifactId> <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version> <properties> <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release> <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding> <juneau.version>10.0.0-SNAPSHOT</juneau.version> </properties> <repositories> <repository> <id>apache-snapshots</id> <url>https://repository.apache.org/snapshots/</url> <releases><enabled>false</enabled></releases> <snapshots><enabled>true</enabled></snapshots> </repository> </repositories> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> </dependencies> <build> <plugins> <plugin> <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId> <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId> <version>3.6.4</version> </plugin> </plugins> </build> </project>

Money stands in for a class from a library you don't control. It has a private constructor, record-style accessors instead of getters, and a toString() meant for debugging, so it isn't a bean and Juneau has no way to rebuild it. import java.math.*; import java.util.*; /** * An amount of money in one currency. * *

* Stands in for a type you don't control: no public constructor, no getters or setters, and a * debugging-only toString(), so Juneau has no way to turn it into JSON and back. */ public final class Money { private final BigDecimal amount; private final Currency currency; private Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) { this.amount = amount; this.currency = currency; } public static Money of(String amount, String currencyCode) { return new Money(new BigDecimal(amount), Currency.getInstance(currencyCode)); } public BigDecimal amount() { return amount; } public Currency currency() { return currency; } @Override public String toString() { return "Money(amount=" + amount + ", currency=" + currency + ")"; } @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof Money m && amount.equals(m.amount) && currency.equals(m.currency); } @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(amount, currency); } }
documents.s: 2. Add the type Juneau doesn't know

documents.t: Invoice is an ordinary bean with public fields, one of them a Money and one a list of them. import java.util.*; /** * A plain bean with {@link Money} properties. */ public class Invoice { public String number; public Money total; public List<Money> payments = new ArrayList<>(); public Invoice number(String value) { number = value; return this; } public Invoice total(Money value) { total = value; return this; } public Invoice payment(Money value) { payments.add(value); return this; } }

A StringSwap<Money> says "represent Money as a String". swap runs when serializing and unswap when parsing. The session and ClassMeta arguments give access to settings and the exact target type, which this swap doesn't need. import org.apache.juneau.marshall.*; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.swap.spi.*; /** * Serializes {@link Money} as a string such as "12.50 EUR", and parses it back. */ public class MoneySwap extends StringSwap<Money> { @Override public String swap(MarshallingSession session, Money money) { return money.amount().toPlainString() + " " + money.currency().getCurrencyCode(); } @Override public Money unswap(MarshallingSession session, String value, ClassMeta<?> hint) { var parts = value.trim().split("\\s+"); return Money.of(parts[0], parts[1]); } }

If you'd rather not register the swap on every serializer and parser, annotate the field. @Swap also works on a class you own, and on getters and setters. import org.apache.juneau.marshall.*; /** * The same idea with the swap attached to the property, so no serializer setup is needed. */ public class InvoiceAnnotated { public String number; @Swap(MoneySwap.class) public Money total; }
documents.s: 5. Or attach the swap to a field

documents.t: The program first tries the invoice without the swap, then registers MoneySwap on a serializer and a parser built from the default ones, and finally writes the annotated invoice with the plain default serializer. import org.apache.juneau.marshall.parser.*; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json.*; /** * Serializes an invoice with and without the swap, then parses it back. */ public class InvoiceDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println(run()); } public static String run() throws Exception { var invoice = new Invoice() .number("INV-1001") .total(Money.of("12.50", "EUR")) .payment(Money.of("10.00", "EUR")) .payment(Money.of("2.50", "EUR")); // Without the swap, Juneau falls back to toString(), which can't be parsed back. var plain = JsonSerializer.DEFAULT.write(invoice); String plainParse; try { JsonParser.DEFAULT.read(plain, Invoice.class); plainParse = "parsed"; } catch (ParseException e) { plainParse = "fails (" + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ")"; } // Register the swap on the serializer and the parser. var serializer = JsonSerializer.create().swaps(MoneySwap.class).build(); var parser = JsonParser.create().swaps(MoneySwap.class).build(); var json = serializer.write(invoice); var parsed = parser.read(json, Invoice.class); // The annotated bean needs no registration at all. var annotated = new InvoiceAnnotated(); annotated.number = "INV-1002"; annotated.total = Money.of("99.95", "USD"); return String.join("\n", "without swap: " + plain, "parse it: " + plainParse, "with swap: " + json, "round trip: " + parsed.total + ", equal=" + parsed.total.equals(invoice.total), "annotated: " + JsonSerializer.DEFAULT.write(annotated)); } }

From the project directory: mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=com.example.InvoiceDemo Expected output: without swap: {"number":"INV-1001","payments":["Money(amount=10.00, currency=EUR)","Money(amount=2.50, currency=EUR)"],"total":"Money(amount=12.50, currency=EUR)"} parse it: fails (ParseException) with swap: {"number":"INV-1001","payments":["10.00 EUR","2.50 EUR"],"total":"12.50 EUR"} round trip: Money(amount=12.50, currency=EUR), equal=true annotated: {"number":"INV-1002","total":"99.95 USD"}

Why the first attempt fails. Juneau serializes a non-bean by calling toString(). To parse it back, it needs a public constructor taking a String, or a public static method taking one with a name such as fromString, valueOf or parse. Money has neither, so parsing fails. See Swap. A swap replaces the type for marshalling. With MoneySwap registered, every serializer and parser built with it treats Money as a String, wherever it appears: a field, a list element, or a map value. swaps(...) accepts any number of swap classes. Registration or annotation. Registering on the builder keeps the model class untouched and lets different serializers make different choices. @Swap travels with the class or field, so the default serializers pick it up. See @Swap Annotation. Other shapes. A swap can produce a map or a bean instead of a string, can be one-way for types you only write, and can render through a template. See One-way Swaps and Templated Swaps.

Use the swap in a REST API: put @MarshalledConfig(swaps=MoneySwap.class) on the resource class, or keep the @Swap field annotation, then follow Build a REST API on Spring Boot. Read every swap variant and the built-in swaps for dates, enums and more: Swap. Load settings from files instead of code: Externalize config with INI/YAML and variables.
Move settings out of your code into a config file, in INI or YAML, and let variables fill in values from system properties, environment variables and other entries when they are read.
documents.s: Externalize config with INI/YAML and variables

documents.t: A small program that loads the same settings from app.ini and from app.yaml, reads single entries as typed values, reads a whole section through a Java interface, and overrides the port with -Dapp.port without editing either file. The program prints: yaml server section: localhost 8080 http://localhost:8080 with -Dapp.port=9090: http://localhost:9090

Java 17 or later and Maven 3. org.apache.juneau:juneau-config:10.0.0-SNAPSHOT, shown in the POM in step 1. It brings in juneau-marshall, which converts entries to Java types. About 15 minutes. 10.0.0-SNAPSHOT is not on Maven Central, so the POM adds the Apache snapshots repository. See the note in the MCP Quickstart and Install Juneau.

Put each class in src/main/java/com/example/ and start each file with package com.example;. Any package works if you use it everywhere. The two config files go in src/main/resources/ExternalizeConfig/.

Create an empty directory with this pom.xml: <project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"> <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion> <groupId>com.example</groupId> <artifactId>externalizeconfig</artifactId> <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version> <properties> <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release> <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding> <juneau.version>10.0.0-SNAPSHOT</juneau.version> </properties> <repositories> <repository> <id>apache-snapshots</id> <url>https://repository.apache.org/snapshots/</url> <releases><enabled>false</enabled></releases> <snapshots><enabled>true</enabled></snapshots> </repository> </repositories> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-config</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> </dependencies> <build> <plugins> <plugin> <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId> <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId> <version>3.6.4</version> </plugin> </plugins> </build> </project>

Save this as src/main/resources/ExternalizeConfig/app.ini. Sections are in brackets, and a # line before an entry is its comment. The values use three variables: ${S:app.port:8080} reads the app.port system property, defaulting to 8080. ${E:APP_DB_USER:app} reads the APP_DB_USER environment variable, defaulting to app. ${C:server/host} reads another entry from the same config. [server] # Host name clients use to reach the service. host = localhost # Defaults to 8080; start the JVM with -Dapp.port=9090 to override. port = ${S:app.port:8080} # Built from the two entries above. baseUrl = http://${C:server/host}:${C:server/port} [database] # Read from the APP_DB_USER environment variable, falling back to "app". user = ${E:APP_DB_USER:app} poolSize = 10

Save this as src/main/resources/ExternalizeConfig/app.yaml. Top-level keys are sections, nested keys are entries, and the variables work the same way. You need only one of the two files; this guide loads both to show they read the same. server: # Host name clients use to reach the service. host: localhost # Defaults to 8080; start the JVM with -Dapp.port=9090 to override. port: ${S:app.port:8080} # Built from the two entries above. baseUrl: http://${C:server/host}:${C:server/port} database: # Read from the APP_DB_USER environment variable, falling back to "app". user: ${E:APP_DB_USER:app} poolSize: 10
documents.s: 3. Or write the same settings in YAML

documents.t: Juneau can implement an interface over a section for you: each getter reads the entry with the matching name and converts it to the return type. /** * Typed view of the [server] section; Juneau implements it for you. */ public interface AppSettings { String getHost(); int getPort(); String getBaseUrl(); }
documents.s: 4. Describe a section as an interface

documents.t: import org.apache.juneau.config.*; import org.apache.juneau.config.store.*; /** * Loads the same settings from INI and from YAML, reads them three ways, and shows a system-property override. */ public class ConfigDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println(run()); } public static String run() throws Exception { // The file extension picks the format; the classpath store reads from src/main/resources. var ini = Config.create("ExternalizeConfig/app.ini").store(ClasspathStore.DEFAULT).build(); var yaml = Config.create("ExternalizeConfig/app.yaml").store(ClasspathStore.DEFAULT).build(); // One key at a time, converted to the type you ask for. var port = ini.get("server/port").asInteger().orElse(0); var user = ini.get("database/user").asString().orElse(null); var poolSize = yaml.get("database/poolSize").asInteger().orElse(0); // A whole section through an interface. var server = yaml.getSection("server").asInterface(AppSettings.class).orElseThrow(); // ${S:app.port:8080} is resolved every time the value is read. System.setProperty("app.port", "9090"); String overridden; try { overridden = ini.get("server/baseUrl").asString().orElse(null); } finally { System.clearProperty("app.port"); } return String.join("\n", "ini server/port: " + port, "ini database/user: " + user, "yaml database/poolSize: " + poolSize, "yaml server section: " + server.getHost() + " " + server.getPort() + " " + server.getBaseUrl(), "with -Dapp.port=9090: " + overridden); } }

From the project directory: mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=com.example.ConfigDemo Expected output, unless APP_DB_USER is set in your environment: ini server/port: 8080 ini database/user: app yaml database/poolSize: 10 yaml server section: localhost 8080 http://localhost:8080 with -Dapp.port=9090: http://localhost:9090

One API, two formats. Config.create(name) picks the format from the file extension: .yaml or .yml is YAML, anything else is INI. Both produce the same sections and entries, so the code that reads them doesn't change. See INI Config Format and YAML Config Files. Where the file comes from. ClasspathStore reads from the classpath, which suits defaults packaged with the application. The default store, FileStore.DEFAULT, reads files from the working directory instead and can save changes back. See Config Stores. Variables resolve on read. Entries keep the ${S:...}, ${E:...} and ${C:...} text. Juneau resolves them each time you read the entry, which is why setting app.port after loading still changes baseUrl. The default after the comma applies when the property or variable is missing. See Variables and the Simple Variable Language. Typed reads. get(key) returns an entry; asInteger(), asString() and the other as... methods convert it and return an Optional, empty when the entry is missing. getSection(name).asInterface(type) maps a whole section.

Use config values in a REST resource with ${C:...} in annotations, then follow Build a REST API on Spring Boot. Read more about sections, imports, listeners and saving changes: juneau-config. Control how your own types are written: Serialize a type Juneau doesn't know.
Get an OpenAPI 3.1 document, a Swagger v2 document and two browsable UIs for a REST resource, generated from the resource's own annotations with no separate spec file to maintain.
documents.s: Generate OpenAPI docs for your API

documents.t: A small Task API that lists, fetches and creates to-do items. Adding two documentation mixins to it serves the API's contract at /openapi.json, /openapi.yaml and /api, and interactive pages at /redoc and /swagger. A short program fetches the OpenAPI document and prints what it describes: openapi: 3.1.0 title: Task API GET /tasks - List tasks

Java 17 or later and Maven 3. These dependencies, shown in the POM in step 1: org.apache.juneau:juneau-rest-server:10.0.0-SNAPSHOT, which contains the documentation mixins org.apache.juneau:juneau-rest-mock:10.0.0-SNAPSHOT, used here to call the API without starting a server About 10 minutes. 10.0.0-SNAPSHOT is not on Maven Central, so the POM adds the Apache snapshots repository. See the note in the MCP Quickstart and Install Juneau.
Put each class in src/main/java/com/example/ and start each file with package com.example;. Any package works if you use it everywhere.

Create an empty directory with this pom.xml: <project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"> <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion> <groupId>com.example</groupId> <artifactId>openapidocs</artifactId> <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version> <properties> <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release> <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding> <juneau.version>10.0.0-SNAPSHOT</juneau.version> </properties> <repositories> <repository> <id>apache-snapshots</id> <url>https://repository.apache.org/snapshots/</url> <releases><enabled>false</enabled></releases> <snapshots><enabled>true</enabled></snapshots> </repository> </repositories> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-server</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-mock</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> </dependencies> <build> <plugins> <plugin> <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId> <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId> <version>3.6.4</version> </plugin> </plugins> </build> </project>

@Schema adds descriptions to the bean and its properties. They end up in the generated schema for Task. import org.apache.juneau.commons.*; /** * A to-do item. */ @Schema(description="A to-do item.") public class Task { @Schema(description="Server-assigned identifier.") public int id; @Schema(description="What needs doing.") public String title; @Schema(description="Whether the task is finished.") public boolean done; public Task() {} public Task(int id, String title, boolean done) { this.id = id; this.title = title; this.done = done; } }

The title and description in @Rest, and the summary and description on each operation, become the document's info block and the operation summaries. mixins grafts in the documentation endpoints: SwaggerUiMixin brings /swagger and /api, and RedocMixin brings /redoc and the /openapi documents. BasicUniversalConfig adds serializers for HTML as well as JSON, which the two UI pages need. import java.util.*; import java.util.concurrent.*; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*; import org.apache.juneau.commons.*; import org.apache.juneau.http.*; import org.apache.juneau.http.response.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.config.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.docs.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.servlet.*; /** * A small task API that publishes its own Swagger 2.0 and OpenAPI 3.1 documents. */ @Rest( title="Task API", description="Create and list to-do items.", mixins={SwaggerUiMixin.class, RedocMixin.class} ) public class TaskResource extends RestServlet implements BasicUniversalConfig { private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L; private final Map<Integer,Task> tasks = new ConcurrentSkipListMap<>(); private final AtomicInteger nextId = new AtomicInteger(1); @RestGet(path="/tasks", summary="List tasks", description="Returns every task, oldest first.") public Collection<Task> list() { return tasks.values(); } @RestGet(path="/tasks/{id}", summary="Get a task") public Task get(@Path("id") @Schema(description="Task identifier.") int id) { var t = tasks.get(id); if (t == null) throw new NotFound("No task with id {0}", id); return t; } @RestPost(path="/tasks", summary="Create a task") public Task create(@Content Task task) { task.id = nextId.getAndIncrement(); tasks.put(task.id, task); return task; } }
documents.s: 3. Write the resource and add the docs mixins

documents.t: MockRestClient runs the resource in-process. The program fetches /openapi.json and prints its version, title and the task operations. import java.util.*; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.collections.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.classic.*; /** * Starts {@link TaskResource} in-process, fetches /openapi.json and prints the task operations it documents. */ public class TaskDocsDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println(run()); } public static String run() throws Exception { try (var client = MockRestClient.buildJson(TaskResource.class)) { var json = client.get("/openapi.json").run().assertStatus(200).getContent().asString(); var doc = JsonMap.ofString(json); var lines = new ArrayList<String>(); lines.add("openapi: " + doc.getString("openapi")); lines.add("title: " + doc.getMap("info").getString("title")); var paths = doc.getMap("paths"); for (var path : new TreeSet<>(paths.keySet())) { if (! path.startsWith("/tasks")) continue; // Skip the documentation endpoints, which document themselves too. var ops = paths.getMap(path); for (var method : new TreeSet<>(ops.keySet())) lines.add(method.toUpperCase() + " " + path + " - " + ops.getMap(method).getString("summary")); } return String.join("\n", lines); } } }

From the project directory: mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=com.example.TaskDocsDemo Expected output: openapi: 3.1.0 title: Task API GET /tasks - List tasks POST /tasks - Create a task GET /tasks/{id} - Get a task To browse the UIs, deploy TaskResource like any Juneau servlet, for example with Build a REST API on Spring Boot, then open /redoc or /swagger under its path.

The document comes from your code. Juneau builds it from the resource and operation annotations, the Java signatures (@Path, @Content, the return types) and the bean schemas, so it changes when the code does. Mixins choose the endpoints. Each mixin is a small @Rest resource merged into yours. The OpenAPI document lists the mixins' own endpoints as well, which is why the program filters to /tasks. BasicRestServlet and BasicRestResource include both mixins by default; with a plain RestServlet, as here, you pick the ones you want. See API-Docs Mixin Pack. Two spec versions. /openapi, /openapi.json and /openapi.yaml serve OpenAPI 3.1, and /api serves Swagger v2. /openapi and /api follow the request's Accept header; the .json and .yaml URLs always return that format. See BasicRestServlet Swagger and OpenAPI 3.1 and Swagger.

Test the API and its documentation endpoints in JUnit: Test an endpoint with MockRestClient. Call the API from Java through a typed interface: Call an existing REST API with a typed proxy. Require a bearer token on the API: Secure an endpoint with JWT and OAuth.

Protect a REST endpoint so that only callers with a valid bearer token and the right scope get through. The same endpoint accepts signed JWTs, checked locally against the issuer's public keys, and opaque tokens, checked by an OAuth 2.0 introspection call.
documents.s: Secure an endpoint with JWT and OAuth

documents.t: An Orders API with one endpoint, GET /orders. A bearer-token guard runs before the endpoint and rejects missing, forged, expired and wrong-audience tokens with 401. The endpoint then checks for the orders:read scope and answers 403 without it. To stay self-contained, the guide issues its own JWTs from a generated RSA key and runs a small local stand-in for the introspection endpoint, so you don't need a real identity provider. When you run it, you'll see one line per kind of caller: no token: 401 Bearer realm="orders" valid JWT: 200 "orders for alice" ...

Java 17 or later and Maven 3. These dependencies, all shown in the POM in step 1: org.apache.juneau:juneau-rest-server-auth-jwt:10.0.0-SNAPSHOT org.apache.juneau:juneau-rest-server-auth-oauth:10.0.0-SNAPSHOT org.apache.juneau:juneau-rest-mock:10.0.0-SNAPSHOT, used here to call the endpoint without starting a server com.nimbusds:nimbus-jose-jwt:10.9.1 and com.nimbusds:oauth2-oidc-sdk:11.38.2. The two Juneau auth modules mark these as provided, so you declare them yourself. About 20 minutes. 10.0.0-SNAPSHOT is not on Maven Central, so the POM adds the Apache snapshots repository. See the note in the MCP Quickstart and Install Juneau.
Put each class in src/main/java/com/example/ and start each file with package com.example;. Any package works if you use it everywhere.

Create an empty directory with this pom.xml: <project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"> <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion> <groupId>com.example</groupId> <artifactId>secureanendpoint</artifactId> <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version> <properties> <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release> <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding> <juneau.version>10.0.0-SNAPSHOT</juneau.version> </properties> <repositories> <repository> <id>apache-snapshots</id> <url>https://repository.apache.org/snapshots/</url> <releases><enabled>false</enabled></releases> <snapshots><enabled>true</enabled></snapshots> </repository> </repositories> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-server-auth-jwt</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>com.nimbusds</groupId> <artifactId>nimbus-jose-jwt</artifactId> <version>10.9.1</version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-server-auth-oauth</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>com.nimbusds</groupId> <artifactId>oauth2-oidc-sdk</artifactId> <version>11.38.2</version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-mock</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> </dependencies> <build> <plugins> <plugin> <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId> <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId> <version>3.6.4</version> </plugin> </plugins> </build> </project>

The resource registers a BearerTokenGuard as a bean. The guard reads the Authorization: Bearer ... header, hands the token to a TokenValidator, and either rejects the request with 401 and a WWW-Authenticate challenge or stores the validated claims for the endpoint. The endpoint receives them as an @Auth ClaimsPrincipal and does its own scope check. import java.util.*; import org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.*; import org.apache.juneau.http.response.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.auth.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.config.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.guard.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.servlet.*; /** * An endpoint that only answers requests carrying a valid bearer token. */ @Rest(title="Orders API") public class SecureResource extends RestServlet implements BasicJsonConfig { private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L; private final transient TokenValidator validator; public SecureResource(TokenValidator validator) { this.validator = validator; } // Every request must pass this guard before any @RestOp method runs. @Bean public RestGuardList guards(BeanStore beanStore) { return RestGuardList.create(beanStore) .append(BearerTokenGuard.create().realm("orders").validator(validator).build()) .build(); } @RestGet(path="/orders") public String orders(@Auth ClaimsPrincipal caller) { if (! hasScope(caller, "orders:read")) throw new Forbidden("Missing scope orders:read"); return "orders for " + caller.getName(); } private static boolean hasScope(ClaimsPrincipal caller, String wanted) { // A JWT carries "scope" as a space-separated string; an introspection result carries it as a list. var scope = caller.getClaims().get("scope"); if (scope instanceof Collection<?> c) return c.contains(wanted); return scope != null && Arrays.asList(scope.toString().split(" ")).contains(wanted); } }

JwtTokenValidator checks a JWT's signature against the issuer's JSON Web Key Set, and checks its issuer, audience and expiry. In production, point it at the issuer's JWKS URL. OAuthIntrospectionValidator posts an opaque token to the authorization server's introspection endpoint and requires the listed scopes. either sends anything shaped like a JWT (three dot-separated parts) to the first and everything else to the second. import java.net.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.auth.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.auth.jwt.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.auth.oauth.*; import com.nimbusds.jose.jwk.source.*; import com.nimbusds.jose.proc.*; /** * The token validators the endpoint can use. */ public final class SecureValidators { public static final String ISSUER = "https://issuer.example.com/"; public static final String AUDIENCE = "https://api.example.com"; private SecureValidators() {} /** Production: verify JWTs against the identity provider's published keys. */ public static TokenValidator jwt(URI jwksUrl) { return JwtTokenValidator.create().jwksUrl(jwksUrl).issuer(ISSUER).audience(AUDIENCE).build(); } /** Same checks, with the keys supplied directly (used by the test). */ public static TokenValidator jwt(JWKSource<SecurityContext> keys) { return JwtTokenValidator.create().jwkSource(keys).issuer(ISSUER).audience(AUDIENCE).build(); } /** Opaque OAuth 2.0 tokens: ask the authorization server whether the token is active (RFC 7662). */ public static TokenValidator introspection(URI endpoint, String clientId, String clientSecret) { return OAuthIntrospectionValidator.create() .introspectionEndpoint(endpoint) .clientId(clientId) .clientSecret(clientSecret) .requiredScopes("orders:read") .build(); } /** Accept either kind: a JWT has three dot-separated parts, an opaque token doesn't. */ public static TokenValidator either(TokenValidator jwt, TokenValidator opaque) { return token -> token.split("\\.", -1).length == 3 ? jwt.validate(token) : opaque.validate(token); } }

To run without an identity provider, generate an RSA key pair, sign tokens with the private key, and publish the public key as the key set the validator trusts. A real issuer does exactly this on its side. import java.time.*; import java.util.*; import com.nimbusds.jose.*; import com.nimbusds.jose.crypto.*; import com.nimbusds.jose.jwk.*; import com.nimbusds.jose.jwk.gen.*; import com.nimbusds.jwt.*; /** * Stands in for your identity provider: owns an RSA key pair and signs short-lived JWTs with it. */ public class TokenIssuer { private final RSAKey key; public TokenIssuer() throws JOSEException { key = new RSAKeyGenerator(2048).keyID("demo-key").algorithm(JWSAlgorithm.RS256).generate(); } /** The public half, as a JWKS document would publish it. */ public JWKSet publicKeys() { return new JWKSet(key.toPublicJWK()); } public String issue(String subject, String scope, String audience) throws JOSEException { var now = Instant.now(); var claims = new JWTClaimsSet.Builder() .issuer(SecureValidators.ISSUER) .audience(audience) .subject(subject) .claim("scope", scope) .issueTime(Date.from(now)) .notBeforeTime(Date.from(now)) .expirationTime(Date.from(now.plus(Duration.ofMinutes(5)))) .build(); var jwt = new SignedJWT(new JWSHeader.Builder(JWSAlgorithm.RS256).keyID(key.getKeyID()).build(), claims); jwt.sign(new RSASSASigner(key)); return jwt.serialize(); } }

A tiny JDK HTTP server stands in for the authorization server's introspection endpoint. It treats opaque-good as an active token with the orders:read scope, and every other token as revoked. import java.io.*; import java.net.*; import java.nio.charset.*; import com.sun.net.httpserver.*; /** * Stands in for an OAuth 2.0 authorization server's introspection endpoint. * The token "opaque-good" is active with scope orders:read; every other token is inactive. */ public class TokenIntrospectionStub implements Closeable { private final HttpServer server; public TokenIntrospectionStub() throws IOException { server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0), 0); server.createContext("/introspect", exchange -> { var form = new String(exchange.getRequestBody().readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8); var body = form.contains("token=opaque-good") ? "{\"active\":true,\"sub\":\"reporting-job\",\"scope\":\"orders:read\"}" : "{\"active\":false}"; var bytes = body.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8); exchange.getResponseHeaders().add("Content-Type", "application/json"); exchange.sendResponseHeaders(200, bytes.length); try (var out = exchange.getResponseBody()) { out.write(bytes); } }); server.start(); } public URI endpoint() { return URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:" + server.getAddress().getPort() + "/introspect"); } @Override public void close() { server.stop(0); } }

MockRestClient calls the resource in-process, with no servlet container. Each call sends a different token. import java.util.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.classic.*; import com.nimbusds.jose.jwk.source.*; /** * Calls the secured endpoint in-process with no token, good tokens and bad tokens. */ public class SecureDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println(run()); } public static String run() throws Exception { var issuer = new TokenIssuer(); try (var authServer = new TokenIntrospectionStub()) { var validator = SecureValidators.either( SecureValidators.jwt(new ImmutableJWKSet<>(issuer.publicKeys())), SecureValidators.introspection(authServer.endpoint(), "orders-api", "change-me")); try (var client = MockRestClient.buildLax(new SecureResource(validator))) { var lines = new ArrayList<String>(); var res = client.get("/orders").run(); lines.add("no token: " + res.getStatusCode() + " " + res.getHeader("WWW-Authenticate").asString().orElse("")); var good = issuer.issue("alice", "orders:read", SecureValidators.AUDIENCE); lines.add("valid JWT: " + call(client, good)); var otherApi = issuer.issue("alice", "orders:read", "https://other.example.com"); lines.add("wrong audience: " + call(client, otherApi)); var noScope = issuer.issue("bob", "profile", SecureValidators.AUDIENCE); lines.add("missing scope: " + call(client, noScope)); lines.add("opaque token: " + call(client, "opaque-good")); lines.add("revoked token: " + call(client, "opaque-revoked")); return String.join("\n", lines); } } } private static String call(MockRestClient client, String token) throws Exception { var res = client.get("/orders").header("Authorization", "Bearer " + token).run(); return res.getStatusCode() == 200 ? "200 " + res.getContent().asString() : String.valueOf(res.getStatusCode()); } }
documents.s: 6. Call the endpoint as different callers

documents.t: From the project directory: mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=com.example.SecureDemo Expected output: no token: 401 Bearer realm="orders" valid JWT: 200 "orders for alice" wrong audience: 401 missing scope: 403 opaque token: 200 "orders for reporting-job" revoked token: 401

The guard runs first. A RestGuardList bean applies to every operation in the resource. BearerTokenGuard answers 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="orders" when the header is missing or the validator rejects the token, so your @RestOp methods never see an unauthenticated call. See AuthN Guards. Validation is pluggable. TokenValidator is a single-method interface, which is why either can be a lambda. With a JWKS URL, JwtTokenValidator caches the key set for 5 minutes and refetches it early when a token names a key id it hasn't seen, so key rotation needs no restart. Invalid signatures, expired tokens and a wrong aud or iss all fail validation, so the wrong-audience call gets 401, not 403. See OAuth 2.0 / OIDC AuthN Support. Authorization stays in your code. The guard only proves who the caller is. The scope check in orders decides what they may do, and answers 403. A JWT carries scope as a space-separated string and an introspection response carries it as a list, so hasScope accepts both. Other ways in. For authentication that runs at the servlet-filter layer, or that covers several resources at once, see the AuthN Filter Framework and the REST Authenticator.

Let users log in through a browser with an OpenID Connect provider: OIDC Relying Party Login. Get tokens from a real authorization server with the client-credentials or authorization-code (PKCE) flows, and set up OIDC discovery: OAuth 2.0 / OIDC AuthN Support. Write JUnit tests for the endpoint: Test an endpoint with MockRestClient. Publish the API's contract: Generate OpenAPI docs for your API.

A small pet API that runs on Spring Boot's embedded Tomcat. It lists pets, returns one pet by id and adds a pet, and the same methods answer in JSON, XML, HTML and the other formats Juneau registers. The pet store is an ordinary Spring bean that Spring injects into the Juneau resource. When you are done, curl -H "Accept: application/json" http://localhost:8080/pets/1 returns {"id":1,"name":"Fido"}.

Java 17 or newer and Maven 3.9 or newer. org.apache.juneau:juneau-rest-server-springboot:10.0.0-SNAPSHOT, which brings juneau-rest-server and juneau-marshall with it. org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-web:4.1.1, plus the spring-boot-maven-plugin to run the app. Port 8080 free. About 15 minutes. 10.0.0-SNAPSHOT needs the Apache snapshots repository, which the pom.xml below declares; Maven Central has only the 9.2.1 release today (see Install Juneau and Downloads).

Make an empty directory and save this as pom.xml: <project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd"> <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion> <groupId>com.example</groupId> <artifactId>pets</artifactId> <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version> <properties> <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release> <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding> <juneau.version>10.0.0-SNAPSHOT</juneau.version> <spring-boot.version>4.1.1</spring-boot.version> </properties> <repositories> <repository> <id>apache-snapshots</id> <url>https://repository.apache.org/snapshots/</url> <releases><enabled>false</enabled></releases> <snapshots><enabled>true</enabled></snapshots> </repository> </repositories> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-server-springboot</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId> <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId> <version>${spring-boot.version}</version> <exclusions> <!-- Juneau does the JSON, so Jackson is not needed. --> <exclusion> <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId> <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jackson</artifactId> </exclusion> <!-- Spring Boot then logs through java.util.logging. --> <exclusion> <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId> <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-logging</artifactId> </exclusion> </exclusions> </dependency> </dependencies> <build> <plugins> <plugin> <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId> <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId> <version>${spring-boot.version}</version> </plugin> </plugins> </build> </project> Put the Java files from the next steps in src/main/java/com/example/pets/, and start each one with package com.example.pets;.

Pet.java is a plain bean. Juneau serializes its public fields, so it needs no annotations: /** * A pet, serialized as {@code {"id":1,"name":"Fido"}}. */ public class Pet { /** The pet's id, assigned by {@link PetStore}. */ public int id; /** The pet's name. */ public String name; /** Used by the parser. */ public Pet() {} /** * Creates a pet. * * @param id The id. * @param name The name. */ public Pet(int id, String name) { this.id = id; this.name = name; } }

PetStore.java keeps the pets in memory. Spring creates one instance and shares it: import java.util.*; import java.util.concurrent.*; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*; /** * An in-memory pet store. Spring creates one and injects it into {@link PetResource}. */ public class PetStore { private final Map<Integer,Pet> pets = new ConcurrentSkipListMap<>(); private final AtomicInteger nextId = new AtomicInteger(1); /** Creates the store with one pet in it. */ public PetStore() { add("Fido"); } /** * Adds a pet. * * @param name The pet's name. * @return The new pet, with its id. */ public Pet add(String name) { var pet = new Pet(nextId.getAndIncrement(), name); pets.put(pet.id, pet); return pet; } /** * Looks up a pet. * * @param id The id. * @return The pet, or empty if there is none with that id. */ public Optional<Pet> get(int id) { return Optional.ofNullable(pets.get(id)); } /** * Returns every pet, in id order. * * @return The pets. */ public List<Pet> list() { return new ArrayList<>(pets.values()); } }

PetResource.java is the API. It extends BasicRestResource, the base class for child resources, and takes the store in its constructor: import java.util.*; import org.apache.juneau.http.*; import org.apache.juneau.http.response.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.servlet.*; import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.*; /** * The pet API, mounted at {@code /pets} under {@link PetRootServlet}. */ @Rest(path = "/pets", title = "Pets") public class PetResource extends BasicRestResource { private final PetStore store; /** * Called by Spring. * * @param store The pet store bean. */ @Autowired public PetResource(PetStore store) { this.store = store; } /** * Lists the pets. * * @return Every pet. */ @RestGet("/") public List<Pet> listPets() { return store.list(); } /** * Returns one pet. * * @param id The pet id from the URL. * @return The pet. * @throws NotFound If there is no pet with that id. */ @RestGet("/{id}") public Pet getPet(@Path("id") int id) throws NotFound { return store.get(id).orElseThrow(() -> new NotFound("No pet with id " + id)); } /** * Adds a pet. * * @param pet The pet to add; only {@code name} is used. * @return The new pet, with its id. */ @RestPost("/") public Pet addPet(@Content Pet pet) { return store.add(pet.name); } }

PetRootServlet.java is the servlet Spring Boot mounts. It extends BasicSpringRestServletGroup, so its children are looked up as Spring beans: import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.springboot.*; /** * The servlet Spring Boot mounts. Its children are looked up as Spring beans. */ @Rest(title = "Pet service", children = { PetResource.class }) public class PetRootServlet extends BasicSpringRestServletGroup { private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L; }

PetApplication.java declares the beans and mounts the root servlet at /*: import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.*; import org.springframework.boot.builder.*; import org.springframework.boot.web.servlet.*; import org.springframework.context.annotation.*; /** * Starts Spring Boot with the pet API on embedded Tomcat (port 8080 by default). */ @SpringBootApplication public class PetApplication { /** * Starts the application. * * @param args Spring Boot arguments, for example {@code --server.port=9090}. */ public static void main(String[] args) { new SpringApplicationBuilder(PetApplication.class).run(args); } /** * The store shared by every request. * * @return A new store. */ @Bean public PetStore petStore() { return new PetStore(); } /** * The pet API, as a Spring bean so the store is injected. * * @param store The store bean. * @return The resource. */ @Bean public PetResource petResource(PetStore store) { return new PetResource(store); } /** * The root servlet. * * @return The servlet. */ @Bean public PetRootServlet petRootServlet() { return new PetRootServlet(); } /** * Mounts the root servlet at {@code /*}, so the API answers at {@code /pets}. * * @param servlet The root servlet bean. * @return The registration. */ @Bean public ServletRegistrationBean<PetRootServlet> petServlet(PetRootServlet servlet) { return new ServletRegistrationBean<>(servlet, "/*"); } }

Start the app: mvn spring-boot:run When the log shows Tomcat started on port 8080, call it from a second terminal: curl -H "Accept: application/json" http://localhost:8080/pets/1 {"id":1,"name":"Fido"} Add a pet: curl -H "Accept: application/json" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"name":"Rex"}' http://localhost:8080/pets {"id":2,"name":"Rex"} List them: curl -H "Accept: application/json" http://localhost:8080/pets [{"id":1,"name":"Fido"},{"id":2,"name":"Rex"}] Ask for a pet that does not exist and print only the status code: curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -H "Accept: application/json" http://localhost:8080/pets/99 404 Leave out the Accept header, or open http://localhost:8080/pets in a browser, and you get the HTML view of the same data. Press Ctrl+C to stop the app.

Mounting. Spring Boot registers PetRootServlet through the ServletRegistrationBean, the same pattern Spring Boot Overview uses. If you would rather not write that bean, the opt-in auto-configuration (juneau.rest.auto-register=true) mounts servlets from their own @Rest paths; see REST Server Self-Registration. Spring beans as children. BasicSpringRestServletGroup resolves each class in children from the Spring context before it tries to create one itself, so PetResource is the petResource bean with PetStore already injected. The module and its auto-configuration classes are described in juneau-rest-server-springboot. Operations. @RestGet and @RestPost map methods to HTTP verbs and paths, @Path binds the {id} segment, and @Content parses the request body into a Pet. Throwing NotFound sends a 404. The same annotations are introduced in Your first REST app. Formats. BasicRestResource carries Juneau's universal configuration, so the Accept header picks the serializer. JSON is Juneau's job here, which is why the pom.xml excludes Spring's Jackson starter.

Test an endpoint with MockRestClient: test resources like this one without starting a server. Secure an endpoint with JWT and OAuth: put a guard in front of the API. Generate OpenAPI docs for your API: publish a description of it.

A small greeting resource and a JUnit test class that calls it through MockRestClient. The mock client sends real requests and parses real responses, but hands them straight to the resource in the same JVM, so no server starts and no port is opened. The three tests check a JSON response, a request body round-trip and a 400 error, and mvn test reports them passing.

Java 17 or newer and Maven 3.9 or newer. org.apache.juneau:juneau-rest-server:10.0.0-SNAPSHOT for the resource. org.apache.juneau:juneau-rest-mock:10.0.0-SNAPSHOT (test scope), which brings the REST client with it. org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:6.0.3 (test scope). About 10 minutes. 10.0.0-SNAPSHOT needs the Apache snapshots repository, which the pom.xml below declares; Maven Central has only the 9.2.1 release today (see Install Juneau and Downloads).

Make an empty directory and save this as pom.xml: <project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd"> <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion> <groupId>com.example</groupId> <artifactId>greetings</artifactId> <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version> <properties> <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release> <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding> <juneau.version>10.0.0-SNAPSHOT</juneau.version> </properties> <repositories> <repository> <id>apache-snapshots</id> <url>https://repository.apache.org/snapshots/</url> <releases><enabled>false</enabled></releases> <snapshots><enabled>true</enabled></snapshots> </repository> </repositories> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-server</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-mock</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> <scope>test</scope> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId> <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId> <version>6.0.3</version> <scope>test</scope> </dependency> </dependencies> <build> <plugins> <plugin> <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId> <version>3.5.4</version> </plugin> </plugins> </build> </project> The two main classes go in src/main/java/com/example/greetings/ and the test in src/test/java/com/example/greetings/. Start each file with package com.example.greetings;.

Greeting.java: /** * The bean the greeting service returns. */ public class Greeting { /** Who is greeted. */ public String name; /** The greeting text. */ public String message; /** Used by the parser. */ public Greeting() {} /** * Creates a greeting for a name. * * @param name Who is greeted. */ public Greeting(String name) { this.name = name; this.message = "Hello, " + name + "!"; } }

GreetingResource.java has one GET and one POST. The POST rejects a blank name with a 400: import org.apache.juneau.http.*; import org.apache.juneau.http.response.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.servlet.*; /** * A small greeting service: one GET, one POST that validates its body. */ @Rest(path = "/greetings", title = "Greeting service") public class GreetingResource extends BasicRestServlet { private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L; /** * Greets the name in the path. * * @param name The name from the URL. * @return The greeting. */ @RestGet("/{name}") public Greeting greet(@Path("name") String name) { return new Greeting(name); } /** * Greets the name in the request body. * * @param body A greeting with only {@code name} set. * @return The completed greeting. * @throws BadRequest If the name is missing or blank. */ @RestPost("/") public Greeting create(@Content Greeting body) throws BadRequest { if (body.name == null || body.name.isBlank()) throw new BadRequest("name is required"); return new Greeting(body.name); } }

GreetingResource_Test.java: import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.*; import org.junit.jupiter.api.*; class GreetingResource_Test { @Test void a01_getReturnsJson() throws Exception { try (var mock = MockRestClient.create(GreetingResource.class); var resp = mock.get("/Ada").header("Accept", "application/json").run()) { resp.assertThat().isOk().body().contains("\"message\":\"Hello, Ada!\""); } } @Test void a02_postParsesBodyIntoBean() throws Exception { try (var mock = MockRestClient.builder(GreetingResource.class).defaultParser(JsonParser.DEFAULT).build(); var resp = mock.post("/").body(new Greeting("Grace")).run()) { resp.assertOk(); var greeting = resp.body().as(Greeting.class); assertEquals("Hello, Grace!", greeting.message); } } @Test void a03_blankNameIsRejected() throws Exception { try (var mock = MockRestClient.builder(GreetingResource.class).noTrace().build(); var resp = mock.post("/").bodyString("{\"name\":\"\"}").header("Content-Type", "application/json").run()) { resp.assertStatus(400); } } }

mvn test The end of the output: [INFO] Results: [INFO] [INFO] Tests run: 3, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0 [INFO] [INFO] BUILD SUCCESS Each request also leaves a one-line INFO access record in the log, with its status, method and path.

No server. MockRestClient.create(GreetingResource.class) builds the resource's RestContext and gives you a RestClient whose transport calls it directly. The context is built once per resource class and reused, so creating a mock client in every test is cheap. See NG Mock REST Client. Paths are relative to the resource. The mock client's root URL already ends in the resource's @Rest(path), so mock.get("/Ada") reaches /greetings/Ada. Ask for the format you test. With no Accept header the resource answers with its HTML view, so the first test sends Accept: application/json. To read a response as a bean with body().as(...), give the builder a parser with defaultParser(...), as the second test does. Expected errors stay quiet. noTrace() sends No-Trace: true, so the 400 the third test expects does not put a stack trace in the log. Two flavors. This guide uses org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.MockRestClient, which pairs with the next-generation REST client. Tests written against the classic client use org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.classic.MockRestClient, described in Mock REST Client Overview. Both ship in juneau-rest-mock.

Build a REST API on Spring Boot: a fuller resource to test the same way. Call an existing REST API with a typed proxy: the client side; test it with MockHttpTransport from NG Mock REST Client. Secure an endpoint with JWT and OAuth: test a guarded resource.

A typed Java client for a books REST API. You describe the API's endpoints as a Java interface, the next-generation RestClient implements the interface for you, and your code calls ordinary methods that send HTTP requests and return beans. So the guide runs anywhere, step 2 starts a small stand-in API on the JDK's built-in HTTP server; point the client at your real API instead when you have one. The client prints five lines, ending with Book 99: 404 Not Found.

Java 17 or newer and Maven 3.9 or newer. org.apache.juneau:juneau-rest-client:10.0.0-SNAPSHOT. It sends requests with the JDK's HttpClient, so there is no other HTTP library to add. Port 8080 free, for the stand-in API. About 15 minutes. 10.0.0-SNAPSHOT needs the Apache snapshots repository, which the pom.xml below declares; Maven Central has only the 9.2.1 release today (see Install Juneau and Downloads).

Make an empty directory and save this as pom.xml: <project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd"> <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion> <groupId>com.example</groupId> <artifactId>books</artifactId> <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version> <properties> <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release> <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding> <juneau.version>10.0.0-SNAPSHOT</juneau.version> </properties> <repositories> <repository> <id>apache-snapshots</id> <url>https://repository.apache.org/snapshots/</url> <releases><enabled>false</enabled></releases> <snapshots><enabled>true</enabled></snapshots> </repository> </repositories> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-client</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> </dependencies> <build> <plugins> <plugin> <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId> <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId> <version>3.6.4</version> </plugin> </plugins> </build> </project> Put the Java files from the next steps in src/main/java/com/example/books/, and start each one with package com.example.books;.

BookStubServer.java answers GET /books, GET /books/1 and POST /books with fixed JSON, and 404 for anything else. Skip this step if you already have an API to call: import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.*; import java.io.*; import java.net.*; import com.sun.net.httpserver.*; /** * A stand-in for the real books API, on the JDK's built-in HTTP server. Answers with fixed JSON, and echoes a * posted book back with id 3. */ public class BookStubServer { /** * Serves the stand-in API on port 8080 until the process is stopped. * * @param args Unused. * @throws IOException If the port cannot be bound. */ public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { start(8080); System.out.println("Books API stand-in on http://localhost:8080/books"); } /** * Starts the server. * * @param port The port, or {@code 0} for any free port. * @return The running server; call {@code stop(0)} to shut it down. * @throws IOException If the port cannot be bound. */ public static HttpServer start(int port) throws IOException { var server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress("localhost", port), 0); server.createContext("/books", x -> { var path = x.getRequestURI().getPath(); var method = x.getRequestMethod(); if (method.equals("GET") && path.equals("/books")) reply(x, 200, "[{\"id\":1,\"title\":\"Dune\",\"author\":\"Frank Herbert\"}," + "{\"id\":2,\"title\":\"Emma\",\"author\":\"Jane Austen\"}]"); else if (method.equals("GET") && path.equals("/books/1")) reply(x, 200, "{\"id\":1,\"title\":\"Dune\",\"author\":\"Frank Herbert\"}"); else if (method.equals("POST") && path.equals("/books")) reply(x, 200, new String(x.getRequestBody().readAllBytes(), UTF_8).replace("\"id\":0", "\"id\":3")); else reply(x, 404, "{\"error\":\"Not found\"}"); }); server.start(); return server; } private static void reply(HttpExchange x, int status, String json) throws IOException { var bytes = json.getBytes(UTF_8); x.getResponseHeaders().set("Content-Type", "application/json"); x.sendResponseHeaders(status, bytes.length); try (var out = x.getResponseBody()) { out.write(bytes); } } }

Book.java matches the JSON the API sends: /** * A book, as the books API sends it: {@code {"id":1,"title":"Dune","author":"Frank Herbert"}}. */ public class Book { /** The id the API assigned. */ public int id; /** The title. */ public String title; /** The author. */ public String author; /** Used by the parser. */ public Book() {} /** * Creates a book that has no id yet. * * @param title The title. * @param author The author. */ public Book(String title, String author) { this.title = title; this.author = author; } }

BookApi.java is the typed proxy interface. @Remote(path) is the common prefix, and each method says which request it sends: import java.util.*; import org.apache.juneau.http.*; import org.apache.juneau.http.remote.*; import org.apache.juneau.http.response.*; /** * The books API, described as a Java interface. {@code RestClient.remote(BookApi.class)} implements it. */ @Remote(path = "/books") public interface BookApi { /** * Calls {@code GET /books}. * * @return Every book. */ @RemoteGet List<Book> listBooks(); /** * Calls {@code GET /books/{id}}. * * @param id The book id. * @return The book. * @throws NotFound If the API answers 404. */ @RemoteGet("/{id}") Book getBook(@Path("id") int id) throws NotFound; /** * Calls {@code POST /books} with the book as a JSON body. * * @param book The book to add. * @return The stored book, with its id. */ @RemotePost Book addBook(@Content Book book); }

BookClient.java builds the client, asks it for a BookApi and calls the methods: import java.io.*; import org.apache.juneau.http.response.*; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; /** * Calls the books API through {@link BookApi} and prints what comes back. */ public class BookClient { /** * Runs against the API root given as the first argument, or {@code http://localhost:8080}. * * @param args The API root URL, optional. * @throws IOException If the API cannot be reached. */ public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { run(args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "http://localhost:8080", System.out); } /** * Makes the calls and prints the results. * * @param rootUrl The API root URL. * @param out Where to print. * @throws IOException If the API cannot be reached. */ public static void run(String rootUrl, PrintStream out) throws IOException { try (var client = RestClient.builder() .rootUrl(rootUrl) .defaultSerializer(JsonSerializer.DEFAULT) .defaultParser(JsonParser.DEFAULT) .allowPrivateUrls(true) // Only because the stand-in API runs on localhost. .build()) { BookApi books = client.remote(BookApi.class); for (var b : books.listBooks()) out.println(b.id + ": " + b.title + " by " + b.author); var added = books.addBook(new Book("Kindred", "Octavia E. Butler")); out.println("Added " + added.title + " as id " + added.id); out.println("Book 1 is " + books.getBook(1).title); try { books.getBook(99); } catch (NotFound e) { out.println("Book 99: 404 Not Found"); } } } }

Start the stand-in API in one terminal: mvn compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=com.example.books.BookStubServer Run the client in a second terminal: mvn exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=com.example.books.BookClient It prints: 1: Dune by Frank Herbert 2: Emma by Jane Austen Added Kindred as id 3 Book 1 is Dune Book 99: 404 Not Found The client also logs one INFO line per request, with its status, method and URL. To call your own API, pass its root URL with -Dexec.args=https://api.example.com and remove the allowPrivateUrls(true) line.

The proxy. client.remote(BookApi.class) returns a dynamic proxy. Each call joins the client's root URL, the @Remote path and the method's path, fills {id} from the @Path argument, serializes the @Content argument as the body and parses the response into the return type. The annotations are listed in Remote Proxy Interfaces and explained in REST Proxies. Errors. Because getBook declares throws NotFound, a 404 response is thrown as NotFound. Declare the error types your code wants to handle. Formats are explicit. The 10.0 client has no implicit JSON fallback, so the builder names the serializer and parser it uses with defaultSerializer(...) and defaultParser(...). Private addresses are refused by default. Proxy calls to loopback, private and cloud-metadata addresses are blocked to guard against server-side request forgery. The stand-in runs on localhost, so the client opts out with allowPrivateUrls(true). See NG Client Security. Which client. This is the next-generation client, org.apache.juneau.rest.client.RestClient, the recommended one for new code; Choosing a REST Client compares it with the classic client. Its proxies also support constant headers, timeouts, retries and more; see Declarative Remote-Proxy Features.

NG Remote Proxies: constant headers and query values, retries, timeouts and multipart bodies on the same interface. Test an endpoint with MockRestClient: test the server side in-process. HTTP Transport Adapters: swap the JDK HttpClient for Apache HttpClient, OkHttp or Jetty.

Three new opt-in modules add a themeable, security-hardened admin-console "chrome" (CSS theme tokens, a status/domain pill component, and FreeMarker-macro composition) on top of juneau-rest-server, without bleeding a template engine or the DataTables toolkit into the core: Module Adds Depends on juneau-console ConsoleChromeMixin (dynamic, per-mount-themed chrome.css endpoint), Theme (--jc-* token allowlist grammar), the chrome.css / juneau-console.js shell assets, the page-contract schema, and PageContractAssert (test helper) juneau-rest-server, juneau-bean-html5 juneau-console-freemarker ConsoleFreemarkerMixin (reserved-classpath base.ftlh + the <@tag> macro, and the <@console> / <@page> / <@navigation> / <@card> directives) juneau-rest-server-view-freemarker (provided), juneau-console <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-console</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <!-- FreeMarker composition (base.ftlh, <@tag>): --> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-console-freemarker</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> A chrome-only consumer (no FreeMarker, or FreeMarker without DataTables) pulls in exactly one or two of these — never all three, and never the unrelated -datatables module unless it explicitly asks for the macro.

Letting a consumer supply arbitrary CSS custom-property values (colors, fonts, a page background) is an XSS/CSS-injection surface: a naive var(--jc-page-bg: url(javascript:...))- style value sunk into an unescaped stylesheet can exfiltrate data or inject markup. Theme closes that gap with a normalize-then-accept-known-safe pipeline, not a denylist: Reject the raw value if it contains any C0/C1/DEL control character (checked before trimming, so a value like "\u0000 url(evil)" can't hide a control character at the boundary). Trim, then strip CSS /* ... */ comments. Case-insensitively reject any url( production outright — style values in this module never carry a URL token, structurally. Match what remains against an accept-known-safe grammar: hex/functional colors, length units, font-family lists, and a small set of gradient functions (linear-gradient, radial-gradient, etc.) with a grammar tight enough that a gradient argument list cannot itself smuggle a nested function call outside the allowed shape. Colors, fonts, and lengths sink only into non-URL-capable CSS properties (color, background-color, border-color, font-family, sizes/spacing, etc.). The only URL-capable sink for a var(--jc-*) token is background-image, and it's restricted to two specific tokens: --jc-page-bg and --jc-avatar-bg. Since step 3 above structurally rejects any url() production before a value is ever accepted, neither of those two tokens can be used to inject a URL anyway — v1 has no url() token form at all. The console logo is a static constant baked into the shipped chrome.css, never a consumer-suppliable token.
documents.s: Why a security-hardened theme, not a raw CSS override?

documents.t: ConsoleChromeMixin serves the structural chrome stylesheet with Theme.OPEN's tokens appended, plus the five stock theme stylesheets (juneau-theme-<name>.css). @Rest(mixins=ConsoleChromeMixin.class) public class ConsoleAssetsRest extends BasicRestServlet { @Bean public ConsoleChromeMixin consoleChrome() { return ConsoleChromeMixin.create().build(); // Theme.OPEN // or: ConsoleChromeMixin.create().theme("gray").build(); } }

open (default), light-red, light-brown, red and gray. Select one per page in the FreeMarker chrome with <@theme name="gray"/>, which links that theme's stylesheet. Use the builder's theme("gray") only to bake a palette into the served chrome.css itself. The petstore themes page shows every stock theme side by side.

Custom palettes are authored in FTL, not Java. Nest <@token> overrides in <@theme>, and <@console> emits the stock-theme <link> followed by an inline <style>html:root{...}</style> block: <@console> <@theme name="light-red"> <#-- A leaf: a literal value. --> <@token name="--jc-pill-red-bg" value="#fdeceb"/> <#-- An alias: a live reference that follows its target through the cascade. --> <@token name="--jc-tab-bar-bg" alias="var(--jc-card-bg)"/> </@theme> <@main/> </@console> Every value goes through the same allowlist grammar and escaper as the stock palettes. A var() in value= is resolved to a literal at render time; an alias= stays a reference. A new name in the reserved --jc-chrome-* namespace is rejected; only the two such tokens that Theme.OPEN already defines (--jc-chrome-bg, --jc-chrome-icon) can be overridden.

Every stock theme has a dark counterpart. The console picks the scheme before first paint and sets data-jc-scheme (light or dark) on the root element. The choice comes from, in order: the visitor's stored choice, only on pages that opt in with a toggle; the page's pin (light or dark), when it has one; the operating system's prefers-color-scheme. auto is the default pin, which means "follow the operating system".

In FreeMarker, set both on the console directive. scheme accepts auto, light or dark. schemeToggle is a strict boolean that adds the header's Auto / Light / Dark control and lets the visitor's stored choice win over the pin: <@console brand="Admin" scheme="auto" schemeToggle=true> <@main/> </@console> Programmatic pages use PageSpec.scheme("dark") and PageSpec.schemeToggle(true).

Add scheme="dark" to a <@token> to set it for the dark scheme only. Dark declarations render in their own rule after the light block. A dark value= must be a literal, because a var() would resolve against the light palette. A dark alias= may point at a stock theme token, at another dark token name, or at one of the console role aliases such as --jc-surface. <@theme name="light-brown"> <@token name="--jc-pill-red-bg" value="#fdeceb"/> <@token name="--jc-link" value="#d9a65c" scheme="dark"/> </@theme>

Write your own dark rules with the selector the console itself uses, so they win over the light rules at the same specificity: html:root[data-jc-scheme="dark"] .my-panel { background: var(--jc-surface); }

The pre-paint script is inline and its text is a constant. Allow it with its hash instead of a nonce by adding ConsoleChromeMixin.SCHEME_SCRIPT_CSP_HASH to script-src. The hash covers only that script. When the request carries a CSP nonce, the script is stamped with it as well, so a script-src that allows the nonce works without the hash. The inline <style> blocks (theme and token overrides) still need the request nonce, or 'unsafe-inline', in style-src.

ConsoleChromeMixin.schemeHead(req, pin, toggle) returns a SchemeHead with two pieces. Put htmlAttributes() on the <html> start tag and head() first in <head>: it holds the pre-paint script and the dark stylesheet link. The page still emits its own chrome.css and palette links. SchemeHead h = ConsoleChromeMixin.schemeHead(req, "auto", true); // <html lang="en" {h.htmlAttributes()}><head>{h.head()} ...
documents.s: Pages that do not use the FreeMarker chrome

documents.t: JuneauConsole.schemeControl(doc) builds the Auto / Light / Dark radio group for a page that wants the control somewhere other than the header, and keeps it in step with the page. The page must still set schemeToggle=true (the data-jc-scheme-toggle attribute on the root element), because the stored choice is honoured only on pages that opt in; without it the control cannot hold a choice. Whenever the effective scheme changes (the operating system, another tab, or any control), the document receives a juneau:theme-changed event whose detail.scheme is light or dark: document.addEventListener('juneau:theme-changed', e => redrawChart(e.detail.scheme));

Status/domain pills are rendered by the <@tag> macro (defined in the reserved base.ftlh, see below). It takes a domain and a value and emits , which chrome.css styles as a pill: <@tag domain="status" value=release.status/> <#-- ... --> value may be a string or an enum constant (its name() is used). Both arguments are lowercased and validated against ^[a-z0-9_-]+$; anything else (including HTML-significant characters) fails the render with a TemplateModelException rather than emitting unsafe markup.

ConsoleFreemarkerMixin extends FreemarkerMixin: register it exactly where you'd register a plain FreemarkerMixin, typed as FreemarkerMixin (the return type is load-bearing — FreemarkerViewRenderer looks it up by that exact type): import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.view.freemarker.*; import org.apache.juneau.console.freemarker.*; @Rest(mixins=FreemarkerMixin.class) public class AdminResource extends BasicRestServlet { @Bean public FreemarkerMixin freemarker() { return ConsoleFreemarkerMixin.create().basePath("/templates/").build(); } } ConsoleFreemarkerMixin augments the resolved Configuration's TemplateLoader with a second, classpath-root-rooted ClassTemplateLoader — your own basePath-relative templates are tried first, so nothing under your /templates/ tree is ever shadowed. Pull in the reserved chrome template with a loader-root-absolute include (a bare relative path resolves against the including template's own directory, not the classpath root, and would miss): <#include "/org/apache/juneau/console/base.ftlh"> ... <@tag domain="status" value=release.status/> For tables, use <@card type="datatables"> (see Building a Console Page). Server-side processing uses the data-juneau-datatable-ajax attribute described in DataTables. Consumer-supplied Configuration is honored, not augmented.
