If your BeanStore already has a freemarker.template.Configuration bean (Spring Boot autoconfig, or a microservice BasicBeanStore.put), resolveConfiguration returns that exact instance untouched — the console loader (and, transitively, the <@tag> macro) is not spliced in. Add the console template location to your own Configuration's loader if you need it in that setup.

DataTablesTable.of(MarshallingContext, String, Collection<?>, Class<?>) — the bean-row-type overload — now resolves and applies each property's @Html(render=...) the same way the ordinary HtmlSerializer/HtmlDocSerializer path already does. This is not a purely additive change: a bean already using @Html(render=...) for the existing serializer path now also renders through that same render when passed through this DataTablesTable overload, where previously it rendered the raw value. Map-based rows (no BeanPropertyMeta to resolve a render from) are unaffected and continue to render raw values.
documents.s: DataTablesTable now honors @Html(render=...) (behavior change, not purely additive)

documents.t: ConsoleFreemarkerMixin registers these directives as shared variables on the Configuration, each only if you have not already defined a variable of that name. Every directive rejects an unknown attribute, and rejects a format= attribute, with a TemplateModelException that names the directive. Attribute values that are lists (init, css, toolkit) accept either a comma-delimited string or a sequence. Nesting: <@page> is the outermost directive. Its body holds the page content and <@card> elements; it then includes the chrome template (default base.ftlh, settable with the builder's chromeTemplate(String)), and that template must contain the <@console> element. Everything else that describes the chrome nests inside <@console>. Directive Attributes Where it goes <@page> tab, init, css, toolkit Outermost; needs a body; cannot be nested or repeated. <@console> theme, icon, favicon, brand, title, chrome, scheme, schemeToggle Inside the chrome template, once; cannot be nested. Writes the whole HTML document. <@navigation> layout Inside <@console>; not nestable. <@node> id, label, href, visible, selected Inside <@navigation> or another <@node>. <@main/> none Inside <@console>; self-closing, marks where the page body goes. <@badge> id, src, refreshMs, href, placement, table, tone, labelOne, labelOther, labelMine, tooltipMax, refreshes, refreshesAllowMissing, scopeParam, scopeBy, stateFilterColumn Inside <@console>; repeatable, one per badge id. See <@badge> and BadgeDef. <@card> type, id, title, src, template, requires, class Inside <@page>; not nestable. <@theme> / <@token> name / name, value, alias, scheme <@theme> inside <@console>; <@token> inside <@theme>. slots: <@head>, <@scripts>, <@brand>, <@actions>, <@title>, <@footer>, <@body> phase (head, scripts), text (footer) Inside <@console>.

class - space-separated CSS class names added to the card's outer wrapper element (div.jc-card), after the built-in jc-card class. Each name must match [A-Za-z_-][A-Za-z0-9_-]*; anything else fails the render. Use it to keep an existing page-scope selector working, for example <@card id="skills" class="ssc-skills"> keeps .ssc-skills .row rules and closest(".ssc-skills") lookups matching. It applies to cards that have a wrapper; the markup between cards is not wrapped and takes no class.

tab - the active navigation path as node ids joined by / (for example tab="new/input"). An unknown path fails the render and the message lists the known paths. init - script URLs emitted as <script src> after the toolkit scripts, in the order given. css - stylesheet URLs emitted as <link rel="stylesheet"> after the theme. toolkit - toolkit packs to load. views is always registered; calendar is registered too and is never inferred from a card type, so a calendar page lists toolkit="views,calendar". An unknown pack name fails the render. Register your own with the builder's registerToolkitPack(name, cssPaths, jsPaths). The template function jcHasToolkit("views") reports whether a pack was requested.

theme - one of open (default), light-red, light-brown, red, gray; anything else fails the render listing the built-in names. A nested <@theme> takes precedence. brand - header title text. title - the document <title>; defaults to brand. icon - header logo URL, resolved against the context:/ URI. favicon - emitted as <link rel="icon">. chrome - strict boolean (true or false only; anything else, including an empty string, fails). Default false. scheme - auto (default), light or dark; the page's pin for the color scheme. schemeToggle - strict boolean, default false; adds the header's Auto / Light / Dark control. See Dark scheme. The directive also emits the chrome.css link, the theme link, any inline token override block, <meta name="page-tab">, and, when the request carries a CSRF token, a csrf-token meta tag and the data-juneau-csrf body attributes.

layout - horizontal or vertical; any other value fails the render. id - required; must match ^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_-]{0,63}$. label - required. href - optional for a node with children, required for a leaf. visible - strict boolean, default true. When false the node and its children are omitted, which is how you gate entries on a permission check. selected - strict boolean, default false; selects that node's id path as the active navigation. <@navigation layout="vertical"> <@node id="setup" label="Setup" href="/rest/setup"/> <@node id="admin" label="Admin" visible=user.admin> <@node id="users" label="Users" href="/rest/users"/> </@node> </@navigation>

Each slot captures its body as markup. <@head> adds to <head>; <@scripts> adds before </body>; <@body> supplies extra attributes for the <body> tag; <@brand> and <@actions> fill header slots; <@title> replaces the header title; <@footer> fills the footer. <@head phase="before-page-css"> places the markup before the page's css links. <@scripts phase="after-toolkit"> places the markup immediately after the toolkit scripts. Any other phase value fails the render. <@footer text="..."> sets plain text; a <@footer> with a body supplies markup. Giving both fails the render.

A badge is a count pill in the console header (or in a table's ribbon). juneau-badges.js polls a same-origin JSON endpoint that returns {total, mine?, items?[]}, shows a label such as "3 changes pending", hides itself at zero, and lists up to tooltipMax items in a hover popover. BadgeDef is the Java form, added with PageSpec.badge(BadgeDef); <@badge> is its FreeMarker twin and builds the same BadgeDef. Both end up in the page contract's header.badges[] array. <@console theme="open" brand="Petstore"> <@navigation layout="horizontal"> ... </@navigation> <@badge id="pending" src="/console/pets/changes/pending" href="/console/pets/changes" refreshMs=60000 placement="header" refreshesAllowMissing="pets"/> </@console> The same badge in Java: BadgeDef badge = BadgeDef.create("pending") .src("/console/pets/changes/pending") .href("/console/pets/changes") .refreshMs(60_000) .placement(BadgeDef.Placement.HEADER) .refreshesAllowMissing("pets"); badge.validate(); pageSpec.badge(badge); Attributes (the BadgeDef method is the same name unless noted): id - required; unique across every PageSpec and <@badge> badge on the page. A duplicate fails the render. src - required, a same-origin path (SafePathTemplate.isSameOriginPath). href - optional click target, also same-origin; the script refuses an unsafe src or href again at run time. refreshMs - poll interval in milliseconds. The script defaults to 60000; a value below 5000 (BadgeDef.MIN_REFRESH_MS) is rejected by validate(), not clamped. placement - header (default) or toolbar. toolbar renders at the right end of the ribbon of the card named by table, so it requires table. tone - info, warning (default) or danger. labelOne, labelOther, labelMine (BadgeDef.label(Map) with keys one, other, mine) - templates using {total} and {mine}. Stock defaults: {total} change pending, {total} changes pending and ({mine} yours). tooltipMax - items listed in the popover, 0 to 50 (the script clamps); default 10. scopeParam and scopeBy (BadgeDef.scope(param, by, values)) - the query parameter sent with each poll and how its value is keyed: nav (the leaf of the active navigation) or view (the active tab of the card named by table, so scopeBy="view" requires table). In the directive both must be given together; the Java form defaults a missing by to nav. The per-key value lists come from the body (below). A scoped badge whose key has no values on the current page hides itself and keeps polling. stateFilterColumn (stateFilter(column)) - the destination table's filter column. With a scope, the click URL gets a state= parameter built by JuneauViews.urlState.encode(...). refreshes and refreshesAllowMissing - card ids to reload when an item id seen on one poll is missing from the next. Every table and refreshes id must name a card on the page, or the render fails at </@console>; ids in refreshesAllowMissing are exempt, for a header badge that refreshes a card on another page (the client skips a card that is not mounted). The directive's optional body is JSON5 with three keys, because those fields have no flat shape: visibleWhen (a list of {field, op, value} rules, all of which must match; op is eq, ne, present, absent, in or contains), scopeValues (a map from nav node id, or view tab id, to a list of values) and params (extra query parameters). Any other key fails the render. For scopeBy="nav", each scopeValues key must be a node id in the navigation tree. <@badge id="health" src="/rest/health" refreshMs=30000 tone="warning"> {"visibleWhen": [{"field": "status", "op": "eq", "value": "degraded"}]} </@badge> A badge is presentation only. The src endpoint must still authorize the caller, and a page should not declare a badge for users who cannot read it. The script sends Accept: application/json (Juneau negotiates content, so a plain GET would be answered with HTML), treats a 401 or 403 as "remove the badge and stop polling", and retries any other failure with exponential backoff. validate() throws IllegalArgumentException for a missing src, an unsafe src or href, an out-of-range refreshMs, placement="toolbar" without table, and scopeBy="view" without table; the directive reports the same messages as render failures. Source: BadgeDef in juneau-console-views; BadgeDirectiveModel, PageSpec.badge and PageCapture in juneau-console-freemarker; juneau-badges.js in juneau-console. For a worked example with its endpoint, see Petstore: Pending Changes.

<@card type> is html (the default), datatables, terminal-view, terminal, chart or job-log (see Terminal View Region and Terminal Region); js, json and calendar were removed in 10.0.0 and fail with a message naming the replacement. An html card takes exactly one of a body, template= or src=; a datatables card requires id and takes a table URL or JSON catalog as its body. <@token> requires exactly one of value or alias; scheme="dark" limits it to the dark scheme.

These are the tokens defined by Theme.OPEN; the four other stock themes override a subset (page background, accent, link, text and border colors, chrome and button colors, avatar gradient) and inherit the rest. Token names match ^--jc-[a-z0-9-]+$, and theme names ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]*$. Group Tokens Typography and shape --jc-font, --jc-radius, --jc-card-padding, --jc-card-shadow Page surfaces --jc-page-bg, --jc-main-bg, --jc-card-bg, --jc-chrome-bg, --jc-white, --jc-table-stripe-bg Text and borders --jc-text, --jc-text-soft, --jc-text-muted, --jc-border, --jc-border-2, --jc-link Accent and focus --jc-accent, --jc-accent-wash, --jc-accent-selected, --jc-focus Buttons and status --jc-btn-primary, --jc-btn-primary-hover, --jc-danger, --jc-danger-wash, --jc-success, --jc-success-wash Header and icons --jc-header-icon-color, --jc-header-height, --jc-chrome-icon, --jc-avatar-bg Navigation --jc-nav-indicator-width, --jc-page-nav-hairline, --jc-page-nav-section-font-size, --jc-page-nav-child-font-size Spacing --jc-space-1 through --jc-space-6 Pills (<@tag> colors) --jc-pill-{green,blue,amber,neutral,red}-{bg,text,border}; --jc-tag-*-{bg,text,border} are aliases of the matching pill tokens Probe status --jc-probe-{ok,fail,warn,neutral}-{bg,text,dot} --jc-page-bg and --jc-avatar-bg hold gradients; every other color token takes a plain color.

Every <@console> page carries one JSON document, the page contract, in <script type="application/json" id="juneau-page">, and loads one script, /juneau-console/juneau-console.js. The server still renders <head> (CSS, theme, CSP-sensitive links). Everything else is drawn by the shell in the browser: the header, the nav (any depth), the cards and the footer. The contract's schema ships as org/apache/juneau/console/juneau-page.schema.json in juneau-console. <script type="application/json" id="juneau-page"> {"contractVersion":"1","title":"Releases","theme":{"name":"open"}, "header":{"title":"Release Manager","chrome":true}, "nav":[{"id":"setup","label":"Setup","href":"/rest/setup"}, {"id":"releases","label":"Releases","href":"/rest/releases"}], "activeNav":["releases"], "cards":[{"id":"releases","type":"datatables","table":{"dataUrl":"/rest/releases/data"}}], "footer":{"text":"Apache Juneau Release Manager"}} </script>
documents.s: The page contract and the console shell

documents.t: The FreeMarker directives write the contract; you never write JSON by hand. <@console brand="Release Manager" chrome="true"> <@navigation> <@node id="setup" label="Setup" href="/rest/setup"/> <@node id="new" label="New Release" href="/rest/runs"> <@node id="input" label="Input" href="/rest/runs?tab=input"/> <@node id="exec" label="Execution" href="/rest/runs?tab=exec"/> </@node> </@navigation> <@main/> <@footer text="Apache Juneau Release Manager"/> </@console> <@page tab="new/input"> sets activeNav. The shell stamps aria-current="page" on every node of that path and draws one child row per selected ancestor. With no tab=, the shell falls back to the longest node href that prefixes the current URL, on path-segment boundaries (/rest/runs matches /rest/runs/7 but not /rest/runsx). Query strings count only when the node's href has one. Markup in a <@page> body becomes <template data-card> elements, which are inert until the shell mounts them. Inline <script>s in them run at mount, in document order. <@card type="html"> takes exactly one of a body, template= or a same-origin src=. <@card type="datatables" id="…"> carries its table catalog in the contract. The shell hands it to JuneauViews.regions.mount on DOMContentLoaded, so views JS may load after the shell. An html card's src= fragment is inserted as served, so the endpoint must be first-party and must escape any data it embeds. Add sanitize=true ("sanitize": true in the page contract, CardSpec.sanitize(true) in Java) to rebuild the fragment through the views attribute-allowlist sanitizer instead: script, on* handlers, javascript: and data: URLs and every attribute off the allowlist are dropped, and benign markup (text, tables, links, images) survives. sanitize= needs src= and the views toolkit on the page; without the toolkit the card paints nothing and reports E-JS-8. The default stays off. Turn it on when the fragment's content is not fully under your control (it embeds user-supplied or third-party markup, or comes from an endpoint you do not own); leave it off for a fragment that needs class, id, style, forms, SVG or iframes, which the allowlist drops. Plain-text footers use <@footer text="…"/>. A <@footer> body is a markup slot. jcHasToolkit("views") reports whether the page asked for the views toolkit. A <@card type="datatables"> loads jQuery, DataTables and the Juneau glue (juneau-datatables.js) before the views runtime, client or server mode. The host composes DataTablesMixin (the glue) and WebJarsMixin (the libraries). Other cards can require more packs. See Card Asset Dependencies.

window.JuneauConsole exposes contract(), card(id) (both deep-frozen), registerCard(type, handler) for custom card types, mount(contract, {root}), chrome (user menu and detail-bar hydration), and schemeControl(doc) (the Auto / Light / Dark color-scheme control; see Dark scheme). The shell dispatches juneau:console-mounted on document with {activeNav, activeNavSource, cards}.

A template mistake fails the render with an HTTP 500 and a message naming the directive and the fix (error codes E-1 to E-18): an unknown attribute, a non-literal boolean, a duplicate card id, an unknown tab= path (the message lists the known paths), stray markup outside <@main/>, or one of the removed card types. In the browser, a contract the shell cannot use (unsupported page contractVersion, an unknown card type, a missing template, a cross-origin src) shows a .jc-console-error banner and logs [juneau-console] … to the console (E-JS-1 to E-JS-13). It never renders a blank page silently.

PageContractAssert (in org.apache.juneau.console.test, no JUnit dependency) parses the contract from a rendered page: assertPage(body) .isValid() .hasActiveNav("new", "input") .hasNavChildren("new", "input", "exec") .hasCard("releases", "datatables") .hasFooterText("Apache Juneau Release Manager"); ConsoleTemplateValidator lints templates without rendering them: var findings = ConsoleTemplateValidator.create() .templateRoot(Path.of("src/main/resources/templates")) .chromeTemplate("base.ftlh") .validateAll(); assertTrue(findings.isEmpty(), findings::toString); Set ConsoleFreemarkerMixin.create().devMode(true) (or -Djuneau.console.devMode=true) to validate every contract against the schema at render time (E-14).

No server-rendered chrome. Header, nav, cards and footer exist only as the page contract and are drawn by juneau-console.js. A page viewed without JavaScript shows its <head> styling and nothing else. Tests should assert on the contract (PageContractAssert), not on chrome HTML. No url() token form. Every var(--jc-*) value is validated by the accept-known-safe grammar described above, which structurally excludes url() productions; a future release may add a javascript:/data:/url()-scheme allowlist alongside an actual url() token form, but v1 ships with neither. The logo is a static chrome.css constant, not a configurable token.

This is the end-to-end tutorial for adding a page to an admin console built on Juneau: a resource that serves the
A console card can need scripts and stylesheets beyond the views toolkit. A datatables card needs jQuery,
A chart card draws a line, bar or donut chart from rows of JSON. Juneau draws it as inline SVG with no third-party
A job-log card starts a long-running job and shows its progress as it runs. It has a small form and a log pane.

An AI coding agent such as Claude Code runs a shell command and shows its output when the command finishes. A six-minute push.py or Maven gate is therefore a silent wait: no progress, no sign of which module is building. This page shows how to give the run a live pane beside the chat, using tmux and juneau-terminal's board view.
documents.s: Watching a Run from an AI Agent

documents.t: Run the agent inside tmux. Have the agent start the long command in a side pane. The pane has a real terminal, so juneau-terminal draws its live view there, and focus stays where you are typing. This is the leader pane. A second pane, the follower, sits below it. It runs tail -F on the full log, so you also see every line of output, not only the board rows. The agent blocks until the command is done. It reads the result back from the pane's last lines and the command's exit code, and carries on. You watch the run as it happens. The agent still gets what it needs: the final rows and a pass or fail.

With JUNEAU_TERMINAL_CONSOLE=board (or --console board), a run in the leader pane shows: one row per step, with its time, a progress bar, counts and a line of summary; the module bar for a Maven build, and a dot line under each running module, test file or check; a header that prints the tail -f command for the full log. By default the full log is written under ~/.cache/juneau-terminal/ (the newest 20 are kept), so the agent can read the details of a failure without scrolling the pane. A run also accepts the paths up front, in JUNEAU_TERMINAL_FULL_LOG and JUNEAU_TERMINAL_BOARD_LOG; watch-run.sh uses that. See Console view for the options.

The toolkit zip, org.apache.juneau:juneau-terminal:<version>:zip, carries two bash scripts in juneau_terminal_scripts/bin/: tmux-pane.sh runs a command in a side pane, blocks until it ends and exits with its code. It also cancels, lists, closes and equalizes such panes. It knows nothing about juneau-terminal. watch-run.sh is a wrapper for a juneau-terminal script (push.py, release.py, deploy*.py). It picks the log and result paths, opens the follower pane, and prints a result summary when the script ends. They need bash, tmux, ps, pgrep and perl; python3 (for the summary) and lsof (for the listening ports in the orphan report) are optional. They are tested on macOS.

With the juneau-terminal command installed (see Installing juneau-terminal), use its watch and pane subcommands; they find the packaged scripts themselves: juneau-terminal watch -d . -t push -- python3 scripts/push.py "message" Without the command, a repository gets the scripts with its copy of the toolkit; there is nothing separate to install. A repository that vendors the toolkit (a tree pinned to a manifest-checked copy of juneau-terminal) gets juneau_terminal_scripts/bin/ on its next refresh of that copy. A repository with scripts/bootstrap.py (the loader every push script vendors) asks it for the path with --bin. It never runs mvn, and it looks at the installed zip, the in-tree sources and the ~/.m2 copy for the pom's <juneau.version>. The Juneau repository has the scripts in juneau-terminal/src/main/python/juneau_terminal_scripts/bin/, and runs them in place. Locate a script, check it, then use it: wr=$(python3 scripts/bootstrap.py --bin watch-run.sh) && [ -x "$wr" ] && "$wr" -d . -t push -- python3 scripts/push.py "message" Without a vendored bootstrap.py, the installed zip is itself runnable: J=~/.m2/repository/org/apache/juneau/juneau-terminal/<v>/juneau-terminal-<v>.zip wr=$(python3 "$J" --bin watch-run.sh) && [ -x "$wr" ] && echo "$wr" When the source is a zip, the scripts are extracted to ~/.cache/juneau-terminal/bin/<version>/, outside target/ so that mvn clean never deletes the cancel path of a run still going. Each file is renamed into place, so a running script keeps the file it opened.

"$wr" -d ~/git/some/repo -t "push" -- python3 scripts/push.py "message" "$wr" --no-tail -- python3 scripts/release.py watch-run.sh prints tail -f <full log> and board: <board log> first; hand the tail -f line to the person watching, since it works from any terminal. When the script ends it prints the pane's last lines, a result: summary and exit=N, so read the last exit= line. It also closes finished panes left by earlier runs before opening a new one; a pane that is still running is left alone. Options (both scripts take the first group; watch-run.sh passes them to tmux-pane.sh): -d DIR working directory, -n LINES how many trailing pane lines to print, -t TITLE the leader pane's title. -k fail|always|never when to keep the panes open after the command ends (default fail, until Enter in the leader), and -K MIN to close kept panes by themselves after MIN minutes. --reap stops anything the command left running; --keep-on-cancel keeps a cancelled run's panes per -k. --no-tail (watch-run.sh) leaves out the follower. --pane 'CMD' (tmux-pane.sh, repeatable, with --size N% before a follower) runs several panes; the first is the leader. Subcommands of tmux-pane.sh: cancel [PANE|TITLE|--all] stops a run from any shell. It sends INT, then TERM, then KILL to the command's process group, TMUX_PANE_GRACE seconds apart (default 10), then stops what is left by PID and start time, never by name. The command that does it is exported to the run as JUNEAU_TERMINAL_CANCEL. list shows each pane (id, title, state, age); close --kept or close PANE closes finished panes with their followers; equalize PANE evens out the column widths. The leader's exit code is the script's. A usage error, or running outside tmux, exits 2; a leader pane closed before the command ended exits 129. Whenever a run ends, processes it started that are still running are listed as orphans, with their listening ports.

The agent pane counts as one column, and each run's leader with its followers is another, so one run gives a 50/50 split and two runs give thirds, and so on. The columns are equalized when a leader opens and again when a run's panes close. The agent pane is remembered in the @tmux_agent pane option. Other panes and other windows are not touched, and a failed resize only prints a warning.

The follower shows the log through a filter; the log file itself is unchanged. U+2028, U+2029 and other format characters (\p{Cf}) become a space, because tmux and the outer terminal disagree on their width and a line's end then overflows into the pane to the left. Control characters other than tab, newline and ESC (so colour survives), and DEL, are dropped. Invalid UTF-8 becomes U+FFFD. watch-run.sh --print-tail-filter prints the filter.
With $TMUX unset both scripts exit 2. Run the command directly and follow its log from another terminal: JUNEAU_TERMINAL_CONSOLE=board python3 push.py > run.log 2>&1 & tail -f run.log

tmux-pane.sh opens the leader pane to the right of the pane it was started from, without taking focus, and gives every pane its environment (a pane otherwise starts with the tmux server's). The command runs as its own process group. While it runs, the script records its descendants about every two seconds, by PID and start time, in a registry under ${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/tmux-pane/; that registry is what lets cancel and the orphan report work from another shell. The script waits for the leader, prints its last lines, and closes or keeps the panes per -k. watch-run.sh adds the juneau-terminal side: it chooses the log paths before anything opens, so nothing has to guess them, exports JUNEAU_TERMINAL_FULL_LOG, JUNEAU_TERMINAL_BOARD_LOG, JUNEAU_TERMINAL_RESULT and JUNEAU_TERMINAL_CANCEL, and reads the result file when the command ends. Each script's header comment is its full usage text.

The panes don't take focus, so typing in the chat is not interrupted. It works for any command juneau-terminal wraps: test.py, push.py, release.py, or a Maven, pytest or Playwright run started through juneau_terminal.py. Hand the person the tail -f line. It works from any terminal and shows the same full log as the follower. Close the panes with Enter in the leader when you have seen enough; the agent already has its output. Give each run its own title (-t) so list and cancel can tell runs apart. Never use pkill -f push.py to stop a run: it kills other people's runs and the next run of the same script. Use cancel. Edit a script while a run is using it by writing a temporary file and mv-ing it over the original. A running Bash reads its script as it goes, so editing in place can break a run that is in progress. A tool that needs structured progress and a machine-readable outcome, rather than the pane's text, can follow a markers file and read a result file; see Driving a Run from Another Tool.
juneau-terminal Driving a Run from Another Tool Terminal Region

The org.apache.juneau.http package contains annotations for defining both server and client side APIs. The server-side APIs also use it for producing auto-generated Swagger documentation through the REST API itself. Contact Content FormData HasFormData HasQuery Header License Part Path PathRemainder Query Request Response StatusCode Tag Url These annotations are used in a variety of places in the server and client side REST interfaces, especially for remote proxies. They are provided by the juneau-rest-common module, so they are available to both server and client code without depending on either. All of them have runtime retention.

These bind a method parameter (or bean property or type) to one part of an HTTP request. All of the following are @Inherited. @Header, @Query, @FormData, @Path and @PathRemainder may be applied to parameters, methods, types and fields; the others are as noted. Annotation Purpose Notable attributes @Content The request body. Targets: parameter, method, type. def, description, summary, schema @Header A request header. name, value (alias for name), def, description, summary, schema @Query A query parameter. name, value, def, description, summary, schema @FormData A form-data entry. name, value, def, description, summary, schema @Path A path variable. name, value, def, description, summary, schema @PathRemainder The remainder of the path after the pattern match. def, description, schema @HasQuery Whether the request has the named query parameter. Parameter only. name, value, description @HasFormData Whether the request has the named form-data parameter. Parameter only. name, value, description

Annotation Purpose Notable attributes @Request Marks an interface or parameter as a request bean exposing several HTTP parts through getters. Targets: parameter, type, method. description @Response Marks a type, method or parameter as a response bean. description, summary, examples, headers, schema @StatusCode Denotes an HTTP response status code. value (int array), description

Annotation Purpose Notable attributes @Part A multipart/form-data part on a remote-proxy method parameter. Parameter only. name, value, fileName, contentType @Url A remote-proxy parameter supplying the entire request URL. Parameter only.

These are not applied to parameters. They are used as nested values of @Swagger (contact, license and tags), which is supplied through @Rest(swagger=...), to populate the generated Swagger document. Annotation Purpose Attributes @Contact Contact information for the API. name, url, email, description @License License information for the API. name, url, description @Tag Metadata for a single Swagger tag. name, description, externalDocs

Server usage: HTTP Part Annotations, Request Beans, Response Beans and Java Method Parameters. Client usage with remote proxies: REST Proxies and its @Content, @FormData, @Query, @Header, @Path, @Request and @Response pages. Swagger generation: Swagger. The server-side @Rest/@RestOp annotations themselves: @Rest and @RestOp.

The Juneau REST server ships with a four-class api-docs mixin pack in org.apache.juneau.rest.server.docs that drives every built-in Swagger / OpenAPI / Redoc endpoint on BasicRestServlet and BasicRestResource. Each class is a single-purpose @Rest-annotated resource designed to be grafted into your servlet via @Rest(mixins=...) — pick the URLs you want, leave the ones you don't. See the guide: Generate OpenAPI docs for your API Migrating from a 9.4.x or earlier resource that used @Rest(apiFormat="…")? See the V10 Migration Guide for the removal table and worked conversions. Short version: stop setting apiFormat, declare the mixins you want instead.

Mixin Default paths Content negotiation Why it exists SwaggerMixin /api Standard Juneau content negotiation (HTML when Accept: text/html; serializer default otherwise). Swagger v2 spec emission via the Swagger bean + SwaggerUI swap. SwaggerUiMixin /swagger Bare browser GET (no Accept) defaults to text/html; explicit Accept is honored normally. Same Swagger v2 spec mounted at an HTML-first URL. Declares @Rest(mixins=SwaggerMixin.class) so transitive resolution brings /api along for free. OpenApiMixin /openapi, /openapi.json, /openapi.yaml /openapi uses standard Juneau content negotiation; /openapi.json and /openapi.yaml are format-pinned (ignore Accept). OpenAPI 3.1 spec emission via the OpenApi bean + RedocUI swap. RedocMixin /redoc Bare browser GET (no Accept) defaults to text/html; explicit Accept is honored normally. Same OpenAPI 3.1 spec mounted at an HTML-first URL. Declares @Rest(mixins=OpenApiMixin.class) so transitive resolution brings /openapi/* along for free. The split is intentional: spec mixins (SwaggerMixin, OpenApiMixin) emit the document and let the standard content negotiation pipeline decide the wire format. UI mixins (SwaggerUiMixin, RedocMixin) tweak content negotiation so a bare browser GET — which sends Accept: */* or no Accept at all — renders the HTML view by default, while machine clients that send Accept: application/json (or application/yaml) still get the spec in their requested format. This keeps the same /swagger URL useful for both "open in browser" and "fetch as JSON" without query-string toggles.
documents.s: The four mixins at a glance

documents.t: Any subclass of BasicRestServlet or BasicRestResource gets the full pack by default. Both classes declare: @Rest(mixins = {SwaggerUiMixin.class, RedocMixin.class}) public abstract class BasicRestServlet extends RestServlet implements ... { ... } Because SwaggerUiMixin transitively pulls in SwaggerMixin and RedocMixin transitively pulls in OpenApiMixin, the mixin walk dedupes by class identity and the resulting servlet serves six URLs: URL Mixin Wire format GET /api SwaggerMixin Swagger v2 spec; content-negotiated. GET /swagger SwaggerUiMixin Swagger UI (HTML default; JSON / XML on explicit Accept). GET /openapi OpenApiMixin OpenAPI 3.1 spec; content-negotiated. GET /openapi.json OpenApiMixin OpenAPI 3.1 spec; always JSON. GET /openapi.yaml OpenApiMixin OpenAPI 3.1 spec; always YAML. GET /redoc RedocMixin Redoc UI (HTML default; JSON / XML on explicit Accept). Subclasses that just want this surface need to declare nothing — extending BasicRestServlet is enough.
The mixins are independent — pick the URLs you want. The four common compositions:

@Rest(path = "/api", mixins = OpenApiMixin.class) public class ApiResource extends RestServlet { @RestGet("/items") public List<Item> items() { ... } } // Serves /api/items, /api/openapi, /api/openapi.json, /api/openapi.yaml.
documents.s: Just the OpenAPI spec (no Swagger v2, no UI)

documents.t: @Rest(path = "/api", mixins = RedocMixin.class) // pulls OpenApiMixin in transitively public class ApiResource extends RestServlet { @RestGet("/items") public List<Item> items() { ... } } // Serves /api/items, /api/openapi, /api/openapi.json, /api/openapi.yaml, /api/redoc.
documents.s: OpenAPI spec plus the Redoc UI

documents.t: @Rest(path = "/api", mixins = {SwaggerUiMixin.class, RedocMixin.class}) public class ApiResource extends RestServlet { @RestGet("/items") public List<Item> items() { ... } } // Serves /api/items, /api/api, /api/swagger, /api/openapi, /api/openapi.json, // /api/openapi.yaml, /api/redoc.
documents.s: Full surface (mirrors BasicRestServlet, but on a plain RestServlet)

documents.t: BasicRestServlet already mixes in both UI halves. To keep only the OpenAPI side on a subclass, opt out of inherited mixins and re-declare the mixin you want: @Rest(noInherit = {"mixins"}, mixins = RedocMixin.class) public class MyApi extends BasicRestServlet { @RestGet("/items") public List<Item> items() { ... } } // Serves /items, /openapi, /openapi.json, /openapi.yaml, /redoc — but NOT /api or /swagger.
documents.s: Drop one half of the inherited pack

documents.t: Each mixin is itself a fully-fledged @Rest-annotated resource and can be subclassed and mounted as its own top-level servlet: @Rest(paths = {"/openapi", "/openapi.json", "/openapi.yaml"}) public class OpenApiDocs extends OpenApiMixin { } Both deployment styles (mixin into an existing servlet vs. mount as a sibling servlet) work the same way under Spring Boot and under the Jetty microservice — see Spring Boot vs. microservice below.

The two UI mixins both declare @Rest(defaultAccept = "text/html"): @Rest(paths = {"/swagger"}, mixins = SwaggerMixin.class, defaultAccept = "text/html") public class SwaggerUiMixin implements BasicUniversalConfig { ... } @Rest(paths = {"/redoc"}, mixins = OpenApiMixin.class, defaultAccept = "text/html") public class RedocMixin implements BasicUniversalConfig { ... } defaultAccept only fires when the request has no Accept header (or sends */*, which collapses to "no preference"). When that happens, the framework injects Accept: text/html before content negotiation runs, and the SwaggerUI / RedocUI swap fires to render the HTML view. That gives the natural behaviors: Request Result on /swagger and /redoc Bare browser GET (no Accept) HTML view via the UI swap. Accept: application/json Spec serialized as JSON via the standard serializer. Accept: application/xml Spec serialized as XML. Accept: */* HTML view (same as bare browser). The spec mixins (/api, /openapi) do not declare defaultAccept, so the standard content-negotiation default (the serializer's preferred media type, typically JSON) wins when no Accept header is sent.

OpenApiMixin declares three @RestGet methods, one per mount path: @RestGet("/*") // content-negotiated public OpenApi getOpenApi(RestRequest req) { ... } @RestGet(path = "/openapi.json", produces = "application/json") public void getOpenApiJson(RestRequest req, RestResponse res) throws Exception { res.getDirectWriter("application/json").write(req.getOpenApi().orElseThrow(NotFound::new).toJson()); } @RestGet(path = "/openapi.yaml", produces = "application/yaml") public void getOpenApiYaml(RestRequest req, RestResponse res) throws Exception { res.getDirectWriter("application/yaml").write(req.getOpenApi().orElseThrow(NotFound::new).toYaml()); } The two .json and .yaml endpoints use RestResponse.getDirectWriter(...) to write the spec directly to the response body in the requested wire format, bypassing the standard content-negotiation pipeline. That means: GET /openapi.json returns JSON regardless of Accept. Even Accept: text/html returns JSON. The path implies the format. GET /openapi.yaml returns YAML regardless of Accept. GET /openapi (no suffix) runs the normal pipeline — Accept: application/json gets JSON, Accept: application/yaml gets YAML, Accept: text/html gets the Redoc UI swap (via the RedocMixin mixin if it's in the pack; otherwise the serializer default). This split lets API docs consumers use direct, unambiguous URLs for the spec (/openapi.json, /openapi.yaml) without trusting the server's content negotiation, while keeping /openapi useful for browsers.

The mixin pack works identically under both deployment paths because mixin instances are resolved through the importing servlet's BeanStore: Microservice path. BasicBeanStore looks up each mixin class via getBean(<MixinClass>.class) first; if no bean is registered, the framework reflects a no-arg constructor on the mixin. Verified end-to-end by BasicApiDocs_JettyMicroservice_Test in juneau-integration-tests, which boots a real Jetty Microservice on an ephemeral port and hits all six URLs over HTTP. Spring Boot path. SpringBeanStore extends BasicBeanStore and delegates unresolved lookups to ApplicationContext.getBeanProvider(beanType).getIfAvailable(). Same fallback to no-arg constructor if no Spring bean is registered. Verified end-to-end by BasicApiDocs_Springboot_Test in juneau-integration-tests, which boots a full Spring Boot context with embedded Tomcat and hits the same six URLs. Both tests share a fixture (BasicApiDocsTestFixtures) so the response-shape assertions are identical across deployment paths. Drift in either direction fails CI.

If your Spring Boot app registers more than one OpenApiProvider @Bean (rare, but possible when you want a default and a custom provider co-existing), mark exactly one of them @Primary: @Configuration public class OpenApiConfig { @Bean @Primary public OpenApiProvider productionProvider() { return new MyCustomOpenApiProvider(...); } @Bean public OpenApiProvider fallbackProvider() { return new BasicOpenApiProvider(...); } } SpringBeanStore.getBean(OpenApiProvider.class) delegates to ApplicationContext.getBeanProvider(OpenApiProvider.class).getIfAvailable(), which honors @Primary correctly. The OpenApiMixin mixin sees the @Primary bean. If you register two OpenApiProvider beans without marking one @Primary, Spring fails the context-load with BeanDefinitionOverrideException (when two @Bean methods declare the same bean id) or falls through to getIfUnique() returning null (when two @Bean methods declare different bean ids and neither is primary). Both failure modes happen before Juneau gets a chance to look the provider up, so Juneau cannot give a friendlier error here. This is a documented "known rough edge"; the fix is always to mark one bean @Primary. Both the success and the collision cases are pinned by BasicApiDocs_Springboot_MultiOpenApiProvider_Test. The same precedence rule applies to SwaggerProvider for the Swagger v2 side: multiple beans require exactly one @Primary marking.
documents.s: Multiple OpenApiProvider beans in Spring Boot

documents.t: The 9.4.x @Rest(apiFormat = "swagger" | "openapi" | "both") annotation member, the juneau.rest.apiFormat system property, the RestContext.getApiFormat() accessor, and the ?Swagger / ?OpenApi query mirrors on group resources are all removed in 10.0.0. Compose the mixins you want instead. The V10 Migration Guide has the full removal table; the short version: Old (9.4.x) New (10.0.0) @Rest(apiFormat = "swagger") Default behavior of BasicRestServlet — no change needed. @Rest(apiFormat = "openapi") @Rest(noInherit = {"mixins"}, mixins = RedocMixin.class) on a BasicRestServlet subclass. @Rest(apiFormat = "both") Default behavior of BasicRestServlet — both halves are always mounted. GET /api?Swagger=… GET /api (or GET /swagger for the HTML view). GET /?OpenApi=… GET /openapi (or GET /redoc for the HTML view). juneau.rest.apiFormat system property Removed. Pick mixins at compile time.

Generate OpenAPI docs for your API: a guided walkthrough. REST Server — Mixins and Multi-Mount Paths — the @Rest(mixins=...) and @Rest(paths=...) primitives this pack builds on, including the parent-chain mixin aggregation rules that govern how mixins compose across an inheritance hierarchy. Mixin Sub-Contexts — per-mixin RestContext inheritance model; each api-docs mixin has its own sub-context so the RestResponse, defaultAccept, and produces settings only affect that mixin's endpoints. Basic REST Servlet Swagger — pre-mixin background on Swagger / OpenAPI emission and components.schemas reuse. V10 Migration Guide — full breaking-change table and worked migration steps for 9.4.x → 10.0.0.

Command-line arguments can be associated with a microservice using the args() method. Example public static void main(String[] args) { Microservice .create() // Create builder. .args(args) // Pass in args. .build() // Create microservice. .start() // Start microservice. .join() // Join thread. ; } When specified, the arguments can be retrieved using the Microservice.getArgs() method which provides an API for easily accessing command-line arguments using common notation: Args args = Microservice.getInstance().getArgs(); One main argument (a1): // a1 String a1 = args.get(0).orElse(null); // "a1" String a2 = args.get(1).orElse(null); // null Two main arguments (a1 a2): // a1 a2 String a1 = args.get(0).orElse(null); // "a1" String a2 = args.get(1).orElse(null); // "a2" One main argument and one optional flag with no value (a1 -a2): // a1 -a2 String a1 = args.get(0).orElse(null); boolean hasA2 = args.has("a2"); // true boolean hasA3 = args.has("a3"); // false One main argument and one optional argument with one value (a1 -a2 v2): // a1 -a2 v2 String a1 = args.get(0).orElse(null); String a2 = args.get("a2").orElse(null); // "v2" String a3 = args.get("a3").orElse(null); // null One main argument and one optional argument with multiple values (a1 -a2 v2a v2b): // a1 -a2 v2a v2b String a1 = args.get(0).orElse(null); List<String> a2 = args.getAll("a2"); // Contains ["v2a","v2b"] List<String> a3 = args.getAll("a3"); // Empty list Same as previous but specifying the argument name multiple times (a1 -a2 v2a -a2 v2b): // a1 -a2 v2a -a2 v2b String a1 = args.get(0).orElse(null); List<String> a2 = args.getAll("a2"); // Contains ["v2a","v2b"] Specifying the command-line arguments also makes them available through $A SVL variables. These can be used in the configuration file and throughout various Juneau annotations. Example // $A used in variable resolver. VarResolver varResolver = Microservice.getInstance().getVarResolver(); System.out.println(varResolver.resolve("Arg #1 is set to ${A:1}")); // $A used in annotation. @Rest( title="${A:title}", ... )

The readArrayRecords(...) / writeArrayRecords(...) factories — declared by the ArrayRecordReadable / ArrayRecordWritable roles — yield a multi-record cursor over the elements of a top-level wire array, without materializing the whole list. This applies to single-rooted formats whose root value happens to be a list — JSON's [...], CBOR's array major-type, etc. For naturally-multi-record formats (csv, sse), use readRecords / writeRecords directly — the wire format IS already a sequence of records. JSONL is also natively line-delimited; its readArrayRecords / writeArrayRecords simply alias that line record stream (rather than wrapping the elements in a bracketed [...] array). See the per-format capability matrix for which formats support array-record reading/writing and whether each streams O(1) or buffers.

// Wire payload is one big JSON array; we want O(1) memory per element. try (RecordReader r = JsonParser.DEFAULT.readArrayRecords(input)) { while (r.canRead()) { Bean b = r.read(Bean.class); process(b); } }
try (RecordWriter w = JsonSerializer.DEFAULT.writeArrayRecords(output)) { for (Bean b : sourceOfBeans()) { w.write(b); } } // output is now: [{...},{...},{...}]

Format Reader Writer Notes JSON / JSON5 streaming streaming O(1) memory per element. CBOR streaming streaming Reader uses indefinite-length array peek (BREAK). Writer always emits indefinite-length so no element count needed. MsgPack streaming buffered; streaming with count overload Reader streams O(1) per element. Writer's no-count writeArrayRecords(output) buffers; writeArrayRecords(output, expectedCount) writes the length-prefix header up front and serializes each element directly. BSON buffered buffered BSON requires byte-length prefix at every nesting level; streaming without buffering isn't possible. Parquet / YAML buffered buffered XML / HTML buffered with caller-specified root not supported (reader only) Reader has the readArrayRecords(input, "rootElementName") overload; there is no array-record writer. JSONL streaming streaming arrayRecords aliases the JSONL line record stream — each top-level line is one element, written/read without a surrounding [...]. O(1) memory per element. CSV / SSE n/a n/a Use readRecords/writeRecords — format is already row-streamed. TOML / HOCON / Hjson / INI / PlainText / Markdown / JsonSchema / JCS / Prototext not supported not supported

For binary formats whose array wire encoding starts with a length prefix, the count overload streams without buffering — the caller pre-declares the element count: ByteArrayOutputStream baos = new ByteArrayOutputStream(); try (RecordWriter w = MsgPackSerializer.DEFAULT.writeArrayRecords(baos, 3)) { w.write(bean1); w.write(bean2); w.write(bean3); } // Bytes equal to: MsgPackSerializer.DEFAULT.write(List.of(bean1, bean2, bean3)) Mismatch between the declared count and the actual write count throws on close(). Writing a 4th element when 3 were declared throws IllegalStateException immediately.

boolean supported = MsgPackSerializer.DEFAULT instanceof ArrayRecordWritable; // true if (MsgPackSerializer.DEFAULT instanceof ArrayRecordWritable w) { boolean streaming = w.isArrayRecordStreaming(); // false — buffered without the count overload }
Token-Streaming Basics Record Streaming Token Streaming

The org.apache.juneau.bct.assertions package in Juneau (provided by the juneau-bct module) is a powerful API for performing fluent style assertions. It is used throughout the REST client and server APIs for performing inline assertions on REST requests and responses. Example // Create a basic REST client with JSON support and download a bean. MyBean bean = RestClient.create() .json5() .build() .get(URI) .run() .assertStatus().asCode().is(200) .assertHeader("Content-Type").isMatches("application/json*") .getContent().assertValue().asString().isContains("OK") .getContent().as(MyBean.class); note The REST API is described later in the documentation. The assertions API is designed to be used in both code (as it's done in the REST APIs) or for standalone use in unit tests. The Assertions class provides various static methods for invoking assertions on a variety of object types for simplified unit testing. Assertions assertAny(T) assertArray(Object[]) assertBean(V) assertBeanList(List) assertBoolean(Boolean) assertBooleanArray(boolean[]) assertByteArray(byte[]) assertBytes(byte[]) assertBytes(InputStream) assertCharArray(char[]) assertCollection(Collection) assertComparable(T) assertDate(Date) assertDoubleArray(double[]) assertFloatArray(float[]) assertIntArray(int[]) assertInteger(Integer) assertList(List) assertLong(Long) assertLongArray(long[]) assertMap(Map) assertObject(T) assertOptional(Optional) assertReader(Reader) assertShortArray(short[]) assertString(Object) assertStringList(List) assertThrowable(V) assertThrown(Snippet) assertVersion(Version) assertZonedDateTime(ZonedDateTime)

Each static Assertions.assertXxx(...) method returns a specific assertion class. All classes are in org.apache.juneau.bct.assertions. Every class inherits the general isX / asX methods of ObjectAssertion (is, isNot, isNull, isNotNull, isExists, isAny, isNotAny, isType, isExactType, isSame, isSameSerializedAs, isString, asString, asTransformed); the table lists the notable additions. Factory method Assertion class Notable methods assertObject(T) ObjectAssertion General POJO tests listed above. assertAny(T), assertOptional(Optional) AnyAssertion asBean, asList, asMap, and other conversions of an untyped value. assertString(Object), assertReader(Reader) StringAssertion isContains, isMatches, isPattern, isStartsWith, isEndsWith, isLines, asLines, asSplit, asTrimmed, asUc, asLc, asLength, asReplace, asReplaceAll, asUrlDecode. assertStringList(List) StringListAssertion asJoin, asTrimmed, plus the list methods. assertBoolean(Boolean) BooleanAssertion isTrue, isFalse. assertInteger(Integer) IntegerAssertion Comparable tests: isGt, isGte, isLt, isLte, isBetween. assertLong(Long) LongAssertion Comparable tests. assertComparable(T) ComparableAssertion isGt, isGte, isLt, isLte, isBetween for any Comparable. assertDate(Date) DateAssertion isBefore, isAfter, isBeforeNow, isAfterNow, isBetween, asEpochMillis, asEpochSeconds. assertZonedDateTime(ZonedDateTime) ZonedDateTimeAssertion Same date tests as DateAssertion. assertVersion(Version) VersionAssertion asMajor, asMinor, asMaintenance, asPart. assertCollection(Collection) CollectionAssertion asSize, isSize, isEmpty, isContains, isAll, isAny. assertList(List), assertList(Stream) ListAssertion asFirst, asLast, asItem, asSublist, asSorted, asCdl, isEach, isHas. assertMap(Map) MapAssertion isContainsKey, asValue, asValues. assertArray(E[]) ArrayAssertion Array size, element and content tests. assertBooleanArray, assertByteArray, assertCharArray, assertDoubleArray, assertFloatArray, assertIntArray, assertLongArray, assertShortArray PrimitiveArrayAssertion Tests on primitive arrays. assertBytes(byte[]), assertBytes(InputStream) ByteArrayAssertion asHex, asBase64, asSpacedHex, asString. assertBean(T) BeanAssertion asProperty, asProperties, asPropertyMap. assertBeanList(List) BeanListAssertion asPropertyMaps, asProperty. assertThrowable(T), assertThrown(Snippet) ThrowableAssertion asMessage, asMessages, asCausedBy, asFind, asStackTrace.

AssertionPredicates provides static factory methods that build AssertionPredicate (a Predicate) arguments for methods such as isEach(...), isAny(...) and is(Predicate): Method Description eq(value), ne(value) Equal / not equal. eqic(value) Equal ignoring case. contains(value) String contains the value. match(pattern) Matches a glob-style pattern. regex(pattern) Matches a regular expression. type(Class), exactType(Class) Instance of / exact class. isNull(), notNull() Null tests. test(Predicate) Wraps an arbitrary predicate. and(...), or(...), not(Predicate) Combinators. any() Always passes (typically equivalent to a null predicate). assertList(names).isEach(eq("foo"), match("bar*"), isNull());

These methods are available on every assertion and return the same assertion: Method Description setMsg(String, Object...) Custom failure message. setOut(PrintStream) Also print failure messages to the given stream. setStdOut() Print failure messages to stdout. setSilent() Suppress printed output. setThrowable(Class) Throw the given RuntimeException subclass instead of the default AssertionError-style exception. For bean-oriented testing with compact expected-value strings (assertBean, assertBeans, assertList, assertMap, assertContains, ...) see Bean-Centric Testing. A lightweight Verify class (Verify.verify(Object)) is also provided for non-throwing checks: is, isTrue, isFalse and isType return an error message string, or null if the check passes.

Assertions have 3 categories of methods: Testing methods (isX methods) Transform methods (asX methods) Configuration methods (setX methods) Examples import static org.apache.juneau.bct.assertions.Assertions.*; import static org.apache.juneau.bct.assertions.AssertionPredicates.*; // Check the contents of a string. assertString("foo, bar") .asSplit(",") .asTrimmed() .isHas("foo", "bar"); // Extract a subset of properties from a list of beans and compare using JSON5. import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json5.Json5Serializer; List myListOfBeans = ...; assertBeanList(myListOfBeans) .asPropertyMaps("a,b") .asString(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT).is("[{a:1,b:'foo'}]"); // Perform an arbitrary Predicate check against a bean. MyBean myBeans = ...; assertBean(myBeans) .is(x -> isValidCheck(x)) // Check that a list of strings has less than 10 entries and the first // 3 entries are [foo, bar*, null] using assertion predicates. List myListOfStrings = ...; assertStringList(myListOfStrings) .asSize().isLt(10) .asFirst(3) .isEach(eq("foo"),match("bar*"),isNull()) // Check that an exception is thrown and is the specified type and has the specified message. assertThrown(()->myBean.runBadMethod()) .isExists() .isExactType(RuntimeException.class) .asMessage().is("foo"); Testing methods (isX methods) perform an assertion on the specified value and throws a AssertionError if the test fails. Otherwise, the method returns the original assertion object to allow you to chain the command. Example // Test a string. assertString(myString) .isNotNull() // Perform test and returns original FluentStringAssertion. .isNotEmpty(); // Perform test and returns original FluentStringAssertion. Transform methods (asX methods) allow you to convert assertions of one type to another type or to convert the tested value to some other form wrapped in another assertion. Example // Customize the behavior of an assertion. assertString(myString) .asLength() // Converts to a FluentIntegerAssertion. .isLt(100) // Runs test and returns original FluentStringAssertion. .asUc() // Converts string to uppercase and returns a new FluentStringAssertion. .isContains("FOO"); // Runs test and returns original FluentStringAssertion. Configuration methods (setX methods) allow you to tailor the behavior of assertions when they fail. They always return the same assertion object. Transformed assertions inherit the configurations of the created-by assertions. Configuration methods start with set. Example // Customize the behavior of an assertion. assertString(myString) .setMsg("My string was null. Value was {VALUE}.") // Custom error message when error occurs. .setOut(myPrintStream) // Print error message to a separate PrintStream. .setThrowable(MyAssertionThrowable.class) // Throw a customized assertion exception. .isNotNull(); The following shows the class hierarchy for the IntegerAssertion class showing the general design pattern for assertion classes: Assertion - Base class for all assertion objects containing common configuration methods.FluentAssertion - Parent class for all fluent assertions.FluentObjectAssertion - Tests and transforms for general POJOs.FluentComparableAssertion<T extends Comparable,R> - Tests and transforms for Comparables.FluentIntegerAssertion - Tests and transforms for Integers.IntegerAssertion - Assertion that returns itself. In the design, the "Fluent" classes (e.g. FluentIntegerAssertion) allow you to specify the object that gets returned when the test method is executed. When used in the RestClient class for example, the return object is the RestResponse object so that you can perform multiple fluent operations against that object. The "Normal" classes (e.g. IntegerAssertion) are simply subclasses of the fluent equivalent which return the assertion itself, meaning the test method returns the original IntegerAssertion so that multiple tests can be performed per assertion. For more information about the capabilities of the Assertions API, refer to the methods on the Assertions methods above.

The org.apache.juneau.rest.server.auth package provides a pluggable servlet-filter authentication framework that runs at the servlet container layer — before Juneau's request routing — so a single URL can support multiple overlapping authentication schemes, short-circuit on the first success, and aggregate roles when more than one scheme succeeds. See the guide: Secure an endpoint with JWT and OAuth This framework is the natural peer of the AuthN Guards that ship in juneau-rest-server: guards run inside RestContext.handleCall(...) (op-level AuthZ); filters run before the servlet is reached (container-level AuthN).

Component Module Purpose AuthFilter (abstract) juneau-rest-server SPI base class with Optional<AuthResult> authenticate(req) contract. AuthResult juneau-rest-server Immutable value: resolved Principal + role set. AuthFilterChain juneau-rest-server Orchestrates multiple AuthFilter instances; first-success principal, role aggregation, all-failure 401. AuthenticatedRequestWrapper juneau-rest-server HttpServletRequestWrapper that surfaces filter-resolved principal and roles to downstream Juneau code. BearerTokenAuthFilter juneau-rest-server Filter impl reusing the TokenValidator SPI. ApiKeyAuthFilter juneau-rest-server Filter impl reusing the ApiKeyStore SPI. JettyServerComponent.addFilter(...) juneau-microservice-jetty New public filter-registration surface for Jetty microservices.

The framework preserves the clean separation between authentication (who is this?) and authorization (may they do this?): HTTP request │ ▼ AuthFilterChain (servlet filter — runs before RestServlet) │ calls authenticate() on matching filters │ wraps request with AuthenticatedRequestWrapper on first success ▼ RestServlet.service(wrappedReq, ...) │ ▼ RestGuardList (RoleBasedRestGuard, etc.) │ reads req.isUserInRole(...) from AuthenticatedRequestWrapper ▼ @RestOp handler │ @Auth Principal p ← reads RestServerConstants.PRINCIPAL_ATTR ▼ AuthenticatedRequestWrapper bridges the two layers: it overrides getUserPrincipal(), isUserInRole(String), getRemoteUser(), and getAttribute(PRINCIPAL_ATTR) so both RoleBasedRestGuard and the @Auth arg resolver see the filter-resolved identity with zero changes.
documents.s: Mental model: filter-time AuthN + op-time AuthZ

documents.t: Each concrete AuthFilter subclass (BearerTokenAuthFilter, ApiKeyAuthFilter, any custom impl) is also a jakarta.servlet.Filter by itself. Use the standalone mode when a single auth scheme is sufficient: // Standalone bearer-token filter registered directly with JettyServerComponent: jsc.addFilter( BearerTokenAuthFilter.create().validator(jwtValidator).build(), "/*"); In standalone mode, AuthFilter.doFilter(req, resp, chain): Calls authenticate(req). On success: wraps the request and passes it through. On Optional.empty(): passes the request through unchanged (no credentials for this filter). On AuthenticationException: writes a 401 response with WWW-Authenticate challenge.

Use AuthFilterChain when multiple auth schemes overlap on the same URL: @Bean public AuthFilterChain authFilters(BeanStore bs) { return AuthFilterChain.create(bs) .append(BearerTokenAuthFilter.create() .validator(jwtValidator) .build()) .append(ApiKeyAuthFilter.create() .store(apiKeyStore) .build()) // /sso/** accepts only SAML (provided by juneau-rest-server-auth-saml, a future sibling module): .append(mySamlFilter, "/sso/*") .build(); } JettyServerComponent auto-mounts the AuthFilterChain bean at /* when it is present in the BeanStore — no explicit addFilter(...) call needed for the common case.

AuthFilter.authenticate(req) returns one of three states: State Meaning Optional.empty() Filter does not apply (no recognizable credentials). Chain continues. Optional.of(AuthResult) Authentication succeeded. throw AuthenticationException Credentials were present but invalid (bad token, revoked key, etc.). This distinction matters for the chain's failure-aggregation logic: If no filter applies (all return empty) the request passes through unchanged — public endpoints need no credentials. If at least one filter actively rejected (threw) the request, the chain sends 401 with aggregated WWW-Authenticate challenges.

Each filter in the chain can be scoped to a URL pattern via append(filter, pattern). Patterns are parsed once at build time via UrlPathMatcher.of(String). Supported forms: Pattern Matches (none) All paths /* All paths /api/* /api/, /api/users, /api/users/123, … /foo/{id}/* /foo/abc/anything, … *.json Any path ending in .json Filters whose patterns do not match the request path are not called — they contribute neither successes nor failures.

When multiple filters match and succeed, the chain aggregates roles across all successful results: The first successful filter's Principal wins for identity (deterministic ordering by registration order). All successful filters' role sets are unioned into a single Set<String>. AuthenticatedRequestWrapper.isUserInRole(String) checks this union. Example: Bearer JWT grants user, API key grants admin. Both succeed on the same request: getUserPrincipal().getName() returns the Bearer principal's name. isUserInRole("user") → true, isUserInRole("admin") → true. RoleBasedRestGuard("user|admin") → passes.

The preferred pattern mirrors the @Bean RestGuardList idiom. Since JettyMicroservice is final, place the @Bean method in a separate @Configuration class: @Configuration public class MyAppConfig { @Bean public AuthFilterChain authFilters(BeanStore bs) { return AuthFilterChain.create(bs) .append(BearerTokenAuthFilter.create() .pattern("/api/*") .validator(jwtValidator) .build()) .append(ApiKeyAuthFilter.create() .pattern("/api/*") .store(apiKeyStore) .build()) .build(); } } Then wire the configuration class at startup: var beanStore = new BasicBeanStore(); beanStore.addBean(Servlet.class, new RootResources()); JettyMicroservice.run(args, beanStore, true, JettyConfiguration.class, MyAppConfig.class); JettyServerComponent.onStart(...) scans the BeanStore for an AuthFilterChain bean and registers it at /* before any servlet is mounted.

For simpler deployments or when bypassing the chain, register standalone filters directly: // In a microservice subclass or test setup: getBeanStore().getBean(JettyServerComponent.class).ifPresent(jsc -> jsc.addFilter(BearerTokenAuthFilter.create().validator(myValidator).build(), "/api/*") ); Both addFilter(Filter, String) (single pattern) and addFilter(Filter, String...) (multiple patterns) are available.

// /api/* accepts Bearer JWT or API key — first to succeed wins; roles aggregate when both do. AuthFilterChain.create(bs) .append(BearerTokenAuthFilter.create() .pattern("/api/*") .validator(jwtValidator) .build()) .append(ApiKeyAuthFilter.create() .pattern("/api/*") .store(apiKeyStore) .build()) .build();

// /api/* → JWT only; /internal/* → API key only; no overlap. AuthFilterChain.create(bs) .append(BearerTokenAuthFilter.create() .pattern("/api/*") .validator(jwtValidator) .build()) .append(ApiKeyAuthFilter.create() .pattern("/internal/*") .store(internalKeyStore) .build()) .build();
When both filters apply and both reject, the response is: HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="api", ApiKey realm="api" Bearer token missing; API key missing

Mirrors BearerTokenGuard extraction logic. Reads Authorization: Bearer <token>, delegates to a TokenValidator. Extracts roles from a ClaimsPrincipal claim (default claim name: "roles"). Builder methods: validator(TokenValidator) (required), realm(String) (default: "api"), rolesClaim(String) (default: "roles"). If absent or non-Bearer scheme → Optional.empty().

Mirrors ApiKeyGuard extraction logic. Reads the key from a configurable source (header / query / cookie), delegates to an ApiKeyStore. Extracts roles from ClaimsPrincipal claims. Builder methods: store(ApiKeyStore) (required), fromHeader(String) (default: X-API-Key), fromQuery(String), fromCookie(String), realm(String) (default: "api"), rolesClaim(String) (default: "roles"). If key absent or blank → Optional.empty().

Spring Security's SecurityFilterChain is the recommended authentication path for Spring Boot users. BearerTokenAuthFilter / ApiKeyAuthFilter can be registered via Spring Boot's FilterRegistrationBean if desired, but the AuthFilterChain @Bean auto-mount is wired for JettyServerComponent only. Do not run both frameworks on the same request path.

Secure an endpoint with JWT and OAuth: a guided walkthrough. REST Authenticator — Resource-Level Authentication — the resource-layer peer that resolves identity + roles inside Juneau dispatch, reusing these same filters. AuthN Guards — Bearer / API-Key / JWT — the op-level guards that compose with this framework. SAML 2.0 AuthN Support — the opt-in juneau-rest-server-auth-saml module that adds a SamlAuthFilter implementation. OAuth 2.0 / OIDC AuthN Support — the opt-in juneau-rest-server-auth-oauth module that adds an OAuthFilter + introspection / OIDC discovery / grant-flow helpers. OIDC Relying Party Login — the opt-in juneau-rest-server-auth-oidc-rp module whose OidcSessionAuthFilter resolves an OIDC login-session cookie into a ClaimsPrincipal. AuthFilterChain AuthFilter BearerTokenAuthFilter ApiKeyAuthFilter JettyServerComponent
The classic Juneau REST client delegates authentication to the underlying Apache HTTP Client, so you configure it with HTTP Client APIs or the builder shortcuts.

Use this when the server you call requires credentials: BASIC with a one-line shortcut, or FORM-based and OIDC logins by customizing the HTTP client. Classic-client-only The auth-shortcut convenience methods shown on these pages (such as basicAuth(...)) are builder methods on the classic RestClient.Builder (org.apache.juneau.rest.client.classic), which wraps Apache HttpClient 4.5. The Next-Generation REST Client has no equivalent auth-shortcut methods at all — it has no dependency on Apache HttpClient, so authentication must instead be configured on the transport you choose (for example, the native Apache HC 4.5/5, OkHttp, or JDK HttpClient builder) before wrapping it in an HttpTransport.

import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.classic.*; public class BasicAuthExample { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { // Create a client that performs BASIC authentication using the specified user/pw. try (RestClient client = RestClient.create() .json() .basicAuth("localhost", 8080, "me", "mypassword") .build()) { System.out.println("Built RestClient"); } } }

Mechanism How BASIC basicAuth(host, port, user, pw) on the builder FORM-based Override createHttpClient() and log in before returning the client OIDC Override createHttpClient() and run the redirect handshake before returning the client

The basicAuth() method can be used to quickly enable BASIC authentication support. RestClient client = RestClient.create() .basicAuth(HOST, PORT, USER, PW) .build(); This is functionally equivalent to the following: RestClient.Builder builder = RestClient.create(); AuthScope scope = new AuthScope(HOST, PORT); Credentials up = new UsernamePasswordCredentials(USER, PW); CredentialsProvider provider = new BasicCredentialsProvider(); provider.setCredentials(scope, up); builder.setDefaultCredentialsProvider(provider);

The RestClient.Builder class does not itself provide FORM-based authentication since there is no standard way of providing such support. Typically, to perform FORM-based or other types of authentication, you'll want to create your own subclass of RestClient.Builder and override the RestClient.Builder.createHttpClient() method to provide an authenticated client. The following example shows an implementation of a client that performs FORM-based authentication against the IBM Jazz platform. /** * Constructor. */ public JazzRestClient.Builder(URI jazzUri, String user, String pw) throws IOException { ... } /** * Override the createHttpClient() method to return an authenticated client. */ @Override /* RestClient.Builder */ protected CloseableHttpClient createHttpClient() throws Exception { CloseableHttpClient client = super.createHttpClient(); formBasedAuthenticate(client); visitAuthenticatedURL(client); return client; } /* * Performs form-based authentication against the Jazz server. */ private void formBasedAuthenticate(HttpClient client) throws IOException { URI uri2 = jazzUri.resolve("j_security_check"); HttpPost request = new HttpPost(uri2); request.setConfig(RequestConfig.custom().setRedirectsEnabled(false).build()); // Charset must explicitly be set to UTF-8 to handle user/pw with non-ascii characters. request.addHeader("Content-Type", "application/x-www-form-urlencoded; charset=utf-8"); List params = List.of( BasicNameValuePair.of("j_username", user), BasicNameValuePair.of("j_password", pw) ); request.setEntity(new UrlEncodedFormEntity(params)); HttpResponse response = client.execute(request); try { int rc = response.getStatusLine().getStatusCode(); Header authMsg = response.getFirstHeader("X-com-ibm-team-repository-web-auth-msg"); if (authMsg != null) throw new IOException(authMsg.getValue()); // The form auth request should always respond with a 200 ok or 302 redirect code if (rc == SC_MOVED_TEMPORARILY) { if (response.getFirstHeader("Location").getValue().matches(".*/auth/authfailed.*")) throw new IOException("Invalid credentials."); } else if (rc != SC_OK) { throw new IOException("Unexpected HTTP status: " + rc); } } finally { EntityUtils.consume(response.getEntity()); } } /* * This is needed for Tomcat because it responds with SC_BAD_REQUEST when the j_security_check URL is visited before an * authenticated URL has been visited. This same URL must also be visited after authenticating with j_security_check * otherwise tomcat will not consider the session authenticated */ private int visitAuthenticatedURL(HttpClient httpClient) throws IOException { HttpGet authenticatedURL = new HttpGet(jazzUri.resolve("authenticated/identity")); HttpResponse response = httpClient.execute(authenticatedURL); try { return response.getStatusLine().getStatusCode(); } finally { EntityUtils.consume(response.getEntity()); } }

The following example shows an implementation of a client that performs OIDC authentication against the IBM Jazz platform. /** * Constructor. */ public JazzRestClient.Builder(URI jazzUri, String user, String pw) throws IOException { ... } /** * Override the createHttpClient() method to return an authenticated client. */ @Override /* RestClient.Builder */ protected CloseableHttpClient createHttpClient() throws Exception { CloseableHttpClient client = super.createHttpClient(); oidcAuthenticate(client); return client; } private void oidcAuthenticate(HttpClient client) throws IOException { HttpGet request = new HttpGet(jazzUri); request.setConfig(RequestConfig.custom().setRedirectsEnabled(false).build()); // Charset must explicitly be set to UTF-8 to handle user/pw with non-ascii characters. request.addHeader("Content-Type", "application/x-www-form-urlencoded; charset=utf-8"); HttpResponse response = client.execute(request); try { int code = response.getStatusLine().getStatusCode(); // Already authenticated if (code == SC_OK) return; if (code != SC_UNAUTHORIZED) throw new RestCallException("Unexpected response during OIDC authentication: " + response.getStatusLine()); // x-jsa-authorization-redirect String redirectUri = getHeader(response, "X-JSA-AUTHORIZATION-REDIRECT"); if (redirectUri == null) throw new RestCallException("Expected a redirect URI during OIDC authentication: " + response.getStatusLine()); // Handle Bearer Challenge HttpGet method = new HttpGet(redirectUri + "&prompt=none"); addDefaultOidcHeaders(method); response = client.execute(method); code = response.getStatusLine().getStatusCode(); if (code != SC_OK) throw new RestCallException("Unexpected response during OIDC authentication phase 2: " + response.getStatusLine()); String loginRequired = getHeader(response, "X-JSA-LOGIN-REQUIRED"); if (! "true".equals(loginRequired)) throw new RestCallException("X-JSA-LOGIN-REQUIRED header not found on response during OIDC authentication phase 2: " + response.getStatusLine()); method = new HttpGet(redirectUri + "&prompt=none"); addDefaultOidcHeaders(method); response = client.execute(method); code = response.getStatusLine().getStatusCode(); if (code != SC_OK) throw new RestCallException("Unexpected response during OIDC authentication phase 3: " + response.getStatusLine()); // Handle JAS Challenge method = new HttpGet(redirectUri); addDefaultOidcHeaders(method); response = client.execute(method); code = response.getStatusLine().getStatusCode(); if (code != SC_OK) throw new RestCallException("Unexpected response during OIDC authentication phase 4: " + response.getStatusLine()); cookie = getHeader(response, "Set-Cookie"); Header[] defaultHeaders = new Header[] { BasicStringHeader.of("User-Agent", "Jazz Native Client"), BasicStringHeader.of("X-com-ibm-team-configuration-versions", "com.ibm.team.rtc=6.0.0,com.ibm.team.jazz.foundation=6.0"), BasicStringHeader.of("Accept", "text/json"), BasicStringHeader.of("Authorization", "Basic " + StringUtils.base64EncodeToString(user + ":" + pw)), BasicStringHeader.of("Cookie", cookie) }; setDefaultHeaders(List.of(defaultHeaders)); } finally { EntityUtils.consume(response.getEntity()); } } private void addDefaultOidcHeaders(HttpRequestBase method) { method.addHeader("User-Agent", "Jazz Native Client"); method.addHeader("X-com-ibm-team-configuration-versions", "com.ibm.team.rtc=6.0.0,com.ibm.team.jazz.foundation=6.0"); method.addHeader("Accept", "text/json"); if (cookie != null) { method.addHeader("Authorization", "Basic " + StringUtils.base64EncodeToString(user + ":" + pw)); method.addHeader("Cookie", cookie); } }
