Various methods can be defined on a class directly to affect how it gets serialized. This can often be simpler than using ObjectSwaps.

Objects serialized as Strings can be parsed back into their original objects by implementing one of the following methods on the class: public static T fromString(String) method. Any of the following method names also work: valueOf(String) parse(String) parseString(String) forName(String) forString(String) public T(String) constructor. Note that these methods cover conversion from several built-in Java types, meaning the parsers can automatically construct these objects from strings: fromString(String) - UUID valueOf(String) - Boolean, Byte, Double, Float, Integer, Long, Short, Date, Time, Timestamp parse(String) - DateFormat, MessageFormat, NumberFormat, Date, Level parseString(String) - DatatypeConverter forName(String) - Class If your static factory method doesn't match any of those conventional names (e.g. of(String) or create(String)), you can use the @StringCtor annotation on the class to name the exact method to use, short-circuiting the name-based lookup above: @StringCtor("of") public class Money { public static Money of(String value) { return new Money(value); } ... } Classes without @StringCtor continue to fall back to the conventional-name lookup (and then the single-String-arg constructor) described above. If you want to force a bean-like class to be serialized as a string, you can use the @Marshalled(as=STRING) annotation on the class to force it to be serialized to a string using the toString() method.

Serializing to other intermediate objects can be accomplished by defining a swap method directly on the class: public X swap() method, where X is any serializable object. public X swap(MarshallingSession) method, where X is any serializable object. public static MyPojo unswap(X) method, where X is any serializable object. public static MyPojo unswap(X,MarshallingSession) method, where X is any serializable object.

Serializing to and from Maps can be accomplished by defining any of the following methods: public Map toMap() method. Can be any type of map with string keys and object vals. public JsonMap toMap() method. public Map toMap(MarshallingSession) method. Can be any type of map with string keys and object vals. public JsonMap toMap(MarshallingSession) method. public static MyPojo fromMap(Map) method. Can be any type of map with string keys and object vals. public static MyPojo fromMap(JsonMap) method. public static MyPojo fromMap(Map,MarshallingSession) method. Can be any type of map with string keys and object vals. public static MyPojo fromMap(JsonMap,MarshallingSession) method.

The MarshallingSession parameter allows you access to various information about the current serialization session. For example, you could provide customized results based on the media type being produced (MarshallingSession.getMediaType()). The following example shows how an HTML5 form template object can be created that gets serialized as a populated HTML5 Form bean. import static org.apache.juneau.bean.html5.HtmlBuilder.*; /** * A simple HTML form template whose serialized form is an HTML5 Form object. */ public class FormTemplate { private String action; private int value1; private boolean value2; // Some constructor that initializes our fields. public FormTemplate(String action, int value1, boolean value2) { this.action = action; this.value1 = value1; this.value2 = value2; } // Special swap method that converts this template to a serializable bean public Form swap(MarshallingSession session) { return form(action, input("text").name("v1").value(value1), input("text").name("v2").value(value2) ); } }

Swapped objects can be converted back into their original form by the parsers by specifying one of the following methods: public static T unswap(MarshallingSession, X) method where X is the swap class type. public T(X) constructor where X is the swap class type. The following shows how our form template class can be modified to allow the parsers to reconstruct our original object: import static org.apache.juneau.bean.html5.HtmlBuilder.*; /** * A simple HTML form template whose serialized form is an HTML5 Form object. * This time with parsing support. */ @Marshalled(dictionary=HtmlBeanDictionary.class) public class FormTemplate { private String action; private int value1; private boolean value2; // Our 'unswap' constructor public FormTemplate(Form form) { this.action = form.getAttr("action"); this.value1 = form.getChild(Input.class, 0) .getAttr(int.class, "value"); this.value2 = form.getChild(Input.class, 1) .getAttr(boolean.class, "value"); } public FormTemplate(String action, int value1, boolean value2) { this.action = action; this.value1 = value1; this.value2 = value2; } public Form swap(MarshallingSession session) { return form(action, input("text").name("v1").value(value1), input("text").name("v2").value(value2) ); } }

Migrating from 9.4.x? The @Rest(apiFormat=…) annotation member, the juneau.rest.apiFormat system property, the RestContext.getApiFormat() accessor, and the ?Swagger / ?OpenApi query mirrors on group resources are all removed in 10.0.0. Both Swagger v2 and OpenAPI 3.1 are now always mounted via the four-class api-docs mixin pack on BasicRestServlet / BasicRestResource. See the V10 Migration Guide for the full removal table, and API-Docs Mixin Pack for the new composition story. Any subclass of BasicRestServlet or BasicRestResource gets six auto-generated API-documentation endpoints by default: URL Format UI swap GET /api Swagger v2 spec SwaggerUI swap for Accept: text/html GET /swagger Same Swagger v2 spec at an HTML-first URL SwaggerUI swap for bare browser GET GET /openapi OpenAPI 3.1 spec RedocUI swap for Accept: text/html GET /openapi.json OpenAPI 3.1 spec Format-pinned JSON (ignores Accept) GET /openapi.yaml OpenAPI 3.1 spec Format-pinned YAML (ignores Accept) GET /redoc Same OpenAPI 3.1 spec at an HTML-first URL RedocUI swap for bare browser GET See the guide: Generate OpenAPI docs for your API The six endpoints come from a four-class mixin pack: SwaggerMixin, SwaggerUiMixin, OpenApiMixin, and RedocMixin. BasicRestServlet declares: @Rest(mixins = {SwaggerUiMixin.class, RedocMixin.class}) public abstract class BasicRestServlet extends RestServlet implements ... { ... } SwaggerUiMixin transitively pulls in SwaggerMixin, and RedocMixin transitively pulls in OpenApiMixin, so listing the two UI halves is enough to mount all six URLs. See API-Docs Mixin Pack for the full composition reference (custom compositions, transitive resolution, parent-chain aggregation, defaultAccept content-negotiation behavior, format-pinned /openapi.json / /openapi.yaml).

Both spec endpoints lean on the existing SwaggerProvider and OpenApiProvider infrastructure. The mixins do not implement their own emission paths; they expose what those providers already produce at the canonical URLs: SwaggerMixin returns the Swagger bean produced by the resource's SwaggerProvider. The class-level @MarshalledConfig applies the SwaggerUI swap when an HTML response is being produced. OpenApiMixin returns the OpenApi bean produced by the resource's OpenApiProvider. The class-level @MarshalledConfig applies the RedocUI swap when an HTML response is being produced. Custom emission is supported by registering a custom SwaggerProvider / OpenApiProvider @Bean (Spring Boot) or via the bean-store registration path (microservice). See API-Docs Mixin Pack § Spring Boot vs. microservice for the resolution rules, including the @Primary precedence for multi-provider Spring Boot applications.

To get the same six-URL surface on a resource that does not extend BasicRestServlet, declare the mixin pack directly: @Rest(path = "/api", mixins = {SwaggerUiMixin.class, RedocMixin.class}) public class CustomApi extends RestServlet { @RestGet("/items") public List<Item> items() { ... } } // Serves /api/items, /api/api, /api/swagger, /api/openapi, /api/openapi.json, // /api/openapi.yaml, /api/redoc. To get only the OpenAPI 3.1 half (no Swagger v2, no /api, no /swagger): @Rest(path = "/api", mixins = RedocMixin.class) public class CustomApi extends RestServlet { @RestGet("/items") public List<Item> items() { ... } } // Serves /api/items, /api/openapi, /api/openapi.json, /api/openapi.yaml, /api/redoc. To get the OpenAPI half on a BasicRestServlet subclass while dropping the inherited Swagger half, opt out of inheritance for the mixins property: @Rest(noInherit = {"mixins"}, mixins = RedocMixin.class) public class OpenApiOnly extends BasicRestServlet { @RestGet("/items") public List<Item> items() { ... } } // Serves /items, /openapi, /openapi.json, /openapi.yaml, /redoc. See REST Server — Mixins and Multi-Mount Paths § Parent-chain mixin aggregation for the aggregation rules that govern how noInherit and per-mixin declarations compose across an inheritance hierarchy.

The OpenAPI 3.1 emission path collapses duplicated inline schemas into reusable components.schemas entries. Two layers contribute: Bean-class lift via Swagger v2 definitions. BasicRestServlet carries @JsonSchemaConfig(useBeanDefs="true"), so when the underlying Swagger generator encounters a bean class it lifts the schema into definitions[<beanClassName>] and emits {"$ref":"#/definitions/<beanClassName>"} from each operation slot. The OpenAPI transform rewrites definitions to components.schemas and #/definitions/<name> refs to #/components/schemas/<name> refs. Inline dedup pass. After the JSON-level Swagger-2.0 → OpenAPI-3.1 transform, BasicOpenApiProviderSession walks every operation parameter, request-body, and response-content schema slot. Inline schemas (those without $ref) that appear two or more times are hoisted into components.schemas and each occurrence is rewritten to a {"$ref":"#/components/schemas/<name>"} pointer. The lifted entry is keyed by the schema's title when present and unique; otherwise a synthesized Schema<N> name is assigned with collision avoidance against existing entries. The dedup pass runs equally on the spec served by /openapi, /openapi.json, and /openapi.yaml, so all three deliver the same components.schemas shape.

Let's look at the various parts of the Petstore application Swagger UI to see how they are defined. The top part of the page shows general information about the REST interface: The information is pulled from the @Rest(swagger) annotation. The real PetStoreResource (juneau-petstore-core) keeps things simple and only sets title/description via @Rest without a swagger= member, so the example below is a self-contained illustrative resource — not literally the shipping PetStoreResource — showing the various ways the @Rest(swagger) annotation can be populated.

@Rest( path="/myResource", title="My REST API", ... swagger=@Swagger("${F:MyResource.json}"), ... ) public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet {...} In this particular case, the Swagger is pulled in from a localized Swagger JSON file located alongside the resource class using the $F variable.
documents.s: Example: pulling Swagger info from an external file

documents.t: { "swagger": "2.0", "info": { "version": "1.0.0", "title": "My REST API", "termsOfService": "You are on your own.", "contact": { "name": "Juneau Development Team", "email": "dev@juneau.apache.org", "url": "http://juneau.apache.org" }, "license": { "name": "Apache 2.0", "url": "http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0.html" } }, "externalDocs": { "description": "Find out more about Juneau", "url": "http://juneau.apache.org" }, ... } Note that the $F variable allows for request-locale-sensitive name matching so that you can provide localized Swagger information. The $F variable simply expands to a string to fill the @Swagger(value) annotation. You could equivalently embed JSON directly into your annotation like so: @Rest( path="/myResource", title="My REST API", ... swagger=@Swagger( // Raw JSON5. // Values are concatenated. "{", "swagger: '2.0',", "version: '1.0.0',", ... "}" ), ... ) public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet {...} However, a more typical (and less error-prone) scenario is to define all of your Swagger as annotations: @Rest( path="/myResource", title="My REST API", ... swagger=@Swagger( version="1.0.0", title="My REST API", termsOfService="You are on your own.", contact=@Contact( name="Juneau Development Team", email="dev@juneau.apache.org", url="http://juneau.apache.org" ), license=@License( name="Apache 2.0", url="http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0.html" ), externalDocs=@ExternalDocs( description="Find out more about Juneau", url="http://juneau.apache.org" ) ), ... ) public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet {...} All annotations support SVL Variables, so you could for example pull localized strings from resource bundles using $L variables. @Rest( path="/myResource", title="My REST API", messages="nls/MyMessages", ... swagger=@Swagger( version="1.0.0", title="${L:myTitle}", termsOfService="${L:myTermsOfService}", contact=@Contact( name="${L:myTeam}", email="dev@juneau.apache.org", url="http://juneau.apache.org" ), license=@License( name="Apache 2.0", url="http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0.html" ), externalDocs=@ExternalDocs( description="${L:myExternalDocsDescription}", url="http://juneau.apache.org" ) ), ... ) public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet {...} A third option is to define your Swagger information in your @Rest(messages) resource bundle using predefined Swagger keywords: MyResource.version = 1.0.0 MyResource.title = My REST API MyResource.termsOfService = You are on your own. MyResource.contact = {name:'Juneau Development Team', email:'dev@juneau.apache.org',...} MyResource.license = {name:'Apache 2.0',...} MyResource.externalDocs = {description:'Find out more about Juneau',...} Information defined in multiple locations are merged into a single set of data. When the same information is provided in multiple locations, the following order-of-precedence is used: Java annotations Resource bundle Swagger JSON file

A powerful and intuitive testing framework that extends JUnit with streamlined assertion methods for Java objects. BCT eliminates verbose test code while providing comprehensive object introspection and comparison capabilities.
Overview Quick Start Core Assertion Methods Nested Property Access Advanced Configuration Migration Examples

Custom Error Messages - Enhanced error reporting Customization - Configuration via @BctConfig and BctConfiguration Stringifiers - Custom string conversions Listifiers - Custom list conversions Swappers - Object transformation Property Extractors - Custom property access

The Bean-Centric Testing Framework transforms complex multi-line JUnit assertions into simple, readable one-liners. Instead of manually extracting and comparing individual properties, BCT provides intelligent object introspection with flexible property access patterns.

Concise Assertions: Replace many lines of manual property extraction with single assertion calls Powerful Property Access: Nested objects, collections, arrays, and maps with unified syntax Flexible Comparison: Support for custom converters, formatters, and comparison logic Type Safety: Comprehensive error messages with clear property paths Extensible: Custom property extractors, stringifiers, and conversion logic Minimal Dependencies: Depends only on JUnit 5 - no external libraries or heavyweight frameworks Zero Configuration: Works out-of-the-box with sensible defaults and automatic discovery 100% Test Coverage: Thoroughly tested with comprehensive unit tests ensuring reliability and stability

BCT is used extensively across the Apache Juneau project's own test suite: Broad adoption: a large share of Juneau's test files use BCT assertions in place of hand-written property checks. Code reduction: many lines of verbose property extraction are replaced with concise assertions. Test clarity: complex object validation is simplified to single-line assertions.

Traditional JUnit: // Testing a user object - verbose and repetitive assertEquals("John", user.getName()); assertEquals(30, user.getAge()); assertTrue(user.isActive()); assertEquals("123 Main St", user.getAddress().getStreet()); assertEquals("Springfield", user.getAddress().getCity()); Bean-Centric Testing: // Same test - concise and readable assertBean(user, "name,age,active,address{street,city}", "John,30,true,{123 Main St,Springfield}");
import static org.apache.juneau.bct.BctAssertions.*;

@Test void testUser() { User user = new User("Alice", 25, true); // Test multiple properties at once assertBean(user, "name,age,active", "Alice,25,true"); // Test individual properties assertBean(user, "name", "Alice"); assertBean(user, "age", "25"); } @Test void testMultipleUsers() { List<User> users = List.of( new User("Alice", 25, true), new User("Bob", 30, false), new User("Carol", 35, true) ); // Test same properties across multiple objects assertBeans(users, "name,age", "Alice,25", "Bob,30", "Carol,35"); // Test just names assertBeans(users, "name", "Alice", "Bob", "Carol"); }

@Test void testList() { List<String> colors = List.of("red", "green", "blue"); // Test all elements assertList(colors, "red", "green", "blue"); // Test as bean properties assertBean(colors, "0,1,2", "red,green,blue"); assertBean(colors, "size", "3"); }

Tests properties of a single object using a flexible property syntax with powerful nested access capabilities. This method provides comprehensive property access for any Java object, supporting nested objects, collections, arrays, maps, and custom field access patterns. It uses intelligent property resolution with automatic type handling and supports complex object graphs.

// Simple properties assertBean(user, "name,email", "John,john@example.com"); // Boolean properties assertBean(user, "active,verified", "true,false"); // Null handling assertBean(user, "middleName", "null");

// Single-level nesting assertBean(user, "address{street,city}", "{123 Main St,Springfield}"); // Multi-level nesting assertBean(user, "profile{settings{notifications{email}}}", "{{{true}}}"); // Mixed simple and nested assertBean(order, "id,customer{name,email},total", "12345,{John Doe,john@example.com},99.95");

// Index-based access assertBean(order, "items{0{name},1{name}}", "{{Laptop},{Phone}}"); // Collection iteration (#{} syntax) assertBean(order, "items{#{name}}", "[{Laptop},{Phone},{Tablet}]"); // Collection properties assertBean(order, "items{length,#{price}}", "{3,[{999.99},{699.99},{299.99}]}"); // Array access assertBean(data, "values{0,1,2}", "{100,200,300}");

// Direct key access assertBean(config, "database{host,port}", "{localhost,5432}"); // Map size testing assertBean(user, "settings{size}", "{5}"); // Null key handling assertBean(user, "mapWithNullKey{<null>}", "{nullKeyValue}");

// Public fields (no getters required) assertBean(myBean, "f1,f2,f3", "val1,val2,val3"); // Field properties with chaining assertBean(myBean, "f1{length},f2{class{simpleName}}", "{5},{{String}}"); // Boolean method variations assertBean(user, "enabled,isActive,hasPermission", "true,false,true");

Tests multiple objects in a collection, comparing the same properties across all objects using the same property access logic as assertBean. This method validates that each bean in a collection has the specified property values. It's perfect for testing collections of similar objects, validation results, or parsed data structures. Each expected value string corresponds to one bean in the collection.

List<User> users = Arrays.asList( new User("Alice", 25), new User("Bob", 30), new User("Charlie", 35) ); // Test same properties across all users assertBeans(users, "name,age", "Alice,25", "Bob,30", "Charlie,35" );

// Test nested properties across multiple beans List<Order> orders = getOrderList(); assertBeans(orders, "id,customer{name,email}", "1,{John,john@example.com}", "2,{Jane,jane@example.com}" ); // Test collection properties within beans List<ShoppingCart> carts = getCartList(); assertBeans(carts, "items{0{name}},total", "{{Laptop}},999.99", "{{Phone}},599.99" );

Tests collection elements directly with support for multiple comparison modes: string conversion, functional validation with predicates, and direct object equality. This method supports any object that can be converted to a List, including arrays, collections, iterables, streams, and more. It provides three distinct comparison modes based on the type of expected values provided.

// String collections - compares string representations assertList(List.of("a", "b", "c"), "a", "b", "c"); // Number collections - converts to string for comparison assertList(List.of(1, 2, 3), "1", "2", "3"); // Object collections - uses toString() or converter assertList(productNames, "Laptop", "Phone", "Tablet"); // Arrays and other collection types assertList(myArray, "element1", "element2", "element3");

// Use Predicate<T> for functional testing Predicate<Integer> greaterThanOne = x -> x > 1; assertList(List.of(2, 3, 4), greaterThanOne, greaterThanOne, greaterThanOne); // Mix predicates with other comparison types Predicate<String> startsWithA = s -> s.startsWith("a"); assertList(List.of("apple", "banana"), startsWithA, "banana"); // Complex predicate validation Predicate<User> isActive = user -> user.isActive(); assertList(userList, isActive, isActive);

// Non-String, non-Predicate objects use Objects.equals() comparison assertList(List.of(1, 2, 3), 1, 2, 3); // Integer objects // Custom objects with proper equals() implementation assertList(List.of(myBean1, myBean2), myBean1, myBean2); // Mixed object types assertList(mixedList, stringObj, integerObj, customObj);

Tests objects with custom property access logic using a BiFunction, designed for objects that don't follow standard JavaBean patterns or require specialized property extraction. This method creates an intermediate LinkedHashMap to collect all property values before using the same logic as assertBean for comparison. This ensures consistent ordering and supports the full nested property syntax. The BiFunction receives the object and property name, returning the property value.

// Custom property access for non-standard objects assertMapped(myObject, (obj, prop) -> obj.getProperty(prop), "prop1,prop2", "value1,value2"); // Map-based property access Map<String, Object> data = new HashMap<>(); data.put("name", "Alice"); data.put("score", 95); assertMapped(data, (map, key) -> map.get(key), "name,score", "Alice,95");

// Exceptions become simple class names in output assertMapped(dataSource, (ds, prop) -> { try { return ds.getConnection().getMetaData().getDatabaseProductName(); } catch (SQLException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } }, "databaseName", "PostgreSQL"); // Safe property access with exception conversion assertMapped(webService, (service, endpoint) -> { try { return service.call(endpoint); } catch (Exception e) { return e.getClass().getSimpleName(); // Returns "TimeoutException" } }, "userEndpoint", "TimeoutException");

// Transform complex nested access patterns assertMapped(configSystem, (config, prop) -> { switch(prop) { case "timeout": return config.getSettings().getTimeout(); case "retries": return config.getSettings().getRetries(); case "database": return config.getDatabase().getUrl(); default: return config.getAttribute(prop); } }, "timeout,retries,database", "30000,3,jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/mydb"); // Conditional property access assertMapped(userService, (service, operation) -> { if ("count".equals(operation)) { return service.getUserCount(); } else if ("active".equals(operation)) { return service.getActiveUsers().size(); } return service.getProperty(operation); }, "count,active", "150,45");

// Access legacy objects without standard getters assertMapped(legacyBean, (bean, fieldName) -> { Field field = bean.getClass().getDeclaredField(fieldName); field.setAccessible(true); return field.get(bean); }, "privateField1,privateField2", "value1,value2");
BCT provides several additional assertion methods for common testing scenarios:

Tests that a string appears somewhere within the stringified object. User user = new User("Alice Smith", 25); List<String> items = Arrays.asList("apple", "banana", "cherry"); // Test substring presence assertContains("Alice", user); assertContains("Smith", user); assertContains("banana", items);

Tests that all specified strings appear within the stringified object. User user = new User("Alice Smith", 25); user.setEmail("alice@example.com"); // Test multiple substrings assertContainsAll(user, "Alice", "Smith", "25"); assertContainsAll(user, "alice", "example.com");

Tests that collections, arrays, maps, or strings are empty. List<String> emptyList = new ArrayList<>(); String[] emptyArray = {}; Map<String,String> emptyMap = new HashMap<>(); String emptyString = ""; // Test empty collections assertEmpty(emptyList); assertEmpty(emptyArray); assertEmpty(emptyMap); assertEmpty(emptyString);

Tests that collections, arrays, maps, or strings are not empty. List<String> names = Arrays.asList("Alice"); String[] colors = {"red"}; Map<String,String> config = Map.of("key", "value"); String message = "Hello"; // Test non-empty collections assertNotEmpty(names); assertNotEmpty(colors); assertNotEmpty(config); assertNotEmpty(message);

Tests the size/length of collections, arrays, maps, or strings. List<String> names = Arrays.asList("Alice", "Bob", "Carol"); String[] colors = {"red", "green"}; Map<String,Integer> scores = Map.of("Alice", 95, "Bob", 87); String message = "Hello"; // Test collection sizes assertSize(3, names); assertSize(2, colors); assertSize(2, scores); assertSize(5, message);

Tests the string representation of an object using the configured converter. User user = new User("Alice", 25); List<Integer> numbers = Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3); Date date = new Date(1609459200000L); // 2021-01-01 // Test string representations assertString("User(name=Alice, age=25)", user); assertString("[1, 2, 3]", numbers); assertString("2021-01-01", date);

Tests that the stringified object matches a glob-style pattern (* and ? wildcards). User user = new User("Alice Smith", 25); String filename = "report.pdf"; String email = "alice@company.com"; // Test pattern matching assertMatchesGlob("*Alice*", user); assertMatchesGlob("*.pdf", filename); assertMatchesGlob("*@*.com", email); assertMatchesGlob("User(name=Alice*, age=25)", user);
BCT provides powerful nested property access with intuitive syntax:

// Access nested object properties assertBean(order, "customer{address{city}}", "{{Springfield}}"); // Multiple nested levels assertBean(user, "profile{settings{notifications{email}}}", "{{{true}}}"); // Multiple properties at each level assertBean(order, "customer{name,email},shipping{method,cost}", "{John,john@example.com},{Express,15.99}");

// Index-based access assertBean(order, "items{0{name},1{name}}", "{{Laptop},{Phone}}"); // Iterate over all elements assertBean(order, "items{#{name}}", "[{Laptop},{Phone},{Tablet}]"); // Collection properties assertBean(order, "items{length,#{price}}", "{3,[{999.99},{699.99},{299.99}]}"); // Array access assertBean(data, "values{0,1,2}", "{100,200,300}");

// Direct key access assertBean(config, "database{host,port}", "{localhost,5432}"); // Special characters in keys assertBean(props, "app.version,app.name", "1.0.0,MyApp"); // Null key access assertBean(mapWithNullKey, "<null>", "nullKeyValue");

// Universal size access assertBean(list, "size", "5"); assertBean(array, "length", "10"); assertBean(map, "size", "3"); // Combined with other properties assertBean(user, "orders{size,#{total}}", "{3,[{99.99},{149.99},{79.99}]}");
BCT provides several advanced configuration options for customizing assertion behavior:

The @BctConfig annotation provides a declarative way to configure BCT settings for your tests. It can be applied at the class level or method level, with method-level annotations taking precedence. @BctConfig(sortMaps=TriState.TRUE, beanConverter=MyCustomConverter.class) class MyTest { @Test @BctConfig(sortCollections=TriState.TRUE) void testSomething() { // sortMaps=true (from class), sortCollections=true (from method), // beanConverter=MyCustomConverter (from class) assertBean(order, "items{0{name}}", "{{Laptop}}"); } } The annotation supports: sortMaps: Enable sorting of map entries before comparison sortCollections: Enable sorting of collection elements before comparison beanConverter: Specify a custom bean converter class to use For more details, see Customization.

The default bean converter can be customized on a per-thread basis using BctAssertions.setConverter(BeanConverter) (a thin passthrough to BctConfiguration.set(BeanConverter)) or via the @BctConfig annotation. This is particularly useful in test setup methods to configure a custom converter for all tests in a test class or method. // Set custom converter in @BeforeEach method @BeforeEach void setUp() { var converter = BasicBeanConverter.builder() .defaultSettings() .addStringifier(LocalDate.class, (conv,date) -> date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE)) .addStringifier(Money.class, (conv,money) -> money.getAmount().toPlainString()) .build(); setConverter(converter); } // All assertions now use the custom converter @Test void testWithCustomConverter() { assertBean(order, "date,total", "2023-12-01,99.99"); } // Reset in @AfterEach method @AfterEach void tearDown() { resetConverter(); } Thread Safety: The converter is stored per-thread, allowing parallel test execution without cross-thread interference. Each test method running in parallel will have its own converter instance.

For detailed information on extending and customizing BCT, see: Custom Error Messages - Add contextual information to assertion failures Customization - Configure BCT via @BctConfig annotation and BctConfiguration class Stringifiers - Define how objects are converted to strings for comparison Listifiers - Convert collection-like objects to lists for testing Swappers - Transform objects before processing (unwrap Optional, Supplier, etc.) Property Extractors - Define custom property access logic for non-standard objects

Complex Object Testing: // Before: Traditional JUnit @Test void testOrderTraditional() { assertEquals(12345L, order.getId()); assertEquals("John Doe", order.getCustomer().getName()); assertEquals("john@example.com", order.getCustomer().getEmail()); assertEquals("123 Main St", order.getShipping().getAddress().getStreet()); assertEquals("Springfield", order.getShipping().getAddress().getCity()); assertEquals(3, order.getItems().size()); assertEquals("Laptop", order.getItems().get(0).getName()); assertEquals(new BigDecimal("999.99"), order.getItems().get(0).getPrice()); assertEquals(OrderStatus.PENDING, order.getStatus()); } // After: Bean-Centric Testing @Test void testOrderBCT() { assertBean(order, "id,customer{name,email},shipping{address{street,city}},items{size,0{name,price}},status", "12345,{John Doe,john@example.com},{{123 Main St,Springfield}},{3,{Laptop,999.99}},PENDING"); } Collection Testing: // Before: Traditional JUnit @Test void testUsersTraditional() { assertEquals(3, users.size()); assertEquals("Alice", users.get(0).getName()); assertEquals(25, users.get(0).getAge()); assertEquals("Bob", users.get(1).getName()); assertEquals(30, users.get(1).getAge()); assertEquals("Charlie", users.get(2).getName()); assertEquals(35, users.get(2).getAge()); } // After: Bean-Centric Testing @Test void testUsersBCT() { assertBeans(users, "name,age", "Alice,25", "Bob,30", "Charlie,35"); } Configuration Testing: // Before: Traditional JUnit @Test void testConfigTraditional() { assertEquals("localhost", config.getDatabase().getHost()); assertEquals(5432, config.getDatabase().getPort()); assertEquals("myapp", config.getDatabase().getSchema()); assertEquals(30000, config.getTimeout()); assertEquals(3, config.getRetries()); assertTrue(config.isLoggingEnabled()); } // After: Bean-Centric Testing @Test void testConfigBCT() { assertBean(config, "database{host,port,schema},timeout,retries,loggingEnabled", "{localhost,5432,myapp},30000,3,true"); }

The Bean-Centric Testing Framework transforms verbose, error-prone test code into concise, readable assertions. By leveraging intelligent object introspection and flexible property access patterns, BCT enables developers to write more maintainable tests while improving test coverage and readability. Benefits: Reduced Code Volume: 70-80% less test code Improved Readability: Clear, intention-revealing assertions Better Maintainability: Changes to object structure require minimal test updates Enhanced Error Messages: Precise failure reporting with property paths Flexible Extension: Custom converters for domain-specific needs Start with simple assertBean calls and gradually adopt more advanced features as your testing needs evolve. The framework grows with your project complexity while maintaining simplicity at its core.

Property extractors define custom property access logic for objects that don't follow standard JavaBean patterns or require specialized property extraction. They provide a flexible way to access properties from any object structure.

The Bean Context (BCT — Bean Context Type) is Juneau's core bean-introspection framework. It provides a unified, highly configurable view of Java beans that all serializers, parsers, and other framework components share. Every marshaller in Juneau extends MarshallingContext, which means a single set of bean-modeling settings controls how beans are discovered, read, and written across all formats — JSON, XML, YAML, CSV, MessagePack, and the rest — with no per-format configuration duplication. The framework splits into two layers: Layer Location Responsibility Bean modeling juneau-commons Introspect classes, discover properties, apply @BeanType/@BeanProp/@BeanIgnore/@BeanCtor Marshalling juneau-marshall Extend the bean model with ClassMeta, type swaps, bean dictionaries, format-specific options

MarshallingContext is the root configuration object for bean introspection and marshalling. All serializers and parsers (and their builders) extend from it, so they inherit every builder method on the context directly. Instances are: Immutable — constructed once via a fluent builder and never changed thereafter. Thread-safe — freely shared across serializers and threads. Cache-sharing — contexts with the same settings reuse the same ClassMeta cache, so expensive reflective analysis of a given class happens only once. // Create a standalone context (useful for programmatic bean introspection // without going through a full serializer). MarshallingContext ctx = MarshallingContext .create() .beansRequireDefaultConstructor() // Tighten bean detection .beanFieldVisibility(Visibility.ANY) // Include private fields .notBeanClasses(MyRawType.class) // Exclude this class from bean treatment .build(); The static constant MarshallingContext.DEFAULT provides a pre-built, zero-config context for quick use.

MarshallingSession is an ephemeral, per-operation companion to MarshallingContext. Sessions hold request-scoped state such as locale, time zone, active view, and media type. They are lightweight to create and are typically not shared across threads. // Open a session for the DEFAULT context. MarshallingSession session = MarshallingContext.DEFAULT_SESSION; // singleton no-op session // Or create one with per-call settings. MarshallingSession session = MarshallingContext.DEFAULT.createSession(); Sessions are the entry point for creating BeanMap instances (see below).

BeanMap wraps a Java bean inside a Map<String, Object> interface, letting properties be read and written via the standard get/put methods. All serializers use BeanMap internally to traverse a bean's properties without generating intermediate structures. Although used internally by every serializer and parser, it is often useful on its own. public class Person { public String name = "John Smith"; public int age = 21; } // Wrap an existing bean. BeanMap<Person> bm = MarshallingContext.DEFAULT_SESSION.toBeanMap(new Person()); bm.put("name", "Jane Doe"); String name = (String) bm.get("name"); // "Jane Doe" // Typed accessor — convert the property value on read. int age = bm.get("age", int.class); // Create a new bean through the map. BeanMap<Person> bm2 = MarshallingContext.DEFAULT_SESSION.newBeanMap(Person.class); bm2.put("name", "Alice"); bm2.put("age", 30); Person p = bm2.getBean(); BeanMap iteration follows a deterministic property order: explicit @BeanType(properties=...) list → alphabetical (default) → natural reflection order when @BeanType(unsorted=true) is set.

BeanMeta is the compiled introspection record for a single bean class. It holds the complete, resolved list of BeanPropertyMeta entries — one per logical property — including the underlying field or getter/setter pair, resolved generic types, and any applied annotations. Instances are built once and cached by the context. Retrieve one via: BeanMeta<Person> meta = MarshallingContext.DEFAULT_SESSION.getBeanMeta(Person.class); for (BeanPropertyMeta prop : meta) { System.out.println(prop.getName() + " : " + prop.getClassMeta().getInnerClass()); }

ClassMeta extends BeanMeta with marshalling-layer knowledge: whether a class is a bean, a collection, a map, a primitive, an enum, or something else (the Category enum covers ~20 categories). It also records the active object swaps and format overrides for that type. ClassMeta<Person> cm = MarshallingContext.DEFAULT.getClassMeta(Person.class); cm.isBean(); // true cm.isMap(); // false

The bean-modeling layer lives in juneau-commons and uses a trio of annotations that are independent of any marshalling concern. The marshalling layer in juneau-marshall extends each one with a sibling that carries format-specific attributes.

Applied to a class to declare the canonical property list, sorting, excluded properties, stop class, and more. The marshalling-layer sibling is @Marshalled. // Keep only "id" and "name"; expose them in that exact order. @BeanType(properties = "id,name") public class Person { public int id; public String name; public String internalToken; // excluded — not in properties list } // Exclude a property by name (useful when you cannot edit the class). @BeanType(excludeProperties = "password") public class Account { ... }

Applied to a field, getter, setter, or constructor parameter to rename a property, mark it read-only/write-only, specify a concrete type, or supply a factory. The marshalling-layer sibling is @MarshalledProp. public class Contact { // Rename the serialized property key. @BeanProp("full_name") public String fullName; // Read-only — serialized but ignored on parse. @BeanProp(ro = "true") public String getCreatedAt() { ... } // Write-only — accepted on parse but not serialized. @BeanProp(wo = "true") public void setPassword(String pw) { ... } }

Applied to a class, field, method, or constructor to exclude it from bean introspection. On a class, marks it as not a bean (the marshaller falls back to toString() or a registered swap). On a member, removes it from the property set. // Entire class: never treated as a bean. @BeanIgnore public class RawToken { ... } // Individual member: hidden from serialization and parsing. public class Order { public String orderId; @BeanIgnore public String getDebugString() { ... } // excluded from marshalling }

Applied to a constructor to map its parameters onto the bean's logical property names. Required when a bean is read-only (no setters) and must be instantiated during parsing. Java Records detect their canonical constructor automatically, so @BeanCtor is optional there. public class Point { public final int x, y; @BeanCtor({"x","y"}) public Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } } // Parser can now reconstruct Point from {"x":1,"y":2}. Point p = Json.to("{x:1,y:2}", Point.class);

When a class cannot be introspected as a bean (or needs a different wire representation), the bean context delegates to object swaps — pluggable converters registered on the context builder: MarshallingContext ctx = MarshallingContext .create() .calendarFormat(CalendarFormat.ISO_INSTANT) // Instant → ISO-8601 string .build(); The MarshalledFilter class (implements BeanFilter) is the programmatic API for applying bean-level overrides such as additional include/exclude lists or property namers without touching the annotated source class — useful for third-party types. See Also Swap Basics for the full object-swap reference. Bean Dictionary Basics for polymorphic type resolution.

Every marshaller builder inherits the full set of MarshallingContext.Builder settings. Common properties include: Builder method Effect beanFieldVisibility(Visibility) Include PRIVATE, PROTECTED, or PUBLIC fields as properties beanMethodVisibility(Visibility) Visibility threshold for getter/setter discovery beansRequireDefaultConstructor() Only treat classes with a public no-arg constructor as beans beansRequireSerializable() Only treat Serializable classes as beans notBeanClasses(Class...) Exclude specific classes from bean treatment notBeanPackages(String...) Exclude entire packages from bean treatment sortProperties() Force alphabetical property order globally ignoreUnknownBeanProperties() Silently skip unrecognized keys during parsing swaps(Class...) Register object-swap converters beanDictionary(Class...) Register types for polymorphic _type resolution Any setting that can be applied via a builder can equally be applied via a @MarshalledConfig config annotation, allowing serializer settings to live on an annotated class and be applied via builder.applyAnnotations(MyAnnotatedClass.class). // Config annotation on a class — useful in REST servlet hierarchies. @MarshalledConfig(sortProperties = "true", ignoreUnknownBeanProperties = "true") public class MyApiResource { ... } // Apply the annotations to a serializer at build time. JsonSerializer s = JsonSerializer.create() .applyAnnotations(MyApiResource.class) .build(); See Also Java Beans Support for property-detection rules and examples. Java Records Support for record-specific behavior. Context Annotations for the config-annotation reference.

The @BeanCtor annotation is applied to bean constructors to map constructor arguments to property names on beans with read-only properties. Since method parameter names are lost during compilation, this annotation essentially redefines them so that they are available at runtime and the framework can instantiate read-only beans during parsing. This annotation lives in juneau-commons so the bean-modeling layer can describe constructor argument mappings without depending on the marshalling layer. Migration This annotation was previously named @Beanc. Usages of @Beanc should be updated to @BeanCtor (in org.apache.juneau.commons.bean). This annotation can only be applied to constructors, and only one constructor per class may carry it.

The definition of a read-only bean is a bean with properties with only getters, like shown below: // Our read-only bean. public class Person { private final String name; private final int age; @BeanCtor(properties="name,age") public Person(String name, int age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; } // Read only properties. // Getters but no setters. public String getName() { return name; } public int getAge() { return age; } } // Parsing into a read-only bean. String json = "{name:'John Smith',age:45}"; Person person = Json.to(json, Person.class); String name = person.getName(); // "John Smith" int age = person.getAge(); // 45 Beans can also be defined with a combination of read-only and read-write properties.

The @Name annotation can also be used instead of @BeanCtor(properties) to label individual parameters: @BeanCtor public Person(@Name("name") String name, @Name("age") int age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; } If neither @BeanCtor(properties) nor @Name is used to identify the bean property names, the framework will try to use the parameter names if they are available in the bytecode.

For Java records, the canonical constructor and its property mappings are automatically detected, so this annotation is not required. It can still be used to specify a non-canonical constructor if needed, for example to provide default values for certain components: @BeanType(properties="name") public record WithBeanCtor(String name, int age) { @BeanCtor(properties="name") public WithBeanCtor(String name) { this(name, 0); // Default age to 0 } } When using @BeanCtor with a non-canonical constructor on a record, use @BeanType(properties) to limit the visible properties to match the constructor parameters. See Also @BeanType Annotation - Class-level bean-modeling annotation. @BeanProp Annotation - Property-level bean-modeling annotation. Java Records Support - Full documentation on Java records support.

While parsing into beans, Juneau attempts to determine the class types of bean properties through reflection on the bean property getter or setter. Often this is insufficient if the property type is an interface or abstract class that cannot be instantiated. This is where bean names and dictionaries come into play. Bean names and dictionaries are used for identifying class types when they cannot be inferred through reflection. Bean classes are given names through the @Marshalled(typeName) annotation. These names are then added to the serialized output as virtual _type properties (or element names in XML). On the parsing side, these type names are resolved to classes through the use of bean dictionaries. For example, if a bean property is of type Object, then the serializer will add _type attributes so that the class can be determined during parsing. @Marshalled(typeName="foo") public class Foo { // A bean property where the object types cannot be inferred since it's an Object[]. @MarshalledProp(dictionary={Bar.class,Baz.class}) public Object[] x = new Object[]{new Bar(), new Baz()}; } @Marshalled(typeName="bar") public class Bar {} @Marshalled(typeName="baz") public class Baz {} When serialized as JSON, _type attributes would be added when needed to infer the type during parsing: { x: [ {_type:'bar'}, {_type:'baz'} ] } Type names can be represented slightly differently in different languages. For example, the dictionary name is used as element names when serialized to XML. This allows the typeName annotation to be used as a shortcut for defining element names for beans. When serialized as XML, the bean is rendered as: <foo> <x> <bar/> <baz/> </x> </foo> Bean dictionaries are registered through the following: MarshalledPropdictionaryMarshalleddictionaryMarshallingContext.BuilderbeanDictionary(Class...) The bean dictionary setting can consist of any of the following types: Any bean class that specifies a value for @Marshalled(typeName). Any subclass of BeanDictionaryList containing a collection of bean classes with type name annotations. Any subclass of BeanDictionaryMap containing a mapping of type names to classes without type name annotations. Any array or collection of the objects above. // Create a parser and tell it which classes to try to resolve. ReaderParser parser = JsonParser .create() .beanDictionary(Foo.class, Bar.class) .build(); // Use the predefined HTML5 bean dictionary which is a BeanDictionaryList. ReaderParser parser = HtmlParser .create() .beanDictionary(HtmlBeanDictionary.class) .build(); The _type property name can be overridden through the following: MarshalledtypePropertyNameMarshallingContext.BuildertypePropertyName(String) When using the annotation, you'll typically want to define it on an interface class so that it can be inherited by all subclasses. @Marshalled(typePropertyName="mytype", dictionary={MyClass1.class,MyClass2.class}) public interface MyInterface {...} @Marshalled(typeName="C1") public class MyClass1 implements MyInterface {...} @Marshalled(typeName="C2") public class MyClass2 implements MyInterface {...} MyInterface[] x = new MyInterface[]{ new MyClass1(), new MyClass2() }; // Produces "[{mytype:'C1',...},{mytype:'C2',...}]" String json = JsonSerializer.DEFAULT.write(x); note Type names do not need to be universally unique. However, they must be unique within a dictionary. The following reserved words cannot be used as type names: object, array, number, boolean, null. Serialized type names are DISABLED by default. They must be enabled on the serializer using the Serializer.Builder.addBeanTypes() setting.

The @BeanIgnore annotation (org.apache.juneau.commons.bean) excludes a class, field, method, or constructor from bean introspection — the model-side decision about whether something participates in bean detection at all. This is the model-side annotation. Format-side concerns — skipping a type entirely at the wire-format layer regardless of whether it's a bean — live on the sibling annotation @MarshalledIgnore (org.apache.juneau.marshall), described at the end of this page. The two annotations are independent and may be combined.

When applied to a field or method, @BeanIgnore excludes it from bean property discovery. public class MyBean { // Not a bean property! @BeanIgnore public String foo; // Not a bean property! @BeanIgnore public String getBar() {...} }

When applied to a constructor, @BeanIgnore excludes it from constructor detection (i.e. it won't be considered a candidate bean constructor). public class MyBean { public MyBean() {...} // Excluded from constructor detection. @BeanIgnore public MyBean(String foo) {...} }

When applied to a class, @BeanIgnore marks the class as not a bean for modeling purposes. The marshaller falls through to its other type-detection logic (object swaps, @BeanType-style hints, @Marshalled(as=MarshalledAs.STRING), etc.) instead of treating the class as a bean — it does not by itself suppress output the way @MarshalledIgnore does. // Not treated as a bean for modeling purposes. // The marshaller still tries to render it, e.g. via toString() or an installed swap. @BeanIgnore public class MyType {...} Migration In versions prior to 10.0, @BeanIgnore on a class caused the object to be serialized via toString() rather than as a bean — that historical behavior is what the current @BeanIgnore-on-class semantics above describe. If you specifically want the wire format to render null for a type regardless of bean-modeling status, use @MarshalledIgnore (see below) instead. If you want the explicit toString() serialization behavior, use @Marshalled(as=MarshalledAs.STRING): // Serialize as toString() value. @Marshalled(as=MarshalledAs.STRING) public class MyType { @Override public String toString() { return "my-value"; } }

By default, @BeanIgnore on a field only excludes that field from field-based bean discovery. Public (or otherwise visible) getters/setters can still expose the same logical property — for example when beanFieldVisibility is NONE and only methods are used. That matches patterns such as @BeanIgnore on private f5…f8 with public getF5() while still serializing f5 via the getter. To also exclude the matching JavaBean accessor pair from metadata (so the property does not appear in serialization or parsing), set ignoreAccessors = true on the field annotation: public class MyBean { public String visible = "ok"; // Hidden from Juneau bean metadata: no "foo" in serialization/parsing @BeanIgnore(ignoreAccessors = true) private String foo = "secret"; public String getFoo() { return foo; } public void setFoo(String value) { foo = value; } } The logical property name is derived from the field the same way as for visible fields: @BeanProp / @Name on the field, if present, otherwise the marshalling context's PropertyNamer applied to the field name. That name must match the accessor-derived property name (e.g. field foo with getFoo/setFoo).

Ignoring individual record components is not supported during parsing. Because records are immutable, all components must be provided to the canonical constructor. Applying @BeanIgnore to a record component's accessor method or field will exclude it from serialization output, but the parser will be unable to instantiate the record if the component value is missing from the input. If you need to omit components during parsing, use @BeanCtor with a non-canonical constructor that provides defaults for the omitted components.

@MarshalledIgnore (org.apache.juneau.marshall) is a type-level-only annotation (it has no field/method target and no ignoreAccessors attribute). Serializers output null for instances of the annotated type, and parsers return null when asked to instantiate it — this is a wire-format concern independent of whatever the bean-modeling layer would otherwise do with the type. // Suppressed entirely at the wire-format layer — serializes as null. @MarshalledIgnore public class MyType {...} Because the two annotations are independent, they combine as follows: @MarshalledIgnore alone — the class still participates in bean detection (it may be treated as a bean by the modeling layer), but the marshaller emits null. @BeanIgnore alone — the class is not a bean for modeling purposes, but the marshaller still tries to render it (typically via toString() or an installed swap). Both — the class is not a bean and the marshaller emits null. See Also Java Records Support - Full documentation on Java records support. @BeanType Annotation - The model-side/format-side split pattern this page follows.

The @BeanProp annotation is applied to bean fields, getter/setter methods, and constructor parameters to control bean introspection and property modeling. This is the model-side annotation in juneau-commons. It carries the attributes that describe the bean property itself — its name, accessibility (read/write only), concrete type, generic type parameters, element type, and the bean factory used to instantiate its value. Format-side concerns (wire-format overrides, dictionary) live on @MarshalledProp in juneau-marshall. Migration This annotation was previously named @Beanp. Usages of @Beanp should be updated to @BeanProp (in org.apache.juneau.commons.bean).

The @BeanProp(name) annotation overrides the name of the bean property. public class MyBean { @BeanProp(name="Bar") public String getFoo() {...} } The @Name annotation is a shortcut for specifying a bean property name: public class MyBean { @Name("Bar") public String getFoo() {...} } The @BeanProp(value) annotation is a synonym for name. Use it when you are only specifying a name so the annotation is more concise: // These two annotations are equivalent: @BeanProp(name="foo") @BeanProp("foo") If the beanFieldVisibility setting on the marshalling context excludes this field (e.g. the visibility is set to the default of PUBLIC but the field is PROTECTED), this annotation can be used to force the field to be identified as a property. public class MyBean { @BeanProp protected String getFoo() {...} }

The bean property named * is the designated "dynamic property" which allows for "extra" bean properties not otherwise defined. This is similar in concept to the Jackson @JsonGetterAll and @JsonSetterAll annotations but generalized for all supported marshall languages. The primary purpose is for backwards compatibility in parsing newer streams with additional information into older beans. The following shows various ways of using dynamic bean properties. // Option #1 - A simple public Map field. // The field name can be anything. public class BeanWithDynaField { @BeanProp(name="*") public Map<String,Object> extraStuff = new LinkedHashMap<>(); } // Option #2 - Getters and setters. // Method names can be anything. // Getter must return a Map with String keys. // Setter must take in two arguments, a String and Object. public class BeanWithDynaMethods { @BeanProp(name="*") public Map<String,Object> getMyExtraStuff() { ... } @BeanProp(name="*") public void setAnExtraField(String name, Object value) { ... } } // Option #3 - Getter only. // Properties will be added through the getter. public class BeanWithDynaGetterOnly { @BeanProp(name="*") public Map<String,Object> getMyExtraStuff() { ... } } note If you're not interested in these additional properties, you can use the ignoreUnknownBeanProperties setting to ignore values that don't fit into existing properties.

The @BeanProp(type) annotation identifies a specialized class type for a generalized property. Normally the type is inferred through reflection of the field type or getter return type. However, specify this value if you're parsing beans where the bean property class is an interface or abstract class to identify the bean type to instantiate. Otherwise, you may cause an InstantiationException when trying to set these fields. This property must denote a concrete class with a no-arg constructor. public class MyBean { // Identify concrete type as a HashMap. @BeanProp(type=HashMap.class) public Map p1; }

The @BeanProp(params) annotation is for bean properties of type map or collection. It identifies the class types of the contents of the bean property object when the general parameter types are interfaces or abstract classes. public class MyBean { // Identify concrete map type with String keys and Integer values. @BeanProp(type=HashMap.class, params={String.class,Integer.class}) public Map p1; }

The @BeanProp(ro) annotation identifies a property as read-only. Serializers will serialize such properties as usual, but parsers will silently ignore them. public class MyBean { @BeanProp(ro="true") public float price; } Java Records Marking record components as read-only is not supported during parsing. Because records are immutable, all components must be provided to the canonical constructor.

The @BeanProp(wo) annotation identifies a property as write-only. Parsers will parse such properties as usual, but serializers will silently ignore them. public class MyBean { @BeanProp(wo="true") public float price; }

Specifies the element type for properties of type Stream, BeanSupplier, BeanConsumer, or BeanChannel when type erasure prevents the framework from inferring the generic type argument at runtime. public class OrderCollection { // Stream property - element type cannot be inferred at runtime due to erasure @BeanProp(elementType=Order.class) public Stream<Order> getOrders() { ... } }

Specifies a BeanFactory class to use when instantiating the value of this specific bean property, overriding the class-level @BeanType(factory) if present. public class MyBean { @BeanProp(factory=ItemChannelFactory.class, elementType=Item.class) public BeanChannel<Item> getItems() { ... } }

info @BeanProp and @Name annotations are automatically inherited when bean property methods (getters, setters, extraKeys) are overridden in subclasses. This feature is particularly useful for fluent APIs where you want to override setters to change the return type without needing to re-annotate every method. // Parent class with annotated property public class Parent { private List<String> children; @BeanProp("c") // Custom property name public List<String> getChildren() { return children; } public Parent setChildren(List<String> children) { this.children = children; return this; } } // Child class with fluent setter override public class Child extends Parent { @Override public List<String> getChildren() { return super.getChildren(); } @Override public Child setChildren(List<String> children) { // Automatically inherits @BeanProp("c") from parent. // Property name remains "c" — no re-annotation needed. super.setChildren(children); return this; // Return type changed for fluent chaining } } If you want to override a method and use a different property name, re-annotate explicitly: public class Child extends Parent { @Override @BeanProp("childList") // Explicit new name takes precedence public Child setChildren(List<String> children) { super.setChildren(children); return this; } } See Also @BeanType Annotation - Class-level bean-modeling annotation. Java Beans Support - Overview of bean property detection.

In addition to the bean type name support, Juneau provides simplified support for bean subtypes via the @Marshalled(dictionary=…) attribute declared on a parent bean class. Bean subtypes are similar in concept to bean type names, with two convenience differences: You declare the list of possible subclasses through an annotation on the parent bean class, rather than registering them individually. You do not need to register the subtype classes on the bean dictionary of the parser — the parser discovers them from the parent class's dictionary.

In the following example, the abstract superclass declares its two concrete subclasses, and each subclass declares its _type name: // Abstract superclass declares its subtypes. @Marshalled( dictionary={A1.class, A2.class} ) public abstract class A { public String f0 = "f0"; } // Subclass 1 @Marshalled(typeName="A1") public class A1 extends A { public String f1; } // Subclass 2 @Marshalled(typeName="A2") public class A2 extends A { public String f2; } When serialized, the concrete subtype is emitted as a virtual _type property: A1 object = new A1(); object.f1 = "f1"; String json = Json5.of(object); assertEquals("{_type:'A1',f1:'f1',f0:'f0'}", json); When parsed back into the abstract type, the _type property is used to instantiate the correct concrete subclass: A object = Json.to(json, A.class); assertTrue(object instanceof A1);
The _type property name is the default type-discriminator key. It can be changed globally via MarshallingContext.Builder.typePropertyName(String), or per-class via @Marshalled(typePropertyName=…).
Bean Dictionaries — the general bean-dictionary mechanism. @Marshalled(typeName) Annotation — declaring type names.

The @BeanType annotation is applied to classes to control bean introspection and modeling. This is the model-side annotation in juneau-commons. It carries the attributes that describe the bean itself — which properties to include or exclude, how to name them, what stop class to use, and so on. Format-side concerns (wire format, type names, dictionary, interceptors, implementation class) live on @Marshalled in juneau-marshall. This split lets a class participate in the bean model without dragging in any marshalling concerns, and lets the bean-modeling layer live in juneau-commons independent of juneau-marshall. Migration Prior to the 10.0 refactor, @BeanType's members were part of @Marshalled. @BeanType (in org.apache.juneau.commons.bean) is now the correct annotation for all bean-modeling attributes listed below. The old @Bean annotation has been removed.

Bean property inclusion and ordering can be controlled using @BeanType(properties|p). // Address class with only street/city/state properties (in that order). // All other properties are ignored. @BeanType(properties="street,city,state") public class Address { ... } p is a shortened synonym for properties: @BeanType(p="street,city,state") public class Address { ... }

Bean properties can be excluded using @BeanType(excludeProperties|xp). // Address class with all properties except city and state. @BeanType(excludeProperties="city,state") public class Address { ... } xp is a shortened synonym for excludeProperties: @BeanType(xp="city,state") public class Address { ... } Java Records Excluding record components is not supported during parsing. Because records are immutable, all components must be provided to the canonical constructor. Excluded components will be omitted from serialization output, but the parser will be unable to instantiate the record if the excluded component values are missing from the input.

Specifies one or more properties that are serialized normally but silently ignored during parsing. // city and state are serialized but not parsed. @BeanType(readOnlyProperties="city,state") public class Address { ... } ro is a shortened synonym for readOnlyProperties.

Specifies one or more properties that are parsed normally but silently ignored during serialization. // city and state are parsed but not serialized. @BeanType(writeOnlyProperties="city,state") public class Address { ... } wo is a shortened synonym for writeOnlyProperties.

Bean properties are sorted alphabetically by default. To opt a specific bean out of this default sorting, use @BeanType(unsorted): // Opt this bean out of the default alphabetical property ordering. @BeanType(unsorted=true) public class MyBean { ... } Sorting can also be disabled globally for all beans via MarshallingContext.Builder.unsortedProperties(): WriterSerializer serializer = JsonSerializer .create() .unsortedProperties() // disable sorting for all beans .build(); Or for individual classes without modifying the bean class itself: WriterSerializer serializer = JsonSerializer .create() .unsortedProperties(MyBean.class) // disable sorting for MyBean only .build();

The @BeanType(propertyNamer) annotation is used to provide customized naming of properties. Property namers transform bean property names from standard form to some other form. For example, PropertyNamerDLC converts property names to dashed-lowercase, and these will be used as attribute names in JSON and element names in XML. // Define a class with dashed-lowercase property names. @BeanType(propertyNamer=PropertyNamerDLC.class) public class MyBean { ... }

The @BeanType(interfaceClass) annotation limits the properties of a bean to those declared on a specific interface class. When specified, only the list of properties defined on the interface class will be used during serialization. Additional properties on subclasses will be ignored. // Parent class @BeanType(interfaceClass=A.class) public abstract class A { public String f0 = "f0"; } // Child class public class A1 extends A { public String f1 = "f1"; } A1 a1 = new A1(); String result = Json5.of(a1); assertEquals("{f0:'f0'}", result); // Note f1 is not serialized. Note that this annotation can be used on the parent class so that it filters to all child classes. Or can be set individually on the child classes.

The @BeanType(stopClass) annotation limits which properties are included by halting class hierarchy traversal. It is identical in purpose to the stop class specified by Introspector.getBeanInfo(Class,Class). Any properties in the stop class or in its base classes will be ignored during analysis. For example, in the following class hierarchy, instances of C3 will include property p3 but not p1 or p2: public class C1 { public int getP1(); } public class C2 extends C1 { public int getP2(); } @BeanType(stopClass=C2.class) public class C3 extends C2 { public int getP3(); }

When true, fluent setters are detected as writable bean properties. @BeanType(findFluentSetters=true) public class MyBean { public int getId() { ... } public MyBean id(int id) { ... } // detected as fluent setter for "id" } Fluent setters must be public, non-static, take exactly one parameter, and return the bean itself.

Specifies a BeanFactory class to use for instantiating the bean instead of relying on a no-arg constructor or static getInstance() method. @BeanType(factory=MyBeanFactory.class) public class MyBean { ... }

Attributes that affect wire format — type names, dictionary, interceptors, implementation class, examples, and locale/timezone formats — live on @Marshalled (per-class) and @MarshalledConfig (bulk application via on/onClass on REST classes and methods). The interceptor attribute on @Marshalled can be used to intercept and modify bean getter and setter calls at the marshalling layer: // Interceptor that strips out sensitive information on Address beans. public class AddressInterceptor extends BeanInterceptor<Address> { @Override public Object readProperty(Address bean, String name, Object value) { if ("taxInfo".equals(name)) return "redacted"; return value; } @Override public Object writeProperty(Address bean, String name, Object value) { if ("taxInfo".equals(name) && "redacted".equals(value)) return TaxInfoUtils.lookup(bean.getStreet(), bean.getCity(), bean.getState()); return value; } } // Register interceptor on bean class. @Marshalled(interceptor=AddressInterceptor.class) public class Address { public String getTaxInfo() {...} public void setTaxInfo(String value) {...} }

When using @BeanType with Java records, note the following: @BeanType(properties) can be used to control property order, but all record components should be included. Omitting components will prevent parsing since all components must be provided to the canonical constructor. @BeanType(excludeProperties) will exclude components from serialization output, but excluded components will cause parsing to fail if their values are missing from the input. @BeanType(readOnlyProperties) will cause parsing to fail for the same reason. If you need to omit components during parsing, use @BeanCtor with a non-canonical constructor that provides defaults for the omitted components. See Also Java Beans Support - Overview of bean property detection. Java Records Support - Full documentation on Java records support.
The following guidelines help you get the most out of the Juneau marshalling APIs in terms of performance and maintainability.

Serializers and parsers are immutable and thread-safe, and they maintain internal caches of bean metadata. Reusing a single instance across requests (rather than rebuilding one per call) lets those caches do their job and avoids the cost of re-analyzing the same bean classes repeatedly. // Good — build once, reuse everywhere (e.g. a static field or injected singleton). static final JsonSerializer SERIALIZER = JsonSerializer.create().ws().build(); String json = SERIALIZER.write(myBean); The predefined DEFAULT instances (JsonSerializer.DEFAULT, JsonParser.DEFAULT, …) are already reusable singletons — prefer them when you don't need custom settings. When you do need a variant, use copy() on an existing instance so the derived instance shares the same construction path.

In general, JSON serialization and parsing is roughly 20% faster than XML, and JSON output is more compact. MessagePack is the fastest and most compact of the built-in formats — prefer it for high-throughput or bandwidth-sensitive machine-to-machine traffic where human readability isn't required. RDF has very different performance characteristics from the core marshallers — node traversal in RDF models is inefficient, so building tree structures out of large RDF graphs is comparatively slow. RDF is documented separately in the RDF section; the guidance on this page applies to the core juneau-marshall formats.
documents.s: Choose the right format for the job

documents.t: The MarshallingTraverseContext.Builder.detectRecursions() option adds a performance penalty of around 20% because every object on the traversal stack has to be checked for cycles. Enable it only when serializing models that can actually contain recursive references. See Non-Tree Models and Recursion Detection. The MarshallingContext.Builder.validateSchema() option validates bean property values against their @Schema-declared constraints during parsing and serialization. This adds per-property validation overhead and is disabled by default — turn it on only on the boundaries where you actually need input/output validation (typically inbound parsing), not on every internal marshalling operation.
documents.s: Enable optional features only when needed

documents.t: The Parser methods that take a ClassMeta parameter are slightly faster than the overloads that take a Class or Object, because the latter must perform a hash lookup to resolve the target type to its ClassMeta. On tight loops that repeatedly parse the same type, resolve the ClassMeta once (via BeanContext.getClassMeta(...)) and reuse it.
documents.s: Prefer ClassMeta parse overloads on hot paths

documents.t: For large collections or continuous feeds, don't build a giant in-memory POJO and serialize it in one shot. Juneau's streaming APIs let you emit or consume records one at a time with a bounded memory footprint — see Token & Record Streaming and Large-Dataset Streaming.
documents.s: Stream large datasets instead of buffering

documents.t: The MarshallUtils class provides concise static shortcuts (json(...), xml(...), msgPack(...), …) that are ideal for one-off serialization/parsing, tests, and scripts — especially with static imports. Because they delegate to the shared DEFAULT marshaller instances, they carry no extra construction cost. Reach for an explicit serializer/parser instance instead when you need custom settings (whitespace, quotes, swaps, dictionaries, etc.), since MarshallUtils always uses default configuration.
Marshallers — the marshaller API overview. Serializers and Parsers Token & Record Streaming

Juneau supports converting arbitrary POJOs to and from BSON (Binary JSON) using native serializers and parsers. BSON is the binary serialization format used by MongoDB, extending JSON with typed integers (int32/int64), native datetime, decimal128, and binary data. It uses little-endian byte order and length-prefixed documents. The BsonSerializer converts POJOs directly to BSON format, and the BsonParser creates POJOs directly from BSON. BSON support is included in juneau-marshall. Maven <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency>

// A simple bean public class Person { public String name; public int age; public Person() {} public Person(String name, int age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; } } // Serialize a bean to BSON Person alice = new Person("Alice", 30); byte[] bson = Bson.of(alice); // Parse BSON into a bean Person parsed = Bson.to(bson, Person.class);

// Parse BSON into a bean Person p = Bson.to(bson, Person.class); // Parse into a map JsonMap map = Bson.to(bson, JsonMap.class); // Parse into a typed map Map<String, Object> m = Bson.to(bson, Map.class, String.class, Object.class); // Parse a list (root must be document; use wrapped {"value": [...]} for standalone arrays) List<Person> people = Bson.to(bson, List.class, Person.class);

// Use the default serializer byte[] bson = BsonSerializer.DEFAULT.write(someObject); // Use the marshaller for convenience byte[] bson = Bson.of(someObject); // Custom serializer: write dates as ISO 8601 strings instead of BSON datetime BsonSerializer s = BsonSerializer.create().writeDatesAsDatetime(false).build(); byte[] bson = s.write(someObject);

Java Type BSON Type Notes Bean, Map Document (0x03) Nested structures Collection, array Array (0x04) Document with "0", "1", ... keys String, Enum String (0x02) int, short, byte Int32 (0x10) 4 bytes little-endian long Int64 (0x12) 8 bytes little-endian float, double Double (0x01) IEEE 754 Date, Calendar, Instant Datetime (0x09) When writeDatesAsDatetime=true Duration String ISO 8601 duration byte[] Binary (0x05) Subtype 0x00 BigDecimal, BigInteger Decimal128 (0x13) IEEE 754-2008 null Null (0x0A) Local java.time types with no instant (LocalDate, LocalDateTime, LocalTime, Year, etc.) are always written as ISO 8601 strings. BSON datetime has millisecond resolution, so sub-millisecond precision of Instant, OffsetDateTime and ZonedDateTime is truncated when writeDatesAsDatetime is true; use writeDatesAsDatetime(false) for lossless ISO 8601 output. BigDecimal / BigInteger values outside the Decimal128 range (34 significant digits, exponent -6176..6111) cannot be represented and fail with a SerializeException.

Instance Description BsonSerializer.DEFAULT / BsonParser.DEFAULT Default settings; raw BSON bytes. BsonSerializer.DEFAULT_SPACED_HEX / BsonParser.DEFAULT_SPACED_HEX binaryFormat(SPACED_HEX). BsonSerializer.DEFAULT_BASE64 / BsonParser.DEFAULT_BASE64 binaryFormat(BASE64). The binary format setting only affects the stream-to-string conveniences (such as writeToString); the serializer always emits native BSON bytes from write(...).

Configured through BsonSerializer.create() (see BsonSerializer.Builder). Builder method Default Description addBeanTypesBson(boolean) false Add _type properties to beans whose type cannot be inferred through reflection. writeDatesAsDatetime(boolean) true Write Date / Calendar / Instant as BSON datetime (0x09); when false, write ISO 8601 strings. nullKeyString(String) "<NULL>" Field name used for null map keys (BSON field names cannot be null). binaryFormat(BinaryFormat) NOT_SET Text rendering (SPACED_HEX, HEX, BASE64, BASE64_URL) used by string conveniences. The defaults can also be set with the BsonSerializer.addBeanTypesBson, BsonSerializer.nullKeyString and BsonSerializer.writeDatesAsDatetime environment settings.

Configured through BsonParser.create() (see BsonParser.Builder). Builder method Default Description nullKeyString(String) "<NULL>" A field with this name is stored with a null key in the target map. Must match the serializer value. trimStrings(boolean) false Trim whitespace from parsed string values (inherited from Parser). binaryFormat(BinaryFormat) NOT_SET Binary text-format hint (SPACED_HEX, HEX, BASE64, BASE64_URL); see BinaryFormat. BsonSerializer s = BsonSerializer.create() .writeDatesAsDatetime(false) .nullKeyString("~null~") .build(); BsonParser p = BsonParser.create().nullKeyString("~null~").build(); byte[] bson = s.write(someMap); Map<?,?> m = p.read(bson, Map.class);
Produces: application/bson Accepts: application/bson

// BSON support is included via BasicUniversalConfig (there is no dedicated BSON-only config interface). @Rest public class MyResource extends RestServlet implements BasicUniversalConfig { ... } // RestClient with BSON RestClient client = RestClient.create().uri("http://localhost:8080").bson().build(); byte[] response = client.get("/api/data").bson().run().body();

Root must be a document: BSON requires a top-level document. Standalone scalars, collections, and arrays are wrapped as {value: x}. Map keys must be strings: Non-string keys use toString(). Null keys use a configurable placeholder. ObjectId is read-only: BSON ObjectId (0x07) is parsed as a 24-character hex string; Juneau does not generate ObjectIds. Deprecated types skipped: Undefined, DBPointer, Symbol, JS with Scope are silently skipped during parsing. MongoDB-internal types unsupported: JavaScript, Timestamp, MinKey, MaxKey are not supported.

@BsonConfig sets serializer/parser properties on a REST class or method (see Context Annotations). Attributes are strings: Attribute Description addBeanTypes Add _type properties to beans whose type can't be inferred through reflection (default false). writeDatesAsDatetime Write Date/Calendar/Instant as the BSON datetime type (0x09); if false, write ISO-8601 strings. maxLength Maximum wire-declared length (bytes) for strings, binary payloads and document/array size prefixes when parsing; guards against malicious size prefixes. rank Ordering relative to other config annotations. @Rest @BsonConfig(writeDatesAsDatetime="true", maxLength="1048576") public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet { ... } @Bson is a class/method/field marker (its only attribute is description), and @BsonApply applies it to other classes/members via on()/onClass() (see Dynamically Applied Annotations). See Also BSON Specification for the full format definition. Marshallers for the marshaller API overview. MessagePack Basics for another binary JSON format.

This is the end-to-end tutorial for adding a page to an admin console built on Juneau: a resource that serves the chrome, a navigation tree, a sortable and searchable table backed by a server-side data endpoint, and a test that pins the page contract. The example is a pet inventory page; substitute your own bean. The reference pages cover each piece in depth. Read them when a step here raises a question.
