Admin-Console Chrome: directives, themes and the page contract. Rich Table Views: what a table card can do. DataTables Server-Side Processing and BeanQuery: the data endpoint.

The result looks like the petstore's pets page: the chrome's header and navigation around one table card fed by a server-side data endpoint. A console page is four cooperating parts: Part Provided by The chrome template (header, navigation, footer) <@console> and <@navigation> in one shared FreeMarker template. The page template (its cards) <@page> with one or more <@card> elements. The data endpoint A REST operation returning DataTablesResults<T>, backed by BeanQuery. The assets (CSS, JavaScript) The mixins ConsoleChromeMixin, ViewsMixin and DataTablesMixin. <@page> is the outermost directive in a page template. It captures its body (the cards), then includes the chrome template, which must contain <@console>. The server never renders the chrome as HTML; it writes a JSON page contract into the document and the shell script juneau-console.js draws the header, navigation, cards and footer in the browser.

<dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-console-freemarker</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-console-views</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-console-datatables</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> The module table in Admin-Console Chrome explains what each one adds. juneau-console-datatables is optional, but you need it for any server-mode table, which is the common case. juneau-console-datatables also brings in the jQuery and DataTables WebJars.

The host resource composes every asset-serving mixin. Each one serves scripts and stylesheets relative to the resource's own path, so all of them must be on the resource that serves the page. @Rest( path="/console", mixins={ FreemarkerMixin.class, // renders .ftlh views ConsoleChromeMixin.class, // chrome.css, theme CSS, juneau-console.js ViewsMixin.class, // the views toolkit scripts and CSS DataTablesMixin.class, // juneau-datatables.js WebJarsMixin.class // /webjars/*: jQuery and DataTables } ) public class PetConsole extends BasicRestServlet { @Bean public FreemarkerMixin freemarker() { // Typed as FreemarkerMixin: the return type is load-bearing. return ConsoleFreemarkerMixin.create() .basePath("/templates/") .chromeTemplate("console/chrome.ftlh") .build(); } @RestGet(path="/pets") public View pets() { return FreemarkerView.of("console/pets.ftlh"); } } Compose DataTablesMixin and WebJarsMixin A datatables card loads juneau-datatables.js (served by DataTablesMixin) and the jQuery and DataTables files (served by WebJarsMixin) before juneau-views.js. If either mixin is missing, those URLs 404 and the table fails loudly in the browser console. See Card Asset Dependencies. To set a theme for the whole console, build the mixin with ConsoleChromeMixin.create().theme("gray").build(), or pick one per page with <@console theme="gray">.
documents.s: Step 2: The host resource and its mixins

documents.t: One template holds the chrome and is shared by every page. It contains <@console> exactly once, with the navigation tree and <@main/>, which marks where each page's cards go. <#-- templates/console/chrome.ftlh --> <@console brand="Pet Store Console" chrome="true"> <@navigation> <@node id="catalog" label="Catalog" href="/console/pets"/> <@node id="orders" label="Orders" href="/console/orders"/> <@node id="admin" label="Admin" visible=user.admin> <@node id="users" label="Users" href="/console/users"/> </@node> </@navigation> <@main/> <@footer text="Pet Store"/> </@console> Node ids must match ^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_-]{0,63}$. Set visible= to a boolean to gate a node on a permission check. The page names its active node with <@page tab="catalog">.

<#-- templates/console/pets.ftlh --> <@page tab="catalog" toolkit="views"> <@card type="html">

Pets

<@card type="datatables" id="pets" title="Inventory"> { dataUrl: '/console/pets/data', dataMode: 'server', defaultOrder: [[0, 'asc']], columns: [ { key: 'name', label: 'Name', searchType: 'text' }, { key: 'status', label: 'Status', searchType: 'enum' }, { key: 'price', label: 'Price', searchType: 'numeric' } ] } toolkit="views" asks for the views toolkit pack. A datatables card also loads jQuery, DataTables and the glue, without any toolkit= entry. A datatables card requires an id, and its body is a JSON5 catalog with dataUrl and columns. Do not write a contract version in the catalog; the chrome stamps the current one. src= is the alternative to a body: it points the card at a resource instead of carrying inline content. The body is a JSON5 catalog only. A bare-URL body is rejected (E-25). The reserved card types are html, datatables, terminal-view, terminal, chart and job-log. See Chart Cards and Job-Log Card. Besides dataUrl and columns, the chrome passes these catalog keys through: copyLink, rowActions, rowClassRules and pausePollingWhileEditing onto the view, and selection and bulk onto the slot. See Catalog and Columns for every catalog key, the search types and the operator sets. Adopters can add their own card types. On the server, implement a CardTypeHandler and register it through ConsoleFreemarkerMixin.Builder.cardType(...) or META-INF/services. In the browser, call JuneauConsole.registerCard(type, {render}), or push onto window.JuneauConsoleCards before the shell loads. A PageSpec.card(...) card of your type runs the same handler: the card's body map (or the markup passed to card(spec, markup)) is the authored body, so the handler validates it and shapes the fragment as it does for <@card>, and a bad body fails the render with the same message.
documents.s: Step 4: The page template with a table card

documents.t: The table's dataUrl points at a REST operation that takes the DataTables request and returns results. It runs the request through BeanQuery. private final InMemoryBeanQueryContext<Pet> ctx = InMemoryBeanQueryContext.create(Pet.class).build(); @RestPost(path="/pets/data", parsers=JsonParser.class) public DataTablesResults<Pet> petData(@Content DataTablesRequest req) { try (var s = ctx.getSession(petService.all())) { return DataTablesQuery.run(req, s); } } Restrict the operation to JSON with parsers=JsonParser.class. DataTablesQuery.toBeanQuery lets you add a guard, such as a tenant filter, before the query runs. The full contract is in DataTables Server-Side Processing; the query language is in BeanQuery. Because the table posts JSON, the state-changing checks of the loopback boundary apply if you use it; see Security Model.

You do not write the script tags. The parts of the order you can rely on: The theme stylesheet comes first, then the CSS of any library packs, then css= stylesheets from <@page>, then the toolkit CSS and any <@theme> token overrides. Library packs that the cards need (for a datatables card: jQuery, DataTables, then the glue) load first. The toolkit pack scripts then load in the pack's fixed order: renders, icons, search, pagestate, urlstate (shareable-URL state and the View Settings Copy link button), ribbon, views, config, regions, helpers. Full list on JavaScript API. Any init= scripts from <@page> load after the toolkit scripts, in the order given, and <@scripts phase="after-toolkit"> content is placed immediately after the toolkit scripts. The console shell, juneau-console.js, mounts the cards from the page contract. It hands a datatables card to JuneauViews.regions.mount on DOMContentLoaded, so the views scripts may load after it. The load order is a contract: juneau-views.js must come before juneau-regions.js, and the library packs load before the toolkit. If you add your own scripts, list them in init= so they land after the toolkit.
documents.s: Step 6: What the page loads, and in what order

documents.t: Because the chrome exists only as the contract, assert on the contract rather than on rendered HTML. PageContractAssert lives in org.apache.juneau.console.test and has no JUnit dependency. import static org.apache.juneau.console.test.PageContractAssert.*; @Test void petsPage() throws Exception { var html = client.get("/pets").run().getContent().asString(); assertPage(html) .isValid() .hasActiveNav("catalog") .hasCard("pets", "datatables"); } Also lint your templates without rendering them: var findings = ConsoleTemplateValidator.create() .templateRoot(Path.of("src/main/resources/templates")) .chromeTemplate("console/chrome.ftlh") .validateAll(); assertTrue(findings.isEmpty(), findings::toString); Set ConsoleFreemarkerMixin.create().devMode(true) while developing to validate every rendered contract against the schema.

A template mistake fails the render with an HTTP 500 and a message naming the directive and the fix. The usual ones: Symptom Cause 500, "<@card type=\"datatables\"> requires 'dataUrl' and 'columns'" The catalog is missing one of them. 500 naming the known paths <@page tab=...> names a node that is not in the navigation. 500, duplicate card id Two cards share an id. Blank table and a console warning about the DataTables glue The host does not compose DataTablesMixin or WebJarsMixin. .jc-console-error banner in the browser The contract failed a check in the shell, such as an unsupported page contractVersion or a missing template.

Add row actions, selection and bulk mutation: Row Actions and Bulk Mutation. Add row-detail panels or card bodies drawn by a function: Regions. Let users save and share table layouts: View Settings and Shareable Links. Restyle the console: the theme and token sections of Admin-Console Chrome.

The following URL parameters have special meaning and can be passed in through the URL of the request: GET Parameter Description &plainText=true Response will always be Content-Type: text/plain and the returned text will be human-readable (WriterSerializer.Builder.useWhitespace() enabled). Useful for debugging. &method=X Overload the HTTP method as a GET parameter (e.g. OPTIONS or HEAD). The name is matched case-insensitively and read from the query string only. On a safe request (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE) the override is honored only for another safe method or an operation declared @RestOp(read=true); anything else is refused with 405. On a POST any admitted method is honored. Must be enabled via @Rest(allowedMethodParams) setting. &Header-Name=headerValue Specify a header value as a GET parameter (e.g. &Accept=text/json). Must be enabled via @Rest(allowedHeaderParams) setting. &content=X Pass in the HTTP body content on PUT and POST methods as a UON-encoded GET parameter (e.g. ?content=(name='John%20Smith',age=45)). Honored on PUT/POST only. Can be disabled via @Rest(disableContentParam) setting. &x-response-headers=X Pass-through headers to the response. Must be a UON-encoded map of key-value pairs. &juneauSerializerOptions=X Override serializer session options for this request. Must be a UON-encoded map; keys must be in the @Rest(allowedSerializerOptions) allowlist or the request fails with 400 Bad Request. &juneauParserOptions=X Override parser session options for this request. Must be a UON-encoded map; keys must be in the @Rest(allowedParserOptions) allowlist or the request fails with 400 Bad Request. note Earlier releases documented &debug=true and &noTrace=true URL parameters. These no longer exist. Request debugging is now driven by the JUL logger level (see Logging / Debugging), and the /echo endpoint must be enabled explicitly via EchoMixin.

Juneau serializers treat instances of Readers and InputStreams special by simply serializing their contents directly to the output stream or writer. This allows you to embed fully customized serializer output. public class MyBean { // A bean property that produces raw JSON. public Reader f1 = new StringReader("{'foo':'bar'}"); } // Produces "{f1:{'foo':'bar'}}" String json = Json5.of(new MyBean()); Note that if you're serializing Readers and InputStreams, it's up to you to make sure you're producing valid output (in this case JSON). A more typical scenario where this is useful is by using swaps to convert POJOs to Readers whose contents are determined via the MarshallingSession.getMediaType() method. In the following example, we're customizing the JSON output for a particular bean type but leaving all other renditions as-is: @Swap(MyBeanSwapSometimes.class) public class MyBean {...} // A swap that produces specialized output for JSON but default serialization for // all other media types. public class MyBeanSwapSometimes extends ObjectSwap { public Object swap(MarshallingSession session, MyPojo object) throws Exception { MediaType mediaType = session.getMediaType(); if (mediaType.hasSubType("json")) return new StringReader("{myPojo:'foobar'}"); // Custom JSON output return object; // Otherwise serialize it as a normal bean } } warning Due to the nature of the RDF serializers, Readers and InputStreams are serialized as literals, not as RDF text. This is due to the fact that the RDF serializers use a DOM for serialization so we don't have access to the underlying stream.

A console card can need scripts and stylesheets beyond the views toolkit. A datatables card needs jQuery, DataTables and Juneau's glue script. The card declares that need, and <@page> loads each asset once, in dependency order, after the body has rendered.

A toolkit pack is a named list of CSS and JS assets. A pack can depend on other packs, and it has a kind: VENDOR packs are libraries and their glue. Their CSS comes before the page css=, and their JS comes before every runtime script. RUNTIME packs are Juneau UI runtimes. They keep the position the views pack always had. Pack Kind Loads Depends on jquery VENDOR jquery.min.js (WebJar org.webjars:jquery) datatables VENDOR dataTables.min.js, dataTables.dataTables.min.css (npm WebJars datatables.net, datatables.net-dt) jquery datatables-glue VENDOR juneau-datatables.js (served by DataTablesMixin) datatables datatables-buttons VENDOR dataTables.buttons.min.js, buttons.html5.min.js, buttons.dataTables.min.css datatables views RUNTIME the views runtime calendar RUNTIME juneau-calendar.js, juneau-calendar.css xterm VENDOR xterm.js, xterm.css (npm WebJar @xterm/xterm) terminal RUNTIME juneau-terminal.js, juneau-terminal.css (served by TerminalMixin) views, xterm charts RUNTIME juneau-charts.js (served by ConsoleChromeMixin) joblog RUNTIME juneau-joblog.js (served by ConsoleChromeMixin) datatables-buttons gives copy and CSV export. Excel and PDF export need JSZip and pdfmake, which aren't included; register your own pack for them (below).

<@page> loads the packs in toolkit=, plus the packs its cards require: Card Requires type="datatables" datatables-glue, plus joblog when its detail.region is a job-log region type="html" nothing type="terminal-view" nothing extra (its runtime ships in the views pack) type="terminal" terminal (which pulls in views and xterm) type="chart" charts type="job-log" joblog A card adds more with requires=: <@card type="datatables" id="rel" requires="datatables-buttons">{ ... }</@card> A card type can also require packs from the card's body: a CardTypeHandler overrides requiredPacks(JsonMap body) (empty by default), and the page unions what it returns with the type's packs and requires=. That is how a datatables card with a job-log detail region gets joblog without a requires=. requires= takes a comma-separated string or a sequence. An unknown pack name fails the render with a 500 that names the card. Each pack loads after the packs it depends on, and each asset loads once, however many cards need it. Markup outside a card records nothing. jcHasToolkit reports only toolkit=.

Compose WebJarsMixin (from juneau-rest-server) into the resource that serves the page. It serves /webjars/* from the classpath with a one-year immutable Cache-Control, and the URLs carry the WebJar version. juneau-console-datatables brings the WebJars in as dependencies. @Rest(mixins={FreemarkerMixin.class, ViewsMixin.class, DataTablesMixin.class, WebJarsMixin.class}) public class PetConsole extends BasicRestServlet { ... } If the host doesn't compose WebJarsMixin, the library URLs 404 and the table doesn't start.

All of this is on ConsoleFreemarkerMixin.Builder, and build() checks it: an unknown pack name, a cycle, or a VENDOR pack that depends on a RUNTIME pack fails the build. ConsoleFreemarkerMixin.create() .registerToolkitPack(ToolkitPack.create("datatables-export") .js("/app/jszip.min.js", "/app/pdfmake.min.js", "/app/vfs_fonts.js") .dependsOn("datatables-buttons") .kind(ToolkitPack.Kind.VENDOR) .resolver((req, path) -> req.getUriResolver().resolve("servlet:" + path)) .build()) .cardRequires("datatables", "datatables-export") // every datatables card .providedPacks("jquery") // the chrome already loads jQuery .build(); registerToolkitPack(ToolkitPack) adds a pack. A pack with a built-in name replaces it, including its dependencies, so registerToolkitPack(ToolkitPack.create("datatables")...) swaps in your own DataTables build. The (name, css, js) form registers a RUNTIME pack with no dependencies. cardRequires(type, packs...) adds packs to every card of a type. providedPacks(names...) names packs your chrome already loads. A provided pack loads nothing; its dependencies still load unless they're provided too. If a page already loads a file through init= or css=, a pack asset with the same file name is skipped, and the log gets a WARN naming the template. A copy loaded through init= is not a bridge: it is skipped only when the file name matches, and the pack's other assets still load. An app that has its own copies of the libraries names the packs in providedPacks(...), or mounts WebJarsMixin and lets the packs load them.

<@head phase="before-page-css">, then VENDOR CSS, then the page css=, then RUNTIME CSS. juneau-console.js, then VENDOR JS (for a datatables card: jQuery, DataTables, juneau-datatables.js), then RUNTIME JS, then <@scripts phase="after-toolkit">, then init=.
Building a Console Page Admin-Console Chrome Rich Table Views DataTables Server-Side Processing

Juneau supports converting arbitrary POJOs to and from CBOR (Concise Binary Object Representation) per RFC 8949 using native serializers and parsers. CBOR is a compact binary format designed for extremely small code size, very small message size, and extensibility. It is widely used in IoT, constrained environments, COSE (CBOR Object Signing and Encryption), and WebAuthn. The CborSerializer converts POJOs directly to CBOR format, and the CborParser creates POJOs directly from CBOR. CBOR shares the same data model as JSON: maps, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. Compared to MsgPack, CBOR follows a different specification (RFC 8949) with different encoding rules and a larger ecosystem (IETF standards, COSE, WebAuthn). CBOR support is included in juneau-marshall. Maven <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency>

// A simple bean public class Person { public String name; public int age; public Person() {} public Person(String name, int age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; } } // Serialize a bean to CBOR Person alice = new Person("Alice", 30); byte[] cbor = Cbor.of(alice); // Parse CBOR into a bean Person parsed = Cbor.to(cbor, Person.class);

// Parse CBOR into a bean Person p = Cbor.to(cbor, Person.class); // Parse into a map JsonMap map = Cbor.to(cbor, JsonMap.class); // Parse from InputStream try (InputStream is = new FileInputStream("data.cbor")) { Person p = Cbor.to(is, Person.class); }

// Use the default serializer byte[] cbor = CborSerializer.DEFAULT.write(someObject); // Use the marshaller for convenience byte[] cbor = Cbor.of(someObject); // Serialize to OutputStream try (OutputStream os = new FileOutputStream("data.cbor")) { Cbor.of(someObject, os); }

Java Type CBOR Encoding Notes Bean, Map Map (major type 5) Nested structures Collection, array Array (major type 4) Definite-length String, Enum Text string (major type 3) UTF-8 int, long (positive) Unsigned integer (major type 0) Compact encoding int, long (negative) Negative integer (major type 1) -1-n encoding float Float32 (0xFA) IEEE 754 single double Float64 (0xFB) IEEE 754 double boolean Simple value 20/21 (0xF4/0xF5) null Simple value 22 (0xF6) byte[] Byte string (major type 2) Native binary Date, Instant, etc. Text string ISO 8601 Duration Text string ISO 8601 duration

For debugging and text-based transport, CBOR provides SpacedHex and Base64 variants: // Spaced-hex output: "A2 61 78 01 61 79 02" String hex = CborSerializer.SpacedHex.DEFAULT.write(bean); JsonMap parsed = CborParser.SpacedHex.DEFAULT.read(hex, JsonMap.class); // Base64 output String b64 = CborSerializer.Base64.DEFAULT.write(bean); JsonMap parsed = CborParser.Base64.DEFAULT.read(b64, JsonMap.class);
Produces: application/cbor Accepts: application/cbor
// CBOR support is included via BasicUniversalConfig (there is no dedicated CBOR-only config interface). @Rest public class MyResource extends RestServlet implements BasicUniversalConfig { ... }

BigInteger/BigDecimal: Cast to long/double; precision loss for values exceeding range. Use ObjectSwap for string serialization if needed. Indefinite-length: Parser does not support indefinite-length arrays/maps from external producers. Half-precision float: Serializer always uses float32/float64; parser accepts float16 from external producers. Semantic tags: Parser ignores tag numbers; tagged value is parsed normally. Tag output deferred to future release.

CBOR is a FULL-capability streaming format. The CborParser implements TokenReadable and ArrayRecordReadable; the CborSerializer implements TokenWritable and ArrayRecordWritable. This means you can read and write CBOR using fine-grained structural token cursors in O(1) memory, without materializing the entire document. // Read CBOR tokens one at a time try (TokenReader r = CborParser.DEFAULT.readTokens(cborBytes)) { while (r.next() != TokenType.END_OF_STREAM) { // inspect r.getCurrentToken(), r.getString(), etc. } } // Write CBOR tokens directly ByteArrayOutputStream baos = new ByteArrayOutputStream(); try (TokenWriter w = CborSerializer.DEFAULT.writeTokens(baos)) { w.startObject(); w.fieldName("name"); w.string("Alice"); w.endObject(); } See Token-Streaming Basics for the full capability matrix and API overview, Token Streaming for the TokenReader/TokenWriter API, and Array-Record Streaming for element-by-element streaming over top-level arrays (CBOR uses indefinite-length arrays on write, so the array-record writer needs no element count).

@CborConfig sets serializer/parser properties on a REST class or method (see Context Annotations). Attributes are strings: Attribute Description addBeanTypes Add _type properties to beans whose type can't be inferred through reflection (default false). useTags Use CBOR semantic tags for dates and other typed values (default false). maxLength Maximum wire-declared length for byte/text strings and array/map element counts when parsing. rank Ordering relative to other config annotations. @Rest @CborConfig(useTags="true", maxLength="1048576") public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet { ... } @Cbor is a class/method/field marker (its only attribute is description), and @CborApply applies it to other classes/members via on()/onClass() (see Dynamically Applied Annotations).
RFC 8949 (CBOR) Cbor marshaller org.apache.juneau.marshall.cbor package

A chart card draws a line, bar or donut chart from rows of JSON. Juneau draws it as inline SVG with no third-party chart library. The script is juneau-charts.js, and <@page> loads it for you when a page has a chart card.

<@card type="chart" id="orders-trend" title="Orders" src="/console/store/stats/daily"> { kind: 'line', x: { field: 'day', label: 'Day' }, series: [ { field: 'placed', label: 'Placed' }, { field: 'delivered', label: 'Delivered', tone: 'ok' } ] } </@card> The endpoint returns an array of flat rows, or an object with a rows array: [ { "day": "Mon", "placed": 3, "delivered": 1 }, { "day": "Tue", "placed": 5, "delivered": 2 } ] From Java, build the same card with ChartDef: page.card(ChartDef.line("orders-trend").title("Orders").src("/console/store/stats/daily") .x("day", null, "Day") .series("placed", "Placed") .series("delivered", "Delivered", "ok") .toCardSpec());

Kind Needs Options line x, one or more series y, legend, height bar x, one or more series stacked, orientation: 'horizontal', y, legend, height donut label, value center ('total' or literal text) x is a field name, or { field, type, label } where type is category, time or number. A series is a field name, or { field, label, tone }. A tone is danger, ok or warning, or a palette index from 1 to 8; colors come from the --jc-chart-1 to --jc-chart-8 theme properties when a theme sets them. A donut folds two or more slices under 2% into one "Other" slice.

Key Meaning src= / data Exactly one. data is an inline array of rows. refreshMs Re-fetch src= every N ms, at least 5000; needs src= (inline data never refreshes). If a refresh fetch fails, the last chart stays, dimmed, and polling continues. height Plot height in pixels, at least 120 (default 240). legend bottom (default), right or none. emptyText Shown when there are no rows (default "No data."). onClick.href A same-origin path template (no scheme, no // prefix, no .. segment); {field} is replaced with the clicked row's URL-encoded value. A cross-origin href fails the page in Java (ChartDef and the card check); if one still reaches the browser, juneau-charts.js logs E-JS-79 and ignores the click. Clicking a point, bar or slice fires a juneau:chart-click event with detail = { card, row, series } (series is null for the built-in kinds), whether or not onClick.href is set. (A donut's folded "Other" slice stands for several rows, so it doesn't click.)

A chart can follow a table on the same page through the params subscription role. The chart's src= carries a {token}, the subscription maps a field of the published payload to that token, and the chart re-fetches whenever the payload changes. A datatables card publishes filter:<id> with the search box text in search, so this chart follows the search box of the table changes: <@card type="datatables" id="changes" title="Changes"> { dataUrl: '/api/changes', columns: [ { key: 'id' }, { key: 'owner' } ] } </@card> <@card type="chart" id="byOwner" title="Open changes by owner" src="/api/changes/by-owner?q={q}" subscribes=[{"topic": "filter:changes", "as": "params", "map": {"q": "search"}}]> { kind: 'bar', x: 'owner', series: [ { field: 'open', label: 'Open' } ] } </@card> From Java, wire the card you get from toCardSpec(); ChartDef itself rejects subscribes because wiring is card-level: page.card(ChartDef.bar("byOwner").title("Open changes by owner").src("/api/changes/by-owner?q={q}") .x("owner").series("open", "Open") .toCardSpec() .subscribes(Subscription.to(Topics.filter("changes")).as("params").map("q", "search"))); Until the first payload arrives, the chart waits instead of fetching a URL with an unfilled {q}. params is the only role a chart accepts: a chart does not publish, and any other as: value on a chart subscription fails the page (E-44 in Java, E-JS-47 in the browser).

The chart is an SVG with role="img", or role="group" when the card is clickable (onClick.href is set, so the marks inside it are interactive). Either way it is labelled through aria-labelledby by a caption that summarizes it, for example "Line chart, 2 series, 7 points, Day from 'Mon' to 'Sun'", so a screen reader reads the summary once. The legend swatches are decorative, and the legend lists each series (or slice) by name. A Show data button (it becomes Hide data, and reports aria-expanded) reveals the same rows as a table, which is the accessible alternative to the drawing. Keyboard focus applies only when onClick.href is set. Then each point (line and bar) or slice (donut) is a focusable role="button" with a label such as "Mon: Placed 3, Delivered 1". On a line or bar chart the points form one tab stop and the arrow keys move between them; on a donut each slice is its own tab stop and the arrow keys do nothing. Enter or Space follows the link. Without onClick.href the marks are not focusable and not buttons; use the data table instead. If a refresh cannot redraw the chart (the renderer throws, or a series field has disappeared from the rows), the card shows the error once as an alert, polling stops, and the card fails. A refresh whose fetch fails keeps the last chart, dims it, and tries again on the next tick.

JuneauCharts.register("spark", function (plot, rows, card, c) { const svg = c.svg(plot); // draw with c.node(svg, tag, cls, attrs), c.scaleLinear(...), c.tone(series, i) return { update(rows) { /* redraw */ }, destroy() { /* clean up */ } }; }); A script that loads before juneau-charts.js can queue its kinds instead: (window.JuneauConsoleCharts = window.JuneauConsoleCharts || []).push(["spark", renderer]);. A kind name is lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter, at most 32 characters (^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,31}$); ChartDef and the card check reject any other name. A card whose kind isn't registered yet waits; if the kind still isn't there when the page has loaded, the card shows E-JS-60.

Code When E-JS-60 The card's kind is not registered. E-JS-62 The src= fetch failed. On a refresh the error is only logged and the last chart stays, dimmed. E-JS-63 A series field is missing from the rows. E-JS-64 A kind was registered twice. E-JS-75 refreshMs was below 5000; the minimum is used. E-JS-79 onClick.href resolved to a URL that isn't same-origin. E-JS-80 A kind's renderer threw. It is shown once; a failed refresh also stops polling. Java checks the card body when the page renders: a missing or malformed kind, both or neither of src= and data, a line or bar without x and a series, a series with no field, a donut without label and value, refreshMs below 5000 (or without src=), height below 120, and an onClick.href that isn't a same-origin path all fail the page.

Child Resources are REST servlets or objects that are linked to parent resources through the @Rest(children) annotation. Example /** Parent Resource */ @Rest( path="/parent", children={MyChildResource.class} ) public MyRootResources extends BasicRestServletGroup {...} /** Child Resource */ @Rest( path="/child" // Path relative to parent resource. ) // Note that we don't need to extend from RestServlet. public MyChildResource extends BasicRestResource {...} The path of the child resource gets appended to the path of the parent resource. So in the example above, the child resource is accessed through the URL /parent/child. One advantage of using child resources is that they do not need to be declared in the JEE web.xml file. Initialization of and access to the child resources occurs through the parent resource. Children can be nested arbitrary deep to create complex REST interfaces with a single top-level REST servlet. As explained earlier, child REST objects typically extend from BasicRestResource or BasicRestResourceGroup and not from one of the servlet classes. They also technically don't even need to extend from those classes and can instead just be a normal class annotated with the bare-minimum @Rest and @RestOp annotations.

In addition to declaring children statically via @Rest(children=…), parent resources that extend BasicRestServletGroup or BasicRestResourceGroup can add and remove child resources at runtime. This is useful for plug-in architectures, integration tests, and other scenarios where the set of mounted endpoints is not known ahead of time. The convenience methods on the group classes delegate to RestChildren, which holds children in a thread-safe, copy-on-write snapshot — reads on the request hot path are lock-free, while mutations are serialized through a write lock. Example @Rest(path="/root") public class MyServer extends BasicRestServletGroup {} @Rest(path="/alpha") public class AlphaChild extends BasicRestResource { @RestGet("/ping") public String ping() { return "alpha-pong"; } } var server = new MyServer(); // ... bootstrap into Jetty / Spring Boot / MockRestClient ... // Add by class — path is derived from the child's @Rest(path) annotation. server.addChild(AlphaChild.class); // Add by instance — useful when the child is hand-constructed or comes from a bean store. var beta = new BetaChild(); server.addChild(beta); // Add with an explicit path override. server.addChild("/gamma", new AlphaChild()); // Remove by path or by class. server.removeChild("/alpha"); server.removeChild(AlphaChild.class); // Inspect what is currently mounted. var keys = server.getChildResources().asMap().keySet();

Method Description addChild(Class<?>) Instantiate from the bean store (or via no-arg constructor) and mount at the child's @Rest(path). addChild(Object) Mount an existing instance at the child's @Rest(path). addChild(Object, boolean replace) Same as above but, when replace=true, atomically destroys any existing child mounted at the same path. addChild(String path, Object) Mount an existing instance at an explicit path, ignoring any @Rest(path) on the resource. addChild(String path, Object, boolean replace) Explicit-path variant with replace semantics. removeChild(String path) Remove the child mounted at the given path. Returns the removed RestContext (or null). removeChild(Class<?>) Remove the child whose resource is an instance of the given class. Returns the removed RestContext (or null). getChildResources() Returns the underlying RestChildren for direct inspection.

When a child is added, its @RestInit, @RestPostInit, and @RestPostInitChildFirst hooks run before addChild returns. When a child is removed, its @RestDestroy hooks run and the resource's Servlet.destroy() is invoked (if applicable) — including for any grandchildren mounted underneath. Mutations are atomic: route matching either sees the full pre-add state or the full post-add state, never a partially-mounted child. Adding a second child at the same path without replace=true throws IllegalStateException to prevent silent route shadowing.

By default, all children declared via @Rest(children=...) are constructed eagerly at parent startup. For resource trees with many rarely-touched children (admin panels, diagnostic endpoints, heavyweight integration bridges), this can add significant startup cost. The 10.0 lazy-children feature defers construction until first access.

@Rest( path="/root", lazyChildren="true", children={ HeavyAdminResource.class, DiagnosticsResource.class } ) public class RootResources extends BasicRestServletGroup {} Programmatic equivalent via AbstractRestBuilder: MyRest.builder().lazyChildInit(true).build();

Aspect Description URL matching Routing entries are registered immediately; URLs are reachable from the first request. Construction The full RestContext for each lazy child — including bean-store setup, lifecycle hooks, and memoizers — is built on the first inbound request to that child's URL prefix. Concurrency Concurrent first-requests to the same lazy child are serialized via double-checked locking. Only one thread runs construction; others block until it completes. Never-invoked children A lazy child that receives zero requests is never constructed. Its @RestDestroy / shutdown hooks are skipped at parent destruction time.

Large microservice trees: dozens of rarely-touched admin, debug, or compatibility endpoints that don't need to be materialized unless an operator actually navigates to them. Expensive integration children: a child that initializes a database connection pool or external API client only pays that cost on first use.

The first request to a lazy child pays the full construction cost, which can be significant for heavyweight children. If predictable first-request latency is required, do not opt in — keep the default eager behavior.

Children are deliberately isolated from the host's resolution chain (see Mixin-vs-child divergence) — a child's serializers, parsers, guards, call logger, etc. are resolved against the child's own RestContext only, never walked through the parent. @Rest(childrenDefs=@Child(...)) doesn't change that isolation; it gives the host an explicit, opt-in way to seed a curated set of settings onto a specific child's otherwise-isolated context, at the point the host declares it: @Rest( childrenDefs = @Child(type = AdminResource.class, callLogger = StructuredJsonLogger.class, guards = AdminBearerGuard.class) ) public class ApiResource extends BasicRestServlet { @RestGet("/items") public List<Item> items() { ... } } AdminResource's endpoints now log through StructuredJsonLogger and require AdminBearerGuard — as declared by the host — without editing AdminResource itself and without those settings leaking into ApiResource's own /items resolution chain. childrenDefs is additive to and coexists with children: bare-class entries in children= and rich @Child entries in childrenDefs= are discovered together (bare entries first, then childrenDefs entries). A @Child(type=X.class) with no seed members is the exact equivalent of a bare children=X.class entry; if both name the same class, the rich entry wins (the bare entry is upgraded in place) — the same equivalence rule @Mixin establishes for mixins/mixinDefs.

Unlike a host @Mixin override — which wins over the mixin class's own declarations — a @Child seed can only add to or fill gaps in the child's own configuration. It never lets the child weaken or discard something the host imposed, and it never masks something the child explicitly declared for itself. Every seed member falls into exactly one of two buckets: Bucket Members Behavior Additive-security guards, converters, roleGuard, rolesDeclared The host's contribution is added alongside whatever the child declares — the child can never remove or weaken it. Child-wins scalars callLogger, partSerializer, partParser, debug, defaultCharset, maxInput The seed is a fallback/default. If the child's own @Rest chain explicitly declares the same setting, the child's value wins; the seed applies only when the child is silent. Additive-security, list-shaped (guards, converters) — PREPEND. The host-seeded entries run first (outermost), then the child's own declared entries. A seeded guard degrades to a plain "set" when the child declares no guards of its own, and the child's own guards/converters are never dropped: @Rest(path = "/admin", guards = AdminOwnGuard.class) // the child's own guard public class AdminResource { @RestGet(path = "/threads") public String threads() { ... } } @Rest(childrenDefs = @Child(type = AdminResource.class, guards = HostGateGuard.class)) public class ApiResource extends BasicRestServlet { ... } A request to /admin/threads must satisfy both HostGateGuard (seeded, runs first) and AdminOwnGuard (the child's own, runs second) — neither is optional. Additive-security, role-based (roleGuard/rolesDeclared) — AND-STACK. A host-seeded roleGuard/rolesDeclared and the child's own explicit value both apply as independent, ANDed role checks, rather than one overriding the other. If the host seeds roleGuard="admin" and the child declares its own roleGuard="on-call", a request must satisfy both roles. Child-wins scalars — fallback only. If the child leaves partSerializer (or any other child-wins member) undeclared, the host's seeded value takes effect. If the child declares its own @Rest(partSerializer=...), the child's value wins outright and the seed is ignored for that property — same "does this property have an explicit value anywhere more-derived?" resolution the framework already uses everywhere else.
documents.s: The unifying principle: seeds never remove or override the child's own config

documents.t: defaultAccept and defaultContentType are not @Child seed members. They're resolved through the framework's shared default-request-headers mechanism (HttpHeaderList.setDefault(...)), which keeps the first value set while walking the annotation chain least-derived-first — independently of @Child, this already resolves in favor of the least-derived declaration in any class hierarchy. Seeding these two through @Child would therefore make the host's seed win over the child's own explicit value, the opposite of the child-wins contract every other scalar in this bucket honors. Rather than ship that contract violation, they're deferred until HttpHeaderList's first-wins resolution is revisited.

@Child itself has no noInherit() member — there's no inherited chain to cut in an isolated context. But a child's own @Rest(noInherit="<property>") does cut the corresponding host seed too, for any seedable property, additive-security or child-wins-scalar alike: @Rest(path = "/admin", noInherit = "guards") // opts out of the host's seeded guard entirely public class AdminResource { @RestGet(path = "/threads") public String threads() { ... } } @Rest(childrenDefs = @Child(type = AdminResource.class, guards = HostGateGuard.class)) public class ApiResource extends BasicRestServlet { ... } With noInherit = "guards" on AdminResource, HostGateGuard is not applied at all — the child stays fully in control, exactly as if the host had never seeded it. This falls out of the same generic noInherit cutoff the framework already applies uniformly to every @Rest property; there's no special-casing for seeded vs. non-seeded values.
A @Child seed survives deferred construction under @Rest(lazyChildren="true") — a lazily materialized child receives its seed on first request exactly as an eagerly-built child would.

REST Server — Children vs Mixins — the same-vs-different matrix for choosing children (isolation) vs mixins (inheritance). REST Server — Mixin Sub-Contexts — the inheritance-based alternative composition primitive, including the host-side @Mixin override this page's @Child section mirrors.

Juneau 10 ships two REST client stacks in the same release. Both are supported; they differ in which HTTP library they are built on and how much of the Juneau API surface they expose. See the guide: Call an existing REST API with a typed proxy Which client? juneau-rest-client (org.apache.juneau.rest.client.RestClient) is the recommended REST client. It is generally available in 10.0.0, transport-agnostic, and uses the JDK HttpClient by default. juneau-rest-client-classic (org.apache.juneau.rest.client.classic.RestClient, Apache HttpClient 4.5) stays supported and is not deprecated; it is the stable choice for existing users. See Choosing a REST Client. Next-Generation (NG) client Classic client Maven artifact juneau-rest-client juneau-rest-client-classic Package org.apache.juneau.rest.client org.apache.juneau.rest.client.classic HTTP library Pluggable transport; JDK HttpClient by default (no third-party dependencies) Apache HttpClient 4.5 only Extends HttpClient No Yes (implements org.apache.http.client.HttpClient) HTTP types org.apache.juneau.http.* org.apache.juneau.http.classic.* (HttpCore-based) Mock client org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.MockRestClient org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.classic.MockRestClient SSRF guard for @Remote / @Url Yes, with per-hop redirect re-validation (NG Security) Yes (classic guard classes) Stability Generally available in 10.0.0; the recommended client Stable, unchanged from 9.x; supported, not deprecated

You are starting a new project. You want zero third-party dependencies (the JDK HttpClient transport is the default), or you want to pick OkHttp, Jetty, or Apache HttpClient 4.5/5 per deployment without changing application code. You want the typed response accessors, assertions, and the BodyConverter extension point. You want serverless tests with the NG MockRestClient.

You depend on RestClient being an Apache HttpClient (passing it to libraries that expect one, or customizing it through HttpClientBuilder). You have existing code that uses the classic fluent surface (.json5(), .plainText(), etc.) and you cannot migrate yet. You want the client unchanged from 9.x (stable and supported, not deprecated). Existing 9.x code keeps working by changing imports to the .classic packages; the full rename table is in the V10 Migration Guide.
The two clients can coexist in the same application, including both mock flavors (both live in the juneau-rest-mock module). Migrate one call site at a time.
NG client: overview, requests, responses, body converters, assertions, interceptors, security, transports. Classic client: juneau-rest-client basics.

The ClasspathStore reads configuration files from the JVM classpath (for example files packaged inside your jar or under src/main/resources). Example // Read "MyConfig.cfg" from the classpath. Config config = Config .create("MyConfig.cfg") .store(ClasspathStore.DEFAULT) .build(); String name = config.getString("General/name"); A shared instance is available as ClasspathStore.DEFAULT, or you can create a new one with ClasspathStore.create().build(). The class is thread safe and reusable.

Lookup. read(String) loads the named resource through the current thread's context class loader (Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader().getResourceAsStream(name)). The name is used as-is, so it is a classpath resource path such as MyConfig.cfg or sub/foo2.cfg; no file extension search is performed (unlike FileStore). Missing files. A resource that does not exist reads as an empty string, and exists(String) returns false (it returns true only when the resource has non-empty contents). Caching. Contents are cached per name after the first read. Writes are in-memory only. Classpath resources can't be written back. write(...) and update(...) replace the cached contents, so a Config built on this store can be modified and commit()-ed and will see its own changes, but nothing is persisted and the change is lost when the JVM exits. Writing to a name that does not exist on the classpath creates an in-memory entry. No watcher. There is no file watching; the store does not detect changes to the classpath resource. close(). No-op.
ClasspathStore.Builder exposes no settings beyond those inherited from ConfigStore.Builder.

ClasspathStore.DEFAULT is also what the system default config lookup falls back to: when Config.getSystemDefault() is searching for a config, it first tries the file system via FileStore.DEFAULT and, if the file is not found there, tries the classpath via ClasspathStore.DEFAULT. See System Default Config.
Store Source Persisted writes FileStore File system directory Yes MemoryStore In memory No ClasspathStore JVM classpath No See Config Stores for the store contract.
Client version headers let one REST resource return different responses depending on which version of a client is calling, so you can make breaking interface changes without breaking older clients.

Use client versions when you must change an operation's response in a way older clients cannot handle, and you cannot make every client upgrade at once. You keep one method per version range on the same path, and the framework picks the method whose range contains the version in the request header.

import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.servlet.*; @Rest(clientVersionHeader="Client-Version") public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet { // Called if Client-Version is at least 2.0. // This also matches 2.0.1. @RestGet(path="/foobar", clientVersion="2.0") public String method1() { return "version 2.0 or later"; } // Called if Client-Version is at least 1.1 but less than 2.0. @RestGet(path="/foobar", clientVersion="[1.1,2.0)") public String method2() { return "version 1.1 up to 2.0"; } // Called if Client-Version is less than 1.1. @RestGet(path="/foobar", clientVersion="[0,1.1)") public String method3() { return "versions before 1.1"; } }

RestclientVersionHeaderRestOpclientVersion Setting Meaning @Rest(clientVersionHeader) The name of the request header that carries the client version. @RestOp(clientVersion) The version range the method accepts: "1.0" is at least 1.0, "[0,1.0)" is below 1.0, and "[0,1.0]" is up to and including 1.0.
@RestOp-Annotated Methods

In general, it's good practice to close Config if you're only creating them temporarily so that their listeners get unregistered from the underlying storage APIs. Example // Create a transient config. Config config = Config.create("MyConfig.cfg").build(); // Do stuff with it. // Then close the config to unregister the listeners. config.close();

Configclose() Config.close() unregisters the Config from the underlying config map so that it no longer receives change events from the store. A long-lived config (for example one shared for the lifetime of the application) typically does not need to be closed. Transient configs created repeatedly against a long-lived store should be closed, otherwise the store keeps a listener for each one. Config does not implement java.io.Closeable or AutoCloseable, so it cannot be used directly in try-with-resources. Use try/finally instead: Example Config config = Config.create("MyConfig.cfg").build(); try { String name = config.getString("General/name"); } finally { config.close(); }

Stores are closed separately. ConfigStore implements java.io.Closeable, and closing a store releases its own resources (for example FileStore.close() interrupts the watcher thread if one was started). Closing a Config does not close the store it was built with, since stores are typically shared. ClasspathStore.close() is a no-op (see ClasspathStore).

The Juneau parsers have the ability to parse into complex data types that consist of multidimensional arrays and nested Maps and Collections using the methods below: Parserread(Object,Class)read(Object,Type,Type...) Arrays are simple enough and can be constructed using the first method: String json = "[1,2,3]"; int[] array = Json.to(json, int[].class); For data types consisting of nested Collections and Maps such as Map<String,List<MyBean>>, you need to use the second read method that allows you to define the parameter types of the Collections classes. Example String json = "{foo:[{bar:'baz'}]}"; TreeMap map = Json.to( json, // Input being parsed. TreeMap.class, // Top-level data type. String.class, // Key type of map. LinkedList.class, // Value type of map. MyBean.class // Value type of list. ); Collection classes are assumed to be followed by zero or one objects indicating the element type. Map classes are assumed to be followed by zero or two meta objects indicating the key and value types. The arguments can be arbitrarily long to indicate arbitrarily complex data structures. Similar methods for converting to complex types can be found on the RequestContent and RequestHttpPart classes, and the MarshallingSession.convertToType(Object,Type,Type...) method.

The following methods can be used to define the configuration for your microservice using the powerful Config API. For the Config API itself, see juneau-config. Microservice.Builderconfig(Config)configName(String)configStore(ConfigStore) If you do not specify any of this information, we attempt to resolve it through the following methods: Resolve a file first in the working directory, then in the classpath, using the following names: The "configFile" argument in the command line arguments passed in through the constructor. The value of the Main-Config entry in the manifest file. A config file in the same location and with the same name as the executable jar file. (e.g. java -jar myjar.jar will look for myjar.cfg). Any *.cfg file that can be found in the working directory. Resolve any of the following files in the classpath: juneau.cfg default.cfg application.cfg app.cfg settings.cfg If no configuration file is found, an empty in-memory configuration is used. The configName(String) method allows you to explicitly specify the name of the external configuration file location for your microservice. Microservice .create() .configName("my-files/MyMicroservice.cfg") .build() .start() ; By default, we try to find the file on the file system and then the classpath. If located on the file system, then the configuration is writeable and the microservice can automatically listen for and react to changes in the configuration file on the file system. If located on the classpath, then the configuration can still react to modifications made to it through the Config API but the changes cannot be persisted since the location prevents the file from being modified. The configStore(ConfigStore) method can be used to explicitly specify a configuration store. This can include your own custom configuration store, such as one that's implemented in a relational database. Microservice .create() .configStore(new MyConfigSqlStore()) .configName("MyConfig") .build() .start() ; The config(Config) method can be used to explicitly specify a Config file as the microservice configuration. When this method is used, the above two methods are bypassed entirely. Config config = getMyOwnConfig(); Microservice .create() .config(config) .build() .start() ; Once the configuration is resolved, it is made as the system default configuration available through the Config.getSystemDefault(). This in turn allows it to be used by REST resources that reference the system default configuration via the SYSTEM_DEFAULT such as those extending BasicRestServlet or BasicRestResource.

@Rest( config="${S:juneau.configFile:SYSTEM_DEFAULT}" ... ) The Microservice.getConfig() method can be used to get access to the configuration. Config config = Microservice.getInstance().getConfig(); File logDir = config.get("Logging/logDir").as(File.class).orElse(null); Boolean append = config.get("Logging/append").asBoolean().orElse(null); String format = config.get("Logging/format", "[{date} {level}] {msg}%n").orElse(null); Long limit = config.get("Logging/limit").asLong().orElse(null); Map levels = config.get("Logging/levels").as(Map.class, String.class, Level.class).orElse(null); Changes to the configuration file can trigger notifications that can be used to restart your microservice or make various other on-the-fly changes. This can be accomplished by either overriding the Microservice.onConfigChange(ConfigEvents) or implementing a listener and using the onConfigChange() methods. These will be described in detail later.

As a convenience, the SystemProperties section of your configuration file can be used to define system properties to set during initialization of your microservice: #======================================================================================================================= # System properties #----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # These are arbitrary system properties that are set during startup. #======================================================================================================================= [SystemProperties] # Configure Jetty for StdErrLog Logging # org.eclipse.jetty.util.log.class = org.eclipse.jetty.util.log.StrErrLog # Configure Jetty to log using java-util logging org.eclipse.jetty.util.log.class = org.apache.juneau.microservice.jetty.JettyLogger # Jetty logging level # Possible values: ALL, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, OFF org.eclipse.jetty.LEVEL = WARN derby.stream.error.file = ${C:Logging/logDir}/derby-errors.log

Configuration change events can be listened for with Config.addListener(ConfigEventListener).
Use a listener to react when an entry changes, either through Config.commit() or because the file changed on the file system, for example to reload a cache.

import org.apache.juneau.config.*; import org.apache.juneau.config.event.*; import org.apache.juneau.config.store.*; public class ConfigListenerExample { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { MemoryStore store = MemoryStore.create().build(); store.update("MyConfig.cfg", "[MySection]\nkey1 = a\n"); Config config = Config.create("MyConfig.cfg").store(store).build(); // Add a listener for changes to MySection/key1 config.addListener(events -> { for (ConfigEvent event : events) { if (event.getType() == ConfigEventType.SET_ENTRY && "MySection".equals(event.getSection()) && "key1".equals(event.getKey())) System.out.println("key1 changed to " + event.getValue()); } }); config.set("MySection/key1", "b"); config.commit(); } }

ConfigaddListener(ConfigEventListener)removeListener(ConfigEventListener) The ConfigEventListener interface consists of the following method: ConfigEventListeneronConfigChange(ConfigEvents) The ConfigEvent class provides access to all the information about the updated entry: ConfigEventgetType()getSection()getKey()getValue()getModifiers()getComment()getPreLines() The listener method is triggered: After Config.commit() is called. When the file changes on the file system. In both cases, the listener is triggered after the changes have been committed.
Config Stores File system changes

Starting in 10.0.0, Juneau's config system supports two cloud-native ergonomics borrowed from the Spring Boot world: environment profiles (<name>-<profile> config overlays) and relaxed binding (one logical key resolvable from any common environment-variable spelling). Both are opt-in-friendly and change no existing behavior by default.

A profile layers an environment-specific overlay (dev / stage / prod, etc.) on top of a base config. Given a base config my.cfg and an active profile stage, the overlay file my-stage.cfg is merged over the base: profile wins over base for any section/key the profile redefines; base-only keys survive unchanged; when multiple profiles are active, the last one wins for shared keys (earlier profiles still contribute their unique keys). YAML bases work identically with my-stage.yml overlays.

Set the active profiles with the juneau.profiles.active key — a comma-separated list — via a system property, an environment variable, or a config key: java -Djuneau.profiles.active=stage,cloud -jar myapp.jar # or export JUNEAU_PROFILES_ACTIVE=stage,cloud # relaxed binding maps this to juneau.profiles.active Or programmatically on the config builder: var config = Config.create() .name("my.cfg") .profiles("stage", "cloud") // base my.cfg + my-stage.cfg + my-cloud.cfg (cloud wins) .build(); With no active profiles, the base config is used verbatim — existing single-file configs are completely unaffected.

Profile resolution happens at the store layer: when profiles are active, the configured ConfigStore is wrapped so that a read of the base name returns the base contents with each active profile's overlay merged on top (ProfileConfigStore + the ProfileMerge engine). Because the merged result flows through the normal config parse, variable resolution, format handling, and live reload all behave exactly as for a single-file config.

Profile overlays participate in live reload: a change to the base file or to any active profile overlay file re-runs the merge and fires the usual ConfigEventListener change events, so a running application picks up profile-file edits without a restart.

When the Spring Boot bridge (juneau-rest-server-springboot) is present, juneau.profiles.active piggybacks on Spring's active profiles — Environment.getActiveProfiles() becomes the source of truth, so spring.profiles.active (however it was set: property, env, SpringApplication.setAdditionalProfiles, …) drives Juneau config-profile selection with no separate configuration. An explicit juneau.profiles.active property still wins if you set one.

Relaxed binding lets a single logical configuration key be supplied in any of the common environment conventions and still resolve. This is what makes Kubernetes-style environment variables map cleanly onto config keys: Logical key Also resolvable from my.prop MY_PROP myProp MY_PROP, my.prop MY_PROP my.prop MySection/myKey MY_SECTION_MY_KEY my-prop MY_PROP, my.prop By default the system-environment source in the Settings singleton is wrapped with relaxed binding (Settings.RELAXED_SYSTEM_ENV_SOURCE), so this works out of the box for env-var lookups.

A lookup is always tried verbatim first, so exact-match behavior is preserved and an already-canonical key resolves with no transformation. Only on a miss are relaxed variants tried, in order: verbatim — the requested name, unchanged; UPPER_UNDERSCORE — every run of non-alphanumeric characters, and every lower→upper camel-case boundary, becomes a single _, then the whole name is upper-cased (the dominant env-var form); lower.dotted — the same separator collapse joined with . and lower-cased. The decorator works in the lookup-key → candidate-name direction only (the well-defined direction): you ask for a known logical key and it generates the environment-convention spellings to probe. It never tries to reverse a flat environment name (where the section/key boundary is ambiguous) back into a section/key pair.
To add relaxed binding over any other PropertySource, wrap it: import org.apache.juneau.commons.settings.*; var settings = Settings.create() .addSource(new RelaxedPropertySource(mySource)) .build();
Config Files Property Sources juneau-commons Settings

The @ConfigProperties annotation (introduced in 10.0.0, package org.apache.juneau.commons.inject) is a declarative, prefix-scoped whole-object config binder — Juneau's analog of Spring Boot's @ConfigurationProperties. Where @Value resolves a single configuration value onto a single field or parameter, @ConfigProperties resolves an entire prefix (myapp.host, myapp.port, myapp.timeout, ...) onto the fields of one POJO in a single pass: import org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.ConfigProperties; @ConfigProperties(prefix = "MyService") public class MyServiceProperties { public String host = "localhost"; public int port = 8080; } The two annotations are complementary, not competing — a class can carry @Value fields internally while also being the target of another class's nested @ConfigProperties bind (see Nested config objects below), and @ConfigProperties fields that are themselves annotated @Value/@Inject are left untouched by the config bind (see Coexistence with @Value and @Inject).

Given the MyServiceProperties class above, materializing it through BeanInstantiator runs the bind automatically: BeanStore store = new BasicBeanStore(null); MyServiceProperties props = BeanInstantiator.of(MyServiceProperties.class, store).run(); With MyService.host=example.com and MyService.port=9090 set as system properties (or environment variables, or any other registered PropertySource), props.host is "example.com" and props.port is 9090. A key that isn't present anywhere in the chain leaves the field's initializer value untouched — bind-only-present semantics, the same "default lives in the field initializer" idea @Value's ${key:default} syntax expresses inline. You can also invoke the underlying binder directly, with or without the annotation, via ConfigPropertiesBinder's fluent builder: MyServiceProperties props = ConfigPropertiesBinder.of(new MyServiceProperties(), "MyService") .relaxed(true) // default .run();

relaxed() defaults to true on the annotation (and on the binder). For each field, the candidate key prefix.fieldName is probed in up to three spellings, via RelaxedPropertySource.candidates(String) — the same relaxed-matching logic used elsewhere in juneau-commons: Verbatim — MyService.host SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE — MY_SERVICE_HOST (the env-var-friendly spelling) lower.dotted — my.service.host This is what lets a Kubernetes-style environment variable (MY_SERVICE_HOST=example.com) satisfy a camelCase-prefixed key without any extra configuration. Set relaxed = false on the annotation (or .relaxed(false) on the binder) to require an exact, verbatim key match only.

Each candidate spelling is resolved through the same chain @Value uses — candidate-major: every spelling is checked against the entire chain before the next spelling is tried, in this order per candidate: A Settings.setLocal(...) / Settings.setGlobal(...) test override, if one is recorded for that exact candidate — always wins. Any caller-scoped PropertySource-typed beans registered in a BeanStore passed via ConfigPropertiesBinder.of(...).beanStore(...) (or supplied automatically by the @ConfigProperties resolution hook — see below) — consulted ahead of the global Settings chain, first-match-wins among the scoped sources. The process-wide Settings.get(name) chain — registered PropertySources, system properties, then system environment variables. Because precedence is candidate-major rather than source-major, a verbatim hit in a lower-priority source can outrank a relaxed-spelling override set on a higher-priority source, if that override used a different spelling than the one that resolved first. In practice this rarely matters — most deployments pick one spelling convention per key — but it's worth knowing if a key is set two different ways in two different places. The caller-scoped PropertySource layer is exactly how the RestContext pilot (see RestContext) lets a resource's @Rest(config=...) file participate in binding RestContext.* keys without mutating the shared Settings.get() singleton.

A field whose declared type is itself @ConfigProperties-annotated is bound recursively, using prefix.fieldName as the sub-prefix — the field's own @ConfigProperties(prefix=...) value is ignored for a nested bind (the enclosing prefix always wins): @ConfigProperties(prefix = "unused-when-nested") public class ServerProperties { public String host = "localhost"; public int port = 80; } @ConfigProperties(prefix = "MyApp") public class MyAppProperties { public ServerProperties server = new ServerProperties(); } MyApp.server.host and MyApp.server.port bind onto server's fields. A null nested field is only materialized (via an accessible no-arg constructor) if at least one key resolves anywhere under its sub-prefix — otherwise it's left null, so an optional nested block doesn't force an empty instance into existence. Circular @ConfigProperties nesting (a type that, directly or transitively, nests itself) is detected and raises a RuntimeException rather than recursing indefinitely. This nested-field detection is inheritance-aware: a field whose declared type is a subclass of an @ConfigProperties-annotated type still triggers a nested bind. This is different from the annotation's own top-level trigger — see the note below.

@ConfigProperties and @Value serve different granularities and coexist on the same class without conflict. A field already annotated @Value or @Inject is never bound by ConfigPropertiesBinder, even when a matching prefix.fieldName key exists — injection resolution owns those fields exclusively: @ConfigProperties(prefix = "MyService") public class MyServiceProperties { public String host = "localhost"; // bound by ConfigPropertiesBinder @Value("${MyService.label:default-label}") public String label; // bound by @Value, never touched by the config bind } When materialized through BeanInstantiator, the whole-object config bind runs after @Value/@Inject field-and-method injection and before any @PostConstruct method, so a @PostConstruct hook observes fully-bound config fields either way.

When a @ConfigProperties-annotated class is materialized through BeanInstantiator, the bound instance is automatically registered into the bean store as a framework default (a non-clobbering addDefaultSupplier — lowest priority, so an explicit caller registration still wins), under the declared annotated type. It's then retrievable anywhere downstream: MyServiceProperties props = beanStore.getBean(MyServiceProperties.class).orElseThrow(); or injected directly: public class MyResource { @Inject MyServiceProperties props; } Not @Inherited: the BeanInstantiator trigger fires only when the exact declared type being instantiated carries @ConfigProperties — a subclass or interface implementor of an annotated type does not itself trigger binding or auto-registration. (This is distinct from the nested-field detection described above, which is inheritance-aware.)

No Optional<T> / Supplier<T> field types. Unlike @Value, type conversion here is keyed on the field's raw Class, not its full generic Type — generic container types aren't supported as @ConfigProperties field types. Use a plain field type (e.g. String uriAuthority with a null default, rather than Optional<String>) if you need "unset" to be distinguishable from a real value. Validation is currently a no-op seam. A post-bind extension point, ConfigPropertiesValidator, is invoked once per bound object (innermost-nested first) — but the shipped default, ConfigPropertiesValidator.NO_OP, performs no validation. It exists purely as a placement marker so a future release can add JSR-303-style validation without changing the binder's public shape.

@Value Annotation Basics — the single-value counterpart. Inject Package — the broader org.apache.juneau.commons.inject injection model. RestContext — RestContextProperties, the real-world @ConfigProperties pilot. org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.ConfigProperties org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.ConfigPropertiesBinder org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.ConfigPropertiesValidator org.apache.juneau.commons.settings.RelaxedPropertySource

Configuration files are stored in entities called Stores. The methods that need to be implemented on a store are: ConfigStoreread(String)write(String,String,String)update(String,String) Read is self-explanatory: public String read(String name) { // Return the contents of the specified configuration. } Write is slightly trickier: public String write(String name, String oldContents, String newContents) { // If the old contents match the current stored contents, the new contents will get stored, // and the method returns null indicating success. // If the old contents DO NOT match the current stored contents (i.e. it was modified in some way), // the new contents are NOT stored, and the method returns the current stored contents. // If the old contents are null, then just always write the new contents. } The update method is called whenever the stored file gets modified externally: public String update(String name, String newContents) { // Do something with the updated contents. } Two configuration stores are provided by default: FileStoreMemoryStore The store is defined on the Config object via the following setting: Config.Builderstore(ConfigStore) Example // Create a config with in-memory storage. Config config = Config.create("MyConfig.cfg").store(MemoryStore.DEFAULT).build(); The default store used is FileStore.DEFAULT which defines the execution directory as the file system directory to store and retrieve files.

The MemoryStore class is simply an in-memory storage location for configuration files. There is no hard persistence and is used primarily for testing purposes. However, the implementation provides a good idea on how stores work (especially the write method): public class MemoryStore extends ConfigStore { // Some methods ommitted. private final ConcurrentHashMap cache = new ConcurrentHashMap(); @Override /* ConfigStore */ public synchronized String read(String name) { return emptyIfNull(cache.get(name)); } @Override /* ConfigStore */ public synchronized String write(String name, String expectedContents, String newContents) { // This is a no-op. if (isEquals(expectedContents, newContents)) return null; String currentContents = read(name); if (expectedContents != null && ! isEquals(currentContents, expectedContents)) return currentContents; update(name, newContents); // Success! return null; } @Override /* ConfigStore */ public synchronized MemoryStore update(String name, String newContents) { cache.put(name, newContents); super.update(name, newContents); // Trigger any listeners. return this; } }

The FileStore is the typical store used for configuration files. It provides the following configurable settings: FileStore.Buildercharset(Charset)directory(File)updateOnWrite()enableWatcher()watcherSensitivity(WatcherSensitivity) Example // Create a config store with a watcher thread and high sensitivity. FileStore fileStore = FileStore .create() .directory("configs") .enableWatcher() .watcherSensitivity(HIGH) .build(); // Create a config using the store defined above. Config config = Config .create("MyConfig.cfg") .store(fileStore) .build();

The ConfigStore API has been written to allow easy development of custom configuration storage classes. The example below shows a starting point for an implementation based on polling a relational database. The source can be found here: SqlStore. Completing it is left as an exercise: Example Store Class public class SqlStore extends ConfigStore { private final String jdbcUrl; private final String tableName, nameColumn, valueColumn; private final Timer watcher; private final ConcurrentHashMap cache = new ConcurrentHashMap(); protected SqlStore(ConfigStore.Builder builder) { super(builder); this.jdbcUrl = builder.jdbcUrl; this.tableName = builder.tableName; this.nameColumn = builder.nameColumn; this.valueColumn = builder.valueColumn; int pollInterval = builder.pollInterval; TimerTask timerTask = new TimerTask() { @Override public void run() { SqlStore.this.poll(); } }; this.watcher = new Timer("MyTimer"); watcher.scheduleAtFixedRate(timerTask, 0, pollInterval * 1000); } synchronized void poll() { // Loop through all our entries and find the latest values. for (Map.Entry e : cache.entrySet()) { String name = e.getKey(); String cacheContents = e.getValue(); String newContents = getDatabaseValue(name); // Change detected! if (! cacheContents.equals(newContents)) update(name, newContents); } } // Reads the value from the database. protected String getDatabaseValue(String name) { // Implement me! return null; } @Override /* ConfigStore */ public boolean exists(String name) { // Implement me! return false; } @Override /* ConfigStore */ public synchronized String read(String name) { String contents = cache.get(name); if (contents == null) { contents = getDatabaseValue(name); update(name, contents); } return contents; } @Override /* ConfigStore */ public synchronized String write(String name, String expectedContents, String newContents) { // This is a no-op. if (StringUtils.eq(expectedContents, newContents)) return null; String currentContents = read(name); if (expectedContents != null && StringUtils.ne(currentContents, expectedContents)) return currentContents; update(name, newContents); // Success! return null; } @Override /* ConfigStore */ public synchronized SqlStore update(String name, String newContents) { cache.put(name, newContents); super.update(name, newContents); // Trigger any listeners. return this; } @Override /* Closeable */ public synchronized void close() { if (watcher != null) watcher.cancel(); } }

The ConfigStore class has the following listener methods: ConfigStoreregister(String,ConfigStoreListener)unregister(String,ConfigStoreListener) Note that this is a different listener than ConfigEventListener. In this case, we're just listening for changed files: ConfigStoreListeneronChange(String) This listener is used by the Config class to listen for changes on the file system so that it can be updated in real-time.
