Outdated examples (10.0) Examples on this page using RestContext.Builder is pre-10.0 and kept only for historical context. Use Config parameter injection in @RestOp methods, @Bean beans, or RestContext.getConfig() from a supported @RestInit parameter. See the V10 Migration Guide. The Server API provides methods for associating configuration files with REST servlets so that configuration properties can be defined in external files. It uses the following annotation: Restconfig Example @Rest( // Config file is located at ./config_dir/myconfig.cfg config="config_dir/myconfig.cfg", ... ) public class MyResource {...} In recap, the Configuration API provides support for INI-style configuration files with embedded string variables: Example #-------------------------- # Examples #-------------------------- [MyProperties] path = ${E:PATH} javaHome = ${S:java.home} customMessage = Java home is ${C:MyProperties/javaHome} and the environment path is ${C:MyProperties/path}. These properties are then accessible through the Config class. @RestGet("/") public String sample(Config config) { String path = config.get("MyProperties/path").get(); File javaHome = config.get("MyProperties/javaHome").as(File.class).orElse(null); String customMessage = config.get("MyProperties/customMessage").orElse("Hello"); ... } The annotation itself can contain string variables. For example, the Microservice API BasicRestServlet class defines the location of the config file as a system property juneau.configFile: @Rest( // Config file location is defined as a system property config="${S:juneau.configFile}", ... ) public class MyResource {...} Spring Boot applications typically define an application.properties file. You can reuse it as a config file like so: @Rest( config="application.properties", ... ) public class MyResource {...} Note that properties files are a subset of functionality of INI files (they're basically just INI files with a single default section). It's therefore possible to use INI-style syntax such as sections in your application.properties file. Once a config file has been associated with a REST resource, it can be accessed through RestContext.getConfig(). It can also be accessed by passing in a Config bean to any of your REST OP methods. A common usage is to use this method to initialize fields in your servlet. @Rest( // Config file is located at ./config_dir/myconfig.cfg config="config_dir/myconfig.cfg", ... ) public class MyResource { private String path; private File javaHome; @RestInit public void init(RestContext context) { Config config = context.getConfig(); path = config.get("MyProperties/path").orElse("mypath"); javaHome = config.get("MyProperties/javaHome").as(File.class).orElse(null); } } Another common usage is to refer to config properties through $C variables in your annotations: @Rest // Get stylesheet from myconfig.cfg but default to devops.css if it's not specified @HtmlDocConfig( stylesheet="${C:MyServlet/stylesheet:servlet:/styles/devops.css}", ) public class MyResource {...} It's even possible to reference request-level variables in your config file if you use RestRequest.getConfig() to access the config file: #------------------------------------- # Contents of config_dir/myconfig.cfg #------------------------------------- [HelloWorldResource] message = Hello ${RQ:person}! /** * Sample REST resource that prints out a simple "Hello world!" message. */ @Rest( config="config_dir/myconfig.cfg", ... ) public class HelloWorldResource extends BasicRestServlet { /** * GET request handler. * Specify the GET parameter "?person=X" for a specialized message! */ @RestGet("/") public String sayHello(Config config) { return config.get("HelloWorldResource/message").get(); } } You can even add resource bundles into the mix: #------------------------------------- # Contents of config_dir/myconfig.cfg #------------------------------------- [HelloWorldResource] message = ${L:localizedMessage:${RQ:person}} #------------------------------------------- # Contents of HelloWorldResource.properties #------------------------------------------- localizedMessage = Hello {0}! /** * Sample REST resource that prints out a simple "Hello world!" message. */ @Rest( messages="HelloWorldResources", config="config_dir/myconfig.cfg", ... ) public class HelloWorldResource extends BasicRestServlet { /** * GET request handler. * Specify the GET parameter "?person=X" for a specialized message! */ @RestGet("/") public String sayHello(Config config) { return config.get("HelloWorldResource/message").get(); } } See Also juneau-config

The Microservice API provides support for simple console commands. public static void main(String[] args) { Microservice .create() .args(args) .build() .start() .startConsole() // Start console. .join() ; } When started, the console renders the following output: Running class 'Microservice' using config file 'my-microservice.cfg'. List of available commands: exit -- Shut down service restart -- Restarts service help -- Commands help > The builder methods for controlling the console are as follows: Microservice.BuilderconsoleEnabled(boolean)consoleCommands(ConsoleCommand...)consoleCommands(Class...)console(Scanner,PrintWriter) By default, the supported commands are pulled from the configuration file: #======================================================================================================================= # Console settings #======================================================================================================================= [Console] enabled = true # List of available console commands. # These are classes that implements ConsoleCommand that allow you to submit commands to the microservice via # the console. # When listed here, the implementations must provide a no-arg constructor. # They can also be provided dynamically by overriding the Microservice.createConsoleCommands() method. commands = org.apache.juneau.microservice.console.ExitCommand, org.apache.juneau.microservice.console.RestartCommand, org.apache.juneau.microservice.console.HelpCommand New commands can be added by adding them to the configuration file, or programmatically using the consoleCommands(ConsoleCommand...) builder method. The API for defining console commands is shown below: ConsoleCommandexecute(Scanner,PrintWriter,Args)getDescription()getExamples()getInfo()getName()getSynopsis() By default, the console input and output are taken from System.in and System.out. These can be overridden using the console(Scanner,PrintWriter) method.

The console message bus carries small JSON values between your server code and the pages of a console. The server publishes to a topic; every page that asked for the topic receives the value, and a page that connects later receives the last retained value straight away. Pages can also publish back on a few topics you allow. Use it to push live state (job counts, alerts, a terminal's new bytes) to a page without the page polling for it. The bus is split over three opt-in modules. Add only what you need: Module Package Adds juneau-console-bus org.apache.juneau.console.bus ServerBus, BusPolicy, and the session POST and SSE stream (BusEventsMixin). Server to page only. juneau-console-bus-websocket org.apache.juneau.console.bus.websocket The Jakarta WebSocket transport (BusWebSockets). The only transport that carries page to server frames. juneau-terminal-bus org.apache.juneau.terminal.bus TerminalInput and TerminalNudges, which connect the terminal region to the bus. juneau-console-bus depends on juneau-rest-server. The WebSocket module adds the bus module and the Jakarta WebSocket API; the servlet container supplies the implementation (for example Jetty's jetty-ee11-websocket-jakarta-server or Tomcat's tomcat-embed-websocket).

Type Role ServerBus Holds the retained topic values and the sessions that bridge them to pages. Create one per application and close() it when the application stops. BusPolicy Says what may flow, in which direction, to whom. Everything not allowed is denied. BusEventsMixin Interface you add to a REST resource. It exposes POST /juneau-bus/session and GET /juneau-bus/stream/{sessionId} relative to the resource. UpstreamHandler Handles one page-to-server topic. BusSession A connected page, as your code sees it: bridgeId(), transport(), principalName(), attribute(String), downstream(), upstream() and isConnected(). BusRefusal The exception behind a refused session request; it carries the HTTP status and a bus:* code.

A resource implements BusEventsMixin and returns the bus; the rest of the application publishes to the same bus. @Rest(path="/ops/jobs") public class JobsRest extends BasicRestServlet implements BusEventsMixin { static final ServerBus BUS = ServerBus.create(BusPolicy.create() .downstream("ops.jobs", true) // retained state .downstream("ops.alert:*", false) // events, any key .build()); @Override public ServerBus serverBus() { return BUS; } } // Anywhere in the application: JobsRest.BUS.publish("ops.jobs", JsonMap.of("schemaVersion", 1, "running", running)); Method What it does publish(topic, payload) Sends to every connected session granted the topic. On a retained topic the value is also stored, and a value whose JSON equals the stored one is not sent again (returns false). clear(topic) Removes a retained value and tells the sessions granted the topic. publishTo(audience, topic, payload) Sends only to the sessions the Predicate<BusSession> accepts. Never retained. Returns how many sessions took the frame. retainedJson(topic) The stored JSON of a retained topic, as an Optional<String>. sessions() A snapshot of the live sessions. Payloads are serialized as JSON. A publish to a topic the policy does not allow, or a frame larger than BusPolicy.maxFrameBytes(), throws IllegalArgumentException (E-56), so a typo fails loudly. // Only to one user's pages; never retained. BUS.publishTo(s -> "jb".equals(s.principalName()), "ops.jobs", mine);

Downstream topics are patterns the policy lists, each with a retain flag. A pattern is one of: a custom topic, ns.name (lower case letters, digits and -, a dot between the two parts); a keyed custom topic, ns.name:key, or every key of a family, ns.name:*; a job topic, job:<id> or job:*; a card command topic, cmd:<cardId>. Upstream topics are exact custom topics, each with an UpstreamHandler. BusPolicy policy = BusPolicy.create() .downstream("ops.jobs", true) .downstream("ops.alert:*", false) .upstream("ops.cancel-all", (session, topic, payload) -> jobs.cancelAll()) .authorizer((req, topic) -> req.isUserInRole("ops")) .boundary(boundary) // a LoopbackBoundary or CsrfBoundary .build(); The builder also sets the limits. The defaults are: Setting Default sessionGrace 60 seconds after a session's last connection closes maxSessionAge 12 hours heartbeat a ping frame after 15 seconds idle maxSessions 256 maxQueuedFrames 1024 per connection maxFrameBytes 65536, both directions maxUpstreamPerSecond 20 per session authorizer(BiPredicate<HttpServletRequest,String>) runs once per requested topic when the session opens, in both directions, and can only narrow a grant. sessionAttributes(Function<HttpServletRequest,Map<String,Object>>) captures values from the opening request that BusSession.attribute(String) returns later. boundary(RequestBoundary) puts the application's CSRF or loopback guard in front of the session POST.

A page asks for topics through the bridges in its page contract. In a page test, BusPolicy.check(contract) fails with an IllegalStateException that lists every requested topic the policy would deny (E-55), so a wiring mistake shows up in a test and not in the browser. policy.check(PageCapture.of(html).contract());

documents.t: The page POSTs to <resource>/juneau-bus/session with {"v":1, "bridge":"ops", "transport":"sse", "downstream":[...], "upstream":[...]}. bridge is required; transport is sse (the default) or websocket. BusEventsMixin.openBusSession runs the policy boundary, then ServerBus opens a session and returns the grant: a 256-bit sessionId (the capability for the stream), the heartbeat and grace times, and the topics granted with their retain flags. The page opens the stream. Over SSE that is GET <resource>/juneau-bus/stream/{sessionId}, a held-open text/event-stream with one event: bus per frame. Over WebSocket it is /juneau-bus/ws/{sessionId}. The server sends the retained values as a resync between resync-begin and resync-end, then live frames. A frame is one JSON object with v, type and, for the data types, topic, payload and a session seq. The types are pub, clear, resync-begin, resync-end, ping and error. BusFrames encodes and decodes them. A refused session POST returns {"code":..., "message":..., "denied":[...]} with a status of 400 (bus:bad-request), 403 (bus:topic-denied), 429 (bus:too-many-sessions, with Retry-After), 501 (bus:transport-unavailable) or 503 (bus:closed). A stream request for an unknown or expired id, or from another principal, is a 404. warning The stream URL contains the session capability. Do not log request URIs for /juneau-bus/stream/*. Juneau's debug pipeline logs the request path at INFO or finer, and RestSession logs it at FINE on a client disconnect, so keep the loggers of resources that serve the bus coarser than INFO. If the application has its own CSRF guard, override openBusSession in the resource, apply the guard, and call BusEventsMixin.super.openBusSession(req, res).

SSE needs nothing beyond the bus module. Page-to-server frames need a WebSocket bridge. Register the endpoint once, when the web application starts: public void contextInitialized(ServletContextEvent e) { BusWebSockets.register(e.getServletContext(), JobsRest.BUS); // "/juneau-bus/ws/{sessionId}" } There is also a register(ServerContainer, ServerBus) form for code that holds the container, for example inside Jetty's JakartaWebSocketServletContainerInitializer.configure. Registration is strict and throws IllegalStateException rather than serving an unguarded endpoint: The container must expose a jakarta.websocket ServerContainer. The policy must have an Origin rule. That is LoopbackBoundary.origin() for a LoopbackBoundary, the handshake's own scheme and Host for a CsrfBoundary, or BusPolicy.allowedOrigins when the policy has no boundary. Any boundary type other than LoopbackBoundary and CsrfBoundary is refused, because a handshake cannot apply a boundary it does not know. A handshake that fails the Host, Origin, Sec-Fetch-Site or capability checks is closed with 4403 (bus:refused) or 4401 (bus:unknown-session); a frame over maxFrameBytes is closed with 1009 (bus:frame-too-large). BusWebSocketConfigurator and BusWebSocketEndpoint are public only because the container instantiates them; do not construct them.

An UpstreamHandler receives a frame a page published on an upstream topic: UpstreamHandler cancelAll = (session, topic, payload) -> jobs.running().forEach(AsyncJob::cancel); The bus has already checked the session's upstream grant and that the payload is a JSON object. Handlers run on the container's WebSocket thread, so keep them short or hand the work off. An exception is logged and answered with a generic bus:upstream-failed frame; its text never crosses the wire. Frames above maxUpstreamPerSecond are refused.

juneau-terminal-bus connects the terminal region to the bus. Both classes are built before the bus exists, then bound to it once. TerminalInput is an UpstreamHandler for term.input. It passes a browser terminal's keystrokes to the terminal's input sink and answers each probe or refused frame on term.input-status, to the sending session only. TerminalInput input = TerminalInput.create(access); ServerBus bus = ServerBus.create(BusPolicy.create() .upstream(TerminalInput.TOPIC, input) .downstream(TerminalInput.STATUS_TOPIC, false) .build()); input.bind(bus); TerminalNudges implements TerminalNudgePublisher. Hand it to TerminalProcess or MemoryTerminalSource and it publishes a small {"end": <offset>} hint on term.nudge:<id>, at most four per second per terminal, so a card fetches new bytes at once instead of waiting for its next poll. Its policy must allow term.nudge:* downstream without retention; bind throws otherwise. TerminalNudges nudges = TerminalNudges.create(access); ServerBus bus = ServerBus.create(BusPolicy.create() .downstream("term.nudge:*", false) .build()); nudges.bind(bus); Both call TerminalAccess.canWatch for the caller, and TerminalInput also needs a present inputSink. The terminal region page covers the card side, the audit log, and the status states.

The @Content annotation can be applied to arguments of @RemoteOp-annotated methods to denote that they are the HTTP body of the request. Contentschema Examples // Used on parameter @Remote(path="/petstore") public interface PetStore { @RemotePost("/pets") String addPet(@Content Pet pet); } // Used on class @Remote(path="/petstore") public interface PetStore { @RemotePost("/pets") String addPet(Pet pet); } @Content public class Pet {...} The argument can be any of the following types: Any serializable POJO - Converted to output using the Serializer registered with the RestClient. Content-Type is set to that of the Serializer. Reader - Raw contents of Reader will be serialized to remote resource. Content-Type is set to text/plain. InputStream - Raw contents of InputStream will be serialized to remote resource. Content-Type is set to application/octet-stream. PartList - Converted to a URL-encoded FORM post. Content-Type is set to application/x-www-form-urlencoded. HttpEntity - Bypass Juneau serialization and pass HttpEntity directly to HttpClient. OpenAPI schema based serialization can be used by using the OpenApiSerializer class. @RemotePost("/comma-delimited-pipe-delimited-ints") String addCommaDelimitedPipeDelimitedInts( @Content( schema=@Schema( type="array", collectionFormat="pipes", items=@Items( type="array", items=@SubItems( type="int32", // Auto-validates on client side! minimum="0", maximum="64" ) ) ) ) int[][] input ); // Same as above but using free-form schema. // Format is simplified-JSON (outer {} brackets are optional). @RemotePost("/comma-delimited-pipe-delimited-ints") String addCommaDelimitedPipeDelimitedInts( @Content( schema=@Schema( "type:'array',collectionFormat:'pipes',items:[type:'array',items:[type:'int32',minimum:0,maximum:64]]" ) ) int[][] input ); See OpenAPI Serializers for information about supported data types in OpenAPI serialization. If your RestClient class does not have a serializer associated with it, the body will automatically be serialized to a string using the rules defined in POJO Categories.

Content Security Policy (CSP) is a browser security mechanism that lets a server declare which content sources a page may load and execute, mitigating cross-site-scripting (XSS) and data-injection attacks. Juneau auto-generates HTML with inline <style>/<script> blocks (the HtmlDoc serializer, the Swagger UI, the OpenAPI UI, and menu-item widgets), so a CSP is the standard way to lock those pages down. Juneau models a policy as a first-class, immutable HTTP header bean, ContentSecurityPolicy, assembled with a fluent ContentSecurityPolicy.Builder. Both live in juneau-rest-common alongside the other modern HTTP header beans. note CSP is off by default. Turning a policy on silently would break existing apps, so you must opt in.

The builder exposes typed setters for the common directives plus a generic directive(name, sources...) escape hatch so new directives never require an API change. Source-expression keywords are exposed as constants (SELF, NONE, UNSAFE_INLINE, UNSAFE_EVAL, STRICT_DYNAMIC) and helpers (nonce(token), scheme(scheme), hash(alg, b64)). import static org.apache.juneau.http.header.ContentSecurityPolicy.Builder.*; String value = ContentSecurityPolicy.create() .defaultSrc(SELF) .scriptSrc(SELF, scheme("https")) .imgSrc(SELF, "data:") .objectSrc(NONE) .baseUri(SELF) .frameAncestors(SELF) .build(); // => "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https:; img-src 'self' data:; // object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; frame-ancestors 'self'" Setting the same directive twice replaces its source list (while preserving its original position), and a directive with no sources renders as a bare keyword (e.g. directive("upgrade-insecure-requests")).

Because ContentSecurityPolicy is an ordinary string header, it flows through the existing response-header path. The simplest opt-in is the static string form on the REST annotation: @Rest( defaultResponseHeaders={ "Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; object-src 'none'" } ) public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet { ... } For programmatic assembly, contribute the bean through a defaultResponseHeaders HttpHeaderList factory method: @Rest(...) public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet { @Bean(name="defaultResponseHeaders") public HttpHeaderList responseHeaders() { return HttpHeaderList.of( ContentSecurityPolicy.create() .defaultSrc(SELF) .objectSrc(NONE) .toHeader() ); } } toHeader() returns a ContentSecurityPolicy whose name is Content-Security-Policy (or Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only when report-only mode is enabled).

Operators can deploy a policy in observe-only mode first, watch violations, tune, then enforce. reportOnly() flips the header name to Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only; the reportUri(...) / reportTo(...) directives point a browser at a violation collector (the collector endpoint itself is out of scope — point at your own). ContentSecurityPolicy csp = ContentSecurityPolicy.create() .defaultSrc(SELF) .reportTo("csp-endpoint") .reportOnly() .toHeader(); // Header name => "Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only"

strictStarter() returns a builder pre-populated with a ready, nonce-based baseline: ContentSecurityPolicy.strictStarter().build(); // => "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-{nonce}'; style-src 'self' 'nonce-{nonce}'; // img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; frame-ancestors 'self'" Because Juneau's built-in pages emit inline <script>/<style>, a strict 'self'-only policy needs a per-request nonce to allow those inline blocks. The preset embeds a NONCE_PLACEHOLDER token ({nonce}); the REST layer mints one cryptographically-random nonce per response, rewrites the placeholder via resolveNonce(value, nonce), and stamps the same nonce onto every inline tag the serializer emits so the header and the markup agree. warning Do not combine a nonce with 'unsafe-inline' in script-src — browsers ignore 'unsafe-inline' whenever a nonce (or hash) is present. The strict starter deliberately omits 'unsafe-inline'.
ContentSecurityPolicy ContentSecurityPolicy.Builder Content Security Policy Level 3 (W3C) REST Security — other REST-layer security considerations.

RestClient supports multi-format content negotiation: it automatically sets Accept and Content-Type headers based on its configured serializer/parser registry, and selects the right parser for each response based on the server's Content-Type reply. See Serializer Sets and Parser Sets for the underlying registry API.

With no explicit configuration, RestClient uses JsonSerializer / JsonParser and sends Accept: application/json on every request: RestClient client = RestClient.create(); MyBean bean = client.get("/api/item/1") .run() .body().as(MyBean.class); // parsed with JsonParser

Register multiple serializers and parsers at build time using RestClient.Builder: RestClient.Builderserializer(Serializer...) — append serializers (built into a SerializerSet)parser(Parser...) — append parsers (built into a ParserSet)serializers(SerializerSet) — supply a pre-built serializer registryparsers(ParserSet) — supply a pre-built parser registrydefaultSerializer(Serializer) — fallback when format is not otherwise discernibledefaultParser(Parser) — fallback when response Content-Type is absent or unmatched RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .serializer(JsonSerializer.DEFAULT, CborSerializer.DEFAULT, YamlSerializer.DEFAULT) .parser(JsonParser.DEFAULT, CborParser.DEFAULT, YamlParser.DEFAULT) .defaultSerializer(JsonSerializer.DEFAULT) .defaultParser(JsonParser.DEFAULT) .build(); RestClient derives the Accept header automatically from all registered parsers: Accept: application/json, application/cbor, application/yaml

When you call RestRequest.body(Object) (or the typed body helpers), the client needs a serializer to convert the POJO to bytes. Selection order: If the request carries an explicit Content-Type header, the matching serializer from the SerializerSet is used. If no explicit Content-Type is set, the defaultSerializer is used (falls back to JsonSerializer.DEFAULT if none configured). Override the format for one request by setting the Content-Type header: client.post("/api/items") .body(myBean) .header("Content-Type", "application/cbor") .run() .assertStatus().asCode().is(201);
documents.s: How the client selects a serializer for outbound bodies

documents.t: When you call ResponseBody.as(Class), the client reads the response Content-Type header and calls RestClient.getMatchingParser(contentType). Selection order: The ParserSet is queried for a parser whose media type matches the response Content-Type. If no match is found, defaultParser is used. If defaultParser is null, the first parser in the registry is used. If the registry is empty, JsonParser.DEFAULT is used as a last resort. // Server responds with Content-Type: application/cbor MyBean bean = client.get("/api/item/1") .run() .body().as(MyBean.class); // → CborParser selected automatically
documents.s: How the client selects a parser for inbound responses

documents.t: Force the server to respond in a specific format by setting the Accept header on the request: MyBean bean = client.get("/api/item/1") .header("Accept", "application/yaml") .run() .body().as(MyBean.class); // parsed with YamlParser The per-request header takes precedence over the client-wide default derived from the ParserSet.
documents.s: Overriding the Accept header per request

documents.t: For fine-grained control over media-type ordering, q-factors, or reuse across clients, build the registry objects directly: SerializerSet serializers = SerializerSet.create() .add(JsonSerializer.DEFAULT, CborSerializer.DEFAULT) .build(); ParserSet parsers = ParserSet.create() .add(JsonParser.DEFAULT, CborParser.DEFAULT) .build(); RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .serializers(serializers) .parsers(parsers) .build(); See Serializer Sets and Parser Sets for the full registry API.

Step What happens Client sends request Accept header = union of all registered parser media types Client sends body Content-Type = matched serializer's media type (explicit header wins) Server replies Content-Type response header drives parser selection in getMatchingParser() Fallback defaultParser → first registered parser → JsonParser.DEFAULT

Serializer Sets and Parser Sets — the underlying registry API POJO Marshalling — per-request language shortcuts ResponseBody — parsing the response body (NG; see Response Content for the classic client's ResponseContent) Request Content — setting the request body

All configurable properties described in the previous section have annotation equivalents that can be applied on classes or methods. In the section on the REST server API, we describe how to configure serializers and parsers using @XConfig annotations like those shown below: @Rest( path="/addressBook", title="Address Book REST API" ... ) @SerializerConfig(quoteChar="'") @RdfConfig(rdfxml_tab="5", addRootProperty="true") @MarshalledConfig(sortProperties="true", examples="Feed: ${F:AddressBook_example.json}") @BeanTypeApply(on="Address", value=@BeanType(properties="street,city,state")) public class AddressBookResource extends BasicRestServlet { ... } Config annotations defined on classes and methods can be applied to serializers and parsers using the following methods: MarshallingContext.BuilderapplyAnnotations(Class...)applyAnnotations(Object...) The following example shows how annotations defined on a dummy class can be applied to a serializer: @SerializerConfig(quoteChar="'") @BeanTypeApply(on="Address", value=@BeanType(properties="street,city,state")) public static class DummyClass {} WriterSerializer serializer = JsonSerializer.create().applyAnnotations(DummyClass.class).build(); String json = serializer.write(addressBean); Config annotations are provided for all serializers and parsers: MarshalledConfig CsvConfig HtmlConfig HtmlDocConfig JsonConfig JsonSchemaConfig MsgPackConfig OpenApiConfig ParserConfig PlainTextConfig SerializerConfig SoapXmlConfig UonConfig UrlEncodingConfig XmlConfig BsonConfig CborConfig HjsonConfig HoconConfig IniConfig JcsConfig Json5lConfig JsonlConfig MarkdownConfig ParquetConfig ProtobufConfig PrototextConfig TomlConfig YamlConfig Annotations normally applied to bean classes/methods/fields/parameters can also be programmatically attatched to beans by using the on or onClass annotation values as seen on the @BeanTypeApply annotation in the example above. Annotations can also be applied directly to serializers and parsers using the following method: MarshallingContext.Builderannotations(Annotation...) The following example shows a concrete implementation of an annotation can be applied to a serializer: public class Address {...} BeanType bt = new BeanTypeAnnotation("Address").properties("street,city,state"); WriterSerializer serializer = JsonSerializer.create().annotations(bt).build(); String json = serializer.write(addressBean); // Will print street,city,state Concrete annotation implementations are provided for all annotations. Any number of matching config or concrete annotations can be applied. They are applied in the order they are provided to the context. Therefore any values can be overridden. Config and concrete annotations also override any class or method level annotations @BeanType(properties="street,city") // Will be overridden public class Address {...} BeanType beanTypeAnnotation = new BeanTypeAnnotation("Address").properties("street,city,state"); WriterSerializer serializer = JsonSerializer.create().annotations(beanTypeAnnotation).build(); String json = serializer.write(addressBean); // Will print street,city,state

Serializers and parsers have a wide variety of configurable settings. Their builders all extend from the MarshallingContext.Builder class that allows you to easily construct new instances from scratch or build upon existing instances. For example, the following code shows how to configure a JSON serializer: WriterSerializer serializer = JsonSerializer .create() // Create a JsonSerializer.Builder .simpleMode() // Simple mode .ws() // Use whitespace .sq() // Use single quotes .sortProperties() // Sort bean properties by name .build(); // Create a JsonSerializer However, each of the serializers and parsers already contain reusable instances with common configurations. For example, JSON has the following predefined reusable serializers and parsers: JsonSerializerDEFAULTDEFAULT_READABLEJson5SerializerDEFAULT DEFAULT_READABLEJsonParserDEFAULT DEFAULT_STRICT These can be used directly, as follows: // Serialize a POJO to LAX JSON. String json = Json5Serializer.DEFAULT.write(myPojo); For performance reasons, serializers and parsers are immutable. However, they can be 'copied' and modified using the copy() method. // Clone and customize an existing serializer. WriterSerializer serializer = Json5Serializer.DEFAULT .copy() // Create a new builder with copied settings. .quoteChar('"') // Use a different quote character. .build(); Default values for configurable settings can be set globally using either system properties or environment variables. For example, the default useWhitespace setting can be set by either the system property WriterSerializer.useWhitespace or environment variable WRITERSERIALIZER_USEWHITESPACE. The builder setters will identify when default values can be set this way.

The settings above are context-level — baked into an immutable serializer/parser when it is built. Many of the same settings can also be overridden per-request at the session level via Session.Builder.property(String, Object), without rebuilding the context. See Serializers and Parsers for the override mechanism (short vs. fully-qualified property names, automatic string coercion, and REST integration). The tables below are the complete catalog of per-session properties, grounded in the MarshallingSession hierarchy and its serializer/parser session subclasses (SerializerSession, ParserSession, WriterSerializerSession, and the per-format session classes).

These properties are available on all sessions regardless of format: Property Type Session Class Description locale / MarshallingSession.locale Locale MarshallingSession Locale used for date/number formatting timeZone / MarshallingSession.timeZone TimeZone MarshallingSession Time zone used for date/calendar types mediaType / MarshallingSession.mediaType MediaType MarshallingSession The media type being produced or consumed debug Boolean ContextSession Enable debug mode

These properties apply to all serializers: Property Type Session Class Description addBeanTypes boolean SerializerSession Add _type properties to beans when type cannot be inferred from reflection addRootType boolean SerializerSession Add _type to the root object keepNullProperties boolean SerializerSession Serialize null bean properties (default: false) trimStrings boolean SerializerSession Trim whitespace from serialized strings sortCollections boolean SerializerSession Sort collections before serializing sortMaps boolean SerializerSession Sort maps by key before serializing trimEmptyCollections boolean SerializerSession Omit empty collections from output trimEmptyMaps boolean SerializerSession Omit empty maps from output initialDepth / BeanTraverseSession.initialDepth int BeanTraverseSession Initial depth for indentation maxIndent / WriterSerializerSession.maxIndent int WriterSerializerSession Maximum indentation depth for whitespace formatting quoteChar / WriterSerializerSession.quoteChar char WriterSerializerSession Quote character for string values uriContext UriContext SerializerSession Context for URI resolution
These properties apply to all parsers: Property Type Session Class Description trimStrings / ParserSession.trimStrings boolean ParserSession Trim whitespace from parsed string values

JSON / JSON5​ Property Type Session Class Description escapeSolidus / JsonSerializerSession.escapeSolidus boolean JsonSerializerSession Prefix / characters with \ escape validateEnd / JsonParserSession.validateEnd boolean JsonParserSession Validate that no trailing content follows the parsed value // Escape forward slashes in URLs String json = JsonSerializer.DEFAULT .createSession() .property("escapeSolidus", true) .build() .write("http://example.com"); // Produces: "http:\/\/example.com" // Require clean end-of-input JsonParser.DEFAULT .createSession() .property("validateEnd", true) .build() .read("{\"a\":1}", JsonMap.class); // ok UON (URL-Encoded Object Notation)​ Property Type Session Class Description encoding / UonSerializerSession.encoding boolean UonSerializerSession Percent-encode non-valid URI characters paramFormat / UonSerializerSession.paramFormat ParamFormat UonSerializerSession Format for parameter values (UON or PLAINTEXT) validateEnd / UonParserSession.validateEnd boolean UonParserSession Validate that no trailing content follows the parsed value // Use plain-text parameter format (no UON escaping) String uon = UonSerializer.DEFAULT .createSession() .property("paramFormat", ParamFormat.PLAINTEXT) .build() .write("hello world"); // Produces: hello world URL Encoding​ Property Type Session Class Description expandedParams / UrlEncodingSerializerSession.expandedParams boolean UrlEncodingSerializerSession Serialize array/collection bean properties as separate key=value pairs expandedParams / UrlEncodingParserSession.expandedParams boolean UrlEncodingParserSession Parse repeated keys as array/collection values // Serialize array as repeated parameters: a=1&a=2&a=3 String urlencoded = UrlEncodingSerializer.DEFAULT .createSession() .property("expandedParams", true) .build() .write(JsonMap.of("a", new int[]{1, 2, 3})); XML​ Property Type Session Class Description enableNamespaces / XmlSerializerSession.enableNamespaces boolean XmlSerializerSession Include XML namespaces in output addNamespaceUrisToRoot / XmlSerializerSession.addNamespaceUrisToRoot boolean XmlSerializerSession Add xmlns:x attributes to the root element autoDetectNamespaces / XmlSerializerSession.autoDetectNamespaces boolean XmlSerializerSession Auto-detect namespace usage before serializing defaultNamespace / XmlSerializerSession.defaultNamespace String XmlSerializerSession Default namespace (e.g. "juneau:http://www.apache.org/juneau/") textNodeDelimiter / XmlSerializerSession.textNodeDelimiter String XmlSerializerSession Delimiter for mixed-content text nodes preserveRootElement / XmlParserSession.preserveRootElement boolean XmlParserSession Preserve the root element name when parsing into a generic JsonMap validating / XmlParserSession.validating boolean XmlParserSession Validate XML against its schema during parsing // Parse XML preserving the root element name JsonMap result = XmlParser.DEFAULT .createSession() .property("preserveRootElement", true) .build() .read("1", JsonMap.class); // result = {"root": {"a": "1"}} HTML​ Property Type Session Class Description addKeyValueTableHeaders / HtmlSerializerSession.addKeyValueTableHeaders boolean HtmlSerializerSession Add key / value column headers to bean/map tables detectLinksInStrings / HtmlSerializerSession.detectLinksInStrings boolean HtmlSerializerSession Auto-convert URL strings to anchor tags detectLabelParameters / HtmlSerializerSession.detectLabelParameters boolean HtmlSerializerSession Look for label query parameters in URLs for anchor text labelParameter / HtmlSerializerSession.labelParameter String HtmlSerializerSession Query parameter name to use as the anchor label (default: "label") uriAnchorText / HtmlSerializerSession.uriAnchorText AnchorText HtmlSerializerSession Strategy for generating anchor text from URIs // Use a custom label parameter name String html = HtmlSerializer.DEFAULT .createSession() .property("labelParameter", "title") .build() .write("http://example.com?title=My+Page"); // Anchor text will be "My Page" // Disable auto-link detection String html2 = HtmlSerializer.DEFAULT .createSession() .property("detectLinksInStrings", false) .build() .write("http://example.com"); // Produces plain text, not an tag CSV​ Property Type Session Class Description byteArrayFormat / CsvSerializerSession.byteArrayFormat ByteArrayFormat CsvSerializerSession Format for byte[] values (e.g. BASE64, HEX, SEMICOLON_DELIMITED) allowNestedStructures / CsvSerializerSession.allowNestedStructures boolean CsvSerializerSession Allow nested bean structures in CSV output nullValue / CsvSerializerSession.nullValue String CsvSerializerSession String representation for null values (default: ) // Use "N/A" for null values in CSV output String csv = CsvSerializer.DEFAULT .createSession() .property("nullValue", "N/A") .build() .write(JsonMap.of("name", null, "age", 30));
Serializers and Parsers — the per-session override mechanism and REST integration.

The Juneau REST server ships with a four-class convention-endpoints mixin pack in org.apache.juneau.rest.server.convention covering the small set of de-facto-standard URLs that every public-facing service eventually has to wire up by hand: the browser favicon, the SEO contracts (robots.txt, sitemap.xml), a JSON deployment-introspection endpoint, and the RFC 8615 /.well-known/* discovery root. Each mixin is a single-purpose @Rest-annotated resource designed to be grafted into your servlet via @Rest(mixins=...) — pick the URLs you want, configure them via a @Bean factory, and leave the rest unmounted.

Mixin Default paths Default body Why it exists FaviconMixin /favicon.ico Juneau-branded juneau-favicon.ico shipped on the framework classpath. Stops every browser from logging a 404 on /favicon.ico. SeoMixin /robots.txt, /sitemap.xml User-agent: *\nDisallow: /\n (deny-all) and an empty <urlset>. RFC 9309 + sitemaps.org compliance. Deny-all default is intentional — opt into indexing explicitly. VersionMixin /version, /info, /about JSON map sourced from META-INF/MANIFEST.MF, git.properties, and the running JVM version. Deployment introspection. All three URLs return the same payload (they are synonyms). WellKnownMixin /.well-known/security.txt None — returns 404 Not Found until the importer configures a body. RFC 9116 security.txt discovery; absence is itself meaningful, so v1 ships with no placeholder. All four endpoints carry @OpSwagger(ignore = true) on their handlers — they show up in the runtime URL space but are excluded from any Swagger / OpenAPI spec generated by the api-docs mixin pack. Convention URLs are not API-meaningful, and shipping them in the spec just clutters the contract.
documents.s: The four mixins at a glance

documents.t: Each mixin is independent — drop in only the ones you need. The examples below build on plain RestServlet. If you're building on BasicRestServlet/BasicRestResource instead, note that FaviconMixin (along with ErrorMixin, HtdocMixin, and StatsMixin) is already baked in by default — re-declaring mixins=FaviconMixin.class on the subclass is redundant but harmless, since the mixin walk collects mixins in parent-to-child order and dedupes by class identity (see Mixin Sub-Contexts for the walk details). The plan-A composition mounts all four with builder-driven configuration: @Rest( path = "/api", mixins = { FaviconMixin.class, SeoMixin.class, VersionMixin.class, WellKnownMixin.class } ) public class ApiResource extends RestServlet { @RestGet("/items") public List<Item> items() { ... } @Bean FaviconMixin favicon() { return FaviconMixin.create().bytes(myLogoBytes).build(); } @Bean SeoMixin seo() { return SeoMixin.create() .robotsAllow("*", "/") .sitemapEntry("https://example.com/api/items") .build(); } @Bean VersionMixin version() { // Defaults read MANIFEST.MF + git.properties + JVM version when no entries are set; // override programmatically here: return VersionMixin.create() .entry("name", "my-app") .entry("version", "1.2.3") .fromGitProperties() .fromJavaVersion() .build(); } @Bean WellKnownMixin wellKnown() { return WellKnownMixin.create() .securityTxt("Contact: security@example.com\nExpires: 2027-01-01T00:00:00Z\n") .build(); } } The framework's mixin walk picks up each @Bean <MixinClass> factory before falling back to no-arg construction (see Mixin Sub-Contexts for the underlying lookup), so the host controls the configuration end-to-end without subclassing. Mixins without a @Bean factory get default behavior: FaviconMixin serves the framework icon; SeoMixin returns deny-all robots and an empty sitemap; VersionMixin reads MANIFEST.MF + git.properties from the framework classloader; WellKnownMixin returns 404 on /.well-known/security.txt.

Each mixin is a fully-fledged @Rest-annotated resource and can also be subclassed and mounted as its own top-level servlet: @Rest(paths = {"/favicon.ico"}) public class FaviconResource extends FaviconMixin { } Both deployment styles (mixin into an existing servlet vs. mount as a sibling servlet) work the same way under Spring Boot and under the Jetty microservice — the VersionMixin_JettyMicroservice_Test and VersionMixin_Springboot_Test parity tests cover both paths end-to-end.

Cache-Control: max-age=2592000, public (30 days) by default — favicons rarely change and browsers re-fetch frequently when uncached. Override via Builder.cacheControl(String). Content-Type: image/x-icon. Builder methods: bytes(byte[]), classpath(String), cacheControl(String). bytes and classpath are mutually exclusive — whichever is set last wins. A classpath path that resolves to a missing resource silently falls back to the framework default.

/robots.txt content type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8. Default body is the deny-all User-agent: *\nDisallow: /\n. Replace via Builder.robotsAllow(String, String...) / robotsDisallow(...) for rule-based policies, or robotsTxt(String) for a fully-formed body (useful when you need Sitemap: / Crawl-delay: directives the rule builder doesn't model). /sitemap.xml content type: application/xml; charset=UTF-8. Default body is an empty <urlset>. Add entries via Builder.sitemapEntry(String url) (URL-only) or the four-arg form with lastmod, changefreq, and priority.

Content-Type: application/json — format-pinned via RestResponse.getDirectWriter("application/json") so the endpoint serves JSON even on a vanilla RestServlet host that hasn't wired up JSON serializers explicitly. All three URLs (/version, /info, /about) currently return the same JSON payload. Future iterations may differentiate (e.g. /info = condensed, /about = full). Default builder chain: fromManifest() + fromGitProperties() + fromJavaVersion(). The manifest reader prefers a META-INF/MANIFEST.MF whose Implementation-Title is set; if no candidate has one, the first manifest found wins. Spring Boot fat-jar caveat: the no-arg reader uses the framework classloader, so to see the importer's app manifest under a fat jar call Builder.fromManifest(importerClassLoader) (or Builder.fromManifest(Manifest) with a pre-loaded manifest). Programmatic override: Builder.entry(String, String) / Builder.entries(Map). Calling any builder method suppresses the default chain — you opt into each fromXxx() call you want.

Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8. No default body — per RFC 9116 the file's presence is itself meaningful. If you don't call Builder.securityTxt(String), the endpoint returns 404 Not Found. Document loudly to your ops team. The class reserves room for future /.well-known/* entries (OIDC discovery, change-password, etc.); v1 ships only security.txt to stay scoped.

@Rest(mixins=...) — the underlying composition primitive. Mixin Sub-Contexts — host-to-mixin RestContext inheritance and bean-store layering. Static-Files Mixin — sibling mixin pack for arbitrary classpath-served assets. API-Docs Mixin Pack — Swagger / OpenAPI / Redoc mixins.

Converters can be thought of as "post-processors" for response POJOs before they get passed to the serializer. Converters are associated with resource classes and methods via the following: RestconvertersRestOpconverters Example // GET person request handler. // Traversable conversion enabled to allow nodes in returned POJO tree to be addressed. // Queryable conversion enabled to allow returned POJO to be searched/viewed/sorted. @RestGet( path="/people/{id}/*", converters={Traversable.class,Queryable.class} ) public Person getPerson(@Path("id") int id) { return findPerson(id); } Juneau defines the following converters out-of-the-box: RestConverterQueryable - Provides BeanQuery search/view/sort/paging parameters that transform the response before it is serialized.Traversable - Allows nodes in the POJO response tree to be individually accessed through additional path info on the request.Introspectable - Allows method calls to be made on the response POJO, and for the result of that method call to be serialized as the response.

As of 10.0, Queryable runs on the shared BeanQuery engine. A response that is a Collection or array of beans (or of Maps) can be searched, projected, sorted and paged with these request parameters, which are bound by BeanQueryRequest: Parameter Meaning search Comma-separated column=expression clauses, e.g. name=$contains(smith),age=$gte(18) view Comma-separated columns to return, in order. Rows come back as maps of those columns sort Comma-separated sort columns; append :desc (or -) for descending position 0-based index of the first row (negative is HTTP 400) limit Maximum rows. Defaults to defaultLimit (100) and is clamped to maxLimit (1000) opts key=value options, e.g. counts=true GET /people?search=age=$gte(18)&sort=name,age:desc&view=name,age&position=20&limit=10 A response that is not tabular (not a collection or array, or whose elements are plain strings, numbers, dates or other scalars) is returned unchanged and the parameters are ignored. An empty collection is also returned unchanged. A bean type gets one cached context per element class; Map rows get a context per request, with one column per key of the first row (types inferred from that row's values). A bad column or option (for example ?sort=noSuchColumn) throws BeanQuerySyntaxException, which the server maps to HTTP 400 with an X-BeanQuery-Error: UNKNOWN_COLUMN header (the BeanQuerySyntaxException.Code name) and, with problem details on, a "code" member in the body. A BeanQueryExecutionException becomes HTTP 500 with the body Query execution failed.; the cause is logged, not sent. See BeanQuery: REST binding. Example — counts ?opts=counts=true adds count headers. The body stays a bare list, and each header is set only when that count was computed: GET /people?search=age=$gte(18)&opts=counts=true X-BeanQuery-Total: 42 X-BeanQuery-Matched: 7

Register a QueryableSettings bean to tune the engine per resource. Each setting you leave unset keeps the BeanQuery default, so the defaults are not duplicated here. Example @Rest(converters=Queryable.class) public class PeopleResource extends BasicRestServlet { @Bean public QueryableSettings queryableSettings() { // $regex is allowed by default; allowRegex(false) opts this resource out. return QueryableSettings.create().defaultLimit(20).maxLimit(500).build(); } @RestGet("/people") public List<Person> getPeople() {...} } Setting Default Meaning defaultLimit(int) 100 Page size when the request has no limit maxLimit(Integer) 1000 Largest page size; larger requests are clamped (null = no cap) allowRegex(boolean) true The $regex operator; false makes it a 400 (REGEX_DISABLED) regexTimeout(Duration) 50 ms Time budget for all regex matching in one query countPolicy(CountPolicy) IF_REQUESTED Which counts are computed maxSearchClauses / maxSortKeys / maxSearchLength / maxExpressionDepth 64 / 8 / 4096 / 16 Caps on the request All of these are trusted server-side settings; none is ever read from request data.

Without the converter, take a BeanQueryRequest argument and run the engine yourself. The argument binds all six parameters and documents them in Swagger automatically: private static final InMemoryBeanQueryContext<Person> PEOPLE = InMemoryBeanQueryContext.create(Person.class).build(); @RestGet("/people") public List<Person> getPeople(BeanQueryRequest q) { try (var s = PEOPLE.getSession(people)) { return s.find(q).rows(); } } A concrete @Request class like BeanQueryRequest must have a public no-arg constructor and a setter for every annotated getter; this is checked when the operation table is built (see the V10 Migration Guide).

Example — DataTables server-side processing The optional juneau-console-datatables module ships a DataTablesRequest bean that models the DataTables server-side request (draw/start/length/search/order/columns), and a DataTablesQuery adapter that maps it onto a BeanQuery session and returns a DataTablesResults envelope. private static final InMemoryBeanQueryContext<MyRow> ROWS = InMemoryBeanQueryContext.create(MyRow.class).build(); @RestPost(path="/rows") public DataTablesResults<MyRow> getRows(@Content DataTablesRequest request) { try (var session = ROWS.getSession(loadRows())) { return DataTablesQuery.run(request, session); } } The caller owns the session, so the same adapter works over the in-memory engine or a SQL-backed one. A malformed search expression throws BeanQuerySyntaxException, which propagates to HTTP 400 with the X-BeanQuery-Error header; JuneauDataTables.ajax shows the server's message to the user. See the BeanQuery package topic for the engine itself.

The juneau-console-datatables module also ships thin, first-party browser-side helpers so a server-rendered table can be upgraded into a DataTables grid without hand-duplicating column lists or serving the wiring yourself: DataTablesColumns - Generates the DataTables columns array (one data/title/orderable/searchable entry per column) from a bean's property order, using @Schema(title) titles (falling back to a humanized property name), so the browser-side column list isn't duplicated from the server bean.DataTablesTable - Builds a plain, DataTables-ready HTML <table> DOM bean (stable id, clean <thead>/<tbody>, marked with data-juneau-datatable) from a collection of rows. Rendered by any Juneau HTML serializer — no coupling to the marshall-core HtmlDocSerializer.DataTablesMixin - A @Rest(mixins=...) mixin that serves the first-party juneau-datatables.js glue script at /juneau-datatables.js. The glue auto-initializes every <table data-juneau-datatable> on the page by calling $(table).DataTable(opts) once the DataTables library is present. DataTables library is caller-provided This is an Apache project, and the DataTables library's license is not an ASF category-A license. Juneau therefore does not bundle DataTables' own JS/CSS (nor jQuery) — the only asset it ships is the thin first-party juneau-datatables.js glue. Reference the DataTables library from a CDN or self-host it, and wire it into the page yourself via @HtmlDocConfig. @HtmlDocConfig is resolved per endpoint / per resource-class hierarchy — a mixin cannot inject page assets into your other endpoints — so add the wire-points to the resource (or op) that renders the table: @Rest(path="/releases", mixins=DataTablesMixin.class) @HtmlDocConfig( stylesheet="${S:juneau.datatables.cssUrl\\:https\\://cdn.datatables.net/2.1.8/css/dataTables.dataTables.min.css}", head={ "<script src='${S:juneau.datatables.jqueryUrl\\:https\\://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.7.1.min.js}'></script>", "<script src='${S:juneau.datatables.jsUrl\\:https\\://cdn.datatables.net/2.1.8/js/dataTables.min.js}'></script>", "<script src='servlet:/juneau-datatables.js'></script>" } ) public class ReleasesResource extends BasicRestServlet { @RestGet public Table getReleases() { return DataTablesTable.of("releases", releases, Release.class); } } The URLs are SVL-resolvable, so the DataTables distribution can be overridden per environment without code changes.

The CsvParser class is used to parse CSV into POJOs. The class hierarchy for the builder of this parser is: Context.BuilderMarshallingContextable.BuilderParser.BuilderReaderParser.BuilderCsvParser.Builder Refer to the builder javadocs for configurable settings. The following pre-configured parsers are provided for convenience: CsvParserDEFAULT

Target Type Parsing Strategy Collection<Bean> / Bean[] Header row → property names; each data row → one bean. Collection<Map> / Map[] Header row → map keys; each data row → one map. Collection<SimpleType> / SimpleType[] value column; each row → one value coerced to element type. Single Bean Header row + one data row → one bean. Single Map Header row + one data row → one map. Object Returns a JsonList of JsonMap entries (all values as strings).

Cell values are strings in CSV. The parser automatically coerces them to the target property/element type using the same type conversion machinery used by all Juneau parsers: Primitive types and their wrappers (int, long, double, boolean, etc.) String Enum types (by name) BigDecimal, BigInteger Date/time types (Date, Calendar, Temporal subtypes) — as ISO 8601 strings Duration — as ISO 8601 duration strings (e.g. PT1H30M) Any type whose ClassMeta supports convertToType(String)
The unquoted literal string null in a CSV cell is parsed as Java null. A quoted "null" cell is parsed as the Java String "null".

The parser handles all RFC 4180 quoted field constructs: "hello, world" → hello, world (comma inside quoted field) "line1\nline2" → line1\nline2 (newline inside quoted field) "say ""hi""" → say "hi" (doubled quotes → single quote)

By default, CSV columns that do not match any bean property are silently ignored (the ignoreUnknownBeanProperties parser setting applies). To throw on unknown properties, configure the parser: CsvParser p = CsvParser.create() .disableIgnoreMissingSetters() .build();

Object swaps registered on the parser are applied during cell value conversion: CsvParser p = CsvParser.create().swaps(DateSwap.class).build(); List<Event> events = p.read(csv, List.class, Event.class);
CsvParser consumes input of media type text/csv.

The CsvSerializer class is used to serialize POJOs into CSV. The class hierarchy for the builder of this serializer is: Context.BuilderMarshallingContextable.BuilderMarshallingTraverseContext.BuilderSerializer.BuilderWriterSerializer.BuilderCsvSerializer.Builder Refer to the builder javadocs for configurable settings. The following pre-configured serializers are provided for convenience: CsvSerializerDEFAULT

// Serialize a list of beans to CSV List<Person> people = List.of(new Person("Alice", 30), new Person("Bob", 25)); String csv = CsvSerializer.DEFAULT.write(people); // Creates a custom serializer CsvSerializer s = CsvSerializer.create() .swaps(DateSwap.class) .build(); String csv = s.write(people); // Use the Csv marshaller for convenience String csv = Csv.of(people);

Beans are serialized as a header row followed by one data row per bean: public class Person { public String name; public int age; } List<Person> people = List.of(new Person("Alice", 30), new Person("Bob", 25)); CsvSerializer.DEFAULT.write(people); name,age Alice,30 Bob,25 Maps are serialized using the keys of the first map as the header row: List<Map<String,Object>> rows = List.of( Map.of("city", "Seattle", "pop", 750000), Map.of("city", "Portland", "pop", 640000) ); CsvSerializer.DEFAULT.write(rows); city,pop Seattle,750000 Portland,640000 Simple values are serialized with a single value column: List<String> values = List.of("alpha", "beta", "gamma"); CsvSerializer.DEFAULT.write(values); value alpha beta gamma

Values that contain commas, double-quote characters, or newlines are automatically enclosed in double quotes. Double-quote characters inside a quoted value are escaped by doubling them: List.of(new Person("Smith, John", 40)); // name contains a comma // Produces: name,age // "Smith, John",40 List.of(new Person("say \"hi\"", 40)); // name contains quotes // Produces: name,age // "say ""hi""",40

Java null is serialized as the unquoted literal null. A Java String with the value "null" is serialized as the quoted string "null" to distinguish it: new Bean(null, "null") // Produces: a,b // null,"null"
CsvSerializer produces output of media type text/csv.

The org.apache.juneau.marshall.csv package provides a fully-implemented CSV (Comma Separated Values) serializer and parser. CSV support is included in juneau-marshall. Maven <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency>

CSV is an inherently tabular format: each row represents one entry and each column represents one field. Juneau models this as: Input type CSV output Collection<Bean> or Bean[] Header row = property names; one data row per bean. Collection<Map> or Map[] Header row = keys of the first map; one data row per map. Collection<SimpleType> or SimpleType[] Single value column header; one data row per value. Single Bean Header row + one data row. Single Map Header row + one data row.

// A simple bean public class Person { public String name; public int age; public Person() {} public Person(String name, int age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; } } // Serialize a list of beans to CSV List<Person> people = List.of(new Person("Alice", 30), new Person("Bob", 25)); String csv = CsvSerializer.DEFAULT.write(people); // Produces: // name,age // Alice,30 // Bob,25 // Parse it back List<Person> parsed = CsvParser.DEFAULT.read(csv, List.class, Person.class); Or use the convenience marshaller: String csv = Csv.of(people); List<Person> parsed = Csv.to(csv, List.class, Person.class);

The serializer and parser comply with RFC 4180: Fields containing commas, double-quote characters, or newlines are enclosed in double quotes. Double-quote characters inside a quoted field are escaped by doubling them ("" → "). Both CRLF and LF line endings are accepted on input. The Java null value serializes as the unquoted literal null.

Java null is serialized as the unquoted string null and is parsed back as Java null. A Java String with the value "null" is serialized as a quoted "null" to distinguish it. name,value null,"null" The first row's name cell parses back to Java null. The value cell parses back to the Java String "null".

Object swaps registered via .swaps(...) work exactly as with other Juneau serializers/parsers. Swap classes transform bean property values before serialization and unswap them during parsing. CsvSerializer s = CsvSerializer.create().swaps(DateSwap.class).build(); CsvParser p = CsvParser.create().swaps(DateSwap.class).build();

@CsvConfig applies to both CsvSerializer and CsvParser on a REST class or method (see Context Annotations). Its only attribute today is rank. @Csv is a class/method/field marker (its only attribute is description), and @CsvApply applies it to other classes/members via on()/onClass() (see Dynamically Applied Annotations).
CSV Serializers CSV Parsers Token-Streaming Basics — CSV is a PARTIAL streaming format (record cursor only); a CSV row isn't a clean structural token sequence.
Custom error messages allow you to provide contextual information when BCT assertions fail. This makes test failures more informative and helps identify issues faster during debugging.

BCT supports custom error messages through a Supplier<String> parameter in all assertion methods. This provides: Lazy evaluation - Messages are only generated when assertions fail Format support - Use Shorts.fs() for convenient formatted messages with arguments Flexible composition - Combine custom messages with default assertion messages

// Simple static message assertBean(() -> "User validation failed", user, "email", "john@example.com"); // More descriptive context assertBean(() -> "Expected user to be active but was inactive", user, "isActive", "true"); // Test context information assertBean(() -> "Order status check for order #12345", order, "status", "PENDING");

The Shorts.fs() method provides a convenient way to create message suppliers with format arguments: import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.fs; // Single placeholder String testName = "validateUser"; assertBean(fs("Test %s failed", testName), result, "status", "SUCCESS"); // Multiple placeholders String userName = "Alice"; int iteration = 5; assertBean(fs("User %s validation failed on iteration %s", userName, iteration), user, "isValid", "true"); // Contextual information String orderId = "ORD-123"; String expectedStatus = "COMPLETED"; assertBean(fs("Order %s expected status %s", orderId, expectedStatus), order, "status", expectedStatus);

// Lazy evaluation for expensive computation assertBean(() -> "Test failed at " + Instant.now(), user, "lastLogin", expectedTime); // Complex context information assertBean(() -> { return String.format("Test failed in %s on thread %s", Thread.currentThread().getName(), Thread.currentThread().getId()); }, result, "status", "SUCCESS"); // Conditional message generation assertBean(() -> { if (isDebugMode()) { return "Debug: Full stack trace available"; } else { return "Test failed - enable debug for details"; } }, user, "email", "john@example.com");

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.fs; @Test void testMultipleOrders() { List<Order> orders = getOrders(); for (int i = 0; i < orders.size(); i++) { Order order = orders.get(i); assertBean(fs("Order validation failed at index %s", i), order, "status,total", "PENDING,99.99"); } }

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.fs; @Test void testUsersByRole() { Map<String, User> usersByRole = getUsersByRole(); for (Map.Entry<String, User> entry : usersByRole.entrySet()) { String role = entry.getKey(); User user = entry.getValue(); assertBean(fs("User validation failed for role: %s", role), user, "role,isActive", role + ",true"); } }
@Test void testOrderProcessing() { Order order = processOrder(); assertBean(() -> String.format("Order processed at %s, validation failed", LocalDateTime.now()), order, "status", "COMPLETED"); }

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.fs; @Test void testConfiguration() { Config config = loadConfig(); String environment = System.getProperty("env", "unknown"); assertBean(fs("Config validation failed in environment: %s", environment), config, "database.host,database.port", "localhost,5432"); }

Use custom messages when: Testing in loops or with multiple iterations Test failures need additional context Debugging complex test scenarios Testing with dynamic or generated data Running tests in different environments Testing concurrent or parallel scenarios Avoid custom messages when: The test is simple and self-explanatory The assertion failure message is already clear Adding message overhead provides no value

Be specific: Include relevant context (IDs, names, indices) Be concise: Keep messages short but informative Include values: Add expected/actual values when helpful Add context: Include loop indices, test phases, environment info Use suppliers for expensive operations: Defer message generation until needed Avoid sensitive data: Don't include passwords, tokens, or PII in messages

// Bad - expensive computation always executed String heavyComputation = performExpensiveOperation(); assertBean(() -> "Test failed with: " + heavyComputation, user, "status", "ACTIVE"); // Good - computation only happens on failure assertBean(() -> "Test failed with: " + performExpensiveOperation(), user, "status", "ACTIVE");

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.fs; // Set custom converter in @BeforeEach @BeforeEach void setUp() { var converter = BasicBeanConverter.builder() .defaultSettings() .addStringifier(LocalDate.class, (conv,date) -> date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE)) .build(); setConverter(converter); } // Use custom message with the converter assertBean(fs("Date validation failed for user %s", userId), user, "birthDate", "1990-01-15"); @AfterEach void tearDown() { resetConverter(); }

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.fs; @ParameterizedTest @ValueSource(strings = {"alice@example.com", "bob@example.com", "carol@example.com"}) void testUserEmails(String email) { User user = findUserByEmail(email); assertBean(fs("User validation failed for email: %s", email), user, "email,isVerified", email + ",true"); }

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.fs; @TestFactory Stream<DynamicTest> testOrders() { return orders.stream() .map(order -> DynamicTest.dynamicTest( "Test Order #" + order.getId(), () -> assertBean( fs("Order %s validation failed", order.getId()), order, "status", "PENDING"))); }

@Test void testOrderProcessing() { Order order = createOrder(); // Process order processOrder(order); // Validate with detailed context assertBean(() -> String.format( "Order validation failed:
" + " Order ID: %s
" + " Customer: %s
" + " Processing Time: %s
" + " Thread: %s", order.getId(), order.getCustomer().getName(), Duration.between(order.getCreatedAt(), Instant.now()), Thread.currentThread().getName() ), order, "status,isPaid,isShipped", "COMPLETED,true,true"); } Output on failure: org.opentest4j.AssertionFailedError: Order validation failed: Order ID: ORD-123 Customer: John Doe Processing Time: PT2.5S Thread: main Expected: COMPLETED Actual: PENDING

@Test void testUserLifecycle() { // Creation phase User user = createUser(); assertBean(() -> "User creation phase failed", user, "status", "NEW"); // Activation phase activateUser(user); assertBean(() -> "User activation phase failed", user, "status", "ACTIVE"); // Verification phase verifyUser(user); assertBean(() -> "User verification phase failed", user, "status,isVerified", "ACTIVE,true"); }

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.fs; @Test void testBatchProcessing() { List<Order> orders = loadOrders(); for (int i = 0; i < orders.size(); i++) { Order order = orders.get(i); processOrder(order); assertBean(fs( "Batch processing failed at index %s of %s, Order ID: %s", i, orders.size(), order.getId()), order, "status", "PROCESSED"); } }

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.fs; @Test void testUserPermissions() { User user = loadUser(); String expectedRole = user.isAdmin() ? "ADMIN" : "USER"; assertBean(fs( "Permission check failed for %s user (expected role: %s)", user.isAdmin() ? "admin" : "regular", expectedRole), user, "role,hasAccess", expectedRole + ",true"); }

Bean-Centric Testing Basics - Main BCT documentation Customization - Configuration via @BctConfig and BctConfiguration Stringifiers - Converting objects to strings Listifiers - Converting collection-like objects to lists Swappers - Transforming objects before processing PropertyExtractors - Custom property access logic

BCT provides flexible customization options through the @BctConfig annotation and the BctConfiguration class. These tools allow you to configure assertion behavior, customize property access, and extend BCT's capabilities to match your testing needs.
@BctConfig Annotation BctConfiguration Class Configuration Properties Custom Bean Converters Thread Safety Advanced Customization Topics

The @BctConfig annotation provides a declarative way to configure BCT settings for your tests. It can be applied at both the class level and method level, with method-level annotations taking precedence over class-level annotations.

import org.apache.juneau.bct.BctConfig; import org.apache.juneau.commons.lang.TriState; @BctConfig(sortMaps=TriState.TRUE) class MyTest { @Test @BctConfig(sortCollections=TriState.TRUE) void testSomething() { // sortMaps=true (from class), sortCollections=true (from method) assertBean(order, "items{0{name}}", "{{Laptop}}"); } }

Controls whether map entries are sorted by key before comparison in assertions. @BctConfig(sortMaps=TriState.TRUE) class MyTest { @Test void testMap() { // Map entries will be sorted before comparison Map<String, String> map = Map.of("zebra", "animal", "apple", "fruit"); assertBean(map, "apple,zebra", "fruit,animal"); } } Values: TriState.TRUE - Enable map sorting TriState.FALSE - Disable map sorting TriState.UNSET - Inherit from class-level annotation (default for method-level)

Controls whether collection elements are sorted before comparison in assertions. @BctConfig(sortCollections=TriState.TRUE) class MyTest { @Test void testList() { // List elements will be sorted before comparison List<String> list = Arrays.asList("zebra", "apple", "banana"); assertList(list, "apple", "banana", "zebra"); } } Values: TriState.TRUE - Enable collection sorting TriState.FALSE - Disable collection sorting TriState.UNSET - Inherit from class-level annotation (default for method-level)

Specifies a custom bean converter class to use for all assertions in the test. public static class MyCustomConverter extends BasicBeanConverter { public MyCustomConverter() { super(BasicBeanConverter.builder() .defaultSettings() .addStringifier(LocalDate.class, date -> date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE)) .build()); } } @BctConfig(beanConverter=MyCustomConverter.class) class MyTest { @Test void testWithCustomConverter() { // All assertions use MyCustomConverter assertBean(event, "date", "2023-12-01"); } } Requirements: The converter class must have a no-arg constructor The constructor will be made accessible if needed (for nested classes, etc.) If instantiation fails, the test will fail with a descriptive error message

Method-level annotations override class-level annotations for the same property. Properties not specified in the method annotation inherit from the class annotation. @BctConfig(sortMaps=TriState.TRUE, beanConverter=MyConverter.class) class MyTest { @Test @BctConfig(sortMaps=TriState.FALSE, sortCollections=TriState.TRUE) void testMethod() { // sortMaps=false (from method, overrides class) // sortCollections=true (from method) // beanConverter=MyConverter (from class, inherited) } @Test void testAnotherMethod() { // sortMaps=true (from class) // sortCollections=UNSET (default, not set) // beanConverter=MyConverter (from class) } }

To explicitly use the default converter when a class-level converter is set, use BasicBeanConverter.class: @BctConfig(beanConverter=MyConverter.class) class MyTest { @Test @BctConfig(beanConverter=BasicBeanConverter.class) void testWithDefaultConverter() { // Uses default converter, not MyConverter } }
The BctConfiguration class provides a programmatic API for configuring BCT settings. It's useful when you need dynamic configuration or want to set up converters in test setup methods.

import static org.apache.juneau.bct.BctConfiguration.*; @BeforeEach void setUp() { // Enable map sorting set(BCT_SORT_MAPS, true); // Enable collection sorting set(BCT_SORT_COLLECTIONS, true); // Set custom converter var converter = BasicBeanConverter.builder() .defaultSettings() .addStringifier(LocalDate.class, date -> date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE)) .build(); set(converter); } @AfterEach void tearDown() { // Clear all thread-local settings clear(); }

// Get a setting with a default value boolean sortMaps = BctConfiguration.get(BCT_SORT_MAPS, false); // Get a setting object (can check if set) StringSetting setting = BctConfiguration.get(BCT_SORT_MAPS); if (setting != null && setting.asBoolean()) { // Map sorting is enabled }

Settings can be set globally (affecting all threads) or thread-locally (affecting only the current thread). Thread-local settings take precedence. // Set global setting (affects all threads) BctConfiguration.setGlobal(BCT_SORT_MAPS, true); // Set thread-local setting (overrides global for this thread) BctConfiguration.set(BCT_SORT_MAPS, false); // Clear thread-local settings BctConfiguration.clear(); // Clear global settings BctConfiguration.clearGlobal();

Property name: "Bct.sortMaps" When enabled, map entries are sorted by key before comparison, ensuring consistent assertion results regardless of map implementation or insertion order. BctConfiguration.set(BctConfiguration.BCT_SORT_MAPS, true);

Property name: "Bct.sortCollections" When enabled, collection elements are sorted before comparison, ensuring consistent assertion results regardless of collection implementation or insertion order. BctConfiguration.set(BctConfiguration.BCT_SORT_COLLECTIONS, true);
Bean converters control how objects are accessed and converted to strings for comparison. BCT uses BasicBeanConverter.DEFAULT by default, but you can provide custom converters for specialized needs.

public static class MyCustomConverter extends BasicBeanConverter { public MyCustomConverter() { super(BasicBeanConverter.builder() .defaultSettings() // Add custom stringifier for LocalDate .addStringifier(LocalDate.class, (conv,date) -> date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE)) // Add custom stringifier for Money .addStringifier(Money.class, (conv,money) -> money.getAmount().toPlainString()) .build()); } }
@BctConfig(beanConverter=MyCustomConverter.class) class MyTest { @Test void testWithCustomConverter() { assertBean(order, "date,total", "2023-12-01,99.99"); } }

@BeforeEach void setUp() { var converter = BasicBeanConverter.builder() .defaultSettings() .addStringifier(LocalDate.class, (conv,date) -> date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE)) .build(); setConverter(converter); // BctAssertions.setConverter(...) - a thin passthrough to BctConfiguration.set(...) } @AfterEach void tearDown() { resetConverter(); // BctAssertions.resetConverter() - a thin passthrough to BctConfiguration.clear() }

Must have a no-arg constructor Constructor will be made accessible if needed (for nested classes, private constructors, etc.) If instantiation fails, a RuntimeException is thrown with a descriptive message

All configuration in BCT is thread-safe and uses thread-local storage. This ensures that: Parallel test execution doesn't interfere with each other's settings Each test thread has its own isolated configuration Settings are automatically cleared after each test when using @BctConfig
// Thread 1 BctConfiguration.set(BCT_SORT_MAPS, true); // Thread 2 (running in parallel) BctConfiguration.set(BCT_SORT_MAPS, false); // Each thread has its own setting - no interference

When using @BctConfig, settings are automatically cleared after each test method: @BctConfig(sortMaps=TriState.TRUE) class MyTest { @Test void test1() { // sortMaps is enabled } @Test void test2() { // sortMaps is still enabled (from class annotation) // But if test1 had method-level annotation, it would be cleared } }

For more advanced customization options, see: Stringifiers - Define how objects are converted to strings for comparison Listifiers - Convert collection-like objects to lists for testing Swappers - Transform objects before processing (unwrap Optional, Supplier, etc.)
