📄️2.6.2.2.1. Stringifiers Stringifiers define how specific types should be converted to strings for comparison in BCT assertions. They provide flexible, customizable string representations that can be tailored to your testing needs. 📄️2.6.2.2.2. Listifiers Listifiers convert collection-like objects into lists for use in BCT assertions. They provide a unified way to work with various collection types, iterators, streams, and other iterable data structures. 📄️2.6.2.2.3. Swappers Swappers transform objects before they are processed by BCT assertions. They provide a way to unwrap, evaluate, or transform objects into more testable forms. Swappers are particularly useful for wrapper types like Optional, Supplier, and Future.

Stringifiers define how specific types should be converted to strings for comparison in BCT assertions. They provide flexible, customizable string representations that can be tailored to your testing needs.

Listifiers convert collection-like objects into lists for use in BCT assertions. They provide a unified way to work with various collection types, iterators, streams, and other iterable data structures.

Swappers transform objects before they are processed by BCT assertions. They provide a way to unwrap, evaluate, or transform objects into more testable forms. Swappers are particularly useful for wrapper types like Optional, Supplier, and Future.
The classic REST client exposes the settings of the underlying Apache HttpClient through fluent builder methods and overridable factory methods.

Use this when the defaults are not enough, for example to change redirect handling, supply your own connection manager, or add request interceptors. These methods belong to the classic client (juneau-rest-client-classic), which is built on Apache HttpClient 4.5. The recommended juneau-rest-client configures its HTTP library through a pluggable transport instead.

All methods on the HttpClientBuilder class have been extended with fluent setters on RestClient.Builder. import org.apache.http.HttpRequestInterceptor; import org.apache.http.impl.conn.PoolingHttpClientConnectionManager; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.classic.*; public class CustomizedClientExample { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { HttpRequestInterceptor interceptor = (request, context) -> request.addHeader("X-Trace", "demo"); // Create a client with customized HttpClient settings. try (RestClient client = RestClient .create() .json() .disableRedirectHandling() .connectionManager(new PoolingHttpClientConnectionManager()) .addInterceptorFirst(interceptor) .build()) { System.out.println("Built " + client.getClass().getSimpleName()); } } }

Several methods are provided for customizing the underlying HTTP client and client builder classes: RestClient.BuilderhttpClientBuilder(HttpClientBuilder) - Set the client builder yourself.createHttpClientBuilder() - Override to create the client builder.createHttpClient() - Override to create the client.createConnectionManager() - Override to create the connection management.
Extending RestClient HTTP Transport Adapters HttpClientBuilder in the Apache HttpClient docs

juneau-console-datatables is an opt-in add-on (not bundled in juneau-distrib, the same precedent as juneau-rest-server-management-logging) that wires a DataTables grid's server-side processing contract onto BeanQuery — the request/response envelope, the query-building rules, and a first-party browser glue script. DataTables itself, jQuery, and their CSS remain caller-provided: they are not vendored (their license is not ASF category-A). <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-console-datatables</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency>

A DataTables-backed endpoint takes @Content DataTablesRequest and returns DataTablesResults<T> (or DataTablesResults<List<Object>> for array rows — see "Array rows" below). DataTablesMixin serves the browser glue script; the resource's own data endpoint is plain @RestOp: @Rest(path="/releases", mixins=DataTablesMixin.class) public class ReleaseResource extends BasicRestServlet { private final InMemoryBeanQueryContext<Release> ctx = InMemoryBeanQueryContext.create(Release.class).build(); @RestOp(method=POST, path="/query") public DataTablesResults<Release> query(@Content DataTablesRequest req) { try (var s = ctx.getSession(releases())) { return DataTablesQuery.run(req, s); } } } Restrict the endpoint to JSON Declare parsers=JsonParser.class on the data endpoint, e.g. @RestPost(path="/query", parsers=JsonParser.class). Under BasicUniversalConfig a form-urlencoded body would otherwise also bind to DataTablesRequest, but JuneauDataTables.ajax only ever sends JSON. DataTablesQuery.run(req, session) builds a BeanQuery from the request (via the public DataTablesQuery.toBeanQuery(req, ctx), usable standalone if you need to inspect or adjust the query before running it — for example to add a tenant guard with query.copy().eq("tenant", id).build()), executes it against the session, and maps the Page result onto the DataTables envelope (recordsTotal/recordsFiltered/data). The caller owns the session, so the same adapter works over the in-memory engine or a SQL-backed one.

JuneauDataTables.ajax(url, extra?) builds a DataTables ajax option object that POSTs the DataTables draw state as a JSON body (not DataTables' default form-encoded request) — matching @Content DataTablesRequest. extra is shallow-merged over the defaults (except contentType, which is always application/json). An extra.data object is merged into the outgoing body, and an extra.data function receives the draw state and may mutate it or return a replacement object — useful for a CSRF token or an active-filter toggle, without rebuilding the whole ajax option yourself. Any top-level body property that is not part of the DataTables request — one merged in through extra.data, or one a DataTables extension adds (SearchBuilder's searchBuilder, SearchPanes' searchPanes) — does not fail the parse: it is collected into DataTablesRequest.getExtra(), where the handler can read it. The adapter itself ignores it, so those extensions have no server-side effect unless your handler applies them. The same goes for DataTables 2's search.fixed() terms: they are parsed (Search.getFixed()) but not applied. For a table that needs no extra wiring at all, skip the inline JuneauDataTables.initAll() (already wired into the page's auto-init pass) sees data-juneau-datatable-ajax on a table whose options carry no ajax key, defaults serverSide: true, and installs ajax: JuneauDataTables.ajax(url) for you. A table that relies on a instead of declared columns (for example a server-rendered DataTablesTable) makes DataTables send integer data values, so pair it with runArrays (see "Array rows"), and keep the header order identical to the context's columns() order.

Each DataTablesRequest.Column.data resolves against the context's declared columns (BeanQueryContext.columns(), in declaration order): data value Resolves to A declared column name That column, as-is. All digits (e.g. "2") The n-th declared column, 0-based. null or "" Always skipped — no error, regardless of searchable/orderable. A dotted path or an unknown name, on a column with a non-blank per-column search or an order[] entry BeanQuerySyntaxException: Unknown column 'name'. A dotted path or an unknown name, on a column that is only a candidate for the global search, or never used No error — resolution is lazy; the column is simply left out. A column with searchable: false is ignored for both per-column and global search, and a column with orderable: false is ignored for sorting. Two DataTables columns resolving to the same key are merged (search terms are ANDed; a duplicate sort key keeps its first occurrence).

A per-column search box (columns[i].search.value) is a raw BeanQuery search expression for that one column ($eq(...), $in(...), $contains(...), …), parsed exactly like a server-side BeanQueryRequest.search term for that column. The global search box (search.value) has no column context, so it expands to an $or of one leaf per searchable, resolvable column, chosen by that column's SearchType: SearchType Global-search leaf TEXT, ID $contains VERSION $prefix ENUM $eqic (case-insensitive exact match) NUMERIC $eq, only when the term parses as a decimal number BOOLEAN $eq, only when the term is true or false (case-insensitive) TIMESTAMP $eq, only when the term is an ISO-8601 instant (e.g. 2026-09-30T00:00:00Z) A NUMERIC, BOOLEAN or TIMESTAMP column whose type the term does not parse as is left out of the $or — it is never an error. Java-only numeric spellings such as 1d, NaN, Infinity and hex floats are not treated as numeric. If only one column is eligible the $or collapses to a single leaf, and if none is eligible the global search adds nothing. Every column type participates, not just text. Column and sort-key counts are capped by the context's getMaxSearchClauses()/getMaxSortKeys() (checked against columns.size() and order.size() before any column is resolved). Exceeding either cap is a BeanQuerySyntaxException — raise the cap on the BeanQueryContext if a table legitimately needs more columns or sort keys than the default allows. Paging maps start/length onto the query's page window: length=-1 means all rows, and a negative start is clamped to 0.

DataTablesQuery.runArrays(req, session) is the run sibling for a table whose columns[i].data are integers. The query's view is set to every declared column in BeanQueryContext.columns() order and each row is flattened to a List<Object> in that same order, so data: n and the n-th array cell refer to the same column.

A malformed request (an unknown column referenced by a search or sort, a cap exceeded, a bad search expression, a disallowed operator or restricted column) throws BeanQuerySyntaxException, which DataTablesQuery.run/runArrays let propagate. The central RestContext.convertThrowable mapping turns it into HTTP 400 with an X-BeanQuery-Error: <CODE> header and the exception's message in the body, the same as every other BeanQueryRequest endpoint. DataTablesResults.error(draw, message) and the response's error field remain available as public API but the adapter no longer uses them. On the client, JuneauDataTables.ajax installs an xhr.dt listener. When a request fails with a status of 400 or more and carries the X-BeanQuery-Error header, the listener reads the server's message from the response body (falling back to Invalid query (<status>).), fires DataTables' error.dt event and honors DataTable.ext.errMode (default: a browser alert; 'none', 'throw' or a function also work) instead of showing the generic "Ajax error". Other failures keep DataTables' default handling. An unexpected failure in your bean accessors or query execution (BeanQueryExecutionException) is not caught here; it propagates to the central RestContext.convertThrowable mapping (HTTP 500), the same as every other BeanQueryRequest endpoint. Counts are always requested as CountRequest.BOTH, but the context's own CountPolicy still wins. recordsTotal and recordsFiltered are the long forms of the session's Page.total()/Page.matched(); when a count is absent, recordsFiltered is left unset and recordsTotal falls back to Page.matched() if that is present. DataTables' own protocol has no concept of an absent count, so there is no CountPolicy opt-out at this layer.

BeanQuery — the query bean, builder, and session this adapter sits on top of. Admin-Console Chrome — <@card type="datatables"> (see Building a Console Page) renders a DataTablesTable, and (server-side mode) wires the same data-juneau-datatable-ajax attribute this page describes. Worked example: the petstore Pets page (a server-mode table over BeanQuery) and Audit page.

The View Settings dialog lets a user tailor a datatable view (the juneau-console-views table card) and keep those choices across reloads. This page covers the dialog's tabs, how settings persist and are applied, the Sort tab, auto-refresh, the per-column search announcer and the Copy link button. For the catalog keys that configure a view see Rich Table Views; for the page-state store and the ?state= URL codec see View Settings and Shareable Links.

The dialog has four tabs: View (columns: visibility, order, label, format), Search (which columns take part in the search box), Sort and Options. The tabs follow the WAI-ARIA tabs pattern: each tab carries aria-selected and aria-controls, only the active tab is in the Tab order, and Left, Right, Home and End move between tabs. Every per-row control (visible, move up/down, label, format and so on) has an aria-label that names its column.

A view can show fewer tabs with columnConfig.tabs in its catalog: { "columnConfig": { "tabs": ["columns", "sort"] } } The names are columns, search, sort and options; columns is the tab shown on screen as View. An empty or unknown list falls back to all four tabs. Settings that belong to a hidden tab are not read from, applied from or written to the stored settings for that view.

Apply writes one settings blob per table into the page-state store (browser localStorage by default). The blob carries a schemaVersion, currently 2. When the stored blob has a different (older, newer or missing) schemaVersion, or the sort is in the old string-array form, the runtime deletes it, falls back to the catalog defaults and shows a one-time notice ("your saved settings were reset"). It never tries to migrate a blob it does not recognise. A stored blob is used only by tables whose catalog has columnConfig; it is ignored for any other table.

Stored settings take effect when the page loads, not only when the dialog is opened. On the first draw the runtime restores the View (visible columns, order, labels, formats), Search membership, Sort, and the Options (page size, wrap, density, auto-refresh), each gated on the tabs the view exposes. A column a user hid stays hidden after a reload, in both client and server data modes. The dialog itself opens seeded from the restored settings, so pressing Apply without touching anything does not overwrite them with the catalog defaults.

The Sort tab is an ordered priority list. Each entry names a column and a direction (Asc or Desc); the first entry is the primary sort key. The draft starts from the view's defaultOrder, so an untouched Apply keeps the default order instead of persisting an ascending sort over every column. Sort is stored as a list of {column, direction} entries.

Besides page size, wrap and density, the Options tab has an Auto-refresh choice: Off (the default), 30 seconds, 1 minute, 5 minutes or 15 minutes. It is stored as autoRefreshMs (0 for Off), and a blob written before the option existed reads as Off. Auto-refresh re-draws the table from the server using the same path as the manual refresh. It does not run while: the View Settings dialog is open, a row-detail region is open, a request is already in flight, or the browser tab is hidden. The timer is cleared when the table is torn down or re-initialised. Behavior change The suspension check used by polling, isPollSuspended, now also returns true while the View Settings dialog is open. A view declared with pausePollingWhileEditing therefore pauses its polling while the dialog is open.

Every header cell of a searchable column has a search icon that opens a small popover (it replaces the old ribbon-level columnSearchToggle button). The popover shows a one-line help text for the column's SearchType. The table has a polite aria-live region that announces results to screen readers. When the popover is dismissed with text that has not been applied, it announces "Search for 'x' not applied." so the typed text is not lost silently.

The Copy link button sits beside the settings gear. It copies the shareable ?state= URL described in View Settings and Shareable Links and announces "Link copied." or, if the clipboard is unavailable or denied, "Could not copy link." The button is shown when the table is primary: true, or when it is the only top-level view table on the page. Set primary: false to hide it for a table, or copyLink: false to hide only the button. It is not rendered when juneau-urlstate.js is not loaded. When a page opens with ?state=, the tab is found by matching the value against the data-juneau-strip-tab attribute of the page's tab elements; a value that matches no tab is ignored.
Rich Table Views and its JavaScript API 10.66 DataTables Server-Side Processing v10.0 Migration Guide for the breaking changes to columnSearchToggle, schemaVersion and readViewSettings

juneau-console-widgets is a small, optional module of declarative widget beans: plain Java objects that describe a dialog, a form, a calendar, a row of stat tiles or a badge, plus the first-party browser scripts that paint them. A bean carries data and a fail-closed validate(); it carries no HTML-emitting code. The server-side emitters live in juneau-console-views, which composes these beans, and the dialog/form/bar runtime ships with that module's juneau-views.js. Not the same thing as ${W:...} widgets Juneau has two unrelated things called "widget": This page 10.31.2 Widgets / 10.31.3 Predefined Widgets Module juneau-console-widgets juneau-rest-server Package org.apache.juneau.console.widgets (plural) org.apache.juneau.rest.server.widget (singular) Core type Widget — a marker interface with validate() Widget — an abstract class with getHtml() / getStyle() / getScript() What it is Typed, data-only beans (modal, form, calendar, badges) Code that emits raw HTML/CSS/JS into an @HtmlDocConfig page via ${W:Name} Safety model Typed fields painted with textContent; never an HTML sink Raw markup authored by the application The two share nothing but a simple class name, and a Widget in your imports is ambiguous if you use both. Import one by its fully-qualified name. <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-console-widgets</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> The module depends only on juneau-rest-server and juneau-commons. It deliberately has no dependency on juneau-console-views, so a widget bean can never import a views type. The runtime lives next to the views module The script this module ships (juneau-calendar.js) resolves its icons through the views module's juneau-icons.js and pushes its popovers onto the single layer stack that juneau-views.js publishes. A page that loads it must load both of those too. See the WidgetsMixin section below.

Widget is a one-method marker interface: public interface Widget { void validate(); // throws IllegalArgumentException if not well-formed } Implementers: ModalDef, FormDef, CalendarDef, BarSlot and ServerValues. Every one of them is fail-closed. validate() rejects a malformed bean rather than repairing it, and the REST serving path calls it for you (see the validation gate). Beans that ride the wire also carry a CONTRACT_VERSION string that the browser runtime compares against a literal it bakes in; a mismatch refuses to paint rather than painting something subtly wrong. Bean CONTRACT_VERSION ModalDef "2" FormDef "2" CalendarDef "2" BarSlot "1" ServerValues "1" (Java-only, never on the wire) ModalDef and FormDef move in lockstep with each other and with the runtime; bumping any two of the three makes every form-bearing dialog refuse to open.

Group Types Dialogs and forms ModalDef (+ Field, ChildAction), FormDef (+ Input, Input.Option, Section) Calendar CalendarDef (+ CalendarView, WeekStart), CalendarEvent, EventCategory (+ CategoryColor) Bar slot BarSlot, BarWidget (sealed), BarBadge, BarText Badges and menus Badge, StatusTone, MenuItem Actions ActionBarItem, ActionRef (+ Emphasis, EnabledRule), SafeAction, Behavior, Op Server values ServerValues, ServerValuesValue, ServerValuesRegistry Serving WidgetsMixin (+ WidgetValidationProcessor)

ModalDef is the payload a row action with present=dialog opens: the response to the modal-open confirmation fetch. It is a REST response body, so you return one from an ordinary @RestGet. Example @RestGet("/incidents/{id}/ack-dialog") public ModalDef ackDialog(@Path("id") String id) { var incident = incidents.get(id); return ModalDef.create("Acknowledge this incident?") .field("Incident", incident.number()) .field("Title", incident.title()) .field("Service", incident.service()) .codeField("Correlation id", incident.correlationId()) .form(FormDef.create() .field(FormDef.Input.of("comment", "Comment", "textarea").maxLength(500))) .idempotencyKey(keys.mint("ack", id)); }

The confirmation body is typed fields, not markup. Each ModalDef.Field is a label and a value, painted by the runtime with textContent, never innerHTML. Live data (an incident title anyone can edit) is attacker-influenceable and the page's origin holds the CSRF token, so an HTML sink here would be stored XSS leading to arbitrary writes. There is no way to express one. Field.kind is "text" (the default) or "code" (monospaced and copyable — an id, a URL, a token). Use .field(label, value) and .codeField(label, value) respectively.

Property Meaning contractVersion Always "2" from construction. title The prompt / title. Required, non-blank. fields The typed confirmation fields, in display order. form Optional FormDef. Omit for a confirm-only dialog. idempotencyKey A server-minted key, bound to the action and target, that the runtime echoes verbatim on submit so a double-click or retry collapses to one effect. selfTargeted Opt-in: the key targets itself (a dialog with no row, whose submit creates the thing). See the warning below. keepOpenOnSubmit Opt-in: do not close at confirm-click; paint the write's result into the open dialog as a receipt. childActions A catalog of actions scoped to this one open dialog, for action inputs that open a stacked step. barSlot An optional BarSlot painted immediately after the title. Additive; does not bump the contract version. selfTargeted discards the real target Set selfTargeted(true) only on a modal whose key came from the self-targeted mint helper. On a modal carrying an artifact-bound key it silently replaces the real target with the key itself, which makes the server's binding check vacuous. It defaults to unset, and a dialog that leaves it unset keeps sending the row's real id.

By default the runtime closes a dialog at confirm time and then submits, so the dialog is gone before the result exists. keepOpenOnSubmit suppresses the close and paints the result into the open dialog. A receipt dialog is non-submittable by construction (it has no confirm control, and the runtime refuses to paint one whose payload carries a form), and it is reached only after a committed write. A dialog synthesized from a confirm string alone cannot opt in; a receipt-bearing action must serve a real ModalDef. An older runtime that ignores the flag closes the dialog and drops the receipt; the write still happens.

A type="action" form input names an action id, which the runtime normally resolves against the enclosing view's row-action catalog. A step reached from inside an open dialog (a Review step in a wizard) is not a row action, and publishing it as one would surface it in every row's menu. ModalDef.ChildAction is that missing catalog, scoped structurally to one open dialog because it rides on the per-open payload. The existing row-action lookup runs first and unchanged, so a served payload can never shadow a declared row action. ModalDef.create("Create rule") .form(FormDef.create().field(FormDef.Input.of("review", "Review", "action").actionId("review"))) .childAction(ModalDef.ChildAction.of("review", "Review") .form("/rules/review-form") .endpoint("/rules") .method("POST") .carryDrafts(true)); ChildAction has id, label, form (the child's form-source URL), endpoint, method, onSuccess and carryDrafts. carryDrafts sends the parent dialog's current values to the child's form GET as one URL-encoded juneauDrafts query parameter, so a Review step does not open empty. It requires both a form on the parent and a form URL on the child. Drafts land in access logs and browser history Never carry a secret through carryDrafts.

FormDef is the input form of a modal. A form is either a flat fields list or an ordered list of sections, never both (the flat list is the single-section case). Sections render as a strip above one visible pane; they are a layout of one dialog, not a stack of dialogs, and a value typed into one section survives a trip through another. Example var form = FormDef.create() .field(FormDef.Input.of("resolution", "Resolution comment", "textarea").required().maxLength(1000)) .field(FormDef.Input.of("severity", "Severity", "select") .option("low", "Low").option("high", "High").value("low")) .field(FormDef.Input.of("notify", "Notify owner", "toggle")); // Sectioned: var wizard = FormDef.create() .section(FormDef.Section.of("basics", "Basics") .field(FormDef.Input.of("name", "Name", "text").required())) .section(FormDef.Section.of("advanced", "Advanced") .field(FormDef.Input.of("retries", "Retries", "text").pattern("[0-9]+")));

The type allowlist is the XSS bound: hostile prefill cannot become an element. The client paints native controls with createElement, uses textContent for labels and options, and .value / .checked for prefills. type Notes text, textarea The default is text. Only these two accept pattern and maxLength. password A masked, write-only input (<input type="password" autocomplete="new-password">). It is never pre-filled, so it is blank on edit and on re-open; validate() rejects a value on a password input, and it does not accept pattern or maxLength. Its typed value is excluded from the carryDrafts draft query, so it never lands in a URL. checkbox, toggle Boolean inputs. select Requires at least one Option; a prefilled value must match an option. options is legal only here. action A button that opens the row action (or child action) named by actionId. actionId is required here and illegal elsewhere. Use .action(ActionRef) or .actionId(String). Input properties: name (the submit-body key, required), label (required), type, required, value, options, pattern, maxLength, help, actionId. pattern is capped at 256 characters and must compile (ReDoS defense in depth); maxLength must be positive. FormDef.template names an optional server-side template for authors and is ignored by the client (not an HTML sink). Create such a form with FormDef.ofTemplate(String). validate() additionally rejects duplicate field names (across all sections of a sectioned form), duplicate section ids, and an empty sections list.

CalendarDef describes a month calendar with navigation, categories and a display-only legend. The emitter (CalendarTable) is in the views module; the page mounts an empty data-juneau-calendar marker and juneau-calendar.js hydrates it. The server paints the initial month and seed events (progressive enhancement); the runtime computes later months client-side and fetches their events from a same-origin, data-only per-month GET. Example var cal = CalendarDef.create() .id("oncall") .endpoint("servlet:/oncall/events/{year}/{month}") .categories( EventCategory.create().id("primary").label("Primary").color(EventCategory.CategoryColor.BLUE), EventCategory.create().id("backup").label("Backup").color(EventCategory.CategoryColor.AMBER)) .events( CalendarEvent.create().id("e1").title("Alice").start("2026-03-02").end("2026-03-04").categoryId("primary"), CalendarEvent.create().id("e2").title("Deploy window").start("2026-03-05T09:00").end("2026-03-05T10:00")) .weekStart(CalendarDef.WeekStart.MONDAY) .maxPerDay(4); Property Meaning id Required; must match [A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_-]*. Emitted as data-juneau-calendar. endpoint Same-origin path template containing both {year} and {month}. null makes the calendar seed-only and disables month navigation. categories Legend entries in display order. A seed event's categoryId must be declared here. events Optional initial-month seed events. view CalendarView.MONTH is the only value (default). weekStart SUNDAY (default) or MONDAY. initialYear / initialMonth Set together with .initial(year, month), or neither (the server clock decides). Month is 1–12. maxPerDay Chips per day before "+N more". Default 3, minimum 1. Spanning bars occupy lanes, with a budget equal to maxPerDay clamped to a hard ceiling of 8 per week row. The two caps are separate: a bar crossing a cell does not consume that cell's chip budget.

CalendarEvent has id, title, start, end, allDay, categoryId, href and tooltip. start/end are ISO-8601 local values: yyyy-MM-dd or yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm. A trailing offset or Z is ignored rather than rejected, and the time renders in the server's clock zone. end is layout-significant, with split inclusivity: Shape end is Example All-day (date-only) inclusive start=2026-03-02, end=2026-03-04 fills three day cells Timed (date-time) exclusive 09:00 to 10:00 is [09:00, 10:00) on the start day; crossing midnight makes a spanning bar Omitted start-only, valid an all-day event fills the start day; a timed one is a zero-width chip A timed event whose end equals its start, or any end before start, is malformed. So is an allDay/end disagreement (for example allDay=true with a date-time end). A malformed seed event is dropped, not fatal: it neither fails the definition nor the whole month payload, and a per-month GET handler should apply the same rule with CalendarEvent.retainWellFormed(...). Event titles, tooltips and labels are painted with textContent. href must be a same-origin document URL.

EventCategory has id, label, color and description. color is one of the fixed CategoryColor values BLUE, GREEN, AMBER, RED and NEUTRAL (the default). There is no author-supplied inline color, so the emitted class is built only from a sanitized id and a fixed token — no CSS-injection surface. An unknown categoryId on a wire event paints as NEUTRAL. Why the contract is "2" end became layout-significant, and the constant doubles as the data-juneau-calendar-contract handshake stamp, so a v1 runtime cannot silently draw a multi-day event as one chip.

Badge is an overlay on a header action (a bell count) or inside a BarBadge. It is exactly one of a count badge or a dot badge, never both. Badge.count(7).max(99).tone(StatusTone.ERROR).label("unread notifications"); // "7"; 120 would show "99+" Badge.dot().tone(StatusTone.INFO); // presence only Property Rule count >= 0. Mutually exclusive with dot. dot Presence badge, no number. max >= 1; a larger count renders as max+. tone A StatusTone (INFO, SUCCESS, WARNING, ERROR, NEUTRAL); null keeps the default color. A tone outside that palette fails closed: nothing is painted. label Visually hidden screen-reader context. Counts are painted with textContent. Badge is a plain bean, not a Widget; its validate() is called by the enclosing bean.

BarSlot is an additive trailing region beside the subtab ribbon — a small row of BarWidgets such as "3 changes pending". It is a Widget with id, widgets (at least one, ids unique) and an optional same-origin refreshUrl for demand-refreshing the counts. BarWidget is sealed over two types: BarBadge.of(id).label("change pending").badge(Badge.count(3).tone(StatusTone.WARNING)) BarText.of(id, "Last synced 10:42") var slot = BarSlot.create("pending") .widgets(BarBadge.of("chg").label("changes pending").badge(Badge.count(3).tone(StatusTone.WARNING)), BarText.of("env", "prod")) .refreshUrl("/pending/count"); A BarSlot can be attached to a ModalDef (barSlot(...), anchored right after the title) and, in the views module, to a page and to a Detail View. On the modal it is carried on the wire, because the modal is itself the wire payload.

Type Role ActionBarItem Marker for one item in an action bar: an ActionRef or a SafeAction. ActionRef An opaque id naming a write action on the enclosing view. The action's existence is checked in the views module, not here. SafeAction A client-only action with no endpoint. The one constant is COLLAPSE (collapse the child row), which stays enabled even during an in-flight or failed expand so the user can dismiss it. Behavior How a header or menu action acts when activated: LINK (same-origin href), SAFE (dispatch a format-validated client event token that the host app interprets) or MENU. MenuItem One row of a header or avatar menu: a link (MenuItem.link(id, label, href)), a safe item (MenuItem.safe(id, label, token)) or a divider (MenuItem.divider()). Behavior.MENU is not functional yet The menu manager has not shipped. Until it does, a MENU trigger is disabled and its list is omitted. MenuItem.validate() requires exactly one of href/safe on a non-divider, a same-origin href, and a safe token matching ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,63}$. Dividers are exempt from every id/label/target rule.

ActionRef.of("resolve") .emphasis(ActionRef.Emphasis.PRIMARY) .enabledWhen("status", Op.EQ, "open", "Only open incidents can be resolved.") .enabledWhen("owner", Op.PRESENT, "Assign an owner first."); Op is the shared single-field comparison vocabulary: EQ and NE take a value, PRESENT and ABSENT do not (Op.requiresValue() discriminates; the wrong overload throws). The rules obey a few deliberate constraints: Presentation only, never authorization. The server re-reads the row and refuses on its own authority. Prefer disabled; hide only when irrelevant. An action that is merely impossible right now stays visible and disabled with a reason. A detail-panel action has no visibleWhen; to drop an action from a whole view, omit it from that view's list. (Row actions in a table view can also declare visibleWhen for the case where the action does not apply to a row at all.) The first-declared failing rule wins, and its reason is shown via a tooltip and aria-describedby. Declaration order is the priority mechanism. Fail closed. A rule on a field the panel never declares is rejected at startup; if the field is missing from a row at runtime the rule fails and the action disables (even ABSENT). ActionRef.Emphasis is PRIMARY (solid accent; at most one per bar) or SECONDARY (the default). Both emphasis and enabledWhen are Java-only and never marshalled.
documents.s: Gating an action on row state: ActionRef.enabledWhen

documents.t: ServerValues declares named scalar providers and interpolates them into widget chrome text (titles, labels) as ${FV:name} or ${FV:name:default} at serve time. It is a thin typed facade over the SVL engine, not a second templating language, and it is Java-only (lambda providers are never serialized). ServerValues sv = ServerValues.create() .value("failedCount", session -> metrics.failed()) .value("env", session -> "prod"); // Column title "Failures (${FV:failedCount})" resolves at serve time. A provider returns a String, Number, Boolean or null. Anything else is rejected at resolve time; collections are not joined. A name that is not declared, or a null result, falls through to the ${FV:name:default} default. A provider that throws propagates (fail-closed). Providers are session-aware (Function<VarResolverSession,?>) and re-run on every reference unless the value is declared cacheable through ServerValuesValue.of(name, provider, true). Cache only values that are stable across a whole response. $FV is not $W: $W emits raw widget HTML, while $FV resolves plain, serializer-encoded text and never injects markup. The $FV variable itself (ServerValuesVar) lives in juneau-console-views.

Compose the mixin to serve the three first-party assets: @Rest(mixins=WidgetsMixin.class) public class MyRest extends BasicRestServlet { ... } Path constant Served at Purpose CALENDAR_JS_PATH /juneau-calendar.js Calendar runtime CALENDAR_CSS_PATH /juneau-calendar.css Calendar stylesheet (declares --jc-* token fallbacks) Assets are cacheable for one day and carry a content-sensitive cache-buster. Reference them from a page with WidgetsMixin.widgetAssetUrl(path) (a servlet:-prefixed URL that Juneau's own HTML serializer resolves) or, for a template engine that never sees that rewrite, WidgetsMixin.widgetAssetUrl(req, path) (an absolute, browser-fetchable URL). Load order is a contract juneau-calendar.js must come after the views module's juneau-views.js. The calendar defines no stack of its own and fails loudly if the shared one is absent. The mixin also exposes the handshake stamps the runtimes bake in: CALENDAR_CONTRACT_VERSION ("2", alias of CalendarDef), BAR_CONTRACT_VERSION ("1", alias of BarSlot) and HEADER_CONTRACT_VERSION ("1"). They are deliberately independent, so a calendar-envelope change never forces a bar or header bump. The views module keeps deprecated accessors at the paths it served these assets from before they moved; they read the same bytes from this module, so existing applications keep working.

WidgetsMixin.WidgetValidationProcessor is a ResponseProcessor that calls validate() on any REST response whose content is a Widget, and answers a failure with HTTP 500 (a malformed widget is a server defect, not a client error). It returns NEXT, so it never claims the response or perturbs the chain. It is registered twice, on purpose: through ServiceLoader (so it applies to every resource on a classpath that carries the module, with no opt-in) and through the mixin's own @Rest(responseProcessors=...) (so a host that composes the mixin is covered even if a shading step drops the services file). Things to know: Top level only. It tests getContent() itself. A Widget nested in a List or Map is not walked; nested widgets inside a ModalDef are covered by that bean's own recursive validate(). Non-REST producers are not gated. A direct Json.of(modal) has no processor in front of it. Call validate() or the chaining ModalDef.checked() / FormDef.checked() yourself. Double validation is intentional. A modal that already called checked() is validated again by the processor; validate() is cheap and idempotent. Escape hatch. To serve a deliberately invalid widget, replace the whole chain with a @Bean ResponseProcessorList factory method. There is no narrower opt-out.

By default, HTTP parts that don't have value (such as missing query parameters) end up with null values: @RestPost("/example") public String doGetExample1( @Query("p1") int p1, @FormData("f1") MyBean f1, @Header("Accept-Language") AcceptLanguage h1 ) { if (p1 == null) p1 = -1; if (f1 == null) f1 = DEFAULT_BEAN; if (h1 == null) h1 = AcceptLanguage.of("en"); } You have several options to provide default values for HTTP parts. The most common is to simply use Optional parameters and handle default values programmatically: @RestPost("/example") public String doGetExample1( @Query("p1") Optional<Integer> p1, @FormData("f1") Optional<MyBean> f1, @Header("Accept-Language") Optional<AcceptLanguage> h1 ) { int _p1 = p1.orElse(-1); MyBean _f1 = f1.orElse(DEFAULT_BEAN); AcceptLanguage _h1 = h1.orElse(AcceptLanguage.of("en")); } You can also specify default values on the annotations: @RestPost("/example") public String doGetExample1( @Query(name="p1", def="-1") int p1, @FormData(name="f1", def="foo=bar,baz=qux") MyBean f1, @Header(name="Accept-Language", def="en") AcceptLanguage lang ) { ... } A third option is to specify default values via the Rest and RestOp annotations. RestdefaultAccept defaultCharset defaultContentType defaultRequestAttributes defaultRequestHeaders defaultResponseHeadersRestOpdefaultAccept defaultCharset defaultContentType defaultRequestAttributes defaultRequestFormData defaultRequestHeaders defaultRequestQueryData defaultResponseHeaders Example // Servlet with default headers @Rest( // Assume "text/json" Accept value when Accept not specified defaultRequestHeaders={"Accept: text/json"}, // Add a version header attribute to all responses defaultResponseHeaders={"X-Version: 1.0"} ) public MyRestServlet extends BasicRestServlet { ... } Default parts can also be supplied programmatically via named beans using @Bean (for example name="defaultRequestHeaders", name="defaultResponseHeaders", name="defaultRequestAttributes", name="defaultRequestFormData", name="defaultRequestQueryData"). In 10.0+, prefer annotation attributes and @Bean-named beans over the legacy builder APIs.

By default, all serializers and parsers have built in ObjectSwaps defined for the following common data types: note As of 10.0.0, Iterator, Iterable, Stream, and Enumeration types are serialized natively without swaps. The IteratorSwap and EnumerationSwap classes have been removed. See Release 10.0.0 for details. note As of 10.0.0, date/time types (Calendar, Date, Temporal subtypes, XMLGregorianCalendar) and Duration are serialized and parsed natively as ISO 8601 strings without swaps. The default swap registrations for these types have been removed from this list. The old swap classes (TemporalCalendarSwap, TemporalDateSwap, CalendarSwap, DateSwap, TemporalSwap) have been removed; to customize the output format (e.g. RFC 1123 instead of ISO 8601) use @MarshalledProp(calendarFormat=...) / @Marshalled(calendarFormat=...) / MarshallingContext.Builder.calendarFormat(CalendarFormat...), or register your own ObjectSwap. See Release 10.0.0 for details. Locale Class TimeZone ZoneId The following types are now handled natively (built-in ISO 8601 support, no swap required): Calendar Date Instant ZonedDateTime LocalDate LocalDateTime LocalTime OffsetDateTime OffsetTime Year YearMonth Temporal XMLGregorianCalendar Duration Various other swaps are provided in the org.apache.juneau.marshall.swaps package.

VarResolver.DEFAULT is a reusable, thread-safe VarResolver instance pre-configured with the most commonly-needed source variables. Because it is immutable and shared, you can reference it directly from anywhere without constructing your own resolver.

Variable Class Resolves against ${S:key[:default]} SystemPropertiesVar Java system properties (System.getProperty) ${E:key[:default]} EnvVariablesVar OS environment variables (System.getenv) ${EF:key[:default]} EnvFileVar A .env-style env file on the filesystem ${DE:key[:default]} DotenvVar A .env dotenv file ${A:key[:default]} ArgsVar JVM command-line arguments ${MF:key[:default]} ManifestFileVar Classpath META-INF/MANIFEST.MF entries Each variable accepts an optional comma-separated default that is returned when the key cannot be resolved.

// Resolve a single system-property variable. String s = VarResolver.DEFAULT.resolve("The Java home directory is ${S:java.home}"); Variables can be arbitrarily nested — the resolved value of one variable can itself contain variables, and a variable's default can be another variable: // Look up a value in priority order: // 1) the MYPROPERTY environment variable, // 2) the 'my.property' system property if the env var is not set, // 3) the literal 'not found' if neither is set. String s = VarResolver.DEFAULT.resolve("${E:MYPROPERTY:${S:my.property:not found}}"); Resolving a string that contains no variables is a no-op that returns the input unchanged, so it is safe (and cheap) to run arbitrary text through the resolver.

VarResolver.DEFAULT is a starting point, not a dead end. Use copy() to derive a new resolver that inherits its variables and adds your own: // Derive a resolver that also supports a custom ${MY:...} variable. VarResolver vr = VarResolver.DEFAULT.copy() .vars(MyCustomVar.class) .build();

Simple Variable Language — the full SVL reference, including the #{...} function-call syntax. VarResolvers — creating and configuring your own resolvers. SVL Other Notes — escaping and recursion caveats. Microservice VarResolver — how the microservice adds variables to the default resolver.

Apache Juneau ships two packaging aids that make it easy to depend on a coherent, version-aligned slice of the framework without hand-maintaining a long list of <version> tags: A Bill of Materials (BOM) — org.apache.juneau:juneau-bom — for version alignment. A small set of curated dependency bundles — one per deployment shape — that transitively pull a coherent module set. Both are deliberately dependency-only aids. They register nothing and discover nothing at runtime (see Explicit over magic below).

The ${juneau.version} property is 10.0.0-SNAPSHOT for these docs; the latest release on Maven Central is 9.2.1. See Install Juneau. The BOM is a 10.0 artifact; it is not published for 9.2.1. Import juneau-bom (scope import, type pom) in your <dependencyManagement> and then drop the explicit versions from every Juneau dependency — the BOM supplies them: <dependencyManagement> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-bom</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> <type>pom</type> <scope>import</scope> </dependency> </dependencies> </dependencyManagement> <dependencies> <!-- No <version> needed - the BOM aligns it. --> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-server</artifactId> </dependency> </dependencies> The BOM enumerates the consumer-facing Juneau modules (juneau-core marshalling/config, juneau-rest, juneau-microservice, juneau-bean, juneau-sc), the test-support modules (juneau-bct, juneau-microservice-test, juneau-rest-mock), and the curated *-bundle POMs themselves. It excludes aggregate/non-library artifacts (juneau-shaded/*, juneau-examples, juneau-petstore, juneau-distrib) and the juneau-terminal build tooling.

Every module below is version-managed by juneau-bom. See the Ecosystem Overview for what each one does and what it requires. Area Managed artifacts Core juneau-commons, juneau-config, juneau-marshall, juneau-marshall-rdf, juneau-beanquery-sql, juneau-beanquery-postgres, juneau-bct Secrets juneau-secret-macos-keychain Beans juneau-bean-atom, juneau-bean-common, juneau-bean-hal, juneau-bean-html5, juneau-bean-jsonapi, juneau-bean-jsonpatch, juneau-bean-jsonrpc, juneau-bean-jsonschema, juneau-bean-mcp-v20250618, juneau-bean-mcp-v20260728, juneau-bean-openapi-v3, juneau-bean-rfc7807, juneau-bean-swagger-v2 REST common and mock juneau-rest-common, juneau-rest-common-classic, juneau-rest-mock REST server juneau-rest-server, juneau-rest-server-rdf, juneau-rest-server-springboot, juneau-rest-server-management-logging, juneau-rest-server-reactive, juneau-rest-server-reactive-reactor REST server: MCP juneau-rest-server-mcp, juneau-rest-server-mcp-v20250618, juneau-rest-server-mcp-v20260728 REST server: auth juneau-rest-server-auth-jwt, juneau-rest-server-auth-saml, juneau-rest-server-auth-oauth, juneau-rest-server-auth-oidc-rp, juneau-rest-auth-oauth-flow REST server: observability juneau-rest-server-metrics-micrometer, juneau-rest-server-tracing-otel REST server: view engines juneau-rest-server-view-freemarker, juneau-rest-server-view-jsp, juneau-rest-server-view-mustache, juneau-rest-server-view-thymeleaf REST server: console UI and views juneau-console, juneau-console-freemarker, juneau-console-datatables, juneau-console-views, juneau-console-views-markdown, juneau-console-widgets, juneau-terminal-report REST client juneau-rest-client, juneau-rest-client-classic, juneau-rest-client-apache-httpclient-45, juneau-rest-client-apache-httpclient-50, juneau-rest-client-okhttp, juneau-rest-client-jetty REST client: MCP juneau-rest-client-mcp, juneau-rest-client-mcp-v20250618, juneau-rest-client-mcp-v20260728, juneau-rest-client-mcp-auth Microservice juneau-microservice, juneau-microservice-jetty, juneau-microservice-tomcat, juneau-microservice-test Server config juneau-sc-server Bundles juneau-microservice-jetty-bundle, juneau-microservice-tomcat-bundle, juneau-springboot-bundle, juneau-observability-otlp-bundle Beyond Juneau's own modules, the BOM also pins the small set of starter-relevant third-party versions the bundles need to stay coherent — Micrometer (micrometer-core, micrometer-registry-otlp), OpenTelemetry (opentelemetry-api, opentelemetry-sdk, opentelemetry-exporter-otlp, opentelemetry-sdk-extension-autoconfigure), and Jakarta (jakarta.servlet-api, jakarta.validation-api). It is not a whole-world third-party BOM (unlike Spring Boot's), so it won't collide with a third-party BOM you import yourself.

Juneau also publishes bundle artifacts — <packaging>pom</packaging> Maven coordinates that pull a curated, version-aligned set of Juneau modules (and their transitive dependencies) in a single declaration. Each bundle targets one deployment shape: depend on a single bundle and you transitively pull a coherent module set plus the REST client. Bundles are dependency aggregators only: they contain no code, register no configurations, and perform no classpath auto-discovery. Every bean, server, and resource still needs to be wired explicitly, exactly as if you had listed the individual modules yourself. Because each bundle internally imports juneau-bom, the modules it pulls are already version-aligned. Bundle vs. starter. These *-bundle POMs are dependency aggregators — add one dependency, get a coherent module set. They are not to be confused with the clone-and-go starter project templates on dedicated apache/juneau branches (microservice-*-starter), which are full runnable project templates.

Approach What it is Best for Bundle A POM-type dependency that pulls a curated module set transitively Applications where you control the full classpath and want a quick start Shaded JAR A single fat JAR with Juneau modules merged in Bazel builds or environments that need a single-artifact classpath; see Juneau Shaded Artifacts Individual modules Each Juneau JAR declared explicitly Libraries and frameworks that want fine-grained transitive dependency control
documents.s: Bundles vs shaded JARs vs individual modules

documents.t: Artifact Use when juneau-microservice-jetty-bundle Building an embedded-Jetty microservice juneau-microservice-tomcat-bundle Building an embedded-Tomcat microservice juneau-springboot-bundle Adding Juneau REST resources to Spring Boot juneau-observability-otlp-bundle Exporting metrics + traces over OTLP in one dependency

<dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-microservice-jetty-bundle</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> <type>pom</type> </dependency> Pulls the full embedded-Jetty microservice stack for a standalone service process: Direct dependency What it brings juneau-microservice-jetty Embedded-Jetty launcher, juneau-microservice lifecycle, juneau-rest-server, juneau-marshall, juneau-config, juneau-commons, and the Jetty embedded-server JARs at the tested compatible version juneau-rest-client REST client for typical service-to-service calls Use this when starting a new Jetty-based microservice and you want a single dependency to bootstrap the project. Wire your servers explicitly via Microservice.Builder.configurations(...) — the bundle performs no auto-configuration. See juneau-microservice-jetty for setup instructions.

<dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-microservice-tomcat-bundle</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> <type>pom</type> </dependency> The Tomcat equivalent of juneau-microservice-jetty-bundle: Direct dependency What it brings juneau-microservice-tomcat Embedded-Tomcat launcher, juneau-microservice lifecycle, juneau-rest-server, juneau-marshall, juneau-config, juneau-commons, and the Tomcat embedded-server JARs at the tested compatible version juneau-rest-client REST client for typical service-to-service calls Wire your servers explicitly via Microservice.Builder.configurations(...). See juneau-microservice-tomcat for setup instructions.

<dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-springboot-bundle</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> <type>pom</type> </dependency> Pulls the Juneau REST server stack for a Spring Boot application: Direct dependency What it brings juneau-rest-server-springboot Spring Boot bridge, juneau-rest-server, spring-boot-starter-web, and the shared juneau-rest-common types juneau-rest-client REST client for typical service-to-service calls Wire your @Rest-annotated resources explicitly in your Spring @Configuration classes — the bundle performs no classpath auto-discovery. See juneau-rest-server-springboot for Spring Boot integration details.

<dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-observability-otlp-bundle</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> <type>pom</type> </dependency> Pulls both Juneau observability bridges plus a coherent, version-aligned OTLP exporter stack in one dependency: Direct dependency What it brings juneau-rest-server-metrics-micrometer MicrometerMetricsRecorder — the MetricsRecorder SPI implementation juneau-rest-server-tracing-otel OtelTracerHook — the TracerHook SPI implementation opentelemetry-exporter-otlp OTLP span exporter opentelemetry-sdk OpenTelemetry SDK (satisfies the provided OTel API dependency of the tracing bridge) opentelemetry-sdk-extension-autoconfigure SDK auto-configure extension micrometer-registry-otlp Micrometer OTLP registry (satisfies the provided Micrometer dependency of the metrics bridge) The bundle covers metrics and traces; OTLP log export is not included in v1. Because the bundle is a dependency aggregator only, you still register the beans explicitly: @Configuration public class ObservabilityConfig { @Bean MeterRegistry registry() { // OtlpMeterRegistry is the Micrometer OTLP registry pulled by the bundle. return new OtlpMeterRegistry(OtlpConfig.DEFAULT, Clock.SYSTEM); } @Bean MetricsRecorder recorder(MeterRegistry r) { return new MicrometerMetricsRecorder(r); } @Bean TracerHook tracer() { // Uses GlobalOpenTelemetry, typically wired by the OTel Java agent or SDK autoconfigure. return new OtelTracerHook(); } } See Observability — Micrometer + OpenTelemetry for the full configuration guide including per-operation controls, W3C trace-context propagation, and custom MetricsRecorder / TracerHook implementations.

Starting a new application — one dependency gets you a working, version-aligned stack. You control the full classpath — no other dependency manager can conflict with the bundle's transitive pulls. You want the versions the Juneau team tested — bundle dependencies are pinned against the juneau-bom so all Juneau sub-modules and their third-party peers are mutually compatible.

Writing a library — declare only the modules your library's API surface requires; don't force your consumers to pull a full microservice stack. Mixing with an existing framework — if your project already declares Jetty or Spring Boot at a specific version, depend on the individual Juneau modules and let your build tool resolve the container version. Minimizing JAR footprint — a single microservice module is smaller than the full microservice bundle when you know exactly which Juneau features you use.

A bundle gives you the classpath for a deployment shape. It does not wire anything up for you. Juneau keeps configuration registration explicit — you register your configuration classes yourself through Microservice.Builder.configurations(Class<?>...). There is no ServiceLoader / META-INF/services scan and no @ConditionalOnClass-style classpath auto-discovery that decides what to activate based on what happens to be on the classpath. This is a deliberate design choice, not a missing feature. In the maintainer's words: "No, we want an explicit classpath-driven solution. I actually see auto-configuration as a weakness in Spring Boot that leads to applications with long startup times and impossible-to-understand architectures. We should make this distinction clear in our docs." The two costs called out there are exactly what the explicit model avoids: Startup time. No classpath scanning for conditional configuration to evaluate at boot. What you register is what runs. Comprehensibility. The set of active configurations is the literal list you passed to configurations(...) — readable in one place, with no implicit behavior toggled on by a transitive dependency you didn't realize was present. So the division of labor is clean: the BOM aligns versions, the bundles assemble a coherent classpath, and you stay in explicit control of what gets wired up.

Juneau Shaded Artifacts — fat JARs as an alternative to bundles (Bazel-friendly) Starter projects — clone-and-go runnable project templates Observability — Micrometer + OpenTelemetry — full guide for juneau-observability-otlp-bundle

REST resources are deployed in the following ways: Deployed in a J2EE container as a servlet. Deployed in a Spring Boot environment as a servlet. Deployed as a child of another REST resource. When deployed in a J2EE container, you MUST extend from one of the servlet classes. note When deployed as a child of another resource, you MAY extend from one of the servlet classes but it's not necessary. The only requirement is that the class be annotated with @Rest and have one of the following constructors if they aren't already Spring Beans: public T() public T(RestContext) Deployment in a servlet container is typically done by adding a servlet entry for the top-level resources to the JEE web.xml. Deployment in a Spring Boot environment involves defining your top-level resources as Spring Beans. Top-level resources must extend from BasicSpringRestServlet or BasicSpringRestServletGroup so that Juneau can hook into the injection framework provided by Spring. Child resource CAN be defined as injected Spring Beans as well but it is not a requirement. Example Spring Boot Configuration @SpringBootApplication @Controller public class SpringBootAppConfig { @Bean public MyRootResources getRootResources() { ... } @Bean public MyChildResource getMyChildResource() { ... } @Bean public ServletRegistrationBean getRootServlet(RootResources rootResources) { return new ServletRegistrationBean(rootResources, "/*"); } }

A script built on juneau-terminal draws its live view for whoever is watching the terminal. A tool that starts the script (an AI coding agent, an IDE task, a CI wrapper) needs something else: progress it can follow and an outcome it can read, without scraping a screen. This page shows how to give each of them what they need from the same run.
documents.s: Driving a Run from Another Tool

documents.t: The person gets a real terminal that shows the live view: a tmux pane, an IDE console or a CI log. The tool follows the run's progress in the markers file, JUNEAU_TERMINAL_MARKERS_FILE. When the run ends, the tool reads the result file, JUNEAU_TERMINAL_RESULT: the status, the exit code and one row per step. Anyone else who wants the details reads the logs. The result file names the full log and the board log. Neither file changes what the terminal shows. With TERMINAL_MARKERS unset, the run draws its console view as usual, and the markers go to the file as well.

Both are written by the script that owns the run, the one that calls run() and done() (Juneau's own push.py and test.py are such scripts). JUNEAU_TERMINAL_MARKERS_FILE=<path> : Every terminal-protocol marker, one ##terminal {json} line each. The owner empties the file when the run starts. A script it runs, which inherits JUNEAU_TERMINAL_ACTIVE, appends its steps to the same file. A file that can't be written is reported once on stderr and the run goes on without it. Under --pty the file isn't written. JUNEAU_TERMINAL_RESULT=<path> : One JSON object, written when the run ends (ok, failed, or cancelled by Ctrl-C or SIGTERM). It is written through a temporary file and a rename, so a reader never sees half of it, and an older file at that path is removed when the run starts. Fields with no value are left out. Result field Meaning status ok, fail or cancelled. exit The script's exit code (130 when cancelled). ms The run's duration. project, branch, head, commit As in the run and done markers. rows One entry per row of the console view, in order: id, label, status, ms, summary and, for a test step, tests with total, fail, err and skip. notes The run's note markers: level, text and href. logs full and board: the paths of the session's logs.

This opens a side pane for the person, runs a script in it, waits for it, and reads the result. It assumes the script is a juneau-terminal adopter such as push.py --test-only; replace it with your own. dir=$(mktemp -d) chan="run-$$" # 1. The pane: a real terminal with the live view. -d keeps focus where the person is typing. tmux split-window -h -d "env JUNEAU_TERMINAL_CONSOLE=board JUNEAU_TERMINAL_MARKERS_FILE=$dir/markers \ JUNEAU_TERMINAL_RESULT=$dir/result.json python3 push.py --test-only; tmux wait-for -S $chan; read -r" # 2. Block until the pane signals (no polling). tmux remembers a signal sent before this line runs. tmux wait-for "$chan" # 3. The outcome: a missing result file means the script died before it could write one. if [ -f "$dir/result.json" ]; then jq -r '.status, "exit \(.exit)"' "$dir/result.json" jq -r '.rows[] | "\(.status)\t\(.label)\t\(.summary)"' "$dir/result.json" jq -r '.logs.full // empty' "$dir/result.json" # where to read a failure's details else echo "fail: no result file" fi The pane waits for Enter after the script ends, so the person can read the final view; the tool already has what it needs. For a tmux session that holds both the agent and the pane, see Watching a Run from an AI Agent.

Read the markers file as it grows. A line that has no trailing newline yet is still being written, so wait for it. import json, time def follow(path, still_running): """Yield each marker from the file; stop after `done`, or when the process is gone with no `done`.""" pending = "" with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f: while True: pending += f.read() *lines, pending = pending.split("\n") for line in lines: if line.startswith("##terminal "): try: marker = json.loads(line[len("##terminal "):]) except ValueError: continue # not a marker: an ordinary output line yield marker if marker.get("ev") == "done": return if not still_running(): yield {"ev": "done", "status": "fail"} # EOF with no `done` return time.sleep(0.2) The file doesn't exist until the run starts, so open it once the process is running. Rather than polling the file, a tool that only needs the outcome can skip it and read the result file at the end.

These come from the terminal protocol's consumer rules, and a wrapper that reads either file should follow them: Ignore an unknown ev, and unknown fields on a known ev. Later versions add events and fields. A line with the prefix but bad JSON, or with no ev, is an ordinary output line. done is the last marker. When it arrives, close any step that has no end: as failed if done.status is fail, as skipped otherwise. If the stream ends with no done, for example because the script was killed, treat it as done with status fail, or cancelled if your tool cancelled the run. Treat a missing result file the same way: the run did not finish.
juneau-terminal Watching a Run from an AI Agent Terminal protocol v1

A common coding practice is to use the same Java interface to define both your server and client side REST interfaces. The advantage to this approach is that changes that you make to your REST interface can be reflected in both places at the same time, reducing the chances for compatibility mistakes. What makes this possible is that method-level annotations such as @RestOp and parameter-level annotations such as @Query are inherited from parent classes. This normally isn't possible but the framework will spider up the parent hierarchy of classes to find method and parameter level annotations defined on overridden methods. The general approach is to define your @Remote-annotated interface first. The following example is pulled from the PetStore app: @Remote(path="/petstore") public interface PetStore { @RemoteGet("/pet") public Collection getPets() throws NotAcceptable; @RemoteDelete("/pet/{petId}") public Ok deletePet( @Header( name="api_key", description="Security API key", required=true, example="foobar" ) String apiKey, @Path( name="petId", description="Pet id to delete", example="123" ) long petId ) throws IdNotFound, NotAcceptable; ... Next you define the implementation of your interface as a normal Juneau REST resource: @Rest( path="/petstore", title="Petstore application", ... ) public class PetStoreResource extends BasicRestServlet implements PetStore { ... @Override /* PetStore */ @RestOp( method=GET, path="/pet", summary="All pets in the store", ... ) public Collection getPets() throws NotAcceptable { return store.getPets(); } @Override /* PetStore */ @RestOp( method=DELETE, path="/pet/{petId}", summary="Deletes a pet", ... ) public Ok deletePet(String apiKey, long petId) throws IdNotFound, NotAcceptable { store.removePet(petId); return OK; } Then use the interface as a remote resource like so: RestClient client = RestClient.create().json().rootUrl("http://localhost:10000").build(); PetStore store = client.getRemote(PetStore.class); for (Pet pet : store.getPets()) { store.deletePet("my-special-key", pet.getId()); System.err.println("Deleted pet: id=" + pet.getId()); } In the example above, we chose to add the @RestOp annotation to the implementation class. However, they could have been added to the interface instead. It's personal preference where you want to place the annotations. Note how we didn't need to use the @Header and @Path annotations in our implementation since the annotations were inherited from the interface.

In the section Swaps, you were introduced to annotations that can be applied to bean classes, methods, fields, and constructors such as @BeanType: // Address class with only street/city/state properties (in that order). // All other properties are ignored. @BeanType(properties="street,city,state") public class Address { ... } An alternate way of applying these annotations is to attach them to unrelated classes and methods and then tell your serializer or parser where to find them. Each annotation pairs with a sibling *Apply annotation that separates the targeting (on()/onClass()) from the content (value()). // Unannotated class. public class Address { ... } @BeanTypeApply(onClass=Address.class, value=@BeanType(properties="street,city,state")) public static class DummyClass {} WriterSerializer serializer = JsonSerializer .create() .applyAnnotations(DummyClass.class) .build(); String json = serializer.write(addressBean); The advantage to this approach is it allows you to use Juneau annotations on classes/methods/fields/constructors where you might not have access to the source code, or when you only want to selectively apply the annotation under certain scenarios instead of globally. For example, the following shows the @BeanTypeApply annotation being selectively applied on a single REST method (described later in juneau-rest-server): @RestGet @BeanTypeApply(onClass=Address.class, value=@BeanType(properties="street,city,state")) public List getAddresses() {} Each *Apply annotation has an on()/onClass() targeting method and applies its value() annotation to the specified targets. The available *Apply annotations are: BeanTypeApply MarshalledApply BeanCtorApply BeanIgnoreApply MarshalledIgnoreApply BeanPropApply MarshalledPropApply ExampleApply NamePropertyApply ParentPropertyApply SwapApply UriApply BsonApply CborApply CsvApply HjsonApply HoconApply HtmlApply IniApply JsonApply MarkdownApply SchemaApply MsgPackApply OpenApiApply ParquetApply PlainTextApply ProtobufApply PrototextApply SoapXmlApply UonApply UrlEncodingApply XmlApply The valid pattern matches are: Classes: Fully qualified: com.foo.MyClass Fully qualified inner class: com.foo.MyClass$Inner1$Inner2 Simple: MyClass Simple inner: MyClass$Inner1$Inner2, Inner1$Inner2, Inner2 Methods: Fully qualified with args: com.foo.MyClass.myMethod(String,int), com.foo.MyClass.myMethod(java.lang.String,int), com.foo.MyClass.myMethod() Fully qualified: com.foo.MyClass.myMethod Simple with args: MyClass.myMethod(String,int), MyClass.myMethod(java.lang.String,int), MyClass.myMethod() Simple: MyClass.myMethod Simple inner class: MyClass$Inner1$Inner2.myMethod, Inner1$Inner2.myMethod, Inner2.myMethod Fields: Fully qualified: com.foo.MyClass.myField Simple: MyClass.myField Simple inner class: MyClass$Inner1$Inner2.myField, Inner1$Inner2.myField, Inner2.myField Constructors: Fully qualified with args: com.foo.MyClass(String,int), com.foo.MyClass(java.lang.String,int), com.foo.MyClass() Simple with args: MyClass(String,int), MyClass(java.lang.String,int), MyClass() Simple inner class: MyClass$Inner1$Inner2(), Inner1$Inner2(), Inner2() A comma-delimited list of anything on this list.

The @Example annotation in org.apache.juneau.marshall identifies a canonical example instance of a POJO. Juneau surfaces these examples in generated Swagger/OpenAPI documents and uses them wherever a representative value of a type is needed. @Example can be placed on a static method, a static field, or a class, and can also be applied to @Rest-annotated classes and @RestOp-annotated methods via @ExampleApply.

A public static method annotated with @Example that returns an instance of the enclosing type supplies the example. The method takes either zero arguments or a single MarshallingSession argument. public class Address { public String street; public String city; @Example public static Address example() { Address a = new Address(); a.street = "123 Main St"; a.city = "Springfield"; return a; } } The example is then emitted when the type is serialized as a documentation example: String json = Json5.DEFAULT.of(Address.example()); // {street:'123 Main St',city:'Springfield'}

A public static method simply named example (with no arguments or one MarshallingSession argument) is picked up as the example even without the annotation: public class Address { public static Address example() { ... } // recognized by name }

A public static field annotated with @Example supplies the example directly: public class Address { public String street; public String city; @Example public static final Address EXAMPLE = create("123 Main St", "Springfield"); }

Applied to a class, @Example takes a Lax-JSON (JSON5) string value describing the example — no separate factory method or field is needed: @Example("{street:'123 Main St',city:'Springfield'}") public class Address { public String street; public String city; }

The same JSON5 example can be declared through the @Marshalled(example) attribute, which is useful when you are already using @Marshalled for other marshalling settings: @Marshalled(example="{street:'123 Main St',city:'Springfield'}") public class Address { public String street; public String city; } Both the class-level @Example("...") form and the @Marshalled(example="...") form set the same underlying POJO example.

The JSON5 string forms support VarResolver.DEFAULT substitution, so an example value can reference configuration and other variables that are resolved when the example is read: @Marshalled(example="{apiKey:'${C:Demo/apiKey}'}") public class Credentials { public String apiKey; } See VarResolver.DEFAULT for the set of built-in variables.

When more than one example source is present for a type, Juneau resolves them in this order: The JSON5 string form — @Example("...") on the class or @Marshalled(example="..."). An example method — a static method annotated with @Example or named example. An @Example-annotated static field. The first source that is present wins. See Also @Marshalled Annotation - The example attribute and other class-level marshalling settings. VarResolver.DEFAULT - Variable substitution supported in example strings. Marshallers - The marshaller API overview.

Rest-annotated classes get automated timing and error statistic information for all @RestOp and lifecycle-event annotated methods on the class. If you extend from BasicRestServlet or BasicRestResource, then the statistics are made available through the REST interface via the StatsMixin op-mixin's following method: @RestGet( path="/stats", summary="Timing statistics", description="Timing statistics for method invocations on this resource." ) @Override /* StatsMixin */ public RestContextStats getStats(RestRequest req) { return req.getContext().getStats(); } Rendered in a browser, the method table looks like this. The rows are the methods of the petstore's about resource (/console/about/stats); each shows its run count, timing and error counts: The default REST configuration provides a link to the stats in the navlinks section of the page: When a method throws, the thrownStore column links to the stored exceptions. Each one carries a hash that is also written to the log file, which gives a quick way of locating the exception in the logs. REST interface access to the statistics are provided via the following methods (contributed by StatsMixin): StatsMixin (composed into BasicRestServlet, BasicRestResource, and their groups)getStats(RestRequest) Programmatic access to the statistics are provided via the following methods: RestContextgetStats()

As of 10.0, JettyMicroservice was reshaped — the legacy subclass form was retired, and a thin static-call facade was introduced to collapse the standard Microservice + JettyConfiguration bootstrap. See juneau-microservice-jetty for the new entry point. juneau-microservice-jetty contributes a single JettyConfiguration class that wires Jetty into the standard Microservice. Customization is therefore done by contributing your own @Bean definitions rather than subclassing.

Implement MicroserviceListener and expose it as a @Bean — every MicroserviceListener bean in the store is invoked on start() / stop() / config-change events (start in registration order, stop in reverse order). @Configuration public class MyApp { @Bean Servlet rootResources() { return new RootResources(); } @Bean(name = "lifecycle") MicroserviceListener lifecycle() { return new BasicMicroserviceListener() { @Override public void onStart(Microservice ms) { // custom start-up logic, e.g. warming caches, registering JMX beans, etc. } @Override public void onStop(Microservice ms) { // custom shutdown logic } }; } } public class App { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Microservice .create() .args(args) .configurations(JettyConfiguration.class, MyApp.class) .build() .start() .startConsole() .join(); } }

The relevant Jetty hooks are all keyed by bean type in the store; user-supplied @Beans win over the defaults that JettyConfiguration contributes. Override Replace by contributing Jetty server itself @Bean Server (skips jetty.xml entirely if its "ServletContextHandler" attribute is set). Server factory @Bean JettyServerFactory — used when no @Bean Server is supplied. Ports / jetty.xml content / var resolution @Bean JettySettings (use JettySettings.create().ports(...).jettyXml(...).build()). Servlet auto-mounts @Bean Servlets annotated with @Rest — mounted at @Rest(path = "...").

Contribute a ServletFilterRegistration bean to mount a jakarta.servlet.Filter before the server starts. The same type works on Jetty and on Tomcat. @Bean(name="consoleBoundary") ServletFilterRegistration consoleBoundary() { return ServletFilterRegistration.create(new PetstoreConsoleBoundary()) .urlPatterns("/console/*") .dispatcherTypes(DispatcherType.REQUEST, DispatcherType.FORWARD, DispatcherType.ASYNC, DispatcherType.ERROR) .order(ServletFilterRegistration.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE) .build(); } URL patterns follow the Servlet specification: a prefix (/api/*), an extension (*.json), an exact path, or "" for the context root. At least one is required, and a malformed pattern is rejected when the registration is built. Dispatcher types default to REQUEST only. dispatcherTypes(...) replaces the default, so list REQUEST explicitly when you want it. Order. Lower order values run first. Filters with the same order run by bean name, so give each registration its own @Bean(name=...). @Order on the bean method does not affect filter order. The default is 0, which runs after the auto-mounted AuthFilterChain at ServletFilterRegistration.AUTH_ORDER (-100). A filter that must reject a request before authentication, such as a CSRF boundary, uses HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE and a narrow pattern; on /* it would also intercept authentication redirects and challenges. AuthFilterChain. A bean of that type is mounted automatically. To change its dispatchers or order, register the injected bean instance in your own ServletFilterRegistration; that registration replaces the automatic one. Validation. The same filter instance cannot be registered twice, and explicit name(...) values must be unique. The addFilter(Filter, String...) overloads on the server component are unchanged and still map REQUEST only.

JettyServerComponent jetty = Microservice .getInstance() .getBeanStore() .getBean(JettyServerComponent.class) .orElseThrow(); URI uri = jetty.getURI(); int port = jetty.getPort(); Server server = jetty.getServer();
