New to Juneau? Work through these four short pages in order. They build one small project, a Pet bean, a REST resource that serves it, and a client that calls it, and every code block is complete enough to compile and run as shown.

You need Notes JDK 17 or newer java -version Apache Maven 3.9 or newer mvn -version An empty directory The walkthrough creates pom.xml and four small source files in it. Port 10000 free Page 3 starts a web server there (Ports used in these docs). About 10 minutes The Maven commands themselves run in seconds. The first build is slower because Maven downloads the Juneau modules and Jetty. Juneau 10 is a pre-release (10.0.0-SNAPSHOT), so the project resolves it from the Apache snapshots repository. Page 1 sets that up for you. Install Juneau: create the project and its pom.xml. Your first serializer: turn a bean into JSON and back. Your first REST app: expose a bean over HTTP. Your first client: call it with the REST client.

The walkthrough above does not need them. The Starter Projects are clone-and-go "Hello World" apps for Jetty, Spring Boot, and Tomcat. The Petstore is a fuller showcase, and the Examples cover marshalling and MCP.
documents.s: Prefer to start from a working project?

documents.t: Read the V10 Migration Guide first. It has the module, package, and API rename tables. If you use the REST client, also see Choosing a REST Client.

Guides: task-based walkthroughs, from a Spring Boot API to a typed client. Ecosystem Overview: every module and what it requires. Dependency Management: the BOM and the bundles. Why Choose Juneau? and Framework Comparisons.

The REST client calls the service from the previous page and parses the response into the same Pet bean. With that server still running, create src/main/java/com/example/demo/Client.java: // Artifact: juneau-rest-client package com.example.demo; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json5.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; public class Client { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .rootUrl("http://localhost:10000") .serializer(Json5Serializer.create().build()) .parser(Json5Parser.create().build()) .build()) { try (var resp = client.get("/pets/{id}").pathData("id", 1).run()) { resp.assertOk(); Pet pet = resp.body().as(Pet.class); System.out.println(pet.id + " " + pet.name); } } } } Run it from a second terminal in the project directory: mvn compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=com.example.demo.Client It prints 1 Fido, followed by a log line for the request. Always close the response (it holds the connection) and close the client at shutdown; the try blocks above do both. Which client? juneau-rest-client (org.apache.juneau.rest.client.RestClient) is the recommended REST client. It is generally available in 10.0.0, transport-agnostic, and uses the JDK HttpClient by default. juneau-rest-client-classic (org.apache.juneau.rest.client.classic.RestClient, Apache HttpClient 4.5) stays supported and is not deprecated; it is the stable choice for existing users. See Choosing a REST Client.
For services you call often, declare an interface and let Juneau implement it. See Declarative Remote-Proxy Features.
Requests, responses, assertions, and security.

You now have a serializer, a REST resource, and a client. The Ecosystem Overview lists everything else, and the Starter Projects show a complete deployable app. Next: pick a guide. The Guides each do one task end to end, from a Spring Boot API to a typed client.
Juneau requires Java 17+. All modules are published to Maven Central under the group id org.apache.juneau.

Define the version once as a Maven property; every snippet in these docs uses ${juneau.version}. <properties> <juneau.version>10.0.0-SNAPSHOT</juneau.version> </properties> <repositories> <repository> <id>apache-snapshots</id> <url>https://repository.apache.org/snapshots/</url> <releases><enabled>false</enabled></releases> <snapshots><enabled>true</enabled></snapshots> </repository> </repositories> These docs describe 10.0, which is a pre-release (10.0.0-SNAPSHOT). Maven Central currently has only 9.2.1, the latest release (see Downloads). To build against 10.0 you need the Apache snapshots repository shown above; for 9.2.1, set juneau.version to 9.2.1 and drop the <repositories> block. The juneau-bom and the newer modules shown in these docs are 10.0 only.

Import juneau-bom once, then leave the version off every Juneau dependency. See Dependency Management for details. <dependencyManagement> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-bom</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> <type>pom</type> <scope>import</scope> </dependency> </dependencies> </dependencyManagement>

You want to... Add Serialize and parse beans (JSON, XML, HTML, YAML, and more) juneau-marshall Build a REST API juneau-rest-server (plus one of the starters or a microservice bundle to run it) Call REST APIs juneau-rest-client (see Choosing a REST Client) Test REST code without a network juneau-rest-mock <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId> </dependency> </dependencies> juneau-marshall needs no third-party dependencies. The full list of modules, with their prerequisites, is in the Ecosystem Overview.

The next three pages build one project. Make an empty directory, juneau-demo, and save this as juneau-demo/pom.xml. It combines the version property, snapshot repository, and BOM from above with the four modules the walkthrough uses: the Jetty microservice bundle (which brings in juneau-marshall and juneau-rest-server), the REST client, and the mock client. <project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"> <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion> <groupId>com.example</groupId> <artifactId>demo</artifactId> <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version> <properties> <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release> <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding> <juneau.version>10.0.0-SNAPSHOT</juneau.version> </properties> <repositories> <repository> <id>apache-snapshots</id> <url>https://repository.apache.org/snapshots/</url> <releases><enabled>false</enabled></releases> <snapshots><enabled>true</enabled></snapshots> </repository> </repositories> <dependencyManagement> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-bom</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> <type>pom</type> <scope>import</scope> </dependency> </dependencies> </dependencyManagement> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-microservice-jetty-bundle</artifactId> <type>pom</type> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-client</artifactId> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-mock</artifactId> </dependency> </dependencies> </project> Then create the source directory the later pages write into: mkdir -p juneau-demo/src/main/java/com/example/demo cd juneau-demo Every Java file in this walkthrough goes in src/main/java/com/example/demo/ and starts with package com.example.demo;.
Your first serializer

A Juneau REST resource is a plain class annotated with @Rest. Methods annotated with @RestGet, @RestPost, and friends become endpoints, and return values are serialized according to the client's Accept header. See the guide: Build a REST API on Spring Boot Create src/main/java/com/example/demo/PetResource.java. Pet is the bean from the previous page. package com.example.demo; import org.apache.juneau.http.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.servlet.*; @Rest(path="/pets", title="Pet service") public class PetResource extends BasicRestServlet { @RestGet("/{id}") public Pet getPet(@Path("id") int id) { return new Pet(id, "Fido"); } } The same method answers Accept: application/json, text/xml, text/html (a browsable page), and the other formats registered on the resource, with no extra code.

tip BasicRestServlet is an HttpServlet, so it can be a top-level resource in any servlet container or in the Jetty microservice. BasicRestResource is the same resource without the servlet base class: use it for child resources (@Rest(children=...)) and for Spring Boot beans. See REST Children and Spring Boot REST API.

The Jetty microservice bundle in your pom.xml includes an embedded Jetty server. Create src/main/java/com/example/demo/App.java to start it with PetResource as the root resource: package com.example.demo; import org.apache.juneau.microservice.jetty.*; public class App { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { JettyMicroservice.run(args, new PetResource(), false).join(); } } The server writes its request log to a logs directory in the working directory, creating it if needed. Start the app: mvn compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=com.example.demo.App When it is up (the first build downloads Jetty, so allow a minute), call it from a second terminal: curl -H "Accept: application/json" http://localhost:10000/pets/1 # {"id":1,"name":"Fido"} curl -H "Accept: text/xml" http://localhost:10000/pets/1 # <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?><object><id>1</id><name>Fido</name></object> You can also open http://localhost:10000/pets/1 in a browser to see the HTML view. Leave the server running for the next page, and press Ctrl+C when you are done. The walkthrough assumes the default port, 10000, so stop anything else that is using it first. If port 10000 is taken, the curl commands and the client on the next page can hit the wrong process and return a 404. Prefer a ready-made project? The starter projects package the same idea with Jetty, Spring Boot, or Tomcat. You do not need one for this walkthrough.

juneau-rest-mock dispatches requests to your resource in-process, so there is nothing to start: import org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.*; try (MockRestClient mock = MockRestClient.create(PetResource.class); var resp = mock.get("/1").run()) { resp.assertThat().isOk().body().contains("Fido"); } The mock client mounts the resource at its @Rest(path), so the request path is relative to /pets. Put the snippet in a main method (or a unit test) to run it; the juneau-rest-mock dependency is already in your pom.xml. See NG Mock REST Client for more.
juneau-rest-server: annotations, content negotiation, Swagger, and the rest. Petstore: a complete REST application, including HTML views and a UI.
Your first client

With juneau-marshall on the classpath (the project from the previous page has it), the Json marshaller turns a bean into JSON and back in one call. Create the bean, src/main/java/com/example/demo/Pet.java. The REST pages reuse it: package com.example.demo; public class Pet { public int id; public String name; public Pet() {} public Pet(int id, String name) { this.id = id; this.name = name; } } Then create src/main/java/com/example/demo/Main.java: package com.example.demo; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json.JsonSerializer; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.marshaller.Json; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.marshaller.Json5; public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String json = Json.of(new Pet(1, "Fido")); // {"id":1,"name":"Fido"} System.out.println(json); Pet pet = Json.to(json, Pet.class); // back to a bean System.out.println(pet.name); // Fido System.out.println(Json5.of(new Pet(1, "Fido"))); // {id:1,name:'Fido'} JsonSerializer serializer = JsonSerializer.create().sq().build(); System.out.println(serializer.write(new Pet(1, "Fido"))); // {'id':1,'name':'Fido'} } } Run it from the project directory: mvn compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=com.example.demo.Main Expected output: {"id":1,"name":"Fido"} Fido {id:1,name:'Fido'} {'id':1,'name':'Fido'} Import the marshaller classes by name, as above. A wildcard import of both org.apache.juneau.marshall.json.* and org.apache.juneau.marshall.marshaller.* makes Json ambiguous, because both packages have a class of that name.

Each format has a marshaller with the same of(...) / to(...) methods. Json5 (used in Main above) writes the relaxed, quote-free JSON dialect, which is handy for logs and tests. For XML, HTML, YAML, CSV, MessagePack, and the rest, see juneau-marshall.

The marshaller uses a default serializer and parser. When you need different settings, build your own and reuse it (serializers are thread-safe and cache their class metadata). Main builds one that uses single quotes: JsonSerializer serializer = JsonSerializer.create().sq().build(); String json = serializer.write(new Pet(1, "Fido")); // {'id':1,'name':'Fido'} See Serializers and Parsers for the full set of options.
Your first REST app

See also: Health / Readiness / Liveness Probes — the probe surface (/healthz, /readyz, /livez) this page gates during shutdown. Starting with 10.0.0, both embedded-server microservice flavors — juneau-microservice-jetty and juneau-microservice-tomcat — perform a zero-downtime graceful shutdown suitable for rolling Kubernetes deployments. The two servers share one identical shutdown contract. When a microservice begins shutting down it: Flips readiness out of service first. A shared ReadinessState flag is flipped before the listening connector stops, so GET /readyz immediately returns 503 Service Unavailable (state=OUT_OF_SERVICE) while a load balancer / Kubernetes is still routing. GET /livez and GET /healthz stay healthy so the orchestrator does not kill the pod mid-drain. Optionally settles. An optional shutdownSettleDelay pause between the readiness flip and the connector stop gives the load balancer a window to observe the 503 before draining begins. Drains in-flight requests. The connector stops accepting new connections and the server waits up to a bounded stopTimeout (default 30s) for in-flight requests to complete before it fully stops. This sequencing is what lets Kubernetes shift traffic away from a terminating pod before its in-flight work is interrupted.

shutdown begins │ ├─▶ ReadinessState.markOutOfService() /readyz → 503 (OUT_OF_SERVICE) │ /livez → 200 (still LIVE) │ /healthz→ 200 (still UP) │ ├─▶ sleep(shutdownSettleDelay) LB observes the 503 (default 0ms) │ ├─▶ drain in-flight requests up to stopTimeout (default 30s) │ Jetty: server.setStopTimeout(...) then server.stop() │ Tomcat: connector.pause() then wait for active count → 0, then stop() │ └─▶ server fully stopped

Probe Normal During shutdown Why GET /readyz 200 (when no component is DOWN) 503 OUT_OF_SERVICE Tells the load balancer / k8s readiness gate to stop routing new traffic to this pod. GET /livez 200 200 (unaffected) A 503 here would make k8s kill the pod mid-drain — deliberately not gated. GET /healthz 200 / 503 per indicators unaffected The aggregate (null-probe) health surface is not gated by readiness. The readiness gate is implemented in HealthAggregator: when the shared ReadinessState is out of service it forces the READY probe DOWN and adds a readiness component with {"state": "OUT_OF_SERVICE"} to the payload. Liveness and the aggregate health surface are untouched. { "status": "DOWN", "components": { "readiness": { "status": "DOWN", "details": { "state": "OUT_OF_SERVICE" } } } }

Two knobs control the drain behavior, both expressible programmatically (preferred), via the config file, or left at their defaults. Knob Default Meaning stopTimeout 30s Bounded time the server waits for in-flight requests to drain before stopping the connector. shutdownSettleDelay 0 (none) In-process pause between the /readyz 503 flip and the connector stop. The recommended Kubernetes pattern uses a preStop hook sleep instead (see below).
For both servers the resolved value follows this precedence: programmatic settings > config-file entry > (Jetty only: existing jetty.xml value) > 30s default

Contribute a @Bean JettySettings (or @Bean TomcatSettings) from your own @Configuration class to override the defaults: import java.time.Duration; import org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.Configuration; import org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.Bean; import org.apache.juneau.microservice.jetty.JettySettings; @Configuration public class MyAppConfig { @Bean JettySettings jettySettings() { return JettySettings.create() .stopTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(45)) .shutdownSettleDelay(Duration.ofSeconds(2)) .build(); } } The Tomcat flavor is identical — swap JettySettings for TomcatSettings: import java.time.Duration; import org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.Configuration; import org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.Bean; import org.apache.juneau.microservice.tomcat.TomcatSettings; @Configuration public class MyAppConfig { @Bean TomcatSettings tomcatSettings() { return TomcatSettings.create() .stopTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(45)) .shutdownSettleDelay(Duration.ofSeconds(2)) .build(); } } Any value left null on the settings bean falls back to the config-file entry, then to the default.

Both knobs are documented in the bundled juneau.cfg and read from the server's section ([Jetty] or [Tomcat]) in milliseconds: [Jetty] # Graceful-shutdown drain timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000 (30s) when unset. stopTimeout = 30000 # Settle delay in milliseconds applied between the /readyz 503 flip and the connector stop. # Defaults to 0 when unset. shutdownSettleDelay = 0 For the Tomcat flavor the keys live under the [Tomcat] section instead (Tomcat/stopTimeout, Tomcat/shutdownSettleDelay).

Both servers expose the same knobs, the same defaults, and the same observable readiness contract. They differ only in the underlying mechanism used to drain: Jetty Tomcat Apply drain timeout server.setStopTimeout(...) applied at startup; server.stop() drains connector pause(), then wait up to stopTimeout for the protocol-handler executor's active count to reach zero, then stop() / destroy() Config section [Jetty] [Tomcat] jetty.xml override honored if set (precedence above the default) n/a Default stopTimeout 30s 30s Readiness flip / settle identical identical The bundled jetty.xml deliberately does not set stopTimeout — it is applied in code so the 30s default and the precedence rules apply uniformly. A comment in jetty.xml documents this.

The recommended production pattern pairs the in-process readiness flip with a preStop hook and a generous terminationGracePeriodSeconds, rather than relying on the in-process shutdownSettleDelay: Point the readiness probe at /readyz so k8s stops routing to the pod as soon as it flips to 503. Point the liveness probe at /livez so k8s does not kill the pod while it is draining. Add a preStop hook sleep to give the cluster's endpoint/Service propagation time to remove the pod from rotation before the JVM begins draining. Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to comfortably exceed (preStop sleep + shutdownSettleDelay + stopTimeout) so Kubernetes does not SIGKILL the pod mid-drain. apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment spec: template: spec: # Must exceed preStop sleep + shutdownSettleDelay + stopTimeout. terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60 containers: - name: my-juneau-microservice readinessProbe: httpGet: path: /readyz port: 10000 periodSeconds: 5 livenessProbe: httpGet: path: /livez port: 10000 periodSeconds: 10 lifecycle: preStop: exec: # Give Service/endpoint propagation time to drop this pod before draining. command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 10"] With this setup: the preStop sleep + readiness 503 keep new traffic away, stopTimeout drains the in-flight requests, and terminationGracePeriodSeconds guarantees the JVM gets enough time to finish before a hard kill. See Also Health / Readiness / Liveness Probes

Guards control access to REST classes and methods. When guards are associated at the class-level, it's equivalent to associating guards on all Java methods on the servlet. If multiple guards are present, ALL guards must pass. (Note that this is different in behavior to Matchers which require only one matcher to pass.) Guards are associated with resource classes and methods via the following: RestguardsRestOpguards Example // Define a guard that only lets Billy make a request public class BillyGuard extends RestGuard { @Override /* RestGuard */ public boolean isRequestAllowed(RestRequest req) { return req.getUserPrincipal().getName().equals("Billy"); } } // Servlet with class-level guard applied @Rest(guards=BillyGuard.class) public class MyRestServlet extends BasicRestServlet { // Delete method that only Billy is allowed to call. @RestDelete public void doDelete(RestRequest req, RestResponse res) throws Exception {...} } A common use for guards is to only allow admin access to certain Java methods... // DELETE method @RestDelete(guards={AdminGuard.class}) public void doDelete(RestRequest req, RestResponse res) throws Exception {...} public class AdminGuard extends RestGuard { @Override /* RestGuard */ public boolean isRequestAllowed(RestRequest req) { return req.getUserPrincipal().isUserInRole("ADMIN"); } } A guard failure results in an HTTP 401 Unauthorized response. However, this can be configured by overriding guard() and processing the response yourself. public class AdminGuard extends RestGuard { @Override /* RestGuard */ public boolean guard(RestRequest req, RestResponse res) throws BasicHttpException { if (! isOkay(req)) throw new Forbidden("Access denied!!!"); return true; } } A simplified format is available for matching based on the user role on the request using the following: RestroleGuardRestOproleGuard Example @Rest( path="/foo", roleGuard="ROLE_ADMIN || (ROLE_READ_WRITE && ROLE_SPECIAL)" ) public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet { ... }

REST Authenticator — Resource-Level Authentication — resolves the Principal + roles that roleGuard / RoleBasedRestGuard check. AuthN Guards — Bearer / API-Key / JWT AuthN Filter Framework — Servlet-Layer Authentication

HTTP form posts can be handled two ways: By parsing the entire HTTP body into a POJO using the registered UrlEncodingParser By access the form post entries as HTTP parts. The following example shows the first approach of handling an application/x-www-form-urlencoded request of the form aString=foo&aNumber=123&aDate=2001-07-04T15:30:45Z and loading it into a simple bean. // A simple bean. public static class FormInputBean { public String aString; public int aNumber; @MarshalledProp(calendarFormat=CalendarFormat.ISO_LOCAL_DATE_TIME) public Calendar aDate; } @Rest(...) public class MyRestResource extends BasicRestServlet { // Our form input endpoint. @RestPost("/") public Object doPost(@Content FormInputBean input) { // Just mirror back the request return input; } } The next example shows handling it as individual parts: // Our form input endpoint. @RestPost("/") public Object doPost( @FormData("aString") String aString, @FormData("aNumber") int aNumber, @FormData("aDate") Calendar aDate) { ... } The advantage to the form input bean is that it can handle any of the parsable types (e.g. JSON, XML...) in addition to URL-Encoding while the latter approach only supports URL-Encoding. warning If you're using form input beans: DO NOT use the @FormData attribute or HttpServletRequest.getParameter(String) method since this will cause the underlying JEE servlet to parse the HTTP body as a form post. Your input bean will end up being null since there won't be any content left after the servlet has parsed the body of the request. This applies to WHENEVER you use @Content or RestRequest.getContent(). If you want to be able to consume url-encoded form post bodies as POJOs in Spring Boot, you'll need to add the following Spring Bean to your configuration to prevent Spring Boot from automatically consuming the body itself: @SpringBootApplication @Controller public class SpringBootAppConfig { @Bean public FilterRegistrationBean registration(HiddenHttpMethodFilter filter) { FilterRegistrationBean reg = new FilterRegistrationBean(filter); reg.setEnabled(false); return reg; } }

The Juneau framework does not natively support multipart form posts. However, it can be done in conjunction with the Apache Commons File Upload library or through the Servlet 3.0 API directly. The following is an example that uses the File Upload library to allow files to be uploaded as multipart form posts. info DirectoryResource (subclassed below) lives in the unpublished juneau-microservice-examples module (package org.apache.juneau.microservice.examples), not in juneau-microservice — see Predefined Resource Classes. Treat this as a copy-and-adapt sample rather than a dependency you pull in directly. Example @Rest( path="/tempDir" ) public class TempDirResource extends DirectoryResource { @RestPost(path="/upload", matchers=TempDirResource.MultipartFormDataMatcher.class) public Redirect uploadFile(RestRequest req) throws Exception { ServletFileUpload upload = new ServletFileUpload(); FileItemIterator iter = upload.getItemIterator(req); while (iter.hasNext()) { FileItemStream item = iter.next(); if (item.getFieldName().equals("contents")) { File file = new File(getRootDir(), item.getName()); IOPipe.create(item.openStream(), new FileOutputStream(file)).closeOut().run(); } } return new Redirect(); // Redirect to the servlet root. } /** Causes a 404 if POST isn't multipart/form-data */ public static class MultipartFormDataMatcher extends RestMatcher { @Override /* RestMatcher */ public boolean matches(RestRequest req) { String contentType = req.getContentType(); return contentType != null && contentType.startsWith("multipart/form-data"); } } } The following shows using the HttpServletRequest.getParts() method to retrieve multi-part form posts when using Jetty. This example is pulled from the PetStore application. @RestPost public SeeOtherRoot uploadFile(RestRequest req) throws Exception { // Required for Jetty. MultipartConfigElement mce = new MultipartConfigElement((String)null); req.setAttribute("org.eclipse.jetty.multipartConfig", mce); String id = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); BufferedImage img = null; for (Part part : req.getParts()) { switch (part.getName()) { case "id": id = IOUtils.read(part.getInputStream()); break; case "file": img = ImageIO.read(part.getInputStream()); } } addPhoto(id, img); return new SeeOtherRoot(); // Redirect to the servlet root. }

The @Header annotation can be applied to arguments of @RemoteOp-annotated methods to denote that they are header parameters on the request. @Headername - Header name. Example @Remote(path="/myproxy") public interface MyProxy { // Explicit names specified for HTTP headers. // pojo will be converted to UON notation (unless plain-text parts enabled). @RemoteGet("/mymethod1") String myProxyMethod1(@Header("Foo") String foo, @Header("Bar") MyPojo pojo); // Multiple values pulled from a HeaderList object. // Same as @Header("*"). @RemoteGet("/mymethod2") String myProxyMethod2(@Header HeaderList headerList); // Multiple values pulled from a Map. // Same as @Header("*"). @RemoteGet("/mymethod3") String myProxyMethod3(@Header Map map); // Multiple values pulled from a bean. // Same as @Header("*"). @RemoteGet("/mymethod4") String myProxyMethod4(@Header MyBean myBean); } Header arguments can be any of the following types: Single-part arguments (i.e. those with name != "*"): Any serializable POJO - Converted to a string using the HttpPartSerializer registered with the RestClient (OpenApiSerializer by default). Multi-part arguments (i.e. those with name == "*" or empty): HeaderList - Serialized as individual headers. Map<String,Object> - Converted to key-value pairs. Values serialized using the registered HttpPartSerializer (OpenApiSerializer by default). Bean - Converted to key-value pairs. Values serialized using the registered HttpPartSerializer (OpenApiSerializer by default). See the link below for information about supported data types in OpenAPI serialization. See Also OpenAPI Serializers

See also: REST Server — Mixins and Multi-Mount Paths — the underlying @Rest(mixins=...) and @Rest(paths=...) composition primitives this page is built on. Starting with 10.0.0, Juneau provides an opt-in probe surface for Jetty microservices: GET /healthz GET /readyz GET /livez Probe routing now has two supported integration styles: Preferred: mix probe operations into your existing root resource with @Rest(mixins=HealthMixin.class). Fallback: standalone probe servlet auto-mounted at explicit @Rest(paths={...}) path specs (/healthz, /readyz, /livez) via HealthProbeConfiguration. A third flavor, HealthResource, mounts the same three probes as a routed child (@Rest(children=HealthResource.class)) under a parent's /health subtree — see REST Server — Standalone vs Mixin Resources for how the three flavors relate. This avoids root-path collisions when your app already owns @Rest(path="/"). The endpoints aggregate every HealthIndicator bean from the microservice bean store and return an Actuator-style payload: { "status": "UP", "components": { "dbHealth": { "status": "UP", "details": { "validationQueryMs": 12 } } } } HTTP status is: 200 OK when no component is DOWN. 503 Service Unavailable when any component is DOWN.

import org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.*; import org.apache.juneau.microservice.*; import org.apache.juneau.microservice.jetty.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.health.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.servlet.*; @Rest( path="/", mixins=HealthMixin.class ) public class RootResources extends BasicRestServlet { @Bean(name="dbHealth") HealthIndicator dbHealth() { return () -> Health.up("db").detail("validationQueryMs", 12).build(); } } public class App { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Microservice.create() .args(args) .configurations(JettyConfiguration.class) .build() .start() .join(); } } Each named HealthIndicator method is registered separately; @Bean methods may be package-private.
documents.s: Option A (recommended): mix into existing root resource

documents.t: import org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.*; import org.apache.juneau.microservice.*; import org.apache.juneau.microservice.jetty.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.health.*; import jakarta.servlet.*; @Configuration public class AppConfig { @Bean Servlet root() { return new RootResources(); } @Bean HealthIndicator dbHealth() { return () -> Health.up("db").detail("validationQueryMs", 12).build(); } } public class App { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Microservice.create() .args(args) .configurations(JettyConfiguration.class, HealthProbeConfiguration.class, AppConfig.class) .build() .start() .join(); } } HealthProbeConfiguration contributes a Servlet bean (HealthServlet) and Jetty mounts it at the three explicit path specs declared on the resource via @Rest(paths={...}).

HealthIndicator is a functional interface: @FunctionalInterface public interface HealthIndicator { Health check(); } Return values are created with Health.up(name), Health.down(name, throwable), and Health.unknown(name), with optional .detail(key, value) entries. Indicators can scope themselves to probe types by overriding probes() and returning a set of HealthProbe values: HealthProbe.LIVE HealthProbe.READY HealthProbe.STARTUP By default, indicators participate in both liveness and readiness probes.

Each indicator runs with a timeout from HealthProbeSettings (default: 1 second). If a check times out or throws, the component is marked DOWN and the error is surfaced in details.error. Override defaults by contributing your own settings bean: @Bean HealthProbeSettings probeSettings() { return HealthProbeSettings.create() .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)) .build(); }

The org.apache.juneau.http.header package contains various convenience classes for creating standard HTTP components using static imports. HttpHeaders - Utility class for standard HTTP headers.HttpParts - Utility class for standard HTTP parts.HttpEntities - Utility class for standard HTTP entities.HttpResources - Utility class for standard HTTP resources.HttpResponses - Utility class for standard HTTP responses.

info There are two HttpHeaders classes: the transport-neutral NG org.apache.juneau.http.HttpHeaders (strongly-typed creators only, e.g. accept(String), contentType(String); see HTTP Headers) and the classic org.apache.juneau.http.classic.HttpHeaders documented below, which adds free-form header creators and HeaderList builders on top of the Apache HttpCore-based header types. The HttpHeaders class contains many convenience static methods and fields for working with standard HTTP request and response headers and header lists. Example import static org.apache.juneau.http.classic.HttpHeaders.*; HeaderList headers = headerList( // Arbitrary list of headers CONTENTTYPE_TEXT_XML, // Static constants contentType("text/xml"), // Predefined headers contentType(() -> "text/xml"), // Predefined headers with supplied values stringHeader("Content-Type", "text/xml"), // Freeform headers stringHeader("Content-Type", () -> "text/xml") // Freeform headers with supplied values ); This class is vast in scope and covers all request and response headers defined in RFC2616. In addition to the predefined headers, various methods are provided for free-form headers. Each accepts either static values or values from Suppliers: HttpHeadersbasicHeader(String,Object)booleanHeader(String,String)csvHeader(String,String)dateHeader(String,String)entityTagsHeader(String,String)entityTagHeader(String,String)integerHeader(String,String)longHeader(String,String)mediaRangesHeader(String,String)mediaTypeHeader(String,String)stringHeader(String,String)serializedHeader(String,Object)stringRangesHeader(String,String)uriHeader(String,String) The serializedHeader methods allows for headers serialized using schema-based serializers such as the OpenAPI serializer. Static methods are also provided for instantiating Header-annotated or other HttpComponent-defined header classes: HttpHeadersheader(Class,String,Object)header(Class,Object) Example import static org.apache.juneau.http.classic.HttpHeaders.*; ContentType contentType = header(ContentType.class, "text/xml"); Lists of headers can be produced with the following methods: HttpHeadersheaderList()headerList(Header...)headerList(List)headerList(String...) The capabilities of the HeaderList class is described later.

info There are two HttpParts classes: the transport-neutral NG org.apache.juneau.http.HttpParts (minimal surface: part(String,String), partList(HttpPart...), partListOfPairs(String...)) and the classic org.apache.juneau.http.classic.HttpParts documented below, which adds typed free-form part creators on top of the Apache HttpCore-based NameValuePair types. The HttpParts class contains convenience static methods for generating query/form-data/path parts and part lists. Example import static org.apache.juneau.http.classic.HttpParts.*; PartList formData = partList( // Arbitrary list of parts stringPart("Name", "Bill"), // Freeform part integerPart("Age", () -> calculateAge()) // Freeform part with supplied value ); The following methods are provided for creating parts. Each accepts either static values or values from Suppliers: HttpPartsbasicPart(String,Object)booleanPart(String,Boolean)csvArrayPart(String,String...)datePart(String,ZonedDateTime)integerPart(String,Integer)longPart(String,Long)serializedPart(String,Object)stringPart(String,String)uriPart(String,URI) The serializedPart methods allows for parts serialized using schema-based serializers such as the OpenAPI serializer. Lists of parts can be produced with the following methods: HttpPartspartList()partList(List)partList(NameValuePair...)partList(String...) The capabilities of the PartList class is described later.

The HttpEntities class contains convenience static methods for generating HTTP message entities. Returned objects extend from org.apache.http.HttpEntity but provides the following additional features: Caching. Fluent setters. Fluent assertions. Externally-supplied/dynamic content. The following methods are provided for creating entities. Each accepts either static values or values from Suppliers and returns builders: HttpEntitiesbyteArrayEntity(byte[])fileEntity(File)readerEntity(Reader)serializedEntity(Object, Serializer)streamEntity(InputStream)stringEntity(String) HTTP entities are automatically supported in both the server and client REST APIs for requests and responses. Example import static org.apache.juneau.http.classic.HttpEntities.*; @RestDelete(path="/{id}") public HttpEntity helloWold(...) { return stringEntity("Hello!").contentType("text/plain"); }

The HttpResources class contains convenience static methods for generating HTTP message resources. Returned objects extend from HttpResource which extends from HttpEntity but with additional arbitrary headers. The following methods are provided for creating entities. Each accepts either static values or values from Suppliers and are in the form of builders. HttpResourcesbyteArrayResource(byte[])fileResource(File)readerResource(Reader)streamResource(InputStream)stringResource(String) The most common location where resources are used are as returned types of REST operation methods described later. Example import static org.apache.juneau.http.classic.HttpResources.*; @RestDelete(path="/{id}") public HttpResource helloWold(...) { return stringResource("Hello!").contentType("text/plain").header("Cache-Control", "none"); }

The HttpResponses class contains convenience static methods for standard HTTP responses. Returned objects implement the transport-neutral HttpResponseMessage interface (which mirrors org.apache.http.HttpResponse semantics without the Apache HttpCore dependency) and are in the form of builders. The following methods are provided for creating responses: HttpResponses _continue accepted alreadyReported badRequest conflict created earlyHints expectationFailed failedDependency forbidden found gone httpVersionNotSupported imUsed insufficientStorage internalServerError lengthRequired locked loopDetected methodNotAllowed misdirectedRequest movedPermanently multipleChoices multiStatus networkAuthenticationRequired noContent nonAuthoritiveInformation notAcceptable notExtended notFound notImplemented notModified ok partialContent payloadTooLarge permanentRedirect preconditionFailed preconditionRequired processing rangeNotSatisfiable requestHeaderFieldsTooLarge resetContent seeOther serviceUnavailable switchingProtocols temporaryRedirect tooManyRequests unauthorized unavailableForLegalReasons unprocessableEntity unsupportedMediaType upgradeRequired uriTooLong useProxy variantAlsoNegotiates The most common location where these responses are used are in REST operation methods described later. Example import static org.apache.juneau.http.HttpResponses.*; import static org.apache.juneau.http.HttpHeaders.*; @RestDelete(path="/{id}") public Ok doDelete(...) throws Unauthorized { if (/* user not authorized*/) throw unauthorized(); return ok().content("Delete was successful"); }

Juneau supports converting arbitrary POJOs to and from Hjson (Human JSON) using native serializers and parsers. Hjson is a syntax extension of JSON designed for human-friendly configuration files and hand-edited data. It extends JSON with quoteless strings, multiline strings, comments, optional commas, and unquoted keys. The HjsonSerializer converts POJOs directly to Hjson format, and the HjsonParser creates POJOs directly from Hjson. Hjson support is included in juneau-marshall. Maven <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency>

// A simple bean public class Person { public String name; public int age; public Person() {} public Person(String name, int age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; } } // Serialize to Hjson (readable mode) Person alice = new Person("Alice", 30); String hjson = Hjson.of(alice); Produces: { name: Alice age: 30 }

// Parse Hjson into a bean Person parsed = Hjson.to(hjson, Person.class); // Parse into a map JsonMap map = Hjson.to(hjson, JsonMap.class); // Parse root-braceless Hjson (no outer {}) String rootBraceless = "name: Bob\nage: 25"; Person bob = Hjson.to(rootBraceless, Person.class);

// Readable mode (default) - newlines between members, quoteless strings String hjson = Hjson.of(bean); // Compact mode - single line, comma-separated (via the HjsonC variant marshaller) String compact = HjsonC.of(bean); The compact configuration is exposed as the dedicated HjsonC variant marshaller (backed by HjsonSerializer.DEFAULT_COMPACT). It is a first-class Hjson facade, so it exposes the same static of(...) / to(...) shortcut surface as Hjson itself. (This replaces the former Hjson.DEFAULT_COMPACT constant, removed in 10.0.0.)

Quoteless strings: name: Alice (no quotes when unambiguous) Multiline strings: Triple single-quote blocks with indentation stripping Comments: #, //, and /* ... */ block comments Optional commas: Newlines can separate object members Trailing commas: Ignored Unquoted keys: Object keys need not be quoted when safe

Maps and beans → Hjson objects Collections and arrays → Hjson arrays Strings → Quoteless (when safe), double-quoted, or multiline Numbers → Hjson numbers Booleans → true / false Null → null ObjectSwaps → Applied for non-primitive types (dates, enums, etc.)
Produces: application/hjson Accepts: application/hjson, application/hjson+json
// Hjson is included in BasicUniversalConfig @Rest public class MyResource extends RestServlet implements BasicUniversalConfig { ... }

Root-braceless Hjson can be parsed; serialization always emits root braces by default Strings equal to true, false, null, or parseable as numbers are automatically quoted on output to prevent ambiguity In compact mode, multiline strings use JSON escape sequences instead of ''' blocks

@HjsonConfig sets serializer/parser properties on a REST class or method (see Context Annotations). Attributes are strings ("true"/"false"): Attribute Description useMultilineStrings Use ''' blocks for strings containing newlines (default true). useQuotelessStrings Omit quotes for simple string values. useQuotelessKeys Omit quotes for simple keys. omitRootBraces Omit the root object braces (default false). useNewlineSeparators Separate members with newlines instead of commas. rank Ordering relative to other config annotations. @Rest @HjsonConfig(useQuotelessKeys="true", omitRootBraces="true") public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet { ... } @Hjson is a marker annotation (no attributes) for classes, methods and fields. @HjsonApply applies it to other classes/members via on()/onClass() (see Dynamically Applied Annotations). See Also Hjson Specification for the full format definition. Marshallers for the marshaller API overview.

Juneau supports converting arbitrary POJOs to and from HOCON (Human-Optimized Config Object Notation) using native serializers and parsers. HOCON is a superset of JSON used extensively in the JVM ecosystem (Akka, Play Framework, sbt, Apache Spark, Kafka, Flink) for configuration files. It extends JSON with path expressions, = as key-value separator, unquoted strings, object merging, substitutions (${var}), triple-quoted multi-line strings, and optional root braces. The HoconSerializer converts POJOs to HOCON format, and the HoconParser creates POJOs from HOCON. HOCON support is included in juneau-marshall. Maven <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency>

// A simple bean public class Person { public String name; public int age; public Person() {} public Person(String name, int age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; } } // Serialize to HOCON Person alice = new Person("Alice", 30); String hocon = Hocon.of(alice); Produces: name = Alice age = 30

// Parse HOCON into a bean Person parsed = Hocon.to(hocon, Person.class); // Parse into a map JsonMap map = Hocon.to(hocon, JsonMap.class); // Parse with path expressions String pathExpr = "database.host = localhost\ndatabase.port = 5432"; JsonMap config = Hocon.to(pathExpr, JsonMap.class);

// Readable mode (default) - = separator, unquoted strings, root braces omitted String hocon = Hocon.DEFAULT.of(bean); // With root braces String braced = HoconSerializer.DEFAULT_BRACES.write(bean); // Compact mode - single line String compact = HoconSerializer.DEFAULT_COMPACT.write(bean);

Key-value separators: = (convention), : (JSON-style), or space-brace for objects Path expressions: a.b.c = value expands to nested objects Unquoted strings: Keys and simple values need not be quoted Object merging: Duplicate keys merge instead of overwrite += array append: list += item appends to an array or creates [item] if the key does not exist Substitutions: ${var} and ${?var} (optional) resolved after parse Self-referential substitution: path = ${path}"/bin" appends to the previous value (e.g. /usr → /usr/bin) Value concatenation: Adjacent values concatenate: path = /usr "/local" → "/usr/local" Array concatenation: [1, 2] [3, 4] → [1, 2, 3, 4] Object concatenation: {a: 1} {b: 2} → {a: 1, b: 2} Triple-quoted strings: """...""" for multi-line Comments: # and // single-line Optional root braces: Top-level {} can be omitted

Maps and beans → HOCON objects Collections and arrays → HOCON arrays Strings → Unquoted (when safe), quoted, or triple-quoted Numbers → HOCON numbers Booleans → true / false Null → null ObjectSwaps → Applied for non-primitive types (dates, enums, etc.)
Produces: application/hocon Accepts: application/hocon
// HOCON support is included via BasicUniversalConfig (there is no dedicated HOCON-only config interface). @Rest public class MyResource extends RestServlet implements BasicUniversalConfig { ... }

Path expressions are parsed; serialization always uses nested-brace form Substitutions (${var}) are resolved during parse; the serializer writes concrete values Strings equal to true, false, null, or parseable as numbers are quoted on output to prevent ambiguity

@HoconConfig sets serializer/parser properties on a REST class or method (see Context Annotations). All attributes are strings ("true"/"false"); unset means "inherit". Attribute Description useEqualsSign Use = as the key-value separator (default true). useUnquotedStrings Omit quotes for simple string values. useUnquotedKeys Omit quotes for simple keys. omitRootBraces Omit the root object braces. useNewlineSeparators Separate members with newlines instead of commas. resolveSubstitutions Resolve ${var} substitutions while parsing. rank Ordering relative to other config annotations. @Rest @HoconConfig(omitRootBraces="true", useEqualsSign="true") public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet { ... } @Hocon is a marker annotation (no attributes) for classes, methods and fields. @HoconApply applies an @Hocon to other classes/members via on()/onClass() (see Dynamically Applied Annotations). See Also HOCON Specification for the full format definition. Marshallers for the marshaller API overview.

The @Html annotation can be used to customize how POJOs are serialized to HTML on a per-class/field/method basis. HtmlanchorText format link noTableHeaders noTables render The @Html(link) annotation adds a hyperlink to a bean property when rendered as HTML. Example public class FileSpace { // Add a hyperlink to this bean property. @Html(link="servlet:/drive/{drive}") public String getDrive() {...} } The @Html(anchorText) annotation is used to specify the anchor text of a hyperlink. Example // Produces CLICK ME! when serialized to HTML. public class FileSpace { // Add a hyperlink to this bean property. @Html(link="servlet:/drive/{drive}", anchorText="CLICK ME!") public String getDrive() {...} } The @Html(format) annotation is used to specify what format to use for HTML elements. For example, the HTML beans defined in the html5 package use format=XML so that the beans get serialized as standard XML: Example // Parent class of all HTML DTO bean classes. @Html(format=XML) public abstract class HtmlElement {...} The @Html(noTableHeaders) annotation is used to prevent beans from being serialized with table headers. The @Html(noTables) annotation is used to force beans to be serialized as trees instead of tables

The @Html(render) annotation allows for custom rendering of bean property values when serialized as HTML. Using this class, you can alter the CSS style and HTML content of the bean property. The following example shows two render classes that customize the appearance of the pctFull and status columns in the code below: import static org.apache.juneau.bean.html5.HtmlBuilder.*; // Our bean class public class FileSpace { private final String drive; private final long total, available; public FileSpace(String drive, long total, long available) { this.drive = drive; this.total = total; this.available = available; } @Html(link="drive/{drive}") public String getDrive() { return drive; } public long getTotal() { return total; } public long getAvailable() { return available; } @Html(render=FileSpacePctRender.class) public float getPctFull() { return ((100 * available) / total); } @Html(render=FileSpaceStatusRender.class) public FileSpaceStatus getStatus() { float pf = getPctFull(); if (pf < 80) return FileSpaceStatus.OK; if (pf < 90) return FileSpaceStatus.WARNING; return FileSpaceStatus.SEVERE; } } // Possible values for the getStatus() method public enum FileSpaceStatus { OK, WARNING, SEVERE; } // Custom render for getPctFull() method public class FileSpacePctRender extends HtmlRender<Float> { @Override public String getStyle(SerializerSession session, Float value) { if (value >= 90) return "background-color:red;color:white;"; if (value >= 80) return "background-color:yellow;"; return null; } @Override public Object getContent(SerializerSession session, Float value) { if (value >= 90) return div( String.format("%.0f%%", value), style("@keyframes color_change { from { background-color: red; } to { background-color: yellow; }") ); return String.format("%.0f%%", value); } } // Custom render for getStatus() method public class FileSpaceStatusRender extends HtmlRender<FileSpaceStatus> { @Override public String getStyle(SerializerSession session, FileSpaceStatus value) { return "text-align:center"; } @Override public Object getContent(SerializerSession session, FileSpaceStatus value) { switch (value) { case OK: return img().src(URI.create("servlet:/htdocs/ok.png")); case WARNING: return img().src(URI.create("servlet:/htdocs/warning.png")); default: return img().src(URI.create("servlet:/htdocs/severe.png")); } } }
The HtmlFlavorRest class in the petstore console (the Html subtab at /console/dev/flavors/html) shows how HTML5 beans can be used to generate arbitrary HTML on REST endpoints.

The fragment() method, served at /console/dev/flavors/html/fragment, shows an example of rendering an HTML table, built from live petstore data. @RestGet(path="/fragment", serializers=HtmlSerializer.class) public Table fragment() { var rows = new ArrayList<Object>(); rows.add(tr(th("Name"), th("Species"), th("Price"), th("Status"))); for (var r : FlavorPets.rows(store())) rows.add(tr(td(r.get("name")), td(r.get("species")), td(r.get("price")), td(r.get("status")))); return table(rows.toArray()).class_("petstore-flavor").attr("data-flavor", "html"); } This is the fragment in a browser: The endpoint is limited to HtmlSerializer, so it has no JSON representation; the beans themselves serialize to JSON like any other bean when an endpoint allows it.

The following method shows an example of rendering a div tag with mixed content. (The petstore console has no per-pet card endpoint; this illustrates the bean API directly.) @RestGet("/card") public Div aCard() { return div( p(b("Rex")), p("Species: Dog"), p("Price: $100"), p("Status: AVAILABLE") ); }

The following method shows an example of rendering an HTML form using the Form HTML5 bean. (The petstore samples don't currently host a form-bean demo resource; this illustrates the bean API directly.) @RestGet @HtmlDocConfig( aside={ "", " Example of serialized org.apache.juneau.bean.html5.Form bean.", "" } ) public Form aForm() { return form().action("/submit").method("POST") .children( "Position (1-10000): ", input("number").name("pos").value(1), br(), "Limit (1-10000): ", input("number").name("limit").value(100), br(), button("submit", "Submit"), button("reset", "Reset") ); }

When HtmlDocSerializer wraps a serialized POJO inside a complete HTML document, the layout of that document is controlled by a page template. By default it uses BasicHtmlDocTemplate (described in BasicHtmlDocTemplate), but you can supply your own to take complete control over the generated markup. Custom page templates are created by implementing the HtmlDocTemplate interface and associating it with your serializer using the HtmlDocSerializer.Builder.template(Class) setting. HtmlDocTemplatewriteTo(HtmlDocSerializerSession,HtmlWriter<?>,Object) The interface defines a single writeTo(session, writer, pojo) method, and the implementation is open-ended — you can write out the page contents any way you wish using the HtmlWriter<?> passed to it. The serialized POJO is available from the session (typically written into the body via session.parentSerialize(writer, pojo)).

The BasicHtmlDocTemplate class defines a default template for HTML documents created by HtmlDocSerializer. The HTML document created by this template consists of the following structure: <html> <head> <style type='text/css'> CSS styles and links to stylesheets </style> </head> <body> <header> Page header </header> <nav> Navigation links </nav> <aside> Side-bar text </aside> <article> Contents of serialized object </article> <footer> Footer message </footer> </body> </html> A page drawn by this template, from the petstore's /console/about/beans/BeanDescription endpoint: the header, the navigation links and the serialized bean in the article (this page sets no aside or footer):

The following template ignores the header/nav/aside/footer settings entirely and renders a bare-bones document consisting of just the serialized POJO wrapped in a <body>: public class MyTemplate implements HtmlDocTemplate { @Override public void writeTo(HtmlDocSerializerSession session, HtmlWriter<?> w, Object o) throws Exception { w.sTag("html").nl(0); w.sTag(1, "body").nl(1); // Serialize the POJO into the body using the parent HtmlSerializer. session.parentSerialize(w, o); w.eTag(1, "body").nl(1); w.eTag("html").nl(0); } } Wire it into a serializer using the builder: HtmlDocSerializer serializer = HtmlDocSerializer .create() .template(MyTemplate.class) .build();

Implementing HtmlDocTemplate from scratch means reproducing the entire page structure. In most cases it's easier to subclass BasicHtmlDocTemplate and override only the individual section methods you want to change. BasicHtmlDocTemplate breaks the page down into overridable protected methods, each receiving the session, writer, and POJO: head(session, w, o) — the element (delegates to style(...) and script(...)). header(session, w, o) — the
element (page title/description/branding). nav(session, w, o) — the
element (navigation links). aside(session, w, o) — the
element (side-bar text). article(session, w, o) — the
element (the serialized POJO itself). footer(session, w, o) — the
element (footer message). There are also companion hasHeader(...), hasNav(...), hasAside(...), hasFooter(...), hasStyle(...), and hasScript(...) predicates that control whether each section is rendered. The following example overrides just the footer to append a fixed copyright notice while leaving every other section untouched: public class MyTemplate extends BasicHtmlDocTemplate { @Override protected void footer(HtmlDocSerializerSession session, HtmlWriter w, Object o) throws Exception { // Preserve the default footer behavior... super.footer(session, w, o); // ...then add our own content. w.appendln(3, "

Copyright (c) My Company

"); } }
HtmlDocSerializer for the document serializer that consumes the template.

The @HtmlDocConfig annotation is used to customize the HTML view of POJOs serialized by HtmlDocSerializer. HtmlDocSerializer is an extension of HtmlSerializer that wraps serialized POJOs in a complete HTML document. This class is used extensively in the creation of POJO-based user interfaces in the REST API.

Use HtmlDocSerializer when the output is a page a person opens in a browser: it adds the head, style, navigation links, aside and footer around the serialized data. For an HTML fragment you embed in another page, use HtmlSerializer. In a REST resource you rarely build one yourself; the @HtmlDocConfig annotation sets the same options declaratively.

import org.apache.juneau.marshall.html.*; public class HtmlDocSerializerExample { public static class Person { public String name = "John Smith"; public int age = 45; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { // A serializer with a navigation bar and a side note around the data. HtmlDocSerializer serializer = HtmlDocSerializer.create() .navlinks("up: request:/..") .aside("

One person.

") .build(); String html = serializer.write(new Person()).toString(); System.out.println(html.contains("

One person.

") + " " + html.contains("John Smith")); } } The same options in a REST resource: /** * Sample REST resource that prints out a simple "Hello world!" message. */ @Rest(path="/helloWorld") @HtmlDocConfig( navlinks={ "up: request:/..", "options: servlet:/?method=OPTIONS" }, aside={ "", "

This page shows a resource that simply response with a 'Hello world!' message

", "

The POJO serialized is a simple String.

", "" } ) class HelloWorldResource extends BasicRestServlet { // ... }

This page describes how the different POJO datatypes are represented in HTML. The representations mirror how the same data structures are represented in JSON, and build directly on the XML Methodology: Simple values (strings, numbers, booleans, nulls) render as text, with lightweight type tags added only where the datatype cannot be inferred through reflection. Maps and beans render as <table> elements. Collections and arrays render as <ul> bulleted lists. The examples below show one representative case per category. For the complete set of data-type representations (all Map, array, Collection, and bean shapes), see the reference tables on the HTML Serializers page.

The representation for simple types mirrors those produced by the XML serializer. Tags are added to help differentiate data types when they cannot be inferred through reflection. These tags are ignored by browsers and treated as plain text. Data type JSON example HTML string 'foo' foo boolean true <boolean>true</boolean> integer 123 <number>123</number> float 1.23 <number>1.23</number> null null <null></null>

Maps and beans are represented as tables. The _type='object' attribute distinguishes objects (Maps/beans) from arrays (arrays/Collections), and per-cell type tags are added only where the value type cannot be inferred through reflection. The following representative example shows a bean containing simple values, a nested bean, and array properties: Data type JSON example HTML class MyBean { public String a; public int b; public MyBean2 c; public int[] d; } class MyBean2 { String h; } { a: 'foo', b: 123, c: { h: 'baz' }, d: [789] }
a foo
b 123
c
h baz
d
  • 789

Collections and arrays are represented as
    ordered lists, with type tags added to individual
  • elements as needed. Collections (e.g. List, Set) serialize identically to their array equivalents. The following representative example shows a mixed-type Object[]: Data type JSON example HTML Object[] ['foo', 123, 1.23, true, null]
    • foo
    • 123
    • 1.23
    • true
The HtmlParser class is used to parse HTML into POJOs. They can also parse the contents produced by HtmlDocSerializer.

Use HtmlParser to read HTML that HtmlSerializer or HtmlDocSerializer produced, such as a page you saved or a table you posted, back into POJOs. It understands the table, list and anchor structure Juneau writes; it is not a general web-page scraper.

import org.apache.juneau.marshall.html.*; public class HtmlParserExample { public static class Person { public String name; public int age; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Person person = new Person(); person.name = "John Smith"; person.age = 45; // Serialize to HTML, then parse the HTML back into a bean. String html = HtmlSerializer.DEFAULT.write(person).toString(); Person copy = HtmlParser.DEFAULT.read(html, Person.class); System.out.println(html); System.out.println(copy.name + " " + copy.age); } } A parser also accepts the full document that HtmlDocSerializer writes; it reads the data out of the body and ignores the surrounding template.

The following pre-configured parsers are provided for convenience: Instance Accepts HtmlParser.DEFAULT HTML with the default settings. For anything else, start from the builder's create() method. The settings readers reach for first: Builder method Effect trimStrings() Trim whitespace from parsed string values. validateEnd() Fail if anything but whitespace follows the parsed value. autoCloseStreams() Close the input stream or reader when parsing finishes. beanDictionary(Class...) Classes the parser may instantiate from type attributes. swaps(Class...) Object swaps that convert parsed values into other types. The class hierarchy for the builder of this parser is below. Refer to the builder javadocs for the full set of configurable settings. Context.BuilderMarshallingContextable.BuilderParser.BuilderReaderParser.BuilderHtmlParser.Builder

The org.apache.juneau.rest.server.widget package contains predefined reusable widgets. Not the declarative widget beans These are ${W:...} HTML widgets. For the typed ModalDef, FormDef, CalendarDef and stats beans in juneau-console-widgets, see Declarative Widgets. org.apache.juneau.rest.server.widgetWidget MenuItemWidget ContentTypeMenuItem QueryMenuItem PoweredByJuneau PoweredByApache Tooltip

MenuItemWidget is an abstract class for rendering menu items with drop-downs. It defines some simple CSS and Javascript for enabling drop-down menus in the nav section of the page (although nothing keeps you from using it in an arbitrary location in the page). The script specifies a menuClick(element) function that toggles the visibility of the next sibling of the element. Subclasses implement the following methods: MenuItemWidgetgetLabel(RestRequest,RestResponse) getContent(RestRequest,RestResponse) getHtml(RestRequest,RestResponse) For example, to render a link that brings up a simple dialog in a div tag: @Override public String getLabel(RestRequest req, RestResponse res) { return "my-menu-item"; } @Override public Object getContent(RestRequest req, RestResponse res) { return HtmlBuilder.div("Surprise!").style("color:red"); } The HTML content returned by the getHtml(RestRequest,RestResponse) method is added where the ${W:...} is referenced in the page.

ContentTypeMenuItem is a predefined Widget that returns back a list of hyperlinks for rendering the contents of a page in a variety of content types. The variable it resolves is ${W:ContentTypeMenuItem}. An example of this widget can be found in RootResources (juneau-petstore-jetty), which provides a drop-down menu item for rendering the current page's contents in a variety of content types: @Rest( title="Juneau Petstore (Jetty)", description="Apache Juneau petstore sample application running under Jetty/Microservice.", children={...} ) @HtmlDocConfig( widgets={ ContentTypeMenuItem.class }, navlinks={ "api: servlet:/api", "stats: servlet:/stats", "${W:ContentTypeMenuItem}", "source: ${C:Source/gitHub}/org/apache/juneau/petstore/jetty/RootResources.java" } ) public class RootResources extends BasicRestServletGroup {...} It renders the following popup-box:

QueryMenuItem is a predefined Widget that returns a menu-item drop-down form for entering search/view/sort arguments. The variable it resolves is ${W:QueryMenuItem}. This widget is designed to be used in conjunction with the Queryable converter, although implementations can process the query parameters themselves by taking a BeanQueryRequest method argument (bound from the search, view, sort, position and limit request parameters) and running a BeanQuery session over their data. Neither of the currently-shipping petstore resources pairs this widget with the Queryable converter, so the following is a self-contained, minimal illustrative example rather than a citation of an existing class: @Rest public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet { @RestGet( path="/", converters=Queryable.class ) @HtmlDocConfig( widgets={ QueryMenuItem.class, }, navlinks={ "up: request:/..", "options: ?method=OPTIONS", "${W:QueryMenuItem}", "${W:ContentTypeMenuItem}" } ) public Collection<MyBean> getBeans() { ... } } It renders the following popup-box: Tooltips are provided by hovering over the field names. When submitted, the form submits a GET request against the current URI with the BeanQuery query parameters (e.g. ?search=column1=$prefix(Foo)&view=column1,column2&sort=column1,column2:desc&position=100&limit=100). The Queryable class knows how to perform these filters against collections of POJOs. The tooltips describe the BeanQuery operators ($eq, $contains, $gt, $between, $and/$or/$not, ...); see the BeanQuery page for the full grammar. The old "Ignore-case" checkbox is gone: case sensitivity is a property of each operator.

PoweredByJuneau is a predefined Widget that places a powered-by-Juneau message on a page. The variable it resolves is ${W:PoweredByJuneau}. It produces a simple Apache Juneau icon floating on the right. The HtmlSchemaSerializer class is the HTML-equivalent to the JsonSchemaSerializer class. It's used to generate HTML versions of JSON-Schema documents that describe the output generated by the JsonSerializer class.

public class Person { // Bean properties public String name; public Calendar birthDate; public List addresses; // Getters/setters omitted } public class Address { // Bean properties public String street, city; public StateEnum state; public int zip; public boolean isCurrent; // Getters/setters omitted } The code for creating our POJO model and generating HTML-Schema is shown below: // Get the one of the default schema serializers. HtmlSchemaSerializer serializer = HtmlSchemaSerializer.DEFAULT_SIMPLE_READABLE; // Get the HTML Schema for the POJO. String htmlSchema = serializer.write(new Person()); // This also works. htmlSchema = serializer.write(Person.class); The result is the HTML table shown below: type object properties name type string birthDate type string addresses type array items type object properties street type string city type string state type string enum AL PA NC zip type integer format int32 isCurrent type boolean

Every page served by a BasicRestServlet is styled by one stylesheet. These shots are the petstore's bean-description page (/console/about/beans) in each of the three stock stylesheets. The default "devops" look-and-feel: The "light" look-and-feel: And the "dark" look-and-feel: The stylesheet URL is controlled by the @HtmlDocConfig(stylesheet) annotation. The BasicUniversalConfig interface defines the stylesheet served up as a static file: @HtmlDocConfig( stylesheet="${C:REST/theme:servlet:/htdocs/themes/devops.css}" ) public interface BasicUniversalConfig {...} The ${C:REST/theme:servlet:/htdocs/themes/devops.css} variable says to use the URI defined in your servlet's config file, if there is one, and to default to serving up the file htdocs/themes/devops.css which is in the resource folder of the juneau-rest-server module. To provide your own stylesheet, simply override the stylesheet attribute and point to a different file: @HtmlDocConfig( stylesheet="servlet:/htdocs/themes/my-style.css" ) public class MyResourceBaseClass extends BasicRestServlet {...} Or set REST/theme in the servlet's config file to point every page of the servlet at another stylesheet without touching the code.

Juneau supports converting arbitrary POJOs to and from HTML using ultra-efficient serializers and parsers. The HTML support is built on top of the XML support. The HtmlSerializer converts POJOs directly to HTML without the need for intermediate DOM objects, and the HtmlParser uses a STaX-based reader to reconstruct POJOs directly from that same markup. Like the rest of Juneau, no annotations are required on your POJOs — beans and maps render as tables, collections and arrays render as bulleted lists, and simple values render as text with lightweight type tags where the datatype cannot be inferred through reflection. The primary use case for HTML marshalling is rendering POJOs in an easy-to-read format in REST interfaces. For that use case, the HtmlDocSerializer wraps the serialized POJO inside a complete HTML document (header, nav, aside, article, and footer sections) so that a bean can be rendered as a self-contained, styled web page.

HtmlSerializer / HtmlParser — convert POJOs to and from HTML fragments (tables and lists). HtmlDocSerializer — extends HtmlSerializer to wrap the fragment inside a full HTML document driven by a customizable page template. Its output is also readable back in by HtmlParser. HtmlSchemaSerializer — produces HTML renderings of the JSON-Schema documents that describe your serialized output.

HTML Methodology — how each POJO datatype is represented in HTML. HTML Serializers — the HtmlSerializer class, its builder hierarchy, and the pre-configured serializers. HTML Parsers — the HtmlParser class, its builder hierarchy, and the pre-configured parsers. @Html Annotation — customizing HTML output on a per-class/field/method basis. @Html(render) Annotation — custom CSS/content rendering of individual bean-property values. HtmlDocSerializer — wrapping serialized POJOs in a complete HTML document. BasicHtmlDocTemplate — the default document template and its page structure. Custom Templates — implementing your own HtmlDocTemplate. HTML-Schema Support — generating HTML views of JSON-Schema documents.
Marshallers for the marshaller API overview. XML for the XML support that HTML marshalling is built on.

An important distinction needs to be made about the HTML representations produced by the REST API. These should not be considered User Interfaces but rather Developer Interfaces. UIs should hide the end-user from the underlying architecture. The audience generally consists of non-technical people not interested in how the UI works. DIs, on the other hand, should NOT hide the end-user from the underlying architecture. Instead, it's a thin veneer over the REST interface with the following goals: Make it easy for the developer to explore and understand the REST API. Make it easy for the developer to debug the REST API using simple tools (hopefully just a browser). As a result, the following guidelines are recommended: Use titles/descriptions/asides to describe why the REST interface exists. A developer knowing little about it should be able to access it with a browser and quickly understand what it is and how to use it. Don't hide the raw data! The HTML view should simply be considered an easier-to-read representation of the data normally rendered in JSON or some other format. Limit your use of Javascript! You can use it sparingly if you want to implement something simple like a pull-down menu to simplify some debug task but remember that your audience cares more about interacting with your service programmatically using REST. Remember that the HTML is just icing on the cake. Don't use it to implement a Web 2.0 interface! If you want a Web 2.0 UI, implement it separately ON TOP OF this REST interface. The architecture is flexible enough that you could in theory pull in and use jQuery, React, Angular, or any number of sophisticated Javascript UI frameworks. Resist the urge to do so.

The HTML views of POJOs can somewhat be considered a rudimentary User Interface. In reality, a better term for them would be a Developer Interface as they're meant to be used primarily by developers and not end users. Despite that distinction, it is possible to 'brand' the HTML page to whatever you desire. The sample root page below includes some default branding for Juneau and Apache: http://localhost:10000/helloWorld The Juneau REST framework does not provide specific branding support (i.e. there is no concept of a brand icon). Instead, it just uses the existing open-ended API for defining branding via annotations on your REST classes. @Rest( // Optional external configuration file. config="${S:juneau.configFile}", ) @HtmlDocConfig( // Default stylesheet to use for the page. // Can be overridden from external config file. // Default is DevOps look-and-feel (aka Depression look-and-feel). stylesheet="${C:REST/theme:servlet:/htdocs/themes/devops.css}", // Default page header contents. header={ "${RS:title}", // Use @Rest(title) "${RS:operationSummary:description}", // Use either @RestOp(summary) or @Rest(description) "${C:REST/header}" // Extra header HTML defined in external config file. }, // Default contents to add to the <head> section of the HTML page. // Use it to add a favicon link to the page. head={ "" }, // Basic page navigation links. navlinks={ "up: request:/.." }, // No default page footer contents. // Can be overridden from external config file. footer="${C:REST/footer}" ) public interface BasicUniversalConfig {} Notice how this is implemented using nested @HtmlDocConfig annotations nested within parent configurations.
