The Jetty Microservice API consists of a combination of the Juneau Core, Server, and Client APIs and an embedded Eclipse Jetty Servlet Container. The API builds upon the juneau-microservice classes to produce easy-to-create and easy-to-use microservices in a standard Java 17+ environment. Renamed in 10.0 — juneau-microservice-core is now published as juneau-microservice. The Jetty module is no longer a subclass of Microservice; it contributes a single @Configuration class (JettyConfiguration) that the user adds to Microservice.Builder.configurations(...). The juneau-microservice-jetty library consists of the following classes: org.apache.juneau.microservice.jetty - PackageJettyMicroservice - Zero-config static-call facade that boots a Jetty microservice in a single line.JettyConfiguration - @Configuration class that wires Jetty into a Microservice.JettyServerComponent - Lifecycle-participating bean that owns the Jetty server.JettySettings - Immutable value bean holding programmatic Jetty knobs (ports, jetty.xml, var resolution).JettyServerFactory - Interface for defining custom Jetty server factories.BasicJettyServerFactory - Default factory that builds the server from jetty.xml.HealthProbeConfiguration - Opt-in @Configuration that auto-mounts the health/readiness/liveness probe servlet. The most-basic creation of a Jetty microservice from an entry-point method is shown below: public class App { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Microservice .create() .args(args) .configurations(JettyConfiguration.class, AppConfig.class) .build() .start() .startConsole() .join(); } @Configuration public static class AppConfig { @Bean Servlet rootResources() { return new RootResources(); } } } RootResources (or any @Bean Servlet whose class is annotated with @Rest) is auto-mounted at the path declared in @Rest(path = "...").
Microservice Overview — the core microservice, without Jetty

Juneau microservices are self-contained, deployable REST servers built on top of the Juneau REST server framework. A microservice packages your REST resources, configuration, and an embedded HTTP container into a single executable jar (or WAR) that you can start with a plain java -jar command. The microservice layer builds on top of the full Juneau stack: Juneau Microservice Stackjuneau-microservice — core lifecycle, config, console, inject bootstrapjuneau-rest-server — @Rest / @RestOp REST engine (serialization, routing, guards, …)juneau-marshall — multi-format POJO marshalling (JSON, XML, HTML, YAML, …)Deployment target (one of Jetty / Tomcat / Spring Boot)

Juneau provides three independently-releasable deployment adapters. All three share the same Microservice + @Configuration + @Bean Servlet programming model and the same lifecycle contracts. Module When to use juneau-microservice-jetty Default choice for standalone runnable jars. Ships a zero-config JettyMicroservice.run(args, servlet) one-liner and a classpath-driven jetty.xml knob for advanced connector tuning. juneau-microservice-tomcat Drop-in alternative when your organisation standardises on Tomcat, or when you want to share [Tomcat] config between an embedded dev launcher and a full Tomcat deployment. juneau-rest-server-springboot Integration point for Spring Boot applications. REST resources extend BasicSpringRestServlet / BasicSpringRestServletGroup so Spring @Autowired injection and @Bean resolution flow through the Spring application context instead of the Juneau bean store. All three adapters depend on juneau-microservice for the core lifecycle engine and on juneau-rest-server for the REST framework itself.

Every Juneau microservice follows a builder → configure → start → join/stop lifecycle. MicroserviceMicroservice.create() — obtain a fluent builderbuilder.args(args) — pass CLI argumentsbuilder.configurations(…) — register @Configuration classes (adds the HTTP container)builder.build() — construct the Microservice instancestart() — start all MicroserviceListeners (including the HTTP container)startConsole() — (optional) launch interactive stdin consolejoin() — block the calling thread until stop() is calledstop() — stop all listeners in reverse order; close the bean store All methods on Microservice return this, making it easy to chain the whole bootstrap in one fluent expression.

The core lifecycle engine lives in a small, self-contained set of packages and classes: Microservice APIorg.apache.juneau.microservice - Main packageMicroservice - The base microservice class.Microservice.Builder - Builder for the microservice class.MicroserviceListener - Interface for hooking into lifecycle events of the microservice.BasicMicroserviceListener - No-op adapter for the MicroserviceListener interface.org.apache.juneau.microservice.console - Console packageConsoleCommand - Abstract class for defining interactive console commands. By itself the core API provides only the bootstrap machinery — an executable-jar lifecycle, config resolution, command-line-argument and manifest access, an interactive console, and the inject bean store. The embedded HTTP server is contributed by a deployment adapter (Jetty, Tomcat, or Spring Boot) registered as a @Configuration class.

The following is the smallest complete Juneau microservice: a single REST resource mounted on an embedded Jetty server with automatic JSON/XML/HTML content negotiation. Add the dependency, with juneau-bom imported as on Install Juneau: <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-microservice-jetty-bundle</artifactId> <type>pom</type> </dependency> Define a REST resource: import org.apache.juneau.http.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.servlet.*; @Rest( path = "/hello", title = "Hello World" ) public class HelloResource extends BasicRestServlet { @RestGet(path = "/*", summary = "Returns a greeting.") public String sayHello() { return "Hello, World!"; } } Boot it from main: import org.apache.juneau.microservice.jetty.*; public class App { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { JettyMicroservice.run(args, new HelloResource(), false).join(); } } JettyMicroservice.run(args, servlet, false) is a convenience facade that wires JettyConfiguration into the Microservice builder, registers the servlet at the path in its @Rest annotation, and starts on port 10000 (or as configured in juneau.cfg); join() blocks until the server stops. The false turns the interactive console off, as on Your First REST App; run(args, servlet) turns it on. Point a browser at http://localhost:10000/hello — the default HTML view renders automatically. For the Tomcat or Spring Boot equivalents, see the module-specific pages listed in the Deployment Targets section above.

Port When 10000 Jetty microservice (Getting Started, MCP quickstart, starters, Petstore Jetty). Set by jetty.xml ${S:availablePort:10000}. The Spring Boot starter also uses 10000 (server.port), as does the juneau-examples-mcp Jetty ExampleServer (DEFAULT_PORT = 10000). 8080 Spring Boot's default (Spring guides, the MCP recipe snippets, the juneau-examples-mcp Spring example) and Tomcat. 5000 Petstore Spring Boot (server.port=${PORT:5000}).

Every microservice reads its runtime settings from an INI-style juneau.cfg file that is resolved from the classpath or working directory at startup. Key sections used by the built-in modules: [Microservice] # Name and version shown in the console banner. name = MyApp version = 1.0 [Jetty] # Comma-separated list of candidate ports; first available wins. 0 = random. port = 8080, 0 [Logging] # Root logging level (java.util.logging). level = WARNING # Log file relative to the working directory. logFile = logs/microservice.%g.log The configuration is exposed as a Config object through Microservice.getConfig() and is also registered in the bean store so @Bean factory methods can inject it directly.

Config supports file-watch hot-reload out of the box. When the underlying juneau.cfg file changes on disk, listeners registered via Config.addListener(…) are notified with the full set of changed entries. The microservice uses this to propagate logging level changes and port-list updates without a restart. You can register your own listener from a @Configuration class: import org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.*; import org.apache.juneau.config.event.*; import org.apache.juneau.microservice.*; @Configuration public class AppConfig { @Bean MicroserviceListener configWatcher() { return new BasicMicroserviceListener() { @Override public void onConfigChange(Microservice ms, ConfigEvents events) { System.out.println("Config changed: " + events); } }; } } The onConfigChange(Microservice, ConfigEvents) callback fires on the calling thread of the file-store watcher, not the request thread, so keep it non-blocking. The ConfigEvents argument carries the full set of changed entries — see Listeners for reacting to specific sections.

The Jetty and Tomcat launchers expose several built-in REST endpoints under the root path when management mixins are enabled. These are opt-in: add the appropriate mixin to your root @Rest resource. Endpoint Mixin / feature Description GET /healthz Health Probes Aggregated health/liveness check. Returns 200 OK or 503 Service Unavailable. GET /readyz Health Probes Readiness probe, used by Kubernetes load-balancer pre-stop hooks. GET /livez Health Probes Liveness probe for pod restart decisions. GET /actuator Management Surface Actuator-style endpoint listing all available management sub-paths. GET /api Auto-generated via Swagger / OpenAPI Swagger 2.x JSON schema; OPTIONS on any resource returns an inline schema. GET /stats Execution Statistics Per-operation call counts, error rates, and latency percentiles. The management surface is implemented via the standard Juneau mixin pack mechanism — there are no special microservice APIs. The same mixins work in a plain servlet container too.

Microservice owns an internal WritableBeanStore populated from every @Configuration class registered on the builder. This makes it easy for companion modules — such as JettyConfiguration and TomcatConfiguration — to contribute lifecycle components and for user code to wire in application services without subclassing. @Configuration public class AppConfig { @Bean Servlet rootResources() { return new RootResources(); } // auto-mounted by JettyConfiguration @Bean MyService myService() { return new MyService(); } // available to other @Bean methods } public class App { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Microservice.create() .args(args) .configurations(JettyConfiguration.class, AppConfig.class) .build() .start() .startConsole() .join(); } } JettyConfiguration walks the bean store at startup, finds every @Bean whose declared return type is Servlet and whose runtime class carries @Rest, and mounts it at the path declared in @Rest(path = "..."). TomcatConfiguration follows an identical contract. See Inject-Aware Microservice for a complete reference on resolution priority, @PostConstruct / @PreDestroy callbacks, and external bean store integration.

Apache Juneau provides three minimal clone-and-go starter projects — one per deployment target — that demonstrate a HelloResource, content negotiation, a Swagger/OPTIONS page, @Path/@Query binding, a YAML config file, and a MockRestClient test. Each is a true-orphan branch of apache/juneau: git clone -b microservice-jetty-starter --single-branch https://github.com/apache/juneau.git my-app git clone -b microservice-springboot-starter --single-branch https://github.com/apache/juneau.git my-app git clone -b microservice-tomcat-starter --single-branch https://github.com/apache/juneau.git my-app See Starter Projects for run commands, layout, and Docker notes.

juneau-microservice — core microservice module (lifecycle engine, config, console) juneau-microservice-jetty — embedded Jetty launcher juneau-microservice-tomcat — embedded Tomcat launcher juneau-rest-server-springboot — Spring Boot integration REST Server — the underlying REST server API Config Files — full configuration file reference Microservice with Jetty — adds the Jetty launcher on top of the core module

@MicroserviceTest is a JUnit 5 extension that boots a whole Microservice — config, lifecycle, and an embedded Jetty server on an ephemeral port — for the duration of a test class, then stops it cleanly. It's the standalone-microservice analog of Spring's @SpringBootTest, and it composes the existing @TestBean mock-bean substrate for collaborator substitution. It ships in a small dedicated support module: <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-microservice-test</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> <scope>test</scope> </dependency>

The two integration-test paths are intentionally distinct: Use For @MicroserviceTest A genuine full-microservice test — real server, real connectors, real lifecycle, exercised over HTTP. MockRestClient An in-JVM test of a single @Rest resource — no server, no sockets, dispatched directly against a RestContext. MockRestClient does not talk to a booted server; reach for @MicroserviceTest when you want the actual server, filters, and connector path in the loop.

The SUT is declared explicitly (no classpath scanning), two complementary ways: configurations={...} — one or more @Configuration classes whose @Bean Servlet methods the microservice auto-mounts (the common case). A static Microservice.Builder supplier method on the test class (default name microserviceBuilder, override via builderMethod) — for full control of the builder. Any configurations={...} are appended to whatever the supplier returns. Either way the extension additionally installs an ephemeral-Jetty Server (bound to port 0) and JettyConfiguration, so tests only contribute their resources. The extension currently boots Jetty. @MicroserviceTest(configurations = MyServiceTest.AppConfig.class) class MyServiceTest { @Configuration public static class AppConfig { @Bean Greeter greeter() { return new ProductionGreeter(); } @Bean Servlet greetingResource(Greeter greeter) { return new GreetingResource(greeter); } } @Test void greetingEndpoint(RestClient client) throws Exception { var resp = client.get("/greeting").run(); assertEquals(200, resp.getStatusCode()); } }

Test methods (and lifecycle methods) may declare parameters the extension resolves: RestClient — a real HTTP client bound to the booted server's root URL (the primary convenience). Microservice — the booted instance. WritableBeanStore — the booted instance's bean store. int / Integer — the bound (ephemeral) port.

Substitute collaborators with the existing @TestBean (the @MockBean analog) — there is no parallel injection annotation. The default is Mode INJECT: the override is installed via Microservice.Builder.overridingBeanStore(...) before boot, so the service reads it from startup (the correct mode for whole-service tests, since the microservice resolves its beans at boot). @MicroserviceTest(configurations = AppConfig.class) class MyServiceTest { // Substituted before the microservice boots — the real GreetingResource sees this mock. @TestBean(scope = Scope.CLASS) static Greeter mockGreeter() { return () -> "mocked"; } @Test void usesTheMock(RestClient client) throws Exception { assertEquals("mocked", client.get("/greeting").run().getBodyAsString()); } } @TestBean(mode = Mode.OVERLAY) instead pushes the overrides onto the already-booted instance's bean store (and pops them in teardown) — the opt-in path for per-test substitution against a long-running instance. Note that OVERLAY only affects beans the framework re-resolves through the bean store per call; beans pinned into per-op memoizers at boot need INJECT.

The microservice is booted once per test class (beforeAll) and stopped in afterAll — a fresh instance per class, never reused. Microservice restart is unsupported (its stopped flag is one-way, the bean store is closed on stop, and each start() registers a JVM shutdown hook), so the build→start→stop cycle is repeated per class. stop() also restores the process globals the microservice sets (getInstance(), Config system default, Settings sources), so multiple @MicroserviceTest classes in one JVM stay isolated. Do not boot microservices in parallel within a JVM — they would stomp those globals. The bound port is always read from the live ServerConnector (never hard-coded), so ephemeral-port binding never collides.

The MockRestClient class is used for performing serverless unit testing of @Rest-annotated and @Remote-annotated classes. See the guide: Test an endpoint with MockRestClient Two flavors of MockRestClient org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.classic.MockRestClient — the legacy mock client documented on this page. Extends the classic RestClient (Apache HttpClient 4.5–based) and exposes the full fluent surface (.json5(), .plainText(), deprecated builder methods). org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.MockRestClient — the canonical NG mock client, paired with the transport-agnostic RestClient. Use this for new tests that target the new stack. See Next-Generation REST Client for examples. Both classes live in the juneau-rest-mock Maven module and can be used in the same project. The classic MockRestClient itself extends from RestClient providing it with the rich feature set of that API. The following shows a simple example of invoking a PUT method on a simple REST interface and asserting the correct status code and response body: public class MockTest { // A simple bean with one field. public static class MyBean { public int foo = 1; } // Our REST resource to test. // Simply echos the response. @Rest public static class EchoRest extends BasicRestServlet { @RestPut public MyBean echo(@Content MyBean bean) { return bean; } } // Our JUnit test. @Test public void testEcho() throws Exception { MyBean myBean = new MyBean(); // Do a round-trip on the bean through the REST interface myBean = MockRestClient .create(EchoRest.class) .json5() .build() .put("/echo", myBean) .run() .assertStatus().is(200) .assertContent().is("{foo:1}") .getContent().as(MyBean.class); assertEquals(1, myBean.foo); } } Breaking apart the fluent method call above will help you understand how this works. @Test public void testEcho() throws Exception { // Instantiate our mock client. MockRestClient client = MockRestClient .create(EchoRest.class) .json5() .build(); MyBean myBean = new MyBean(); // Create a request. RestRequest req = client.put("/echo", myBean); // Execute it (by calling RestCallHandler.service(...) and then returning the response object). RestResponse res = req.run(); // Run assertion tests on the results. res.assertStatus().is(200); res.assertContent().is("{foo:1}"); myBean = res.getContent().as(MyBean.class); } The concept of the design is simple. The MockRestClient class is used to create instances of MockServletRequest and MockServletResponse which are passed directly to the call handler on the resource class RestOpInvoker.invoke(RestOpSession). In effect, you're fully testing your REST API as if it were running in a live servlet container, yet not actually having to run in a servlet container. All aspects of the client and server side code are tested, yet no servlet container is required. The actual over-the-wire transmission is the only aspect being bypassed. The create(Object) method can take in either Class objects or pre-instantiated beans. The latter is particularly useful for testing REST APIs written as Spring beans. @RunWith(SpringRunner.class) @ContextConfiguration(classes = {MyApp.class}) @SpringBootTest public class MockTest { @Autowired EchoRest echoRest; MockRestClient client; @Before public void setup() { // Instantiate our mock client. client = MockRestClient .create(echoRest) .json5() .build(); } // Our JUnit test. @Test public void testEcho() throws Exception { MyBean myBean = new MyBean(); // Do a round-trip on the bean through the REST interface myBean = client .put("/echo", myBean) .run() .assertStatus().is(200) .assertContent().is("{foo:1}") .getContent().as(MyBean.class); assertEquals(1, myBean.foo); } } The MockRestRequest object has convenience methods provided to allow you to set properties directly on the underlying HttpServletRequest object. The following example shows how this can be used to directly set roles on the request object to perform security testing. Example @Rest(roleGuard="ADMIN") public class A { @RestGet public String get() { return "OK"; } } @Test public void mytest() throws Exception { MockRestClient client = MockRestClient.build(A.class); // Admin user should get 200 but anyone else should get 403-Unauthorized. client.get().roles("ADMIN").run().assertStatus().is(200); client.get().roles("USER").run().assertStatus().is(403); } The MockRestClient class has a debug mode that will cause your HTTP requests and responses to be sent to the console: MockRestClient client = MockRestClient .create(MyRest.class) .debug() .json5() .build(); The MockRestClient class can also be used for testing of Remote-annotated interfaces against @Rest-annotated resources. Example // Our remote resource to test. @Remote public interface MyRemoteInterface { @RemoteGet("/echoQuery") public int echoQuery(@Query(name="id") int id); } // Our mocked-up REST interface to test against. @Rest public class MyRest { @RestGet public int echoQuery(@Query("id") int id) { return id; } } @Test public void testProxy() { MyRemoteInterface mri = MockRestClient .create(MyRest.class) .json() .build() .getRemote(MyRemoteInterface.class); assertEquals(123, mri.echoQuery(123)); }

The following method can be used to associates entry modifiers to a config: Config.Buildermods(Mod...) Mods are used to modify values before being persisted. This can be used to replace or encode sensitive information. They are denoted by a single character that gets appended between angle brackets on the property name (e.g. key). Multiple modifiers can be denoted by multiple characters (e.g. key) and are applied/removed in the order denoted. The framework comes built-in with a simple xor-encode mod tied to the '*' character. The following shows how it is used: [MyHost] url = http://localhost:9080/foo user = me password = {AwwJVhwUQFZEMg==} Custom encoders can be used to provide your own encoding support by implementing the Mod class. Modapply(String)remove(String)isApplied(String) Unmodified values are encoded when the file is saved using the Config.commit() method. They can also be encoded immediately by calling Config.applyMods() which can typically be done during JVM startup to immediately encode any unencoded passwords in the file.
The MsgPackParser class is used to parse MessagePack into POJOs.
Use MsgPackParser to read MessagePack bytes written by MsgPackSerializer, or by any MessagePack library, into POJOs. The spaced-hex and Base64 instances accept the text forms of the same bytes.

import org.apache.juneau.marshall.msgpack.*; public class MsgPackParserExample { public static class Person { public String name = "John Smith"; public int age = 45; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { // Serialize a bean to bytes, then parse the bytes back. byte[] bytes = (byte[]) MsgPackSerializer.DEFAULT.write(new Person()); Person person = MsgPackParser.DEFAULT.read(bytes, Person.class); System.out.println(person.name + " " + person.age); } }

The following pre-configured parsers are provided for convenience: Instance Accepts MsgPackParser.DEFAULT Binary MessagePack. MsgPackParser.DEFAULT_NATIVE Binary MessagePack, returning native types such as byte[] for binary values. MsgPackParser.DEFAULT_SPACED_HEX MessagePack as a hex string. MsgPackParser.DEFAULT_BASE64 MessagePack as a Base64 string. For anything else, start from the builder's create() method. The settings readers reach for first: Builder method Effect nativeMode() Return native Java types for MessagePack values. maxLength(int) Reject binary, string or collection values longer than this. validateEnd() Fail if anything follows the parsed value. beanDictionary(Class...) Classes the parser may instantiate from _type properties. swaps(Class...) Object swaps that convert parsed values into other types. The class hierarchy for the builder of this parser is below. Refer to the builder javadocs for the full set of configurable settings. Context.BuilderMarshallingContextable.BuilderParser.BuilderInputStreamParser.BuilderMsgPackParser.Builder
MessagePack Serializers: the reverse direction. MessagePack Support Serializers and Parsers
The MsgPackSerializer class is used to serialize POJOs into MessagePack.

Use MsgPackSerializer when you want JSON's data model in a compact binary form: smaller than JSON on the wire and faster to parse, at the cost of not being human readable. It writes byte[], so use it for binary protocols, message queues and caches rather than for browsers.

import org.apache.juneau.marshall.msgpack.*; public class MsgPackSerializerExample { public static class Person { public String name = "John Smith"; public int age = 45; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Person person = new Person(); // Binary output. byte[] bytes = (byte[]) MsgPackSerializer.DEFAULT.write(person); // The same bytes as spaced hex, for reading. System.out.println(bytes.length + " bytes"); System.out.println(MsgPackSerializer.DEFAULT_SPACED_HEX.writeToString(person)); } } The bean is 22 bytes; the same data as JSON is 30 characters.

The following pre-configured serializers are provided for convenience: Instance Output MsgPackSerializer.DEFAULT Binary byte[]. MsgPackSerializer.DEFAULT_SPACED_HEX The same bytes as a hex string. MsgPackSerializer.DEFAULT_BASE64 The same bytes as a Base64 string. For anything else, start from the builder's create() method. The settings readers reach for first: Builder method Effect addBeanTypesMsgPack() Add _type properties to beans whose runtime type differs from the declared one. keepNullProperties() Write bean properties whose value is null. trimEmptyCollections() / trimEmptyMaps() Skip empty collections or maps. sortCollections() / sortMaps() Sort collections or map entries before writing. beanDictionary(Class...) Classes whose _type names the serializer may write. swaps(Class...) Object swaps that convert values before writing. The class hierarchy for the builder of this serializer is below. Refer to the builder javadocs for the full set of configurable settings. Context.BuilderMarshallingContextable.BuilderMarshallingTraverseContext.BuilderSerializer.BuilderOutputStreamSerializer.BuilderMsgPackSerializer.Builder
MessagePack Parsers: the reverse direction. MessagePack Support Serializers and Parsers

The juneau-rest-server-view-mustache module adds Mustache view-rendering to juneau-rest-server without bleeding the Mustache engine dependency into the core. This page covers the Mustache-specific bridge. For the engine-agnostic View interface itself, see the 10.0.0 release notes under the juneau-rest-server section. The sibling JSP View Support, Thymeleaf View Support, and FreeMarker View Support pages cover the JSP, Thymeleaf, and FreeMarker bridges with the same shape.

Mustache is the canonical logic-less templating engine — a small, well-defined spec implemented identically across two dozen languages. The Java implementation com.github.spullara.mustache.java:compiler is fast (compiled to bytecode), has zero servlet-container dependencies, and renders directly to a java.io.Writer, so it runs unchanged under MockRest, Jetty microservices, and Spring Boot. It's the recommended choice when you want a template syntax that's intentionally restricted (no embedded scripts, no inline expressions) and identical to what your JavaScript / Go / Python / Ruby front ends already use.

Class Role View (in juneau-rest-server core) Engine-agnostic contract: getTemplateName(), getAttributes(), getResponseHeaders(). MustacheMixin Mixin. Mounts /mustache/* for raw .mustache template requests; registers MustacheViewRenderer on the response-processor chain. Builder: basePath(String) (default /), templateSuffix(String) (default .mustache), cacheTemplates(boolean) (default true). Builder implements the shared ViewMixinBuilder contract. MustacheView View implementation. Immutable; fluent: MustacheView.of("hello").attr("name", name).header("Cache-Control", "no-store"). MustacheViewRenderer ResponseProcessor that detects MustacheView returns and asks the configured com.github.mustachejava.MustacheFactory to compile and execute the template directly onto the response writer.

juneau-rest-server-view-mustache ships only com.github.spullara.mustache.java:compiler in provided scope. No engine is bundled with the bridge module. Consumers add the engine matching their deployment.

Deployment Recommended setup Maven coordinates Juneau microservice / Jetty / MockRest Bridge-default DefaultMustacheFactory (built on first use, anchored on the importer's classloader and the configured basePath) com.github.spullara.mustache.java:compiler Spring Boot User-supplied @Bean MustacheFactory (Spring Boot's official starter ships jmustache, not mustache.java — see Spring Boot integration below) com.github.spullara.mustache.java:compiler Custom resolvers / caching / preprocessors User-supplied @Bean MustacheFactory (subclass DefaultMustacheFactory or implement your own) Whatever you build on top of compiler The bridge picks up a MustacheFactory bean from the request's BeanStore via BeanStore.getBean(MustacheFactory.class) first; if no factory bean is registered, it constructs a default DefaultMustacheFactory rooted at the classpath directory derived from basePath (e.g. basePath("/templates/") → resource root templates). When no Mustache engine is on the classpath, the renderer surfaces a clear diagnostic naming the missing dependency: No Mustache engine is available on the classpath. Add: - com.github.spullara.mustache.java:compiler Or register a custom @Bean MustacheFactory that supplies your preferred resolvers / caching. See https://juneau.apache.org/docs/topics/MustacheViewSupport for the full matrix.

<dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-server-view-mustache</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <!-- engine: --> <dependency> <groupId>com.github.spullara.mustache.java</groupId> <artifactId>compiler</artifactId> <version>0.9.14</version> </dependency>
src/main/resources/ templates/ hello.mustache
Hello, {{name}}!

import org.apache.juneau.http.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.servlet.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.view.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.view.mustache.*; @Rest(path="/app", mixins=MustacheMixin.class) public class AppResource extends RestServlet { @Bean MustacheMixin mustache() { return MustacheMixin.create() .basePath("/templates/") .build(); } @RestGet("/hello/{name}") public View hello(@Path String name) { return MustacheView.of("hello").attr("name", name); } } GET /app/hello/world returns Hello, world! — MustacheViewRenderer intercepts the MustacheView return, hands the view's attributes to the active MustacheFactory, and asks the compiled Mustache to render /templates/hello.mustache directly onto the response.

To use MustacheView from a host-class @RestGet without adopting the full mixin, add MustacheViewRenderer.class directly to the host's responseProcessors: @Rest(responseProcessors={MustacheViewRenderer.class}) public class AppResource extends BasicRestServlet { @RestGet("/hello/{name}") public View hello(@Path String name) { return MustacheView.of("mustache-templates/hello.mustache").attr("name", name); } } The ResponseProcessorList partition pass (added in 10.0.0) automatically repositions MustacheViewRenderer to run before SerializedPojoProcessor. Because mustache.java renders directly to a Writer with zero servlet-container dependencies, attribute interpolation ({{name}} → "Alice") works under MockRest — verified end-to-end by MustacheView_TypedHandler_Test#a04_renderInterpolatesAttributesFromTypedHandler.

The mixin also installs a default /mustache/* mount that renders raw templates under the configured base path. With basePath("/templates/"), a request for GET /app/mustache/about renders /templates/about.mustache directly — no Java handler required. The handler appends the configured templateSuffix if the requested path doesn't already end with it, so /app/mustache/about.mustache works too. The greedy /* handler is excluded from the generated Swagger / OpenAPI spec via @OpSwagger(ignore=true) since the path isn't API-meaningful.

The default mount /mustache/* can be overridden via the SVL variable ${juneau.mustache.path:mustache} — set via system property (-Djuneau.mustache.path=views), environment variable (JUNEAU_MUSTACHE_PATH=views), or Config key (juneau.mustache.path = views) to change the runtime mount without subclassing.

Builder#cacheTemplates(boolean) (default true) controls whether the bridge-default MustacheFactory (built lazily when no @Bean MustacheFactory is registered) caches compiled templates: @Bean MustacheMixin mustache() { return MustacheMixin.create() .basePath("/templates/") .cacheTemplates(false) // dev hot-reload: rebuild the factory on every render .build(); } true (default, production-safe) — the bridge builds the default factory once and reuses it; mustache.java's own DefaultMustacheFactory compiles-and-caches templates internally, so a template is compiled exactly once. false — the bridge rebuilds the default factory (with an empty compile-cache) on every render, so edited .mustache files under basePath are picked up without a server restart. The flag only affects the bridge-default factory; a user-supplied @Bean MustacheFactory manages its own caching and is returned as-is regardless of this setting. This is the same knob the sibling JSP / Thymeleaf / FreeMarker bridges expose via the shared ViewMixinBuilder contract — see View-mixin builder contract below.

MustacheMixin.Builder implements ViewMixinBuilder, the minimal contract shared by all four view-engine mixin builders (basePath(String) + cacheTemplates(boolean)). Code written against the interface works unchanged if you later swap engines: import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.view.*; ViewMixinBuilder<?> anyEngineBuilder = MustacheMixin.create(); anyEngineBuilder.basePath("/templates/").cacheTemplates(false);

The raw-template handler funnels every user-supplied @Path("/*") String path through FileUtils.resolveVirtualPathSafely(String, String) and rejects any .. traversal that escapes the configured basePath with HTTP 403. Both direct (/mustache/../secret) and nested (/mustache/a/b/../../../secret) traversal attempts are blocked at the handler boundary before reaching the engine resolver. This is the same hardening the JSP and Thymeleaf bridges apply; see MustacheMixin_PathTraversal_Test for the canonical coverage.

Spring Boot's official server-side templating starter for Mustache (spring-boot-starter-mustache) ships jmustache, not com.github.spullara.mustache.java:compiler. The bridge module deliberately targets mustache.java (the implementation spring-boot-starter-mustache does not autowire), so Spring Boot applications wiring MustacheMixin need to register their own MustacheFactory @Bean explicitly: @Configuration public class AppConfig { @Bean public MustacheFactory mustacheFactory() { return new DefaultMustacheFactory("templates"); // classpath:/templates/*.mustache } @Bean public MustacheMixin mustache() { return MustacheMixin.create() .basePath("/templates/") .build(); } } The Spring BeanStore adapter resolves both beans through ApplicationContext.getBean(...); no additional plumbing is required.

MustacheViewRenderer implements ViewRenderer and is automatically positioned before SerializedPojoProcessor by the ResponseProcessorList partition pass. A @RestOp method returning MustacheView reaches the renderer without any extra configuration — the mixin registers the renderer and the framework ensures ordering. MockRest-level typed-handler integration is verified by MustacheView_TypedHandler_Test (attribute interpolation asserted end-to-end).

Some apps want /views/ for the public site and /admin/views/ for the admin console. Register two MustacheMixin beans, each in its own subclass with its own paths override: @Rest(paths={"/views/*"}) public class PublicViewsResource extends MustacheMixin { public PublicViewsResource() { super(MustacheMixin.create().basePath("/templates/public/")); } } @Rest(paths={"/admin/views/*"}) public class AdminViewsResource extends MustacheMixin { public AdminViewsResource() { super(MustacheMixin.create().basePath("/templates/admin/")); } } Both subclasses mount independently and each resolves templates against its own basePath.

jmustache is not supported by the default factory. Spring Boot's spring-boot-starter-mustache autoconfigures jmustache's Mustache.Compiler, which is a different API entirely. The bridge module targets mustache.java's MustacheFactory. Apps preferring jmustache can wire a custom MustacheFactory @Bean that adapts the jmustache API, but the bridge does not ship that adapter. Lambda sections are users' responsibility. Mustache's lambda-section spec lets a template attribute resolve to a function; pass the lambda as an attribute via MustacheView.attr("greet", new Mustache.Lambda() { ... }) exactly as you would directly with mustache.java. The bridge passes attributes through unchanged.

The @NameProperty annotation is used to identify a setter method or field for setting the name of a POJO as it's known by its parent object. This annotation is used by parsers to automatically set the name/key of an object when parsing structured data (e.g., JSON maps, XML elements). A common use case is when parsing a map where the map key should be stored as a property on the bean.

Must be an instance method or field (not static) For methods: Must accept exactly one parameter (any type) For fields: Can be any type The method or field does not need to be public (will be made accessible automatically)
Can be applied to: Bean setter methods or fields @Rest-annotated classes and @RestOp-annotated methods when using the on() parameter

// JSON being parsed: { "id1": {name: "John Smith", sex: "M"}, "id2": {name: "Jane Doe", sex: "F"} } public class Person { @NameProperty public String id; // Gets set to "id1" or "id2" from map key public String name; public char sex; }
public class Person { private String id; @NameProperty protected void setName(String name) { this.id = name; } public String name; public char sex; }

During parsing when an object is created as a value in a map/collection The parser automatically calls the setter or sets the field with the key/name from the parent structure This allows the bean to know its key/name within the parent container

This page covers two packaging concerns for Juneau applications: Docker image layering (a concrete recommendation you can apply today) and GraalVM native-image support (a feasibility assessment with a forward plan).

Juneau itself ships libraries, not runnable applications, so there is no Juneau-side fat-jar to layer. Layering happens in your deployable application image. Two practical levers: Spring Boot apps — spring-boot-maven-plugin's repackage goal produces a layered jar by default (since Spring Boot 2.4), separating slow-changing dependency layers from your fast-changing application classes. Combined with a multi-stage Dockerfile using java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --layers, Docker caches the dependency layer across rebuilds. The Juneau Spring Boot petstore sample is built this way. Embedded-Jetty / plain-jar apps — order your Dockerfile COPY steps coarsest-changing first: copy the dependency jars (which include the stable Juneau artifacts) in an earlier layer than your application jar, so a code-only change re-uploads only the small application layer. The starter projects on the apache/juneau microservice-*-starter branches ship minimal Dockerfiles; a production image can apply the layered COPY shape described above. Depending on Juneau through the version-aligned BOM and curated bundles keeps the dependency layer stable and reproducible across rebuilds, which is what makes the cache hit reliable.

Juneau's marshalling/bean core is reflection-heavy, so native-image (closed-world AOT) support is non-trivial. A feasibility assessment was performed against the reflective source; the verdict is CONDITIONAL GO.

All of Juneau's reflection flows through a single wrapper layer — org.apache.juneau.commons.reflect.* (ClassInfo / MethodInfo / FieldInfo / ConstructorInfo) with one setAccessible() choke point in AccessibleInfo — and there is no sun.misc.Unsafe and no bytecode generation anywhere in main source. The blockers are the standard native-image reflection blockers, not anything pathological. Critically, the same MarshallingContext / BeanMeta / ClassMeta model that drives marshalling already computes exactly the constructor + field + accessor set that reachability metadata needs — so a Juneau-authored metadata emitter is realistic. That is what tips the verdict from no-go to conditional-go.

Open-world bean reflection — every marshalled bean's full member set must be registered; application bean types are unknowable at Juneau-build time. There is no "zero-config native Juneau" — consumers always need a generation step. User-supplied dynamic-proxy interface sets (@Remote clients, interface beans) — proxy metadata can't be derived from Juneau's bytecode; it comes from the GraalVM tracing agent or explicit declaration. _type dictionary class resolution via Class.forName — classes reachable only through a serialized _type string are invisible to static analysis and must be registered by name. Reflective swap/converter/DI instantiation through BeanInstantiator. Classpath resource + NLS ResourceBundle loading — broad but low-risk (regex resource includes cover it). SPIs / ServiceLoader usage, despite intuition, is the easiest category — finite and statically known.
documents.s: The hard blockers (all standard, all addressable)

documents.t: The maintainer-approved direction is option (b): a native-image-ready juneau-marshall core (JSON/XML/HTML/UON + swaps + dictionaries), driven by a Juneau-authored reachability-metadata emitter built on BeanContext introspection, with the GraalVM tracing agent covering the statically-invisible parts (@Remote/interface-bean proxies, _type dictionary classes). Target the modern unified reachability-metadata.json format, delivered as a Maven plugin goal / module the consumer points at their bean classes (not checked-in static metadata, which silently drifts). The REST server (embedded Jetty/Tomcat, ServletContainerInitializer, transport providers) is deferred — most of its residual native-image risk lives in third-party dependencies, not Juneau's own code. Rough effort: a minimal single-bean JSON round-trip to native is S (~1–3 days); a generally-usable native marshalling core is L (~3–6 weeks); the full framework including @Remote proxies + REST server is XL and out of scope. This assessment is a feasibility verdict, not a shipped feature. The native-image emitter is tracked as a dedicated committed follow-on; native-image builds of Juneau are not yet supported.

Which client? juneau-rest-client (org.apache.juneau.rest.client.RestClient) is the recommended REST client. It is generally available in 10.0.0, transport-agnostic, and uses the JDK HttpClient by default. juneau-rest-client-classic (org.apache.juneau.rest.client.classic.RestClient, Apache HttpClient 4.5) stays supported and is not deprecated; it is the stable choice for existing users. See Choosing a REST Client. Juneau 10.0 promotes the next-generation REST client and HTTP type stack to the canonical names under org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*, org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.*, and org.apache.juneau.http.*. The pre-existing Apache HttpClient 4.5–based stack ships unchanged under .classic packages and the new juneau-rest-client-classic Maven module — see V10 Migration Guide for the import-rename table. See the guide: Call an existing REST API with a typed proxy The next-generation stack: Uses only JDK types in its API surface (org.apache.juneau.http). No org.apache.http.* on any signature. Introduces an HttpTransport abstraction so you can plug in any HTTP client (Apache HC 4.5, Apache HC 5, JDK HttpClient, OkHttp, Jetty, or a custom transport) without changing user code. Replaces 40+ Apache HC–specific builder methods on the classic RestClient.Builder with a small, focused builder. Transport-specific configuration lives on the transport builder, not on RestClient.Builder.

Package Module Role org.apache.juneau.http juneau-rest-common JDK-native HTTP types (HttpHeader, HttpPart, HttpBody, status types, ~73 RFC-named headers, ~50 named response types, multipart, remote-proxy annotations). No httpcore dependency. org.apache.juneau.rest.client juneau-rest-client HttpTransport abstraction, canonical RestClient / RestRequest / RestResponse, interceptors, body converters, JUL-level-driven debug logging (RestClientDebugFormatter). No httpcore dependency. org.apache.juneau.rest.mock juneau-rest-mock MockHttpTransport and the canonical MockRestClient for in-process testing against a Juneau RestContext. org.apache.juneau.http.classic juneau-rest-common-classic Pre-existing Apache HttpCore-based types (~170 classes). Kept for the classic stack. org.apache.juneau.rest.client.classic juneau-rest-client-classic (new) Pre-existing RestClient that implements org.apache.http.client.HttpClient. The JDK HttpClient–based JavaHttpTransport is built into the canonical juneau-rest-client artifact and is the default — it requires no third-party dependencies on Java 11+. To swap to a different native HTTP client, add one of the optional transport modules below. Each ships only its own native client and registers a higher-priority HttpTransportProvider via ServiceLoader, which automatically takes over discovery. An explicit RestClient.builder().transport(...) call always wins. Module Artifact ID Native client Apache HttpClient 4.5 juneau-rest-client-apache-httpclient-45 org.apache.httpcomponents:httpclient:4.5.x Apache HttpClient 5 juneau-rest-client-apache-httpclient-50 org.apache.httpcomponents.client5:httpclient5 OkHttp juneau-rest-client-okhttp com.squareup.okhttp3:okhttp-jvm Eclipse Jetty client juneau-rest-client-jetty org.eclipse.jetty:jetty-client Each optional module ships three classes: *Transport — the HttpTransport implementation, with static create() and builder() factories. *TransportBuilder — a final builder whose httpClient(...) method accepts the native client, so all native-client–specific configuration (pooling, proxies, TLS, authentication) is done on that client's own builder (e.g. ApacheHc45Transport.builder().httpClient(HttpClients.custom()….build())). *TransportProvider — ServiceLoader entry for auto-discovery. See HTTP Transport Adapters for the full feature matrix, JavaHttpTransport configuration, and per-transport authentication examples.

import org.apache.http.impl.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json5.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.apachehttpclient45.*; // Pre-build the serializer/parser — configure marshalling externally var serializer = Json5Serializer.create().build(); var parser = Json5Parser.create().build(); // Choose a transport explicitly and configure the underlying native client HttpTransport transport = ApacheHc45Transport.builder() .httpClient(HttpClients.custom().setMaxConnTotal(50).build()) .build(); RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .transport(transport) .serializer(serializer) .parser(parser) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build(); // Always use try-with-resources on the response — close() releases the connection try (var resp = client.get("/users/{id}").pathData("id", 42).run()) { var user = resp.body().as(User.class); } // At application shutdown client.close();

RestClient.create() is a zero-config shortcut — it's shorthand for RestClient.builder().build(): an auto-discovered transport, no default serializer/parser, and no root URL. Reach for it when you just want a client to issue requests against absolute URLs with no marshalling configured up front: RestClient client = RestClient.create(); try (var resp = client.get("https://api.example.com/users/{id}").pathData("id", 42).run()) { var body = resp.body().asString(); } Use RestClient.builder() — as shown above — whenever you need to configure a transport, serializer/ parser, root URL, default headers, interceptors, or any other builder option. create() and builder() are the only two idioms for obtaining an NG RestClient; create() is not a legacy alias for builder() (that shape belongs to the classic client, which is why porting classic code replaces RestClient.create() with RestClient.builder() — see Migration Path below).

If you don't pass an explicit transport, RestClient uses ServiceLoader to pick the highest-priority HttpTransportProvider on the classpath — this applies whether you configure the client via create() or via builder(). The following configures marshalling explicitly while still relying on transport auto-discovery: RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build();

Concern Classic RestClient (...client.classic) Canonical RestClient (...client) Client construction create() returns a Builder (call .build() to get a client) create() returns a built, ready-to-use client (the zero-config shortcut); builder() returns a Builder HTTP integration Implements org.apache.http.client.HttpClient; bound to Apache HC 4.5 Composes an HttpTransport; transport-agnostic Serialization model Multi-language marshallers / format shortcuts (json(), xml(), …) One pre-built serializer/parser pair per client; no multi-language mode Builder surface 40+ Apache HC passthrough methods Small builder with only Juneau-specific concerns Lifecycle RestClient.close() RestClient.close() — same idiom; both implement Closeable Per-request lifecycle RestRequest and RestResponse are both Closeable Only RestResponse is Closeable; close() releases the connection Header/part types Implement org.apache.http.Header / NameValuePair Implement JDK-only HttpHeader / HttpPart interfaces Schema validation on @Query/@Header/@FormData/@Path Supported Not supported — toString() + CollectionFormat only

documents.t: RestResponse — returned by RestRequest.run() — is the single Closeable in the user-facing per-call API. Close it to release the underlying connection and stream: // Correct — try-with-resources releases the connection even if run() or body() throws try (var resp = client.get("/users").run()) { return resp.body().as(UserList.class); } // At application shutdown client.close(); RestRequest does not implement Closeable — it is a disposable fluent builder for a single call, and run() transfers ownership of the connection to the returned RestResponse.

ResponseHeader (obtained via RestResponse.header(String)) has a small set of typed-wrapper convenience methods, mirroring the classic stack's asXxxHeader() family without pulling in any org.apache.http.classic.* types. Each is a thin parse over the header's raw string value using JDK types or the transport-neutral types already in juneau-rest-common: Method Return type Absent / unparseable asBoolean() Optional<Boolean> empty asZonedDateTime() Optional<ZonedDateTime> empty (RFC-1123 HTTP date) asUri() Optional<URI> empty asEntityTag() Optional<EntityTag> empty (e.g. ETag) asEntityTags() EntityTags (never null) EntityTags.EMPTY (e.g. If-Match) asStringRanges() StringRanges (never null) empty (e.g. Accept-Encoding) try (var resp = client.get("/users/123").run()) { Optional<ZonedDateTime> lastModified = resp.header("Last-Modified").asZonedDateTime(); Optional<EntityTag> etag = resp.header("ETag").asEntityTag(); EntityTags ifMatch = resp.header("If-Match").asEntityTags(); } These sit alongside the existing generic accessors (asInteger(), asLong(), asOptional(), asCsvList()); for anything not covered here, parse getValue() directly.

The @Remote / @RemoteOp proxy annotations (and the @RemoteGet / @RemotePost / @RemotePut / @RemoteDelete / @RemotePatch verb annotations) gain a family of declarative capabilities in the next-gen engine, obtained via client.remote(MyProxy.class). These are documented on their own page, NG Remote Proxies: Constant part values — always-applied headers, query and form data Content body defaults Per-part serializers Call policy — interceptors, timeouts, retries, throwOnError Dynamic URLs and base overrides — @Url and baseUrl() Declarative multipart — @Multipart / @Part Per-method format selection Streaming request and response bodies MyProxy proxy = client.remote(MyProxy.class);

multipart/form-data is a first-class body type. Build a MultipartBody explicitly and send it like any other request body via RestRequest.body(HttpBody): var mp = MultipartBody.builder() .field("note", "hello") .file("attachment", new File("report.pdf"), "application/pdf") .build(); try (var resp = client.post("/cases/123/attachments").body(mp).run()) { resp.assertOk(); } RestRequest.formData(...) continues to produce application/x-www-form-urlencoded and should not be used for binary uploads. For a declarative alternative on remote proxies, see Declarative Multipart.

Logging is framework-agnostic and driven by the JUL logger level. There is no .logger(...) builder method and no RestLogger type; configure the debug logger name (and optionally a RestClientDebugFormatter) on the builder, then raise the logger level: RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .debugLoggerName("myapp.http") .build(); // uses the built-in JavaHttpTransport by default // INFO = summary, FINE = + headers, FINEST = + bounded bodies (opt-in) java.util.logging.Logger.getLogger("myapp.http").setLevel(java.util.logging.Level.FINE); try (var resp = client.get("/users/123").run()) { resp.assertOk(); } Body dumping is off unless explicitly opted in, and credentials are redacted by default. See REST Client Logging and Debugging for the tier table, the secure-by-default rules, and request correlation.

MockHttpTransport routes TransportRequest directly to a Juneau RestContext without network I/O. Use org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.MockRestClient for unit tests that exercise serialization, remote proxies, interceptors, and assertions: import org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.MockRestClient; try (MockRestClient mock = MockRestClient.create(MyRestResource.class); var resp = mock.get("/users/123").run()) { var user = resp.body().as(User.class); } For the legacy fluent surface (.json5(), .plainText(), .disableRedirectHandling(), etc.) use org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.classic.MockRestClient — see Mock REST Client Overview.

The classic RestClient and its supporting juneau-rest-common Apache HttpCore types are not deprecated in 10.0; they moved to .classic packages and the new juneau-rest-client-classic module. Migration is opt-in and incremental: Stay on classic — keep using the same RestClient / MockRestClient types you have today; just adjust imports as described in V10 Migration Guide and add a Maven dependency on juneau-rest-client-classic. No behavioral change. Adopt the canonical stack — add the NG transport module for your preferred HTTP stack as a Maven dependency. Replace RestClient.create() with the canonical org.apache.juneau.rest.client.RestClient.builder() and adapt builder calls — some map 1:1 (rootUrl, default headers/query, interceptors, logger); marshaller, errorCodes, and executorService have no NG equivalent — configure marshalling via the discrete serializer(...)/parser(...) builder methods instead. Wrap each call's RestResponse in try-with-resources. Call close() on the client at application shutdown. If you customized Apache HttpClient through httpClientBuilder() / connectionManager() / defaultRequestConfig(), build the equivalent native CloseableHttpClient yourself and pass it to the transport builder's httpClient(...) method (e.g. ApacheHc45Transport.builder().httpClient(...)). If you relied on multi-language marshallers or per-request language overrides, create one RestClient per language. The canonical stack will graduate to stable in a future release, at which point the classic stack may be deprecated and eventually removed.
