RestResponse.assertThat() returns a ResponseAssertion (package org.apache.juneau.rest.client.assertion) for fluent checks. Failures throw AssertionError, so they work directly in JUnit tests. try (var resp = client.get("/users/42").run()) { resp.assertThat() .isOk() .header("Content-Type").contains("json").and() .header("ETag").isPresent().and() .body().contains("\"id\":42").and(); }

Method Checks statusCode() Returns an integer assertion on the status. isOk() Status is 2xx. isClientError() / isServerError() Status is 4xx / 5xx. header(name) Switches to a ResponseHeaderAssertion. body() Switches to a ResponseBodyAssertion. and() Returns to the parent assertion.
isPresent(), isAbsent(), equals(String), contains(String), startsWith(String), integerEquals(int), and().

equals(String), contains(String), startsWith(String), isEmpty(), isNotEmpty(), and(). Body assertions read the body, so they consume it. Use them instead of, not in addition to, body().as(...) on the same response.

assertThat() is for tests: it throws AssertionError. assertOk() / assertStatus(int) on the response are for application code: they throw RestCallException, which you can catch and inspect with getStatusCode().

A BodyConverter<T> turns an object passed to RestRequest.body(Object) into a transport body before the client falls back to the default serializer. public interface BodyConverter<T> { boolean canConvert(Object o); TransportBody convert(Object o) throws Exception; static <T> BodyConverter<T> of(Class<T> type, ThrowingConverter<T> fn); }
RestClient.DEFAULT_BODY_CONVERTERS handles, in order: HttpBody, InputStream, byte[], and File. Anything else is serialized by the client's default serializer.

RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .bodyConverter(BodyConverter.of(Path.class, p -> TransportBody.of(FileBody.of(p.toFile())))) .build(); client.put("/upload").body(Path.of("data.bin")).run().close(); Builder method Effect bodyConverter(...) Prepends converters, so they win over the defaults and keep them as fallbacks. bodyConverters(...) Replaces the whole list, including the built-in converters. The first converter whose canConvert returns true is used.

Sending a type you do not want routed through Juneau marshalling (streams, files, pre-encoded data). Adding a transport body for a domain type (for example, a buffer with a specific content type). For serializing beans, prefer configuring a serializer rather than writing a converter.

The NG RestClient protects outbound calls against server-side request forgery (SSRF) and credential leaks across redirects. This page describes what is enforced, where, and how to opt out. The same URL policy class (org.apache.juneau.http.remote.RemoteUrlPolicy, in juneau-rest-common) is shared with the classic client. Which calls are covered? The SSRF guard (URL deny-list, pin-on-connect, per-hop redirect re-validation) applies to policy-covered calls: @Remote / @RemoteOp proxies and dynamic @Url arguments, or a request where you called remoteUrlPolicy(true, ...). An ordinary client.get("https://...") is treated as trusted application code and is not run through the deny-list.

RemoteUrlPolicy.requireAllowedUrl(url, allowPrivate) rejects a URL unless: the scheme is http or https and the host is non-empty; the host is not on the deny-list: localhost, localhost.localdomain, metadata.google.internal (and its subdomains), or an IP literal that is loopback, any-local, link-local, site-local (RFC 1918), IPv6 unique-local (fc00::/7), IPv4 0.0.0.0/8 ("this network"), IPv4 100.64.0.0/10 (carrier-grade NAT shared space, which stays denied), IPv4 special-purpose ranges 192.0.0.0/24 (IETF protocol assignments), 198.18.0.0/15 (benchmarking), 224.0.0.0/4 (multicast) and 240.0.0.0/4 (reserved, including 255.255.255.255), IPv6 multicast (ff00::/8), IPv6 Teredo (2001::/32) or IPv6 local-use NAT64 (64:ff9b:1::/48). The last two are denied outright, because the embedded IPv4 address is obfuscated or its embedding length is operator-defined. IPv6 addresses that embed an IPv4 address (IPv4-mapped, IPv4-compatible, IPv4-translated ::ffff:0:a.b.c.d, NAT64 64:ff9b::/96, and 6to4 2002::/16) are unwrapped and classified by the embedded IPv4 address. IPv6 zone ids ([fe80::1%25en0]) are ignored for classification, and an unparseable IPv6 literal is denied. To re-permit a lab or appliance network (for example 198.18.0.0/15), set the JVM-wide system property RestClient.allowAddressRanges to a comma- or whitespace-separated CIDR list, such as -DRestClient.allowAddressRanges=198.18.0.0/15. It defaults to nothing allowed, and it is narrow by construction: every entry must lie entirely inside one of the special-purpose ranges 192.0.0.0/24, 198.18.0.0/15, 224.0.0.0/4, 240.0.0.0/4 or ff00::/8; any other entry (including 0.0.0.0/0, ::/0, a private range or the CGNAT range) is rejected with an IllegalArgumentException; it only re-permits addresses denied solely because they fall in one of those ranges. Loopback, link-local and metadata, private, CGNAT, "this network", unique-local, Teredo and local-use NAT64 addresses stay denied, as do IPv6 forms (such as 6to4) that embed such an address; an IPv4 entry matches the IPv4 address or the IPv4 address embedded in an IPv6 form; an IPv6 entry matches only a native ff00::/8 address. the allow applies to both the string check above and the resolved-address (DNS-pinned) check below. Entries are parsed strictly without any DNS lookup: dotted-quad IPv4 with octets 0-255 and no leading zeros, prefix lengths without leading zeros, and empty list items (such as a trailing comma) are ignored. The same allow-list can be set for a single client with RestClient.Builder.allowAddressRanges(String...) (for example .allowAddressRanges("198.18.0.0/15")) on both the classic and next-generation clients and every transport. It has exactly the semantics and validation described above, and an invalid entry makes build() throw an IllegalArgumentException. The client's ranges are combined with the system property as a union, and a client without the setting is unaffected by another client's setting in the same JVM. Relative values pass through, and the client's rootUrl is not re-checked. Bare decimal, octal, or hex IP spellings are not recognized as literals by the string check; they are caught by DNS pinning below. Set allowPrivateUrls(true) on the builder, allowPrivateUrls=true on @Remote / @RemoteOp, or the system property RestClient.allowPrivateUrls=true to permit private addresses (for example, when calling internal services). The effective setting is the logical OR of the three.

A host-name check alone is defeated by DNS rebinding and by names that resolve to private addresses. When the guard is active, each transport resolves the host itself, picks the first address that is not denied (RemoteUrlPolicy.selectAllowedAddress), and connects to exactly that address. If every candidate is denied, the call fails with TransportException. Transport Pinning mechanism JDK JavaHttpTransport (default) Rewrites the request URI to the pinned literal address and keeps the original Host header. It fails closed if pinning is not possible. Apache HttpClient 4.5 PolicyPinningDnsResolver on a dedicated policy-only client with its own connection pool. Apache HttpClient 5 PolicyPinningDnsResolver on a dedicated policy-only client with its own connection pool. OkHttp PolicyPinningDns on a dedicated policy-only derived client (shares the connection pool and dispatcher with the normal client, but OkHttp only reuses a connection for a request with the same Dns). Jetty PolicyPinningSocketAddressResolver Pinning is scoped to policy-covered requests, so normal traffic through the same client is unaffected, and a policy-covered request never reuses a connection that a normal request opened without the pin. The Apache HttpClient 4.5 and 5 transports send policy-covered requests through a second client of their own, whose separate connection pool resolves every connection through the pin. Jetty tags policy-covered requests, which gives them a separate connection pool of their own, and its resolver pins every connection opened for that pool. OkHttp's policy-only client shares the normal client's connection pool, but OkHttp reuses a connection only for a request with the same Dns, so the two never share a connection.

If the guard is active and the transport reports supportsUrlPolicy() == false, RestRequest.run() refuses to send the request and throws TransportException ("Refusing to send a policy-covered @Remote request..."). All bundled transports and the mock transports support the policy. The Apache HttpClient 4.5, Apache HttpClient 5, and Jetty transports support it only with the client they create themselves; built with a caller-supplied client, they report supportsUrlPolicy() == false. The OkHttp transport reports false for a client with an explicit proxy, and refuses a policy-covered request that the client's proxy selector routes through a proxy, because the proxy resolves the target host itself. A custom HttpTransport must override supportsUrlPolicy() once it implements pinning and honors TransportRequest redirect handling.
documents.s: Transports that cannot enforce the policy

documents.t: The classic client (org.apache.juneau.rest.client.classic.RestClient) guards @Remote calls with the same URL policy. The connection manager it builds keeps two separate pools: policy-covered calls lease from a pinned pool whose connections are all opened through PolicyPinningDnsResolver, and every other call leases from the ordinary pool. So a policy-covered call, or any of its redirect hops, never reuses a connection that an ordinary call opened without the pin. This holds for both the default and the pooled() connection manager. The pinned pool uses the ordinary pool's settings (pool limits, socket and connection configuration), so a createConnectionManager() override that configures the manager returned by super configures policy-covered calls too. The connection manager the classic client builds applies the builder's TLS and pool settings to both pools: sslContext(...) (for example one with a custom trust store), sslHostnameVerifier(...), sslSocketFactory(...), maxConnTotal(...) and maxConnPerRoute(...). Apache HttpClientBuilder ignores its own copies of these once a connection manager is set. maxConnTotal(...) or maxConnPerRoute(...) makes the connection manager a pooling one, as pooled() does. Each build() creates a new connection manager, so a builder reused after build() gives every client its own, and closing one client does not break the next. A connection manager you supply with connectionManager(...) is used as is and keeps its own TLS and pool settings. A custom sslSocketFactory(...), or a socket factory set with setSSLSocketFactory(...) on the HttpClientBuilder you pass to httpClientBuilder(...), is also used for policy-covered calls. The pin hands it the address it has already checked, and the factory must connect to exactly that address. A factory that ignores that address and connects by host name, resolving the name again, bypasses the pin. The other settings Apache HttpClientBuilder applies only to a connection manager it builds itself reach both pools too: defaultSocketConfig(...), defaultConnectionConfig(...), connectionTimeToLive(...) (which also makes the connection manager a pooling one) and publicSuffixMatcher(...) (used by the default hostname verifier). So do TLS and pool settings made directly on the HttpClientBuilder you pass to httpClientBuilder(...), and the system properties useSystemProperties() reads: the JVM's default SSL socket factory (the javax.net.ssl.* trust and key stores), https.protocols, https.cipherSuites and, unless http.keepAlive is false, the http.maxConnections limit. A DNS resolver set on the HttpClientBuilder is used for ordinary calls only; policy-covered calls always resolve through the pin. If httpClientBuilder(...) replaces the HttpClientBuilder after you have configured the client builder, these connection-manager settings made with the client builder's own setters carry over, and win over the same setting on the replacement: sslContext(...), sslSocketFactory(...), sslHostnameVerifier(...), publicSuffixMatcher(...) (for the default hostname verifier only; its use for cookies is lost with the replaced builder), maxConnTotal(...), maxConnPerRoute(...), pooled(), connectionTimeToLive(...), defaultSocketConfig(...), defaultConnectionConfig(...) and the TLS and http.maxConnections system properties of useSystemProperties(). Every other setting made before the replacement (interceptors, proxy, the rest of useSystemProperties(), and so on) was made on the replaced HttpClientBuilder and is lost. For these connection-manager settings, a value set with the client builder's own setter always wins over the same setting on the HttpClientBuilder, whichever was set last: unlike Apache's last-write-wins, a later httpClientBuilder().setDefaultSocketConfig(...) does not override an earlier defaultSocketConfig(...). As in Apache HttpClientBuilder, a socket factory wins over an SSL context wherever each was set, so a setSSLSocketFactory(...) on the replacement wins over an earlier sslContext(...). close() shuts down the connection manager the client built for itself, even with connectionManagerShared(true): nothing else can reach it. "Shared" keeps open a connection manager you supply, and any connection manager an overridden createConnectionManager() returns, even one that calls super, because the override may hand the same instance to several clients. The classic client refuses a policy-covered @Remote call ("Refusing to send a policy-covered @Remote request...") when it cannot guarantee the pin. It cannot pin a connection manager it did not build, or a call that goes out through an HttpClient other than the one it wired to its pinning connection manager. The guard travels on the request's HttpContext (each redirect hop gets a context marked for the guard), so it holds on whichever thread runs the request. A replaced call path may still send a copy of the request, or send it with another context, so the refusals below are what keep such a path from going out unpinned. That is the case when: you supply a connection manager with connectionManager(...); you override createConnectionManager() to return a different one; you supply an HttpClient with httpClient(...); you override createHttpClient() to return a different client, or a wrapper around the one super builds; your createHttpClient() override, after calling super.createHttpClient(), sets an HttpProcessor on the HttpClientBuilder, adds a request interceptor with addInterceptorLast(...), or replaces its redirect strategy or request executor, and builds again. Make such changes before calling super. The builder is checked as it is once the client is built, so one of these changes made after the build is refused too; a change that the override undoes before it returns is not detected; you pass httpClientBuilder(...) (or return from createHttpClientBuilder()) an HttpClientBuilder subclass that overrides build(), createMainExec(...), decorateMainExec(...) or decorateProtocolExec(...), or inherits such an override. Any of these can build the client around another connection manager or request executor, even when build() returns the client super built. This includes wrapping or decorating builders such as httpclient-cache's CachingHttpClientBuilder (it overrides decorateMainExec(...)). The check fails closed and has no escape hatch: under the guard, allowPrivateUrls(true) is the only way to use such a builder; you set an HttpProcessor with httpProcessor(...). It replaces all of the client's request interceptors, among them the guard's own and the redirect credential guard. Add interceptors with addInterceptorFirst(...) or addInterceptorLast(...) on the HttpClientBuilder instead; you set a custom RestCallHandler with callHandler(...), or a BasicRestCallHandler bound to a different client; you use a RestClient subclass that overrides run(HttpHost,HttpRequest,HttpContext), execute(HttpHost,HttpRequest,HttpContext) or execute(HttpUriRequest,HttpContext); createRequest(...) returns a RestRequest subclass that overrides run(); an override of createRequest(...) or request(...) returns a RestRequest bound to a different client. That request would go out through the other client's HttpClient. A policy-covered request whose HttpContext lacks the guard marker, for example one a custom call path sent with a fresh context, is refused rather than sent unguarded. So is one that would open or reuse a connection of the ordinary pool. That can only happen when the guard's request interceptor did not run, for example a request with the guard's context sent directly through execute(...) on a client with an HttpProcessor. A refused request leaves nothing behind: the next ordinary request on the same thread is sent normally. A policy-covered call on a proxy route is refused too, because the pin would check the proxy's address instead of the target's. This covers proxy(...), a routePlanner(...) that picks a proxy, and the proxy system properties read by useSystemProperties(). The refusal is reported as a RestCallException, with the connection manager's IllegalStateException as its cause. Ordinary calls are unaffected. Set allowPrivateUrls(true) if the target is an intentional local or intranet service. MockRestClient supplies its own connection manager, so its @Remote calls need allowPrivateUrls(true) too.

For policy-covered calls, Juneau runs the redirect loop itself (PolicyEnforcedRedirects) and turns off the transport's own auto-redirect. For every Location hop: the target URL is re-checked against the URL policy; the hop is sent over a pinned connection; on the classic client, a hop to another origin (or an https-to-http downgrade) drops the caller-set credential headers: the RedirectSecurity set described below, and Proxy-Authorization in every case (a guarded call never goes through a proxy). They stay dropped for the rest of the chain, even if a later hop returns to the first origin. Every hop is compared with the first hop's origin, so the same headers are also dropped when the client's own interceptors or HttpClientBuilder default headers add them to a hop on another origin. With a context(...) setting, which all hops share, the target's authentication state is reset on a hop to another origin, as Apache HttpClient does on a change of host, so credentials that answered the first host's challenge are not sent unasked to the next. Handled status codes are 301, 302, 303, 307, and 308. 301/302/303 rewrite the method to GET and drop the body (unless it was already GET/HEAD); 307/308 preserve the method and body. The call fails if: the redirect has no Location; more than 5 hops are followed (RemoteUrlPolicy.MAX_REDIRECT_HOPS); the Location is invalid, or names a host that java.net.URI cannot parse (such as my_service), so the origins cannot be compared; a 307/308 would have to replay a non-repeatable body (fail closed); the JDK HttpClient was configured to follow redirects itself (Redirect.NEVER, the default, is required). Each of these failures, like a refused pin, is a TransportException.

When a redirect changes origin, credentials must not follow it. RedirectSecurity defines the rule: same origin compares scheme, host (case-insensitive), and port (80/443 normalized); credentials are stripped when the origin differs or the redirect is an https-to-http downgrade; the stripped set is RedactedHeaders.DEFAULT: Authorization, Cookie, Set-Cookie, Proxy-Authorization, and X-API-Key. The OkHttp transport keeps Proxy-Authorization only while the redirected request is still plain HTTP through the same HTTP proxy as the original request, and the original request was also plain HTTP (the header authenticates you to the proxy, so stripping it there makes the proxy answer 407 again). With no proxy, a different proxy, or an https target (reached through a CONNECT tunnel), it is stripped like the rest. The Apache HttpClient 5 transport, on a client you supply, likewise keeps it on a proxied route that is not tunnelled (see below); if the two origins cannot be compared, the guard strips (fail safe). Transports apply this rule through RedirectSecurity when a redirect is followed. The OkHttp and Apache HttpClient 4.5 transports, and the Apache HttpClient 5 transport on ordinary (not SSRF-guarded) requests, compare origins on the library's own host object, so a host name that java.net.URI cannot parse (for example the underscore name my_service) is compared like any other host. The transports apply the rule on the clients they create; the OkHttp, Apache HttpClient 4.5, Apache HttpClient 5 and Jetty transports also apply it to a client you supply (see below for Apache HttpClient 5). On OkHttp the origin is the first request after your application interceptors (so an interceptor that rewrites the URL sets the origin), and only the values you sent are stripped: cookies loaded from the client's CookieJar for the new origin, and credentials from its Authenticator or proxyAuthenticator, still go to the new origin. The classic client strips headers only, too. Its redirect credential guard runs after the client's other request interceptors, so a Cookie header from its CookieStore is dropped on a hop to another origin like any other. But the client still answers an authentication challenge from the new origin with whatever its CredentialsProvider holds for that host. A credential registered for AuthScope.ANY (for example basicAuth(null, -1, user, pw): a null host and a -1 port are AuthScope.ANY_HOST and AuthScope.ANY_PORT) matches any host, so it is sent to the new origin when that origin asks for it. Scope credentials to the host and port they are meant for. On a client you supply to the Apache HttpClient 4.5 or Jetty transport, only the values you sent are stripped on a cross-origin hop, as on OkHttp: cookies from the client's own cookie store, and credentials its CredentialsProvider (Apache HttpClient 4.5) or authentication store (Jetty) answers a challenge with, still go to the new origin. Same-origin redirects keep that library's own header handling (Jetty drops Authorization, Cookie and Proxy-Authorization on every redirect, including same-origin ones). The strip happens before the client's own request processing, so a header your client adds itself on every request (an Apache HttpClient 4.5 HttpRequestInterceptor, or a Jetty request listener, that sets a fixed Authorization or X-API-Key) is added again on the hop to the new origin; add credentials per request, or scope such code to the hosts it is meant for. On Jetty, the transport creates each request itself, so that its redirect copies are guarded, and does not call the client's newRequest(URI); an override of that method on a client you supply is not used. On the client the Apache HttpClient 5 transport creates itself, a redirect to another origin is followed, as on the other transports, with the stripped set removed from that hop and from every later hop in the chain, including a hop back to the first origin; a same-origin redirect keeps your headers. It uses the same per-request context as a client you supply (below), with a redirect strategy that lets the guarded hop go ahead instead of refusing it. Otherwise HttpClient's own redirect handling applies: 301, 302, 303, 307 and 308 are followed, a POST redirected by 301/302, or any method other than GET or HEAD redirected by 303, becomes a new GET that carries none of your headers, at most 50 redirects are followed, and a circular redirect fails with a TransportException. Cookies that the transport's own cookie store holds for the new host are still sent, under HttpClient's cookie rules (cookies are not scoped to a port). An Authorization that a CredentialsProvider adds, and the resends after a retry (such as a 503 with Retry-After) or an authentication challenge, are stripped from a cross-origin hop the same way as on a client you supply. Unguarded requests on this client now connect to a cross-origin Location host (credentials stripped, other headers and the body of a 307/308 forwarded); only SSRF-guarded requests re-check each hop against the policy. They do not use this client; they follow redirects through the policy-checked loop described above. On a client you supply to the Apache HttpClient 5 transport, the client's own redirect settings decide which redirects are followed: its RedirectStrategy, maxRedirects and circular-redirect settings, and disableRedirectHandling() or HttpClients.createMinimal() (no redirects) behave exactly as you configured them. The transport marks every header in the stripped set as sensitive, and DefaultRedirectStrategy (5.6) refuses, in isRedirectAllowed, a cross-origin redirect that replays sensitive headers: with it, a redirect that replays your headers is not followed to another origin while it carries any of them. You get the 3xx response instead, and the other origin is not contacted. A POST redirected by 301/302, or any method other than GET or HEAD redirected by 303, is followed as a new GET that carries none of your headers. Whichever strategy follows a redirect to another origin (HttpClient's LaxRedirectStrategy, which allows every redirect, or a custom one), the transport passes each request a context that removes the caller-set credential headers from that hop and from every later hop in the chain, including a hop back to the first origin; same-origin hops before the first cross-origin hop keep them. On a proxied route that is not tunnelled (a plain http target through an HTTP proxy), Proxy-Authorization is kept on every hop, because it authenticates to the proxy that every hop goes through and removing it would make the proxy answer 407 again; on a direct route, or a tunnelled (https) one, it is removed with the rest. Other headers you set, and a 307/308 request body, still go to the new origin, as HttpClient sends them. The strip runs where HttpClient records each hop in the request context, before the client's own request interceptors run, so cookies from the client's cookie store for the new origin and headers its interceptors add still go to the new origin. HttpClient 5 adds a credential from the client's CredentialsProvider before that point, so on a cross-origin hop that Authorization is removed too: a client that relies on its CredentialsProvider to authenticate to a redirect target on another origin is not authenticated there. The guard is the per-request context the transport passes to execute; a client that replaces that context (for example by wrapping it as the parent of a context of its own) is not guarded.

Keep-alive connections that the server closed while idle fail on reuse. The JDK, Apache HttpClient 4.5, and Jetty transports detect that specific failure and replay the request once on a fresh connection. A failure counts as stale when it is an EOFException, ClosedChannelException, a connection-reset SocketException, or the JDK client's "received no bytes" message (TransportException.isStaleConnectionFailure). The replay is only attempted when TransportRequest.isSafeToReplay() is true: an idempotent method (GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, TRACE) and a body that is absent or repeatable. A POST is never replayed by this mechanism. This is separate from the @Remote(retries=...) policy retries described in Next-Generation REST Client, which retry on application-visible failures according to your configuration.
Choosing a REST Client HTTP Transport Adapters REST Security, server-side counterparts

A RestCallInterceptor observes or modifies a call at three points. All methods have no-op defaults, so implement only what you need. public interface RestCallInterceptor { default void onInit(RestRequest req) throws Exception {} default void onConnect(RestRequest req, RestResponse res) throws Exception {} default void onClose(RestRequest req, RestResponse res) throws Exception {} } Hook Runs Typical use onInit After the request is built, before it is sent. Add headers (signing, correlation ids). onConnect After the response status and headers arrive, before the body is read. Metrics, auth refresh checks. onClose In run()'s finally block, before the debug logger; res can be null if the call failed before a response. Cleanup, timing. RestCallInterceptor stamp = new RestCallInterceptor() { @Override public void onInit(RestRequest req) { req.header("X-Start", String.valueOf(System.nanoTime())); } }; RestClient client = RestClient.builder().interceptors(stamp).build();

Interceptors can be registered on the client builder, on a @Remote interface, on a @RemoteOp method, or on a single request with RestRequest.interceptors(...). They run in that order (builder, interface, method/request). The built-in request-id interceptor always runs first; it adds a UUIDv7 X-Request-Id header unless you disable it with sendRequestId(false) or set your own with requestId(...). See Declarative Remote-Proxy Features for the annotation forms, and Logging and Debugging for the debug pipeline.

The juneau-rest-mock module provides two ways to test code that uses the NG RestClient without a network: Class Use it to test org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.MockRestClient A @Rest resource, in-process. The request is dispatched straight to the resource's RestContext. org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.MockHttpTransport Client code (a RestClient or @Remote proxy) against canned responses that you define. See the guide: Test an endpoint with MockRestClient The classic mock client is documented in Mock REST Client Overview.

MockRestClient wraps a RestClient whose transport calls the resource directly. The argument is a @Rest bean instance or class. Request paths are relative to the resource's @Rest(path), so for a PetResource annotated @Rest(path="/pets"), mock.get("/1") reaches /pets/1. A path of /pets/1 would look for /pets/pets/1 and return a 404. try (MockRestClient mock = MockRestClient.create(PetResource.class); var resp = mock.get("/1").run()) { resp.assertThat().isOk().body().contains("Fido"); } The verb methods (get, post, put, patch, delete, head, request) return the same RestRequest as a real client, so assertions, interceptors and typed bodies all work. getClient() exposes the underlying RestClient, for example to create a @Remote proxy: PetApi api = mock.getClient().remote(PetApi.class);

MockRestClient mock = MockRestClient.builder(new PetResource()) .contextPath("/app") .defaultParser(Json5Parser.create().build()) .build(); Method Purpose contextPath(String) Simulates a servlet context path. The root URL becomes http://localhost + context path + servlet path. overridingBeanStore(BeanStore) Supplies beans to the resource. Disables the per-class RestContext cache so your beans are used. defaultParser(Parser) Parser for body().as(...). noTrace() Sends No-Trace: true on every request; see below. Without an overriding bean store, the RestContext is created once per resource class and reused across tests, so mock clients are cheap to create.

A test that asserts a 404, 405 or 415 normally makes the server log a stack trace for an outcome the test expects. Send No-Trace: true to keep the trace off the log record while the one-line access record (status, method, path) is still logged. Use noTrace() on the builder for every call from that client: try (MockRestClient mock = MockRestClient.builder(PetResource.class).noTrace().build(); var resp = mock.get("/1/missing").run()) { resp.assertStatus(404); } or on a single request, which leaves the other calls from the same client unchanged: try (var resp = mock.get("/1/missing").noTrace().run()) { resp.assertStatus(404); } No-Trace is opt-in only: ignoreErrors() and the other builder options do not turn it on. See Logging / Debugging for what the server does with the header. Redirect and URL-policy behavior matches the real client; see NG Client Security.
documents.s: Keeping expected-error traces out of the log

documents.t: MockHttpTransport is an HttpTransport with routes you define. Plug it into a real RestClient: var transport = MockHttpTransport.builder() .on("GET", "/pets/1", req -> TransportResponse.builder() .statusCode(200) .header("Content-Type", "application/json") .body(new ByteArrayInputStream("{\"name\":\"Fido\"}".getBytes(UTF_8))) .build()) .on("POST", "/pets", req -> TransportResponse.builder().statusCode(201).build()) .recordRequests() .build(); var client = RestClient.builder().transport(transport).rootUrl("http://mock").build(); try (var resp = client.get("/pets/1").run()) { resp.assertOk(); } assertEquals(1, transport.getRecordedRequests().size()); on(method, path, handler) matches the HTTP method and the exact path. A null method or path matches anything. fallback(handler) handles unmatched requests. Without one, unmatched requests get a 404 with the body No mock route matched: METHOD path. recordRequests() keeps every TransportRequest; read them with getRecordedRequests() and reset with clearRecordedRequests(). A handler can throw TransportException to simulate a network failure. MockHttpTransport.of(status, body) is a one-liner that always returns the same response. The transport reports supportsUrlPolicy() == true and follows redirects with the same re-validation loop as the production transports, so @Remote tests exercise the SSRF guard too.

MockPathResolver resolves an incoming URL into the artifacts an HttpServletRequest would report: getTarget(), getContextPath(), getServletPath(), getRemainder(), getURI(), and getError(). Its constructor takes (target, contextPath, servletPath, pathToResolve, pathVars); {name} tokens in the context and servlet paths are filled from pathVars, and a null target defaults to http://localhost. It is used by the classic org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.classic.MockRestClient. The NG MockRestClient does not use it; it derives its root URL from contextPath and the resource's servlet path. You only need MockPathResolver directly when writing your own classic-style mock harness. The classic MockRestClient supplies its own connection manager, which the classic SSRF guard cannot pin, so its getRemote(...) proxies need allowPrivateUrls(true) on the builder (see NG Client Security).
Test an endpoint with MockRestClient: a guided walkthrough. Next-Generation REST Client juneau-rest-mock Mock REST Client Overview (classic)

The next-generation engine adds a family of declarative capabilities to the REST proxy annotations (@Remote, @RemoteOp, and the verb annotations @RemoteGet / @RemotePost / @RemotePut / @RemoteDelete / @RemotePatch). This page covers those capabilities; the client itself is described in the Next-Generation REST Client overview. Mostly next-gen engine only Most features on this page are honored only by the next-generation proxy engine obtained via RestClient.remote(MyProxy.class) → RemoteClient. The classic engine obtained via RestClient.getRemote(...) ignores those annotation members; where an attribute is visible on a shared annotation, its Javadoc states that the classic engine currently ignores it. The one exception is dynamic URLs and base overrides (@Url / baseUrl()), which the classic engine also honors, with the same SSRF guardrail. // Next-gen proxy — honors everything on this page. MyProxy proxy = client.remote(MyProxy.class); // Classic proxy — also honors @Url / baseUrl() (see below); ignores the other next-gen-only // members on this page. MyProxy classic = client.getRemote(MyProxy.class, "https://api.example.com");

@Remote (interface) and @RemoteOp / the verb annotations (method) can declare always-applied constant headers, query parameters, and form-data fields that are emitted on every call — with no corresponding method parameter and no dummy null argument. Interface-level: @Remote(headers=…, queryData=…, formData=…). Method-level: @RemoteOp(headers=…, queryData=…, formData=…) (and the verb annotations). headers use the "Name: value" form; queryData / formData use the "name=value" form. All values resolve through VarResolver.DEFAULT (e.g. "${S:mySystemProperty}"). A method-level constant of the same name takes precedence over an interface-level constant. A caller-supplied parameter value of the same name still composes with the constant (the constant is not suppressed). This is distinct from parameter-level def defaults, which only fill a null argument. Constant path values are out of scope There is no constant path attribute at either level. Path segments remain driven by the path template's {var} tokens and @Path parameters. @Remote( path="/api", queryData="api_key=${S:petstore.apiKey}" // every call carries ?api_key=… ) public interface PetStore { @RemoteGet( path="/pets", headers="X-View: full", // every getPets() call sends this header queryData="view=full" // …and ?view=full ) Pet[] getPets(); } @Remote(headerList=…) is classic-only The @Remote(headerList=…) member (a supplier of an Apache-HttpClient HeaderList) remains classic-only. The next-gen engine does not consume it — use the transport-agnostic headers="Name: value" form instead.

The next-gen engine honors @Content(def=…) — both the parameter-level default (used when a body argument is null) and the param-less, method-level constant body (used when a method has no body parameter at all). This matches the classic engine's behavior and the documentation under Default Values. Provided values still win. @Remote(path="/petstore") public interface PetStore { // Parameter-level default — fills a null argument. @RemotePost("/pets") Pet addPet(@Content(def="{name:'Unknown',price:0}") CreatePet pet); // Param-less constant body — sent on every call. @RemotePost("/pets/ping") @Content(def="{}") void ping(); }

A specific request part (query / header / path / form-data) can be marshalled with a custom HttpPartSerializer via @HttpPartMarshalling(serializer=…), instead of the engine's default OpenApiSerializer. The annotation can sit on a parameter, on the method, or on the interface, with precedence parameter › method › interface; when absent, the existing default serializer is used unchanged. @Remote(path="/api") public interface MyApi { @RemoteGet("/search") String search( @Query("filter") @HttpPartMarshalling(serializer=MyFilterPartSerializer.class) // this part only Filter filter ); } Serializer side only Only the serializer (request) side is wired in the next-gen engine; the parser member is not consumed because the next-gen engine has no response-part parse path. This applies to HTTP parts only — request bodies are handled by per-method format selection and full serializers, not HttpPartSerializer.

@Remote and @RemoteOp / the verb annotations can declare cross-cutting call behavior declaratively, instead of configuring it only on the RestClient builder. See also the Interceptors page. Member Type Behavior interceptors() Class<?>[] Classes implementing the client RestCallInterceptor SPI (public no-arg constructor). timeout() String Per-call response/read timeout as a duration string (e.g. "30s", "1500ms"). retries() int Maximum automatic retry attempts (0 = disabled). retryNonIdempotent() boolean Opt POST/PATCH into auto-retry. throwOnError() boolean Throw a generic exception on an unmatched error response. @Remote(path="/api", interceptors=AuthInterceptor.class, timeout="30s") public interface MyApi { @RemoteGet(path="/flaky", retries=3, throwOnError=true) Data getData(); @RemotePost(path="/orders", retries=2, retryNonIdempotent=true) Order createOrder(@Content Order order); } Interceptors are applied as a union in the order builder → interface → method (the method-level interceptor runs closest to the call). Timeout / retries / throwOnError scalars follow method › interface › builder default precedence (throwOnError and retryNonIdempotent are the logical-OR of the method and interface values). The per-call timeout is the response/read timeout; the connect timeout remains a client-level setting. Timeouts and transports The declarative timeout() is passed to the transport as the per-request timeout. Of the built-in transports, only JavaHttpTransport applies it; see the transport feature matrix. Safe retries are deliberately conservative (hard gates, all must pass): Trigger — a connection failure, or a retryable HTTP status (429 or any 5xx), with a short exponential backoff between attempts. Idempotent verbs only — GET/PUT/DELETE/HEAD auto-retry; POST/PATCH retry only when retryNonIdempotent=true. Repeatable bodies only — a request whose body is not repeatable (e.g. a streaming InputStream / Reader body) is never resent. A serialized-POJO body is repeatable. Buffered return modes only — retries are disabled for RESPONSE, raw InputStream / Reader returns, streaming cursors, and Future / CompletableFuture returns. throwOnError composes after the typed-exception mapping from the method's throws clause: a declared exception type whose status matches the response is still thrown in preference; only when no declared type matches and the status is >=400 does the generic exception fire.
documents.s: Call Policy: Interceptors, Timeouts, Retries, throwOnError

documents.t: Honored by both engines Unlike the other declarative features on this page, @Url and baseUrl() are honored by both the next-gen engine (RestClient.remote(...)) and the classic engine (RestClient.getRemote(...)). The classic engine resolves the same precedence order and enforces the same SSRF guardrail described below. Two complementary ways to point a call at a runtime- or annotation-chosen endpoint: @Url parameter (org.apache.juneau.http.Url) — the Retrofit @Url pattern. The argument's value becomes the effective URL for that single call. A value containing a scheme (://) is absolute — it replaces the whole endpoint and bypasses the client root URL; a value with no scheme is relative — it resolves against the client root URL only (not against the interface @Remote(path)). {var} tokens are still filled by @Path parameters. At most one @Url per method; a null/blank value is rejected. baseUrl() attribute on @Remote / @RemoteOp / the verb annotations — substitutes only the authority+root of the URL while preserving the interface base path, the method path, and {var} templating. Resolves through VarResolver.DEFAULT. Precedence (most-specific first): @Url parameter › method baseUrl › interface baseUrl → client rootUrl. @Remote(path="/api", baseUrl="${S:myservice.baseUrl}") public interface MyApi { // Caller chooses the endpoint at runtime. @RemoteGet String fetch(@Url String url); // Overrides the host for this one method only. @RemoteGet(path="/health", baseUrl="http://health-host:8080") String health(); } SSRF guardrail Only http / https schemes are permitted on a URL/base override — other schemes (file:, gopher:, jar:, …) are rejected with a clear error, allowPrivateUrls or not. Beyond the scheme check, every absolute effective URL (an absolute @Url value, a baseUrl() override, or a default-path URL that already carries a scheme) is checked against a deny-private policy by default: loopback (127.0.0.1, ::1), RFC1918/unique-local private ranges, link-local (including the 169.254.169.254 / 169.254.170.2 cloud-metadata addresses), localhost, and *.metadata.google.internal are all rejected. This is enforced at connect time against the actually-resolved address (pin-on-connect) — not just lexically against the hostname string — so a DNS name that resolves to a blocked address is rejected even if the hostname itself looks public, and a rebinding attack (blocked address swapped in after the initial check) cannot bypass it. Every hop of a redirect chain on a guarded call is re-validated the same way before it is followed; scheme-less relative @Url values (resolved against the client root) are not re-checked. Opt out for an intentional local-dev or intranet target via allowPrivateUrls(true) on the client builder, @Remote(allowPrivateUrls=true) on the interface, or the RestClient.allowPrivateUrls system property — any one of the three is sufficient (there is no per-method override), and http/ https is still required either way.

Beyond manually building a multipart body, the next-gen engine supports a Retrofit-style declarative multipart/form-data surface: @Multipart (org.apache.juneau.http.remote.Multipart) — a method-level marker. The multipart/form-data Content-Type (with a generated boundary) is applied automatically. @Part (org.apache.juneau.http.Part) — a parameter annotation with name() / value() (synonym), fileName(), and contentType() members. @Remote(path="/api") public interface UploadService { @RemotePost("/upload") @Multipart String upload( @Part("title") String title, @Part(name="attachment", fileName="report.pdf", contentType="application/pdf") byte[] data ); } Accepted part-source types (mapped automatically from the argument type): Argument type Part behavior String / CharSequence / scalars Text field byte[] Binary, sent verbatim (repeatable) File Streamed; fileName defaults to the file's name InputStream Streamed (one-shot; makes the body non-repeatable) Reader Streamed as UTF-8 (one-shot) HttpBody Used directly any other object (bean) Serialized with the client's default serializer A null @Part argument contributes no part. File / stream / reader / bean parts stream (they reuse the streaming bodies described under Streaming Bodies). Body-mode exclusivity is validated at proxy-build time (IllegalArgumentException): a method is either multipart (@Multipart + one or more @Part) or single-body (@Content), never both; @Multipart with no @Part, or @Part without @Multipart, is also rejected. Escape hatch (Option B) For advanced cases you can still hand-assemble a MultipartBody and pass it as a single @Content body without @Multipart — that path is unchanged.

@Remote (interface default) and @RemoteOp / the verb annotations (method) expose contentType() and accept() media-type attributes that drive marshaller selection — not merely header values. This lets a single method switch its actual wire format without changing the client default for every other call (e.g. one legacy XML endpoint on an otherwise-JSON API, or a binary format on a few endpoints). See also Content-Type Negotiation. contentType selects the matching registered request serializer from the client's serializer set (so the body bytes are actually written in that format) and sets a single, clean Content-Type header — replacing the serializer's default content type with no duplicate header. accept sets the Accept header and acts as a fallback parser only. The response Content-Type stays authoritative for parser selection; the accept media type is used only when the response is unlabeled or its Content-Type matches no registered parser. No-match media type falls back to the default marshaller but still sends the overridden label (supporting vendor types such as application/vnd.example.v2+json). Precedence: method › interface › client default. A dedicated contentType/accept attribute beats a constant Content-Type/Accept header (the constant is dropped, no duplicate), but a genuinely caller-supplied @Header("Content-Type"/"Accept") parameter still wins. @Remote(path="/api") // interface defaults to the client's JSON marshaller public interface MyApi { @RemoteGet("/items") Item[] getItems(); // JSON request/response // This one legacy endpoint speaks XML in both directions. @RemotePost(path="/legacy", contentType="application/xml", accept="application/xml") Result postLegacy(@Content Payload payload); }

The next-gen engine streams large bodies in both directions instead of buffering them in memory, matching the classic engine's efficiency. See also Streaming Cursors. Streaming POJO request bodies — a POJO @Content body is serialized straight to the wire (chunked, Content-Length: -1) rather than pre-serialized to a String/byte[]. This body is repeatable, so it is safe to auto-retry. Streaming Reader request bodies — a Reader @Content body streams as UTF-8 rather than being drained to a String first. (Non-repeatable — never auto-retried.) Reader and InputStream return types — a method may declare a Reader or InputStream return type and receive a lazy stream over the live response. The caller owns the stream; the underlying connection is released when the caller closes it. Always close the returned stream (try-with-resources). @Remote(path="/api") public interface MyApi { // Streams the POJO body straight to the socket. @RemotePost("/bulk") void bulkUpload(@Content List<Record> records); // Caller owns the returned stream — close it to release the connection. @RemoteGet("/export") InputStream export(); } MyApi api = client.remote(MyApi.class); try (InputStream in = api.export()) { in.transferTo(System.out); }

A request is built fluently from a RestClient verb method and executed with run(). Each verb (get, post, put, patch, delete, head, and request(method, url)) returns a RestRequest. RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .serializer(Json5Serializer.create().build()) .parser(Json5Parser.create().build()) .build(); try (var resp = client.post("/users/{id}/notes") .pathData("id", 42) .queryData("notify", true) .header("X-Trace", "abc") .body(new Note("hello")) .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)) .run()) { resp.assertOk(); }

Method Purpose header(name, value) / headers(...) Request headers. queryData(name, value) Query-string parameters. formData(name, value) application/x-www-form-urlencoded form fields. pathData(name, value) Substitutes {name} in the URL path. timeout(Duration) Per-request timeout. requestId(String) Overrides the generated X-Request-Id. Defaults set on the builder (header, headers, queryData) apply to every request made by that client.

Method Behavior body(HttpBody) Sent as-is. body(Object) Runs the body converter chain first (HttpBody, InputStream, byte[], File, plus any you registered); if none matches, the object is serialized with the client's default serializer. With no default serializer configured, an IllegalStateException is thrown. bodyString(String) Sent as text/plain. streamBodyEntity(RecordStreamBody) Streams a record sequence without buffering it. See Streaming Cursors.

run() sends the request and returns a RestResponse. Transport-level failures (DNS, connect, TLS, I/O) throw TransportException. HTTP error statuses do not throw unless you ask for it with assertOk(), assertStatus(int), or throwOnError on a remote proxy; those throw RestCallException, which carries getStatusCode(). openEventStream() runs the request and returns the response as a server-sent event stream.

interceptors(...) adds interceptors for this request only. remoteUrlPolicy(boolean enforced, boolean allowPrivateUrls) controls the SSRF guard for a single request. Ordinary client.get(url) calls are not policy-covered by default; @Remote and @Url calls are. See NG Security.

Builder method Purpose transport(HttpTransport) Explicit transport; otherwise auto-discovered. rootUrl(String) Prefix for relative request URLs. header(s), queryData Defaults for every request. serializer(s), parser(s) Marshalling. defaultSerializer / defaultParser choose the one used when several are registered. bodyConverter(s) Body converters. interceptors(...) Interceptors. allowPrivateUrls(boolean) Opt out of the private-address deny-list for policy-covered calls. sendRequestId(boolean) Toggles the automatic X-Request-Id header (on by default). debugFormatter, debugLoggerName See Logging and Debugging. client.remote(MyApi.class) creates a remote proxy that uses this same client.

run() returns a RestResponse. It is Closeable and holds the connection until closed, so always use try-with-resources. try (var resp = client.get("/users/42").run()) { int status = resp.getStatusCode(); String type = resp.header("Content-Type").orElse("unknown"); User user = resp.body().as(User.class); }

getStatusCode(), getReasonPhrase(), and getRequestId() (the X-Request-Id that was sent). assertOk() and assertStatus(int) throw RestCallException (with getStatusCode()) when the status does not match.

getHeaders() and getFirstHeader(name) return the raw values. header(name) returns a typed ResponseHeader: Accessor Returns isPresent(), getName() Presence and name. getValue(), orElse(String), asOptional() Raw string value. getValues(), asCsvList() Repeated or comma-separated values. asInteger(), asLong(), asBoolean() Numeric and boolean parsing. asZonedDateTime() HTTP-date parsing. asUri(), asEntityTag(), asEntityTags(), asStringRanges() Structured header types. See also Typed Response Header Accessors.

body() returns a ResponseBody. The body can be consumed once. Method Result asString() Decoded text. asBytes() / readAllBytes() Entire body as a byte array. asStream() The raw InputStream; you must close it. as(Class<T>) Parses into a POJO using the parser selected by the response Content-Type. Throws a 415 UnsupportedMediaType if no registered parser matches. See Content-Type Negotiation. as(Parser, Class<T>) Parses with an explicit parser. asCursor(...) Lazy record iteration. See Streaming Cursors. asEventStream() Server-sent events. getBodyAsString() and getBodyStream() on the response are shortcuts for the common cases.
assertThat() returns a ResponseAssertion for test-style checks; see NG Assertions.

Juneau gives you fine-grained control over what gets emitted on the wire and what happens when a null arrives during parsing. The two surfaces are co-designed so the round-trip behavior is predictable across every format (JSON, JSON5, XML, HTML, YAML, MsgPack, …). This page documents: The serializer inclusion knobs that suppress empty / default values. The parser Nulls policy that decides what to do when an incoming null reaches a bean property. The shared Optional contract that both sides honor. A short Jackson @JsonInclude / @JsonSetter(nulls=…) mapping table.

All inclusion knobs live on Serializer.Builder and apply uniformly across every format. They are evaluated in a fixed precedence order — the first one that decides "omit" wins: Order Knob Default What it omits 1 keepNullProperties() off null (and Optional.empty()) properties are omitted unless this is enabled. 2 trimStrings() off Trims whitespace from string values (does not omit; normalizes). 3 trimEmptyCollections() off Omits properties whose value is an empty Collection/array. 4 trimEmptyMaps() off Omits properties whose value is an empty Map. 5 nonDefault() off Omits properties whose value equals the type's default. Note: null is governed by keepNullProperties, not by nonDefault. The two knobs compose — see below.

The nonDefault() knob suppresses any property whose value is equal to its default. "Default" means: For primitives and boxed wrappers — the Java type default (0, 0L, 0.0, false, '\u0000', null). For bean properties — the value the property holds on a freshly-constructed instance of the owning bean via its no-arg constructor. The reference instance is built once and cached on the bean's ClassMeta. If a bean's no-arg constructor cannot be invoked (private, throws, etc.), nonDefault is silently skipped for that bean and properties are emitted normally. The knob never aborts a serialization. Equality is by value, not by reference. Numeric comparisons use a BigDecimal.compareTo-style check so 1 ≡ 1.0, 0.0 ≡ -0.0, 0 ≡ 0L, and so on. For everything else, Objects.equals decides. public class Person { public String name = "Anonymous"; public int age = 0; public boolean active; } var s = JsonSerializer.create().nonDefault().build(); var p = new Person(); s.write(p); // → {} p.name = "Alice"; s.write(p); // → {"name":"Alice"} p.age = 21; s.write(p); // → {"name":"Alice","age":21}

Because nonDefault does not govern null, the two knobs compose cleanly: public class Bean { public Integer boxed; // default = null public String s; // default = null public int i; // default = 0 public double d; // default = 0.0 } var s = JsonSerializer.create().nonDefault().keepNullProperties().build(); s.write(new Bean()); // → {"boxed":null,"s":null} The primitive defaults i:0 / d:0.0 are omitted by nonDefault; the explicit null properties are kept by keepNullProperties.
The same setting is available on @SerializerConfig: @SerializerConfig(nonDefault = "true") @Rest(serializers = JsonSerializer.class) public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet {}

When a JSON null (or its equivalent in any format) reaches a bean property during parsing, you can choose what value the setter actually receives via the Nulls enum: Mode Behavior LEAVE Pass the null straight through to the setter (default — matches historical Juneau behavior). EMPTY Substitute the type's "empty" value: "" for strings, an empty mutable collection / map for collection-typed properties, Optional.empty() / OptionalInt.empty() / … for Optional properties. DEFAULT Substitute the value the property holds on a freshly-constructed reference instance of the owning bean (same cached instance used by serializer nonDefault). SKIP Do not invoke the setter at all — any pre-existing field initializer or earlier assignment is preserved. The policy can be set at three levels (per-property wins, then session, then context): public class Bean { @MarshalledProp(nulls = Nulls.EMPTY) public String s; @MarshalledProp(nulls = Nulls.SKIP) public String t = "initial"; public String u; } var p = JsonParser.create().nulls(Nulls.LEAVE).build(); var b = p.read("{\"s\":null,\"t\":null,\"u\":null}", Bean.class); // b.s == "" (per-prop EMPTY wins) // b.t == "initial" (per-prop SKIP preserves initializer) // b.u == null (no per-prop override; falls through to context LEAVE)
The context-level default is also configurable on @ParserConfig: @ParserConfig(nulls = "EMPTY") @Rest(parsers = JsonParser.class) public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet {}

Optional<T>, OptionalInt, OptionalLong, and OptionalDouble participate in both the inclusion and the null-coercion contracts as first-class types: Wire form Java value Notes absent property Optional.empty() parser fills in via ClassMeta.getOptionalDefault() null literal Optional.empty() the null is never stored bare inside the Optional value v Optional.of(v) parser unwraps and re-wraps automatically On serialization, Optional.empty() (and OptionalInt.empty() / OptionalLong.empty() / OptionalDouble.empty()) is treated identically to null: omitted unless keepNullProperties() is set, in which case it is emitted as null. A present Optional is emitted as its unwrapped value. On per-property null-coercion of an Optional property: LEAVE — the setter receives null (the Optional reference itself is null). This is the historical behavior; most callers prefer EMPTY. EMPTY / DEFAULT — the setter receives Optional.empty() (or the bean's reference-instance value for DEFAULT). Never a bare null wrapped inside the Optional. SKIP — the setter is not invoked; the field's initializer value (or earlier assignment) survives.

For migrators coming from Jackson, the rough equivalents are: Jackson Juneau @JsonInclude(NON_NULL) (default on most setups) default behavior (keepNullProperties is off) @JsonInclude(NON_EMPTY) trimEmptyCollections() + trimEmptyMaps() (+ trimStrings() for whitespace-only) @JsonInclude(NON_DEFAULT) nonDefault() @JsonSetter(nulls = Nulls.AS_EMPTY) @MarshalledProp(nulls = Nulls.EMPTY) @JsonSetter(nulls = Nulls.SKIP) @MarshalledProp(nulls = Nulls.SKIP) @JsonSetter(nulls = Nulls.SET) (Jackson default) Nulls.LEAVE (Juneau default) DeserializationFeature.READ_UNKNOWN_ENUM_VALUES_AS_NULL + setter coercion Nulls.DEFAULT on the offending property The Juneau knobs are intentionally at the model level (Serializer.Builder / Parser.Builder / @MarshalledProp), so the behavior is identical across every format — there is no format-specific opt-in.
