The @ParentProperty annotation is used to identify a setter method or field for adding a parent reference to a child object. This annotation is used by parsers to automatically establish parent-child relationships when parsing nested objects. When a child object is created within a parent object (e.g., in a list or as a property), the parser automatically sets the parent reference on the child.

Must be an instance method or field (not static) For methods: Must accept exactly one parameter (the parent object type) For fields: Can be any type (typically the parent object type) The method or field does not need to be public (will be made accessible automatically)
Can be applied to: Bean setter methods or fields @Rest-annotated classes and @RestOp-annotated methods when using the on() parameter

public class AddressBook { public List<Person> people; } public class Person { @ParentProperty public AddressBook addressBook; // Automatically set to containing AddressBook public String name; public char sex; }

public class AddressBook { public List<Person> people; } public class Person { private AddressBook parent; @ParentProperty protected void setParent(AddressBook parent) { this.parent = parent; } public String name; public char sex; }

During parsing when a child object is created within a parent object The parser automatically calls the setter or sets the field with a reference to the parent object This allows child objects to navigate back to their parent if needed Useful for bidirectional relationships where child objects need access to their parent context

In the example above, each Person is not a direct property of AddressBook — it's an element of the List<Person> people field. When resolving a @ParentProperty member, the parser skips over any intervening List, Set, array, and Map containers, regardless of nesting depth, and injects the nearest enclosing bean instead. So Person.addressBook is set to the AddressBook, not to the List that directly contains it. A bean that has no enclosing bean — for example, one parsed at the document root, or one that's an element of a top-level collection passed directly to the parser — has nothing to inject, so its @ParentProperty member is simply left null.
documents.s: Enclosing Bean Through Collections and Maps

documents.t: When a @ParentProperty back-reference is also a normally-visible bean property (e.g. a public field or getter, as in the field example above), it forms a parent/child cycle. Unlike Jackson's @JsonBackReference, Juneau does not auto-omit the @ParentProperty member on the write (serialize) side — the annotation is a parse-time convenience only. This is intentional. The serialization behavior of such a cyclic graph therefore depends on the serializer's recursion settings (see Non-Tree Models and Recursion Detection): Default configuration (detectRecursions=false, ignoreRecursions=false): the traversal is silently truncated at maxDepth (default 100), producing finite but semantically-incomplete output. No exception is thrown — maxDepth is a size guard, not a cycle detector. detectRecursions(): fail-fast on the cycle with a SerializeException ("Recursion occurred, stack=..."). ignoreRecursions(): omit the repeated node so the output round-trips cleanly — parsing re-injects the parent via @ParentProperty. Using the AddressBook/Person classes from the field example above, ignoreRecursions() round-trips cleanly end to end: AddressBook book = new AddressBook(); book.people = new ArrayList<>(); Person person = new Person(); person.name = "John Smith"; person.sex = 'M'; book.people.add(person); // Clone an existing serializer and enable ignoring of recursions. WriterSerializer serializer = Json5Serializer .DEFAULT_READABLE .copy() .ignoreRecursions() .build(); // Serialize to JSON. The Person.addressBook back-reference is omitted to break the cycle. String json = serializer.write(book); // Parse it back. The parser re-injects the enclosing AddressBook into each Person. AddressBook parsedBook = JsonParser.DEFAULT.read(json, AddressBook.class); Person parsedPerson = parsedBook.people.get(0); assert parsedPerson.addressBook == parsedBook; // Restored, even though person is nested inside a List

The org.apache.juneau.marshall.parquet package provides Juneau serializer and parser implementations for the Apache Parquet columnar storage format. Parquet support is included in juneau-marshall. Maven <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> The ParquetSerializer and ParquetParser classes integrate with the standard Juneau Serializer / Parser APIs and support the @Parquet and @ParquetConfig annotations for format-specific configuration. The Parquet marshaller (in org.apache.juneau.marshall.marshaller) provides the usual static shortcuts. Media type: application/vnd.apache.parquet (both produced and consumed). Parquet is collection-oriented: each bean is one row and each bean property is one column. The serializer accepts a Collection, an array, or a single bean (wrapped in a one-element list) at the root. The parser always returns a List<T>, never a bare T.

public class Person { public String name; public int age; } List<Person> people = List.of(/* ... */); // Serialize rows to a Parquet file image. byte[] bytes = Parquet.of(people); // Parse back. The result is always a List. List<Person> parsed = Parquet.to(bytes, List.class, Person.class); // Or with the serializer/parser instances directly. byte[] bytes2 = ParquetSerializer.DEFAULT.write(people); List<Person> parsed2 = ParquetParser.DEFAULT.read(bytes2, List.class, Person.class);

Configured through ParquetSerializer.create() (see ParquetSerializer.Builder). Builder method Default Description compressionCodec(CompressionCodec) UNCOMPRESSED Page compression on write. UNCOMPRESSED or GZIP. null resets to UNCOMPRESSED. rowGroupSize(int) 128 MiB Target row group size in bytes. Values below 1024 are raised to 1024. pageSize(int) 1 MiB Target page size in bytes. Values below 1024 are raised to 1024. addBeanTypesParquet(boolean) false Adds a _type column for polymorphic beans. writeDatesAsTimestamp(boolean) true Dates/temporals as INT64 TIMESTAMP_MILLIS; when false, as ISO 8601 strings. emitLogicalTypes(boolean) false Also writes the Parquet LogicalType union into the footer for columns whose physical encoding is ambiguous (currently UUID only). Legacy convertedType is still written. nativeLogicalTypes(boolean) false Writes binary-native DECIMAL, DATE, TIME and TIMESTAMP (micros) columns. See below. cycleHandling(ParquetCycleHandling) NULL How to handle cyclic references: THROW fails with SerializeException; NULL writes cycles as null. maxRecursionDepth(int) 5 Expansion depth for self-referential bean types (e.g. Node.next). Deeper structure is truncated to null. Values below 1 are clamped to 1. nullKeyString(String) "<NULL>" Placeholder written for null Map keys (Parquet MAP keys are UTF-8). The defaults for emitLogicalTypes, maxRecursionDepth and nullKeyString can be overridden with the ParquetSerializer.emitLogicalTypes, ParquetSerializer.maxRecursionDepth and ParquetSerializer.nullKeyString environment settings. ParquetSerializer s = ParquetSerializer.create() .compressionCodec(CompressionCodec.GZIP) .rowGroupSize(32 * 1024 * 1024) .pageSize(256 * 1024) .writeDatesAsTimestamp(true) .cycleHandling(ParquetCycleHandling.THROW) .build();

Builder method Default Description nullKeyString(String) "<NULL>" A Map key equal to this string is restored as null. Must match the serializer's value for round trips. The parser detects the compression codec per page from the file itself. Supported codecs are UNCOMPRESSED, GZIP and SNAPPY (decode-only); any other codec is reported as a parse error.

Given a bean property type, the serializer writes the following Parquet column (default settings): Java type Parquet physical / converted type boolean / Boolean BOOLEAN byte, short, int and wrappers INT32 (INT_8, INT_16, INT_32) long / Long INT64 (INT_64) Number (abstract) INT64, re-typed to the concrete INT32 / INT64 / DOUBLE type when a runtime sample is available float / double and wrappers FLOAT / DOUBLE String and other CharSequence types BYTE_ARRAY (UTF8) Enums BYTE_ARRAY (ENUM) byte[] BYTE_ARRAY Date / Calendar / java.time temporals INT64 (TIMESTAMP_MILLIS), or ISO 8601 UTF8 string when writeDatesAsTimestamp(false) Duration UTF8 string UUID FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY(16) Nested bean Optional group with one child per property Collection / array LIST Map MAP (keys stored as strings; non-string keys use toString() / enum name) Optional<X> Optional group with a value child of type X Anything else (including BigDecimal / BigInteger by default) UTF8 string Properties marked with @ParentProperty are excluded from the schema.

The parser reads spec-compliant Parquet produced by external writers (parquet-mr / Spark / Hive), not just files Juneau itself emits: Multi-page column chunks — a column chunk split across several data pages is read end-to-end. Multi-row-group files — every row group is read and concatenated, not just the first. Dictionary-encoded pages — a DICTIONARY_PAGE followed by PLAIN_DICTIONARY / RLE_DICTIONARY data pages (the parquet-mr default) is decoded back through its dictionary. Snappy compression — Snappy-compressed pages are decompressed by a built-in, dependency-free Snappy block decoder. Snappy is decode-only; on write use UNCOMPRESSED or GZIP. LZ4, Zstd, Brotli, and LZO remain unsupported and are reported as a hard error rather than silent garbage. The pageSize and rowGroupSize builder settings control how Juneau splits its own output into pages and row groups (useful for streaming large datasets and for interop testing).

The parser always decodes the binary-native logical types external tools emit: INT96 — legacy 12-byte timestamps (Impala / Hive / older Spark) decode to instants. DECIMAL (INT32 / INT64 backed) decodes to BigDecimal with the schema's scale. DATE, TIME (micros), TIMESTAMP (micros) decode to the matching java.time types, preserving sub-millisecond precision. On write, these native encodings are opt-in via ParquetSerializer.create().nativeLogicalTypes(true). By default Juneau keeps its portable string / TIMESTAMP_MILLIS normalization, so default output is unchanged. Enable nativeLogicalTypes() for sub-millisecond-precise, parquet-mr-interoperable output. With nativeLogicalTypes(true), the following mappings replace the defaults in the type-mapping table: Java type Native column BigDecimal / BigInteger DECIMAL on INT64, scale 9, precision 18 (extra fractional digits are rounded HALF_UP) LocalDate DATE (INT32) LocalTime / OffsetTime TIME(MICROS) (INT64) Other date / calendar / temporal types TIMESTAMP(MICROS) (INT64) // Emit binary-native DECIMAL / DATE / TIME / TIMESTAMP-micros columns. ParquetSerializer s = ParquetSerializer.create().nativeLogicalTypes(true).build();

The @ParquetConfig annotation (on classes or methods) applies serializer settings declaratively. Attribute values are strings and support variables. Attribute Description compressionCodec GZIP (case-insensitive); any other non-empty value selects UNCOMPRESSED. rowGroupSize Row group size in bytes. pageSize Page size in bytes. addBeanTypes true to add the _type column. @ParquetConfig(compressionCodec="GZIP", pageSize="262144") public class MyResource { ... }

Both classes also implement the low-level record cursor interfaces (RecordWritable / RecordReadable and the array variants), exposed on the marshaller as Parquet.ofRecords(...), Parquet.toRecords(...), Parquet.ofArrayRecords(...) and Parquet.toArrayRecords(...). Parquet cursors are buffered, not O(1) streaming (isRecordStreaming() returns false). See Also Marshallers for general serializer/parser configuration patterns. The Javadoc for ParquetSerializer, ParquetParser, and ParquetConfig for the full list of available options.

The Juneau parsers are not limited to parsing back into the original bean classes. If the bean classes are not available on the parsing side, the parser can also be used to parse into a generic model consisting of Maps, Collections, and primitive objects. You can parse into any Map type (e.g. HashMap, TreeMap) but using JsonMap is recommended since it has many convenience methods for converting values to various types. The same is true when parsing collections. You can use any Collection<T> (e.g. HashSet<String>, LinkedList<MyBean>) or array (e.g. Object[], String[], String[][]) but using JsonList is recommended. When the map or list type is not specified, or is the abstract Map<String,Object>, Collection<Object>, or List<Object> types, the runtime type the parser creates depends on the parser's flavor: JsonParser produces JsonMap / JsonList. Json5Parser produces Json5Map / Json5List. All other parsers (XmlParser, YamlParser, UonParser, HoconParser, MsgPackParser, CborParser, BsonParser, HtmlParser, JsonlParser, HjsonParser, MarkdownParser, CsvParser, RDF parsers, etc.) currently produce the neutral MarshalledMap / MarshalledList. All three pairs extend the same neutral MarshalledMap / MarshalledList base, so the generic-model API shown in the examples below (getString(...), getInt(...), getMap(...), getList(...), cast(MyBean.class), etc.) works identically whether the parser handed you a JsonMap, a Json5Map, or a MarshalledMap. Typing variables as MarshalledMap / MarshalledList (or as Map<String,Object> / List<Object>) keeps callers parser-flavor-agnostic. If you specifically want the strict-JSON JsonMap / JsonList runtime type — for example because downstream code casts to it — pass it as the explicit target class (e.g. parser.read(text, JsonMap.class)); the parser will then produce exactly that type instead of the flavor default. For example, given the following JSON: { id: 1, name: 'John Smith', uri: 'http://sample/addressBook/person/1', addressBookUri: 'http://sample/addressBook', birthDate: '1946-08-12T00:00:00Z', addresses: [ { uri: 'http://sample/addressBook/address/1', personUri: 'http://sample/addressBook/person/1', id: 1, street: '100 Main Street', city: 'Anywhereville', state: 'NY', zip: 12345, isCurrent: true } ] } We can parse this into a generic JsonMap: // Parse JSON into a generic POJO model. JsonMap map = Json.to(json, JsonMap.class); // Convert it back to JSON. String json = Json5.of(map); What we end up with is the exact same output. Even the numbers and booleans are preserved because they are parsed into Number and Boolean objects when parsing into generic models. { id: 1, name: 'John Smith', uri: 'http://sample/addressBook/person/1', addressBookUri: 'http://sample/addressBook', birthDate: '1946-08-12T00:00:00Z', addresses: [ { uri: 'http://sample/addressBook/address/1', personUri: 'http://sample/addressBook/person/1', id: 1, street: '100 Main Street', city: 'Anywhereville', state: 'NY', zip: 12345, isCurrent: true } ] } Once parsed into a generic model, various convenience methods are provided on the JsonMap and JsonList classes to retrieve values: // Parse JSON into a generic POJO model. JsonMap map = Json.to(json, JsonMap.class); // Get some simple values. String name = map.getString("name"); int id = map.getInt("id"); // Get a value convertable from a String. URI uri = map.get("uri", URI.class); Calendar birthDate = map.get("birthDate", Calendar.class); // Get the addresses. JsonList addresses = map.getList("addresses"); // Get the first address and convert it to a bean. Address address = addresses.get(0, Address.class); As a general rule, parsing into beans is often more efficient than parsing into generic models. And working with beans is often less error prone than working with generic models.

Juneau comes with three basic marshaller types for serializing and parsing Header, Query, Form, and Path parts: HttpPartSerializerSimplePartSerializer - Serializes directly to strings.UonSerializer - Serializes to UON notation.OpenApiSerializer - Serializes using OpenAPI schema rules.HttpPartParserSimplePartParser - Parses directly from strings.UonParser - Parses from UON notation.OpenApiParser - Parses using OpenAPI schema rules. By default, the REST API uses the OpenAPI serializer and parser which allows for schema-based marshalling. You also have the option to use UON marshalling which is schema-less but allows for JSON-equivalent data structures (object/array/primitives/...) using URL-encoding notation. This can be done by overriding the part marshallers through the following APIs: RestpartSerializerpartParser The OpenAPI marshallers themselves also have the ability to support UON notation for individual parts via the schema itself: @Query(..., schema=@Schema(format="uon")) Map myMap

The @Path annotation can be applied to arguments of @RemoteOp-annotated methods to denote that they are path parameters on the request. @Pathname - Path variable name. Example @Remote(path="/myproxy") public interface MyProxy { // Explicit names specified for path parameters. // pojo will be converted to UON notation (unless plain-text parts enabled). @RemoteGet("/mymethod1/{foo}/{bar}") String myProxyMethod1(@Path("foo") String foo, @Path("bar") MyPojo pojo); // Multiple values pulled from a PartList object. // Same as @Path("*"). @RemoteGet("/mymethod2/{foo}/{bar}/{baz}") String myProxyMethod2(@Path PartList partList); // Multiple values pulled from a Map. // Same as @Path("*"). @RemoteGet("/mymethod3/{foo}/{bar}/{baz}") String myProxyMethod3(@Path Map map); // Multiple values pulled from a bean. // Same as @Path("*"). @RemoteGet("/mymethod4/{foo}/{bar}/{baz}") String myProxyMethod4(@Path MyBean myBean); } Path arguments can be any of the following types: Single-part arguments (i.e. those with name != "*"): Any serializable POJO - Converted to a string using the HttpPartSerializer registered with the RestClient (OpenApiSerializer by default). Multi-part arguments (i.e. those with name == "*" or empty): PartList - Serialized as individual path parameters. Map - Converted to key-value pairs. Values serialized using the registered HttpPartSerializer (OpenApiSerializer by default). Bean - Converted to key-value pairs. Values serialized using the registered HttpPartSerializer (OpenApiSerializer by default). See the link below for information about supported data types in OpenAPI serialization.

For capturing the path remainder (the part matched by /*), you can use the @PathRemainder annotation as a more intuitive alternative to @Path("/*"). Example @Remote(path="/myproxy") public interface MyProxy { // Using @PathRemainder (preferred) @RemoteGet("/files/{+remainder}") String getFile(@PathRemainder String remainder); // Equivalent using @Path("/*") @RemotePost("/upload/{+remainder}") void uploadFile(@Path("/*") String remainder, @Content File file); } See Also OpenAPI Serializers @PathRemainder

The @RestOp(path) annotation allows you to define URL path patterns to match against. These patterns can contain variables of the form {xxx} that can be passed in directly to the Java methods as extra parameters. In the following example, 3 separate GET request handlers are defined with different path patterns. Note how the variables are passed in as additional arguments on the method, and how those arguments are automatically converted to the specified class type... // Default method @RestGet(path="/*") public void doGetDefault() { ... } // Method with path pattern @RestGet(path="/xxx") public void doGetNoArgs(...) { ... } // Method with path pattern with arguments @RestGet(path="/xxx/{foo}/{bar}/{baz}/{bing}") public void doGetWithArgs( @Path("foo") String foo, @Path("bar") int bar, @Path("baz") MyEnum baz, @Path("bing") UUID qux ) { ... } By default, path patterns are matched using a best-match heuristic. When overlaps occur, URLs are matched from most-specific to most-general order: // Try first @RestGet("/foo/bar") public void method1() { ... } // Try second @RestGet("/foo/{bar}") public void method2(...) { ... } // Try third @RestGet("/foo/*") public void method3(...) { ... } // Try last @RestGet("/*") public void method4(...) { ... } Paths that end with /* will do a prefix match on the incoming URL. Any remainder after the match can be accessed through RequestPathParamList.getRemainder() or parameters with the @Path("/*") annotation. On the other hand, paths that don't end with /* (e.g. / or /foo) will require an exact URL match, and if any remainder exists, a 404 (not found) error will be thrown. The following example shows the distinction. @RestGet("/*") public void doGet(@Path("/*") String remainder) { // URL path pattern can have remainder accessible through req.getRemainder(). } @RestPut("/") public void doPut() { // URL path pattern must match exactly and will cause a 404 error if a remainder exists. }

The path can contain variables that get resolved to @Path parameters or access through the RestRequest.getPathParams() method. Example @Rest( path="/myResource/{foo}/{bar}" ) public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet { @RestPost("/{baz}") public void doX(@Path String foo, @Path int bar) { ... } } Variables can be used on either top-level or child resources and can be defined on multiple levels. Path variables resolved in parent resource paths are also available to the child resources. note All variables in the path must be specified or else the target will not resolve and a 404 will result.

The path remainder (the part matched by /*) can be captured using either @Path("/*") or the more intuitive @PathRemainder annotation. Example @Rest public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet { // Using @PathRemainder (preferred) @RestGet("/files/*") public File getFile(@PathRemainder String path) { return new File(path); } // Equivalent using @Path("/*") @RestPost("/upload/*") public void uploadFile(@Path("/*") String path, @Content File file) { ... } } The @PathRemainder annotation supports the same features as @Path, including: Default values via def() property Custom parsers and serializers Schema validation OpenAPI/Swagger documentation generation

The About page (/console/about) is the smallest page in the petstore console: three prose cards and no data. It is worth reading as the minimal shape of a console page, and because its third card links to live examples of the REST utility beans.

The three html cards, each wrapped in a jc-prose block: Card id Title Content overview About the petstore What the sample is, and that its data is seeded the same way on every start links Elsewhere Links to /petstore/api (the REST API and its Swagger page), /petstore-ui (the React app) and the petstore docs beans REST utility beans Links to three bean endpoints, shown against the Pet bean The bean endpoints live under /console/about/beans and each returns one utility bean: Endpoint Bean /console/about/beans/BeanDescription BeanDescription, the properties of the Pet class /console/about/beans/Hyperlink Hyperlink, a link back to /console/about /console/about/beans/SeeOtherRoot SeeOtherRoot, a redirect to the servlet root

<@page tab="about"> <@card id="overview" title="About the petstore">

The petstore is Apache Juneau's sample application and its console regression suite. ...

<@card id="links" title="Elsewhere"> ...

return PageSpec.create().tab("about") .html("overview", "About the petstore", """

The petstore is Apache Juneau's sample application and its console regression suite. ...

""") .html("links", "Elsewhere", "...") .html("beans", "REST utility beans", "..."); Source: AboutRest in juneau-petstore/juneau-petstore-core/src/main/java/org/apache/juneau/petstore/console/; AboutPageBuilders.about in .../console/pages/; about.ftlh under .../console/templates/. Tests: AboutRest_Test.

The Audit page, served at /console/ops/audit, is the smallest server-mode table in the petstore and a leaf of the navigation tree: one resource, one template, one query endpoint. It is a read-only view of the store's audit trail, with a search box on every column and a date range on the timestamp. Start here if you want the shortest path from a bean to a searchable table.

A leaf page. AuditRest has a page operation, a POST /query operation and a convenience GET /rows. It has no child resources and no write operations. Server mode over BeanQuery. query hands the DataTables request to DataTablesQuery.run against store().queryAudit(). A malformed search expression comes back as a 200 error envelope. Typed column search. Each column declares a searchType: timestamp for at and text for the rest. The at column takes a range as its search value, in the BeanQuery form $between(2026-09-30T00:00:00Z,2026-10-01T00:00:00Z), and the query layer parses the ISO-8601 instants. Newest first. The default order is at descending. Mutations made through the console (for example a pet saved, an order approved or a restock job) write an AuditEntry with the actor, entity, entity id, action and detail. Export. Copy and CSV buttons in the ribbon.

The whole page is audit.ftlh, a single card: <@card type="datatables" id="audit">{ dataMode: 'server', dataUrl: '/console/ops/audit/query', defaultOrder: [{ key: 'at', dir: 'desc' }], columns: [ { key: 'at', label: 'When', render: { id: 'timestamp' }, searchType: 'timestamp' }, { key: 'actor', label: 'Actor', searchType: 'text' }, { key: 'action', label: 'Action', searchType: 'text' } ], ribbon: [ { type: 'export', buttons: ['copy', 'csv'] }, { type: 'refresh', id: 'refresh' } ] }</@card> The excerpt trims three columns (entity, entityId and detail); the real card has six.

This is the shortest builder twin in the tour. OpsPageBuilders.audit is one expression of about ten lines, and ?builder renders it in place of the template. PageSpec.create().tab("ops/audit").toolkit("views") .table(TableSpec.create("audit").dataMode(DataMode.SERVER).dataUrl("/console/ops/audit/query") .operators(SearchOperatorSet.standard()) .defaultOrder("at", Sort.DESC) .columns( Column.create("at").label("When").render("timestamp").searchType(SearchType.TIMESTAMP), Column.create("actor").label("Actor").searchType(SearchType.TEXT)) .ribbon(RibbonItem.export("copy", "csv"), RibbonItem.refresh().id("refresh"))); Compare it with the template: the card body keys (dataMode, dataUrl, defaultOrder, columns, ribbon) each have a builder method of the same name. The builder also sets operators(SearchOperatorSet.standard()), which the template does not spell out.

Source: juneau-petstore/juneau-petstore-core, classes AuditRest (in the ops package), OpsPageBuilders (in the pages package), AuditEntry and PetStore (in the service package), and the template audit.ftlh. Tests: AuditRest_Test (the seeded trail is queryable, the timestamp $between range, a console write shows up, newest first), PetstorePages_ContractTest and PetstoreTwins_Test.

Twin pattern: see 19.17. Template and Builder Twins. Petstore: Jobs: the restock job writes audit entries. Petstore: Pending Changes: applying a change writes one too. Data Tables: the request and response envelopes, and DataTablesQuery. Rich Table Views: what a table card can do. Rich Table Views: Catalog: column types and search types.

Every petstore console page shares one chrome: the header with the brand and theme toggle, the navigation tree, the pending-changes badge and the footer. That chrome is defined once, in the shared base.ftlh template, and every page template wraps itself in it. This page walks the chrome, the navigation tree and the contract test that pins the pages. For the directives themselves, see Admin-Console Chrome.

Each page's template calls <@page>, which captures the page's cards and includes base.ftlh. The base template holds the <@console> directive, so the chrome is declared exactly once. Source: juneau-petstore-core/src/main/resources/org/apache/juneau/petstore/console/templates/base.ftlh. <@console brand="Juneau Petstore" title=(pageTitle!"") theme=(petstoreTheme!"open") schemeToggle=true> <@scripts phase="after-toolkit"><script src="${assetUrl('/console/petstore.js')}"></script></@scripts> <@navigation> <@node id="store" label="Store" href="/console/store"/> <@node id="pets" label="Pets" href="/console/pets"> <@node id="sold" label="Sold" href="/console/pets/sold"/> <@node id="changes" label="Pending changes" href="/console/pets/changes"/> </@node> ... </@navigation> <@badge id="pending" src="/console/pets/changes/pending" href="/console/pets/changes" ... placement="header"/> <@main/> <@footer text="Apache Juneau petstore sample"/> </@console> Three things to notice: The theme comes from the model (petstoreTheme), so the Themes page can switch it. A custom theme layers <@token> overrides inside a nameless <@theme> in the same template. petstore.js is the one petstore-specific script, loaded after the toolkit on every page. The <@badge> sits after </@navigation> and is unscoped on purpose; see Pending Changes.

The tree goes four levels deep, which is the deepest the shell draws: Level Nodes 1 Store, Pets, Orders, Users, Operations, Developer, About 2 Pets: Sold, Pending changes (plus a node for the open pet, see below). Operations: Jobs, Audit. Developer: Custom cards, Themes, Rendering flavors, Secure 3 The open pet's tabs (summary, photo, orders, history). The four rendering flavors (Html, Freemarker, Mustache, React) 4 An order under a pet's orders tab The pet nodes are not in the static tree: the pet detail page builds its own activeNav (for example pets/p1/summary) and passes it to <@page tab=activeNav>. See Pet Detail. Pages normally state their node with <@page tab="ops/jobs">. A page that omits it, such as the Sold Pets page, falls back to the longest node href that prefixes the current URL, on path-segment boundaries. That is why /console/pets/sold highlights the Sold node without naming it. The fallback is described under the page contract in Admin-Console Chrome.

PetstorePages_ContractTest is the pattern to copy into your own console. It holds a list of Page records, each a path plus a set of assertions on the contract the server wrote into the document: the active nav path, the card order, each card's type, and selected keys of a card's catalog (for example that the Pets table is server-mode with a persistent selection). Adding a page to the console means adding one row. new Page("audit", "/console/ops/audit", p -> p.hasActiveNav("ops", "audit").hasCard("audit", "datatables")), Source: juneau-petstore-core/src/test/java/org/apache/juneau/petstore/console/PetstorePages_ContractTest.java. Because the assertions are on the JSON contract, not on rendered HTML, the test needs no browser. The browser tests (PetstoreNav_BrowserTest and friends) cover what only a browser can show, such as the current-page marker at each nav level.
PetstorePages_ContractTest, PetstoreConsoleShell_Test, PetstoreNav_BrowserTest.

Twin pattern: see 19.17. Template and Builder Twins. Porting these patterns to your own console: see 19.19. Porting to the Console. Admin-Console Chrome: the directives, themes and the page contract. Building a Console Page: the end-to-end tutorial. juneau-petstore: the tour landing page.

The Custom cards page (/console/dev/cards) shows how an adopter adds a card type of their own. It carries one card type that needs no Java at all (kpi), one whose body the server validates and reshapes (inventory-gauge), two ordinary chart cards fed by the same page, and two prose cards that exercise the card API from a button row. Read it next to Building a Console Page when you need a card the stock types do not cover.

A card type is a JavaScript handler registered under a type id. A Java class is optional, and is worth adding only when the server should validate or enrich the body before the page ships. Type Java Body What the handler draws kpi none label and dataUrl One number from /console/dev/cards/stats/available, with its label inventory-gauge InventoryGaugeCardType species, low, high A gauge for one species, read from /console/dev/cards/inventory?species= Both handlers live in the page script petstore-cards.js, served beside CustomCardsRest. The page loads it through init, and the handlers register by pushing onto window.JuneauConsoleCards. That queue works whether your script runs before or after the console shell: (window.JuneauConsoleCards = window.JuneauConsoleCards || []).push(['kpi', { render(card, el, ctx) { ... } }]); With no registered Java handler, a type falls back to the generic passthrough: the JSON5 body becomes the card fragment unchanged. That is all kpi is.
documents.s: Two ways to write a card type

documents.t: InventoryGaugeCardType implements CardTypeHandler. Its toFragment rejects a body with no species, an unknown species, a non-whole low or high, a negative low, or low at or above high. low defaults to 0 and high to 100. A good body is reshaped into a gauge object that adds the dataUrl for that species, which is what the browser handler draws. A bad body fails the page at render time, so a typo fails loudly and does not produce a broken gauge. The host registers the type once, on the console's FreeMarker mixin (PetstoreConsolePage.freemarker()): ConsoleFreemarkerMixin.create().basePath(TEMPLATES).chromeTemplate("base.ftlh") .adopterAssets(PetstoreConsolePage.class.getClassLoader(), "org/apache/juneau/petstore") .cardType(new InventoryGaugeCardType()).requirePacks("charts").build();

A new type id must match ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,31}$. These ids belong to the framework and cannot be registered: html, datatables, terminal-view, terminal, chart and job-log. A bad name, a reserved id and a duplicate each fail when the mixin is built. A JSON body that sets a base key (id, type, title, src, template, ref) fails the page at render time, because those are set as attributes. kpi and inventory-gauge are free ids.

<@page tab="dev/cards" init=["/console/dev/cards/petstore-cards.js"]> <@card id="available" type="kpi" title="Pets available">{label:'Pets available', dataUrl:'/console/dev/cards/stats/available'}</@card> <@card id="gauge" type="inventory-gauge" title="Dog inventory">{species:'DOG', low:20, high:120}</@card>

var gauge = CardSpec.of(InventoryGaugeCardType.TYPE, "gauge").title("Dog inventory") .body("species", "DOG").body("low", 20).body("high", 120); return PageSpec.create().tab("dev/cards").init("/console/dev/cards/petstore-cards.js") .card(CardSpec.of("kpi", "available").title("Pets available") .body("label", "Pets available").body("dataUrl", "/console/dev/cards/stats/available")) .card(gauge) ... PageSpec runs the gauge body through the same registered handler, so both pages carry the same validated fragment. ?builder renders the twin.

The toolbar card has buttons that call JuneauConsole.refreshCard and JuneauConsole.cardApi, and the script listens for the juneau:card-mounted event to record mount order. The script also reads and writes its own ?state=species(CAT) directive for the gauge. The Store page loads the same script for its kpi alone; see Petstore: Store. The page's charts load their assets through the charts pack named in requirePacks; see Card Asset Dependencies for how packs and init scripts are ordered. Source: CustomCardsRest, InventoryGaugeCardType and petstore-cards.js in juneau-petstore/juneau-petstore-core/src/main/java/org/apache/juneau/petstore/console/dev/; DevPageBuilders.cards in .../console/pages/; cards.ftlh under .../console/templates/. Tests: CustomCardsRest_Test, InventoryGaugeCardType_Test, PetstoreCustomCard_BrowserTest.

Under the Developer tab the petstore keeps a set of pages that exercise parts of the console framework rather than the pet store itself. Three of them are about charts and data: Charts, Data sources and Dashboard. All three are builder-only pages. Each is written as a PageSpec in Java and has no FreeMarker twin and no navigation node of its own; all three use the Developer tab, and DevRest lists them as children. The other Developer pages have their own tour pages: Custom Cards, Themes, Rendering Flavors and Secure.

ChartsRest (/console/dev/charts) draws a line chart, trend ("Orders this week"), fed by /console/dev/charts/daily. The chart has Markers and Thresholds decorators and publishes a click on a point to the topic app.day-picked. Below it, a client-mode days table loads the same rows, and its ribbon has a "Highlight Monday" item that publishes a highlight command to the topic cmd:trend, which the chart executes. See Chart Cards for the chart card and its decorators.

DataRest (/console/dev/data) shows a chart that reads a large series from a data source instead of a single JSON response. /console/dev/data/orders serves hourly CSV for a requested window, limited to 31 days. The page declares a DataSourceDef for it: CSV, chunked by day and cached in IndexedDB, so panning back over a day already fetched does not hit the server again. The script data.js publishes the visible range as a topic, and the chart ordersChart follows it.

DashboardRest (/console/dev/dashboard) is a configurable dashboard over the same pieces. A ?variant= query parameter takes ok, slow, truncated, error or right, which choose how /console/dev/dashboard/series/{variant} answers, so you can see how the page behaves when the data source is slow, cut short or failing. A ?v= parameter sets the persist version. The rail (left, or right for variant=right) has range, search, choice, card and custom sections, and dashboard.js supplies the custom one. The grid has two columns holding three chart panels, and the range, search, reasons and zoom state persists and can be shared as a link.

There is no template to compare against, so the builder method is the whole definition and ?builder changes nothing. Because they have no twin, the three paths are not in PetstorePages_ContractTest.PAGES, the list the twin and vocabulary tests walk. They are in a separate list, PetstorePages_ContractTest.BUILDER_ONLY, and each page's own test class (ChartsRest_Test, DataRest_Test, DashboardRest_Test) asserts its contract. A trimmed example from DevPageBuilders.charts: PageSpec.create().tab("dev").toolkit("views") .card(ChartDef.line("trend").title("Orders this week").src(rows).x("day") .series("placed", "Placed").series("delivered", "Delivered") .decorate(Thresholds.at(6).label("Target").tone("ok")) .on("click", "app.day-picked") .toCardSpec()) .table(TableSpec.create("days").dataMode(DataMode.CLIENT).dataUrl(rows), "Days"); Source: ChartsRest, DataRest, DashboardRest and DevRest in juneau-petstore/juneau-petstore-core/src/main/java/org/apache/juneau/petstore/console/dev/; DevPageBuilders in .../console/pages/; data.js and dashboard.js under the matching console/dev/ resources directory. Tests: ChartsRest_Test, DataRest_Test, DashboardRest_Test, PetstoreChart_BrowserTest, PetstoreData_BrowserTest, PetstoreDashboard_BrowserTest.

A console page that is misconfigured must fail where the mistake is, with a message that names it. It must not render a half-working page, drop a card, or fall back to a default without telling anyone. The petstore calls this FailLoud. This page explains the rule, shows how the tests exercise it, and lists every case the petstore pins.

When a template or a PageSpec is wrong, the render stops with HTTP 500 and the body names the directive, the id and what to do instead. For example, a badge declared twice, a nav path that does not exist, a body key that is reserved, or a bytesUrl that points off-site. The message is the contract. The tests assert the text of the message, not just the status, so a rewording that loses the useful part fails the build. Two things are worth knowing before you read the table: Most cases pin a message, not a code. The reason codes the console used to print (the E-B series for the server-side directives) were replaced by plain messages, so the table lists a code only where an assertion still pins one. A code that appears only in a comment does not count. Some failures are client-side. The server renders the page successfully and the browser script reports the problem. Those are covered separately, below the main table.

PetstoreFailLoud_Test renders small fixture templates through three hosts. Each is a minimal REST servlet with the console FreeMarker mixin: FixtureHost renders failloud/<name>.ftlh inside the production base.ftlh chrome, so a fixture is a page in the real petstore frame. It also has two builder routes (/s/badge-duplicate and /s/facts-duplicate) for mistakes that start in a PageSpec, and it registers the petstore's custom card type so the custom-card cases run for real. DevHost is the same chrome with dev mode on. Dev mode validates each page contract against its schema before writing it, so a bad contract is rejected on the server instead of in the browser. ChromeHost uses a small test chrome that includes one fixture. The directives <@navigation>, <@badge> and <@facts> are legal only in a chrome, never in a page, so cases about them need a chrome to put them in. The fixtures live under src/test/resources/org/apache/juneau/petstore/console/failloud/. Each test renders one, asserts a 500 and checks that the body contains the expected message. A manifest, docs-catalogue.txt, lists every FailLoud test with its fixture and any pinned code. A second test, PetstoreDocsCatalogue_Test, fails the build when a FailLoud test is added without a manifest row, when a catalogued test or fixture disappears, or (when pointed at a docs checkout) when this page stops mentioning a test id or code. That is why every test id below appears in the table.

Some mistakes can only be detected in the browser, by the console scripts. The server returns 200 and the script raises a coded error. These codes are pinned by the petstore's browser tests: Code Test What is asserted E-JS-12 PetstoreCustomCard_BrowserTest Registering a card type that is already registered (kpi) reports E-JS-12 card type 'kpi' is already registered E-JS-62 PetstoreDashboard_BrowserTest A data source or chart fetch that fails reports E-JS-62 with the source or card id E-B4 ThemesRest_Test Asserted absent: a nameless <@theme> must not raise a theme error, so the page renders

The Jobs page, served at /console/ops/jobs, is the petstore's reference for asynchronous work. A restock adds new pets in the background: the browser submits it once, the server answers 202 with a job reference, and the page follows the job's progress until it settles. The page also hosts a terminal demo, a "groom pet" job whose output is streamed into a terminal card. If a write in your app takes longer than a request, copy this page.

The mixin. JobsRest implements AsyncJobsMixin and TerminalMixin. AsyncJobsMixin serves the stream and cancel operations under /juneau-jobs; the resource supplies the AsyncJobRegistry through asyncJobRegistry(). Submit once. POST /console/ops/jobs/restock builds an IdempotencyKey from the body's idempotencyKey and calls AsyncJobRegistry.tryCreate(key). A resubmit with the same key returns the same job, so the resource keeps no key map of its own. Self-targeted keys. The ribbon "Restock" dialog has no row to bind a key to, so restockForm() returns a ModalDef carrying IdempotencyKey.mintSelfTargeted("restock") and the selfTargeted flag. The two must travel together; see Rich Table Views: Actions for the pairing rule. Completion. The job finishes with a success ActionResult (ActionResult.success(null), which ActionResult.ok() is the readability alias for) and a message such as "Restocked 3 pets". A job-log card. The "Restock inventory" card is a job-log card: a small submit form (counts per species, plus two timing knobs) that posts the same restock in its flat form, shows the job's progress lines and offers Cancel. slowMs waits before touching the store, so a cancel changes nothing; holdMs holds after the pets are added, so a late cancel reports that the change was made. A per-instance hard timeout. The registry's hard timeout is 30 seconds. A host overrides it by declaring a JobsRest.HardTimeout bean, which is per resource instance, so one test host's short timeout does not leak into another. A job that exceeds it settles with unknown and app:hard-timeout-exceeded. A concurrency limit. At most two restocks run at once (system property petstore.jobs.limit; the registry's own cap is 8). A replay of an existing key never counts against the limit. When the limit is hit the server answers 429 with the refusal app:job-limit, and the message names the running count. A hold knob for tests. System property petstore.jobs.speciesHoldMs (read on every request, at most 10000) sets how long a species row's restock holds after its effect, so a test can land a cancel in that window. A terminal card. The groom job (GroomRuns) streams its output through TerminalMixin, shown twice: a card over the in-memory output and a second over the same run's file-backed transcript. Row jobs. The "species" table has one row per species with its available count. Expanding a row opens a job-log region that restocks that species only: the panel fetches a key bound to the row from POST /console/ops/jobs/species/{id}/key, and POST /console/ops/jobs/species/{id}/restock verifies it with RowJobSubmit and JobKeyLedger. The species comes from the verified targetId; the panel's hidden species field is sent but ignored, so editing it changes nothing. When the job ends, the panel's "Available" value is updated from the result's row. While the open panel's job runs, the table's poll waits and its pill shows Paused. A replay of the same key returns the same job, and a key issued for one species is refused for another with 409. A job button. Each groom run's detail panel has a "Groom again" button, painted by the petstore's petstore-regroom populator with helpers.jobButton. It posts to POST /console/ops/jobs/groom-runs/{id}/regroom with a key from that run's key endpoint, and the endpoint answers synchronously with an ActionResult, so no stream opens. The pet comes from the server's run record, not from the request. The dialog's /groom endpoint keeps its self-targeted key; the row endpoint accepts ledger keys only.

The template is jobs.ftlh. The job-log card is configured entirely by its submit block. <@card type="job-log" id="restock" title="Restock inventory">{ submit: { endpoint: '/console/ops/jobs/restock', submitLabel: 'Restock', fields: [ { name: 'DOG', label: 'Dogs (0-50)', type: 'number', default: 1 }, { name: 'slowMs', label: 'Wait before restocking (ms, 0-10000)', type: 'number', default: 0 }, { name: 'holdMs', label: 'Hold after restocking (ms, 0-10000)', type: 'number', default: 1000 } ] }, urlParam: 'job' }</@card> The species table declares its job-log region in the card body: <@card type="datatables" id="species">{ dataMode: 'client', dataUrl: '/console/ops/jobs/species', pollIntervalMs: 2000, columns: [ { key: 'species', label: 'Species' }, { key: 'available', label: 'Available' } ], detail: { endpoint: '/console/ops/jobs/species/{id}', region: { id: 'restock-species', populate: 'job-log', config: { submit: { endpoint: '/console/ops/jobs/species/{id}/restock', envelope: 'action', action: 'restock-species', keyUrl: '/console/ops/jobs/species/{id}/key', submitLabel: 'Restock', fields: [ { name: 'count', label: 'How many (1-50)', type: 'number', default: 1, required: true }, { name: 'species', type: 'hidden', source: 'row.species' } ] }, detail: { renderer: 'fieldGrid', fields: [ { data: 'available', label: 'Available' } ] }, output: { target: { field: 'available' }, from: 'row.available' } } } } }</@card>

OpsPageBuilders.jobs takes the two TerminalDef values and builds the same cards. The species table's region is built with RowDetail.region(JobLogRegion.create("restock-species")...toRegion()), and the groom runs' detail with a RegionDef that allows the petstore-regroom populator. .card(CardSpec.of("job-log", "restock").title("Restock inventory") .body("submit", Map.of("endpoint", "/console/ops/jobs/restock", "submitLabel", "Restock", "fields", List.of( Map.of("name", "DOG", "label", "Dogs (0-50)", "type", "number", "default", 1), Map.of("name", "holdMs", "label", "Hold after restocking (ms, 0-10000)", "type", "number", "default", 1000)))) .body("urlParam", "job")) .card(CardSpec.of("terminal", "groom-output").title("Groom run").body("terminal", groomOutput.toMap()))

Source: juneau-petstore/juneau-petstore-core, classes JobsRest and GroomRuns (in the ops package), OpsPageBuilders (in the pages package), and the template jobs.ftlh. The Orders page, served at /console/orders, is the petstore's workflow table. Orders move through PLACED, APPROVED and DELIVERED; each row offers only the transitions that are legal for its status, and creating an order is a two-step dialog. It shows what row actions, dialogs, confirmations and a ribbon dialog button look like when they are wired to real state changes.

Server mode with BeanQuery, like the Pets page, plus two URL-state directives, day and window. The query endpoint accepts ?day=yyyy-mm-dd, or ?start= and ?end= for a date window (both ends inclusive, either may be omitted), and applies them before the column filters. A missing or malformed value is ignored. The Store page's trend chart links here with ?state=day({day}). Row actions with visibleWhen. Approve appears only on PLACED rows and Deliver only on APPROVED rows. Each posts to /console/orders/{id}/approve or /console/orders/{id}/deliver; an illegal transition is a 409. A dialog from an action. Cancel opens a form (GET /console/orders/{id}/cancel-form, with a reason and a notify checkbox) and submits a DELETE to /console/orders/{id}. The reason is recorded in the audit trail. A typed confirmation. Delete uses confirmRenderer: 'typed', so the user must type to confirm. The row action's tone is danger. A two-step wizard. The ribbon's "+ New order" button opens a ModalDef: step one picks an available pet and an optional ship date; its child action "Review order" stacks a second dialog, carrying the first step's inputs as drafts, and Confirm posts to /console/orders. Only pets that are for sale are offered.

The template is orders.ftlh. The excerpt keeps the URL state and two of the row actions. <@card type="datatables" id="orders" title="Orders"> { rowType: 'Order', dataMode: 'server', dataUrl: '/console/orders/query', urlState: { day: {}, window: {} }, rowActions: [ { id: 'approve', label: 'Approve', endpoint: '/console/orders/{id}/approve', method: 'POST', onSuccess: 'redraw', visibleWhen: [ { field: 'status', op: 'eq', value: 'PLACED' } ] }, { id: 'cancel', label: 'Cancel', form: '/console/orders/{id}/cancel-form', present: 'dialog', endpoint: '/console/orders/{id}', method: 'DELETE', onSuccess: 'redraw' } ] } </@card> The ribbon also carries a "+ New order" dialog item whose form is /console/orders/new-form; see the wizard above.

OrdersPageBuilders.orders builds the same table. Request /console/orders?builder to render it. TableSpec.create("orders").rowType("Order").dataMode(DataMode.SERVER).dataUrl("/console/orders/query") .urlState("day", "window") .rowActions( RowAction.create("approve").label("Approve").endpoint("/console/orders/{id}/approve").method(Method.POST) .onSuccess(OnSuccess.REDRAW).visibleWhen(VisibilityRule.when("status").eq("PLACED")), RowAction.create("delete").label("Delete").endpoint("/console/orders/{id}").method(Method.DELETE) .confirm("Delete order '{id}'?").tone(Tone.DANGER).confirmRenderer("typed").onSuccess(OnSuccess.REDRAW)); The wizard is not part of the template or the builder: both pages point the ribbon button at the same two form endpoints on OrdersRest, which return ModalDef beans (newForm and reviewForm).

Source: juneau-petstore/juneau-petstore-core, classes OrdersRest (in the orders package) and OrdersPageBuilders (in the pages package), and the template orders.ftlh. Tests: OrdersRest_Test (query, day and window, transitions and their 409s, cancel, the wizard steps and order placement), PetstorePages_ContractTest and PetstoreTwins_Test.

The Pending changes page (/console/pets/changes) lists edits that were staged from the pet detail page but not yet written to the pet. A staged change can be applied, retried if the write failed, or discarded. The same page is the data source for the count badge in the console header, which is why this page is also where the <@badge> directive is documented: the framework has no page of its own for it yet.

PendingChanges (obtained from PetStore.pendingChanges()) holds the staged edits, and a PendingChange has one of three states: State Meaning Allowed next step PENDING Staged. The pet is unchanged. Apply, or discard APPLIED Written to the pet, and the write is audited. None FAILED The apply failed, for example because the pet is gone. message says why. Retry Staging records the field, the old value, the new value, the author and a one-line summary in the form <pet name>: <field> '<old>' -> '<new>'. The staging call is POST /console/pets/{id}/stage, served by PetsRest. The photo is not stageable Every editable Pet field stages into a pending change except the photo. The photo is a binary payload with no meaningful diff and nothing sensible to discard, so staging it is rejected with a 400, Field 'photo' cannot be staged; use one of: name, price, species, status, tags. The pet detail Photo tab edits it directly. See Petstore: Pet Detail.

Route Does Errors POST /console/pets/changes/{id}/apply Writes one PENDING change to its pet 404 unknown change, 409 not pending POST /console/pets/changes/{id}/retry Re-applies one FAILED change 404 unknown change, 409 not failed POST /console/pets/changes/discard Discards many PENDING changes in one call 400 missing ids or idempotencyKey Apply and retry answer with an action result: a success toast (Applied '<summary>') when the write landed, or a failure carrying the changed row and its message when the pet is gone and the change is now FAILED. Discard takes {ids, idempotencyKey} and returns a BulkResult. PendingChanges.discard produces a DiscardOutcome with three lists: succeeded, notFound (including ids that do not parse) and failed (ids that exist but are not pending, with the reason). A discarded change is removed from the list and an audit entry is recorded. Replaying the same idempotencyKey returns the stored answer instead of discarding again. The demo toggle ?fail=discard answers 503 so you can watch the table handle a transport failure. Only PENDING rows are selectable (selectableWhen), so a failed row offers only its Retry row action. The ribbon's "Pending only" option is on by default, so turn it off to see FAILED rows.

selection: { rowIdField: 'id', selectAll: true, scope: 'persistent', labelField: 'summary', selectableWhen: [ { field: 'state', op: 'eq', value: 'PENDING', reason: 'Only pending changes can be discarded or applied.' } ] }, bulk: { actions: [ { id: 'discard', label: 'Discard', endpoint: '/console/pets/changes/discard', method: 'POST', bulkMode: 'aggregate', confirmTitle: 'Discard changes', confirm: 'Discard the selected changes?', tone: 'danger', confirmRenderer: 'typed' }, { id: 'apply', label: 'Apply', endpoint: '/console/pets/changes/{id}/apply', method: 'POST', bulkMode: 'perRow' } ] }

var selection = SelectionDef.create("id").selectAll(true).scope(SelectionDef.Scope.PERSISTENT).labelField("summary") .selectableWhen(RowActionEnabledRule.of("state", Op.EQ, "PENDING", "Only pending changes can be discarded or applied.")); ... .bulk(BulkMutateDef.create(WritePermit.forCapability("pets.changes"), selection).actions( RowAction.create("discard").label("Discard").endpoint("/console/pets/changes/discard").method(Method.POST) .bulkMode(BulkMode.AGGREGATE).confirmTitle("Discard changes").confirm("Discard the selected changes?") .tone(Tone.DANGER).confirmRenderer("typed"), RowAction.create("apply").label("Apply").endpoint("/console/pets/changes/{id}/apply").method(Method.POST) .bulkMode(BulkMode.PER_ROW))) For selection, bulk modes and WritePermit, see Row Actions and Bulk Mutation.

base.ftlh declares one badge inside <@console>, after the navigation: <@badge id="pending" src="/console/pets/changes/pending" href="/console/pets/changes" refreshMs=60000 placement="header" refreshesAllowMissing="pets"/> It is unscoped on purpose. A nav scope would hide the badge on every page except the pets page. BadgeDef is the Java form (PageSpec.badge(BadgeDef)); the FreeMarker directive builds the same definition. The full directive and BadgeDef reference is in Admin-Console Chrome (BadgeDef javadoc).

Attribute BadgeDef Meaning id create(id) Required. Unique among all badges on the page. src src Required. Same-origin JSON endpoint to poll. refreshMs refreshMs Poll interval. Default 60000; below 5000 is an error, not clamped. href href Same-origin path the badge navigates to when clicked. placement placement header (default) or toolbar. toolbar needs table. table table Card id the badge belongs to. Needed for toolbar and for scopeBy="view". tone tone info, warning (default) or danger. labelOne, labelOther, labelMine label Templates using {total} and {mine}. Defaults: {total} change pending, {total} changes pending, ({mine} yours). tooltipMax tooltipMax Items listed in the hover popover, 0 to 50. Default 10. refreshes refreshes Card ids to reload when a previously seen item leaves the response. Each must exist on the page. refreshesAllowMissing refreshesAllowMissing Like refreshes, but the card may live on another page. The petstore uses "pets". scopeParam, scopeBy scope Query parameter to send and how to key it: nav or view. Give both or neither. stateFilterColumn stateFilter Column the destination page filters on, added to the click URL as ?state=. Needs a scope. The directive's body is optional JSON5 with visibleWhen (a rule list), scopeValues (nav or view id to value list) and params (extra query parameters). Any other key is rejected.

ChangesRest.pending (GET /console/pets/changes/pending) returns {total, mine, items}. Each item is {id, label, href, mine, kind}: mine is true when the caller authored the change, and href points at the pet summary. The badge script reads total, mine, and each item's id, label, href and mine. A badge is presentation only; the endpoint still decides who may read it. The script behaves as follows: It sends Accept: application/json on every poll. Juneau negotiates content, so a plain GET with no Accept header would be answered with HTML. It hides itself at zero, and pulses when the count rises. A response without a numeric total is an error. A 401 or 403 removes the badge and stops polling. Any other failure shows a stale ! and retries with exponential backoff, starting at the interval and capping at five minutes. A fetch aborted by an AbortError, or by the page unloading (pagehide; pageshow re-arms it for a restored page), is silent. It logs nothing and does not mark the badge stale. A failure on a live page still logs. When an item id seen on one poll is missing from the next, it reloads the refreshes cards. That is how applying or discarding a change refreshes the pets table; a card that is not mounted is skipped. An unsafe src, href or item href (an absolute URL, //, .., a backslash or a control character) is refused. The pet detail page is where a console page gets a nested identity. One pet has four tabs (Summary, Photo, Orders and History) and each tab is its own URL under /console/pets/{id}/{tab}. The Orders tab goes one level deeper: /console/pets/{id}/orders/{orderId} selects one of the pet's orders. The navigation tree grows to match, so this is also the petstore's example of depth-4 navigation with nodes that are added per request.

Per-request navigation nodes. The page appends nodes under the pets node: p<petId> with children summary, photo, orders and history, and o<orderId> under orders when an order is selected. Node ids must start with a letter, so the numeric ids are prefixed. The active tab is pets/p<id>/<tab>, or pets/p<id>/orders/o<orderId> at depth 4. Summary is a one-row client-mode table over GET /console/pets/{id}/row. The name and price cells use the edit renderer: a pencil that commits an inline edit through a hidden row action. Photo is an html card holding an <object> that points at the API's own photo endpoint, with fallback text when no photo is uploaded. Admins also get an "Upload photo" card; for other viewers the template leaves it out on the server. Orders is a table of this pet's orders with a row detail, plus an html card for the selected order. History is the pet's audit entries, newest first. Not found. An unknown pet renders pet-not-found.ftlh inside the chrome with a 404 status, rather than an error page. An unknown tab, or an order that does not exist or belongs to another pet, is a plain 404. The bare URL /console/pets/{id} answers with a 303 to the Summary tab.

The pencil does not write to the pet. It posts to POST /console/pets/{id}/stage, which records a pending change that someone reviews on the Pending changes page before it is applied. The body is either {field, value} or the inline-edit envelope {fields: {<field>: value}} with exactly one field. Staging accepts name, price, species, status and tags; the Summary table's pencil cells edit name and price. The sold-pet case is handled by the actions' visibleWhen rule: a sold pet shows no edit actions. Photo-field exception Every editable Pet field stages into pending changes except the photo. The photo is not stageable: it is a binary payload, so there is no meaningful before-and-after to show in a review, and no sensible way to discard half of an upload. Staging it is refused with HTTP 400 and the message Field 'photo' cannot be staged; use one of: name, price, species, status, tags. The Photo tab edits the photo directly, through the API's own PUT /petstore/pets/{id}/photo.

The template is pet.ftlh, one template for all four tabs, switched on a tab model attribute. The nodes and the Summary card, trimmed: <@page tab=activeNav toolkit="views"> <@node under="pets" id="p${pet.id?c}" label=pet.name href="/console/pets/${pet.id?c}/summary"> <@node id="summary" label="Summary" href="/console/pets/${pet.id?c}/summary"/> <@node id="orders" label="Orders" href="/console/pets/${pet.id?c}/orders"> <#if order??><@node id="o${order.id?c}" label="Order ${order.id?c}" href="/console/pets/${pet.id?c}/orders/${order.id?c}"/></#if> </@node> </@node> <#if tab == "summary"> <@card type="datatables" id="pet" title=pet.name> { rowType: 'Pet', dataMode: 'client', dataUrl: '/console/pets/${pet.id?c}/row', columns: [ { key: 'name', label: 'Name', render: { id: 'edit', meta: { action: 'rename', column: 'name', input: 'text' } } } ], rowActions: [ { id: 'rename', label: 'Rename', endpoint: '/console/pets/{id}/stage', method: 'POST', present: 'inline' } ] } </@card>

PetsPageBuilders.pet takes the pet, the tab, the active nav path, the selected order and the viewer's roles, and returns a PageSpec. The roles go into the page facts, so a client-side rule could read them too. PageSpec.create().tab(activeNav).toolkit("views").title(pet.getName()) .facts(Map.of("viewer", Map.of("roles", roles))) .navUnder("pets", n -> { var node = n.add("p" + id, pet.getName(), href + "/summary"); node.add("summary", "Summary", href + "/summary"); var orders = node.add("orders", "Orders", href + "/orders"); if (order != null) orders.add("o" + order.getId(), "Order " + order.getId(), href + "/orders/" + order.getId()); }); Request any tab with ?builder to render it through this path.

The Pets page, served at /console/pets, is the petstore's main table. It lists every pet with server-side searching, sorting and paging, a ribbon of filters, row actions, multi-row selection with a bulk "Mark sold" action, and export. It is the best single page to read if you want to see what a server-mode Rich Table View looks like in a real app.

Server mode. The table posts a DataTables request to /console/pets/query. PetsRest.query runs it against the pet collection with DataTablesQuery.run, so searching and ordering are BeanQuery expressions evaluated on the server. A malformed search expression comes back as a 200 response carrying an error envelope, so the table can show the message instead of failing. Ribbon. Two option groups ("Pet status" with Available and Pending, and "Species" with Mammals and Others) that set column filters, an "+ Add pet" dialog button, copy and CSV export (Excel and PDF when available) and a refresh button. Row actions. Edit (a dialog form, merges the row on success) and Delete (with a confirmation). Selection and bulk. Rows can be selected across pages, except sold pets, which carry the reason "Already sold." The bulk action "Mark sold" calls POST /console/pets/{id}/sell once per selected row. URL state. The ids URL-state directive carries a comma-separated list of pet ids in the page URL. The query endpoint accepts it as ?ids= and narrows the rows to those ids before the column filters apply. Polling. The table refreshes every 30 seconds and pauses while a cell is being edited.

The template is pets.ftlh. The excerpt keeps the data mode, the URL state and the bulk definition. <@card type="datatables" id="pets" title="Pets"> { rowType: 'Pet', dataMode: 'server', dataUrl: '/console/pets/query', urlState: { ids: {} }, pollIntervalMs: 30000, selection: { rowIdField: 'id', selectAll: true, scope: 'persistent', labelField: 'name', selectableWhen: [ { field: 'status', op: 'ne', value: 'SOLD', reason: 'Already sold.' } ] }, bulk: { actions: [ { id: 'sell', label: 'Mark sold', endpoint: '/console/pets/{id}/sell', method: 'POST', bulkMode: 'perRow', confirmTitle: 'Mark pets sold', onSuccess: 'redraw' } ] } } </@card>

PetsPageBuilders.pets builds the same table. Selection and bulk are two separate opt-ins; the bulk definition is created from a WritePermit and the selection it applies to. var selection = SelectionDef.create("id").selectAll(true).scope(SelectionDef.Scope.PERSISTENT).labelField("name") .selectableWhen(RowActionEnabledRule.of("status", Op.NE, "SOLD", "Already sold.")); TableSpec.create("pets").rowType("Pet").dataMode(DataMode.SERVER).dataUrl("/console/pets/query") .urlState("ids").pollIntervalMs(30_000) .selection(selection) .bulk(BulkMutateDef.create(WritePermit.forCapability("pets.sell"), selection).actions( RowAction.create("sell").label("Mark sold").endpoint("/console/pets/{id}/sell") .method(Method.POST).bulkMode(BulkMode.PER_ROW).onSuccess(OnSuccess.REDRAW)));

Request /console/pets?mixed and the page is "half FTL": pets-mixed.ftlh lays out the page and places the table with <@card ref="pets"/>, while the table itself comes from PetsPageBuilders.petsMixed(). Both paths share one petsTable() method, so they cannot drift. Use this shape when you want a hand-written layout around a builder-defined card. ?builder renders the all-builder page, and ?builder&mixed renders the mixed one through the builder path.

The Pets bulk action is in perRow mode: the browser submits N independent single-row requests to the same sell endpoint, each with its own result. The other mode, aggregate, sends one request listing every selected id and expects one BulkResult back, with a per-id outcome. The request body is a BulkRequest: the ids, plus an idempotencyKey so a retried submit never double-applies. The petstore uses the aggregate shape on the Pending changes page, not here; see Petstore: Pending Changes. Selection and bulk mutation are introduced in Rich Table Views: Actions.

The Rendering flavors section (/console/dev/flavors) shows the same list of ten pets drawn by four different view technologies, each inside the console chrome: the HTML5 bean builder, FreeMarker, Mustache and the standalone React app. It replaces the earlier standalone view resources with pages inside the console. Each flavor is a level-3 subtab under Developer, so a reader can flip between them and compare the output.

FlavorsRest (/console/dev/flavors) redirects / to the first flavor with a 303 to html. The enum Flavor holds each flavor's id, nav label, caption and the GitHub link to its source. The nav tree in base.ftlh lists them as the nodes html, freemarker, mustache and react under flavors. FlavorPets.rows returns the first ten pets by id with display-ready strings (the price has two decimals), so the engines differ only in markup.

Each server flavor is a child resource that serves two things: its console page at /, and a bare fragment at /fragment with no page chrome. The console page is one html card whose content comes from the fragment through src=. The fragment is a <table class="petstore-flavor" data-flavor="...">, so a test can tell the engines apart and compare their cells exactly. The FreeMarker fragment carries no <@page> for the same reason: it is loaded into a card, not served as a page. The React flavor has no fragment. Its page carries an iframe pointing at /petstore-ui, the same app that talks to the /petstore API on its own. /petstore-ui is PetstoreUiResource, which is not part of the console.

The Secure page (/console/dev/secure) pairs an open console page with a bearer-token protected API underneath it. Its "Try it" card calls the API from your browser with no token, with a demo token and with a wrong token, and prints the status and body, so you see the 401 and the success side by side. The page also marks the line between two different protections: the bearer guard on the API, and the CSRF boundary that guards writes to the console itself. This page covers both, adds the separate CSRF boundary on the /petstore API, and shows how the Jetty and Spring Boot runners install the boundaries.

The page is open. The API under /console/dev/secure/api is SecureApiRest, and every operation on it is gated by a fail-closed BearerTokenGuard with the realm petstore, backed by StubBearerTokenValidator: Request Result No Authorization header 401, with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="petstore" Authorization: Bearer petstore-user 200, principal alice Authorization: Bearer petstore-admin 200, principal admin Any other token 401 The API has GET /pets, GET /pets/{id} (404 for an unknown pet) and GET /whoami, which returns the caller's name through an @Auth Principal parameter. The guard is one @Bean returning a RestGuardList, so it covers every operation on the resource. The siblings stay open: the guard does not touch /petstore or the other console pages. From a shell: curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer petstore-user' http://localhost:10000/console/dev/secure/api/pets With a single mechanism, the op-level guard is the whole story. AuthFilterChain is for composing several mechanisms; it is fail-open by design, so a downstream guard still decides.

Everything under /console is also behind PetstoreConsoleBoundary, a servlet Filter over the framework's LoopbackBoundaryFilter. It pins the Host header on every console request, and on console writes it also requires a same-origin Origin, a JSON body and the per-process synchronizer token, which the page renderer stamps on <body data-juneau-csrf>. The checks are listed in Security Model. The boundary judges the method a request claims, not only its request line. A method query parameter, or an X-Method, X-HTTP-Method-Override, X-HTTP-Method or X-Method-Override header naming a non-safe method, makes the request a write. Behind a Docker port mapping or a reverse proxy, set the petstore.console.authority setting to the host and port the browser uses, or the pinned Host check answers 421. The /petstore-ui app and the Jetty admin resources are outside this boundary. The /petstore API has a boundary of its own, described next, and so do the admin resources.

Everything under /petstore is behind PetstoreApiBoundary, a servlet Filter over the framework's CsrfBoundary (through a RequestBoundaryFilter). This is separate from the bearer guard above, which covers only /console/dev/secure/api; the petstore API has no bearer guard. The framework's checks are described in CSRF protection: loopback vs general, and the console side in Security Model. Browser writes. A write from a browser must come from the page's own origin and carry the API's token in the X-Csrf-Token header. The token travels only in that header, so an HTML <form> POST to the API is refused, the application's own forms included. The console's Photo tab. It is the console's one write to the API. The console boundary hands the page an API token, the page stamps it on the upload form as data-petstore-csrf, and petstore.js sends it as X-Csrf-Token. This token is not the console's data-juneau-csrf token, and each boundary refuses the other's. The token is per process. A restart invalidates it, so reload any open page after restarting the server. Command-line and program clients need nothing special, provided the request is not a simple form-type request. A request with no Origin is admitted when it carries a JSON, XML or UON body, or uses PUT, DELETE or PATCH. A urlencoded, multipart or text/plain POST with no Origin is refused with SIMPLE_REQUEST_WITHOUT_ORIGIN: curl -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{...}' http://localhost:10000/petstore/pets curl -d a=b http://localhost:10000/petstore/pets The first is admitted; the second is answered with 403. Method overrides count. Requests are judged on their effective method, so GET /petstore/pets/1?method=DELETE is treated as a write. Past the filter, the router refuses it too: an override of a GET to a write is answered 405. Refusals name their reason in the X-Request-Boundary response header. The /petstore-ui app stays outside: it only reads. The Jetty runner's admin resources (/config, /logs and /shutdown) are provided by the microservice, not by the petstore, and are behind their own boundary, AdminBoundary (see Protecting the admin resources). It answers to the host names in its own setting, petstore.admin.allowedHosts; while that is unset, only localhost, 127.0.0.1 and [::1] are answered, and any other Host gets 421 HOST_NOT_ALLOWED, reads included. petstore.api.allowedHosts does not apply to it. The admin resources have no forms, so every browser write to them is refused; curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' http://localhost:10000/shutdown and other PUT, DELETE or JSON POST requests from the command line are admitted. The boundary does not authenticate, and the admin resources are not read-only (/shutdown is not), so do not expose them on an untrusted network.

Loopback development. Nothing needs to be set. A plain-HTTP host. Set petstore.api.allowedHosts (a system property, an environment setting or any registered setting source) to the comma-separated host names the browser uses, without ports. Any other Host is answered with 421 HOST_NOT_ALLOWED; this is the DNS-rebinding defence. It is read once at startup, and a malformed entry fails startup. The admin resources stay loopback-only unless you also set petstore.admin.allowedHosts the same way to the names you reach them under. Behind a TLS-terminating proxy. The boundary compares the browser's https origin with the http request the container sees, and it never reads forwarded headers, so writes are refused. Such a deployment needs the container's forwarded-header support together with the framework boundary's CONTAINER origin source. The petstore does not ship that switch. The console. petstore.console.authority is unchanged and still applies to the console boundary.

The console boundary covers PetstoreConsoleBoundary.URL_PATTERN, which is /console/*. The API boundary covers PetstoreApiBoundary.URL_PATTERN, which is /petstore/*. The two patterns never overlap. Each runner builds one PetstoreApiBoundary and gives that same instance to both registrations, because the console boundary mints the API token its pages carry and a token from any other instance is refused. Spring Boot. App declares a FilterRegistrationBean for the boundary on that pattern with the highest precedence, for the REQUEST, ASYNC, ERROR and FORWARD dispatcher types, so a dispatch that lands on a console path is checked too. Jetty. App.AppConfig in juneau-petstore-jetty contributes a ServletFilterRegistration bean for the boundary on that pattern with HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE, for the same four dispatcher types. The server component mounts it as a container filter before the servlets, ahead of authentication, so the Jetty runner and the Spring Boot runner behave alike. INCLUDE dispatches are deliberately not mapped. See Registering servlet filters for the registration API. The API registration. On Spring Boot, a second FilterRegistrationBean named apiBoundary covers PetstoreApiBoundary.URL_PATTERN with Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 10. On Jetty, App.AppConfig has an apiBoundary @Bean returning a ServletFilterRegistration for the same pattern with ServletFilterRegistration.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 10. Both are registered for the REQUEST dispatcher type only, so an internal forward or error dispatch to the API is not checked again. The order puts the API boundary just after the console boundary; the petstore mounts no authentication filter between them.

The Sold pets page, served at /console/pets/sold, is the smallest table page in the petstore: every pet that has been marked sold, with a species filter. It exists to show the contrast with the main Pets page. Same bean, but a different data mode and a much shorter template.

A table in client mode. The endpoint returns all the rows in one response and the browser does the filtering, sorting and paging. There is no server-side query, so the endpoint is a plain GET returning a list. A ribbon option group that filters on the species column in the browser, with no request to the server. A minimal page template: no tab attribute, no URL state, no row actions. Client mode is the right choice when the full row set is small. When it is not, use server mode, as the Pets page does.

The template is pets-sold.ftlh. The card body is trimmed here to its essentials. <@page toolkit="views"> <@card type="datatables" id="sold" title="Sold pets"> { rowType: 'Pet', dataMode: 'client', dataUrl: '/console/pets/sold/rows', columns: [ { key: 'id', label: 'Id' }, { key: 'name', label: 'Name' }, { key: 'species', label: 'Species' } ], ribbon: [ { type: 'optionGroup', id: 'species', title: 'Species', options: [ { id: 'dogs', title: 'Dogs', column: 'species', value: '$eq(DOG)' }, { id: 'cats', title: 'Cats', column: 'species', value: '$eq(CAT)' } ] }, { type: 'refresh' } ] } </@card> </@page> The filter values use the BeanQuery search syntax ($eq(DOG)). In client mode the table applies them locally; in server mode the same strings are sent to the server.

PetsPageBuilders.sold builds the same page. Request /console/pets/sold?builder to render it. PageSpec.create().toolkit("views") .table(TableSpec.create("sold").rowType("Pet").dataMode(DataMode.CLIENT).dataUrl("/console/pets/sold/rows") .columns(Column.create("id").label("Id"), Column.create("name").label("Name")) .ribbon( RibbonItem.optionGroup("species", RibbonItem.option("dogs").title("Dogs").column("species").value("$eq(DOG)"), RibbonItem.option("cats").title("Cats").column("species").value("$eq(CAT)")).title("Species"), RibbonItem.refresh()), "Sold pets");

GET /console/pets/sold/rows is served by PetsRest.soldRows. It returns every pet whose status is SOLD, sorted by id. Marking a pet sold is a separate action on the Pets page (POST /console/pets/{id}/sell), after which the pet appears here on the next refresh.
