Reference for the attributes of the @Rest, @RestOp and @Mixin annotations that configure a REST resource.

This page is a consolidated reference for the attributes of the three annotations that configure a REST resource: @Rest - class-level configuration of a resource. @RestOp and its verb-specific variants (@RestGet, @RestPut, @RestPost, @RestDelete, @RestPatch, @RestOptions) - per-method configuration. @Mixin - a rich mixin declaration used inside @Rest(mixinDefs=...). All three live in the org.apache.juneau.rest.server package of the juneau-rest-server module. @Rest is applied to classes (@Target(TYPE)); @RestOp and the verb annotations are applied to methods (@Target(METHOD)); all are @Inherited. @Mixin has an empty @Target and can only be used as a value of @Rest(mixinDefs). Unless stated otherwise, string attributes support SVL variables. Tri-state attributes are strings taking "true", "false" or "" (the default, meaning "inherit from the enclosing level").

Attribute Type Description path String Resource path. Child-to-parent search. Only effective when the class is registered directly as a top-level resource; when the class is a mixin the host's path governs. See Path Variables. paths String[] Additional top-level mount paths. Each element is SVL-resolved and then comma-split. children Class<?>[] Child resources, each mounted under its own URL subtree. See Child Resources. childrenDefs Child[] Rich child definitions (host-side seed form of children). mixins Class<?>[] Operation-provider classes whose @RestOp methods are composed into this resource. See Mixin Sub-Contexts. mixinDefs Mixin[] Rich mixin definitions with host-side overrides. See @Mixin attributes below. mergeResponseProcessorsIntoHost boolean Mixin-declared opt-in: when this class is composed as a mixin via a plain mixins= reference, fold its own responseProcessors into the host's chain. Default false. lazyChildren String Opt the parent into deferred (first-invocation) construction of its children. eagerInit String Eagerly initialize framework-managed memoizers during RestContext construction. config String Location of the configuration file. The keyword SYSTEM_DEFAULT refers to Config.getSystemDefault(). See Configuration Files. messages String Location of the resource bundle for this class. staticFiles Class<? extends StaticFiles> Static-file provider. Default StaticFiles.Void.class. authenticator Class<? extends RestAuthenticator> Resource-level authenticator. Default RestAuthenticator.Null.class. See Authenticator.

Attribute Type Description serializers Class<? extends Serializer>[] Serializers for response bodies. parsers Class<?>[] Parsers for request bodies. encoders Class<? extends Encoder>[] Compression encoders (e.g. gzip). See Encoders. converters Class<? extends RestConverter>[] Class-level response converters. produces String[] Supported Accept media types, overriding those inferred from the serializers. consumes String[] Supported Content-Type media types, overriding those inferred from the parsers. partSerializer Class<? extends HttpPartSerializer> Part serializer for headers, query/form parameters and URI parts. Default HttpPartSerializer.Void.class. partParser Class<? extends HttpPartParser> Part parser for headers, query/form parameters and URI parts. Default HttpPartParser.Void.class. defaultAccept String Default Accept header when not on the request. defaultContentType String Default Content-Type header when not on the request. defaultCharset String Default character encoding when not on the request. maxInput String Maximum allowed request input size, in bytes. allowedSerializerOptions String[] Serializer session option keys that clients are allowed to set. See Session Options. allowedParserOptions String[] Parser session option keys that clients are allowed to set. See Session Options. debugMarshalling String Tri-state opt-in to REST-driven serializer/parser debug behavior.

Attribute Type Description defaultRequestHeaders String[] Default request headers used when not sent by the client. defaultRequestAttributes String[] Default request attributes used when not already set. defaultResponseHeaders String[] Default response headers used when not set by the method. headerParams Header[] Default definitions for @Header method parameters across the class. queryParams Query[] Default definitions for @Query method parameters across the class. formDataParams FormData[] Default definitions for @FormData method parameters across the class. pathParams Path[] Default definitions for @Path method parameters across the class. allowedHeaderParams String Headers (e.g. Accept, Content-Type) that may be passed as URL query parameters. allowedMethodParams String HTTP methods that may be requested through a method URL parameter. "*" means all. On a safe request (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE) an admitted method is honored only if it is safe or its operation is declared read=true; otherwise the request is refused with 405. See Overloading HTTP Methods. allowedMethodHeaders String HTTP methods that may be requested through an X-Method, X-HTTP-Method-Override, X-HTTP-Method or X-Method-Override header. "*" means all. Empty (off) by default. Conflicting overrides are refused with 400. The same safe-request rule as allowedMethodParams applies. See Overloading HTTP Methods. disableContentParam String Set to true to disable the content URL parameter on PUT and POST requests. clientVersionHeader String Name of the header carrying the client version (see @RestOp(clientVersion)). For the allowed*Params/allowedMethodHeaders attributes, the value "NONE" (case-insensitive) suppresses inheriting a value from a parent class.

Attribute Type Description guards Class<? extends RestGuard>[] Guards applied to all operations of the class. See Guards. roleGuard String Role expression required to access operations, e.g. "ROLE_ADMIN". rolesDeclared String Comma-delimited list of all possible user roles. responseProcessors Class<? extends ResponseProcessor>[] Processors that convert returned POJOs into HTTP responses. restOpArgs Class<? extends RestOpArg>[] Additional Java method parameter resolvers. See Java Method Parameters. problemDetails String Tri-state opt-in to RFC 7807 / RFC 9457 application/problem+json error responses. See Problem Details. renderResponseStackTraces String Render stack traces in HTTP response bodies when errors occur. virtualThreads String Tri-state opt-in to per-request virtual-thread dispatch (Java 21+; silently ignored with a warning on older JVMs). asyncTimeoutMillis String Timeout for CompletableFuture-returning handlers. Default 30,000 ms; "0" disables. On timeout the response is 504 Gateway Timeout. See Async Dispatch. asyncCompletionExecutor String Name of the Executor bean on which CompletableFuture completion callbacks are run. observability String Per-resource observability opt-in/opt-out. See Observability. noInherit String[] Property names for which less-derived contributions are not inherited (see below).

Attribute Type Description title String[] Servlet title; populates the Swagger title. description String[] Servlet description; populates the Swagger description. siteName String Site name applied to the entire site. swagger Swagger Swagger metadata (which uses @Contact, @License, @Tag; see Annotations). swaggerProvider Class<? extends SwaggerProvider> Swagger provider. Default SwaggerProvider.Void.class. openApiProvider Class<? extends OpenApiProvider> OpenAPI 3.1 provider. Default OpenApiProvider.Void.class. uriAuthority String Overrides the authority path for this resource and its children. uriContext String Overrides the context path for this resource and its children. uriRelativity String How relative URIs are interpreted by serializers. uriResolution String How relative URIs are resolved by serializers.

On @Rest, accepted values are allowedParserOptions, allowedSerializerOptions, allowedHeaderParams, allowedMethodHeaders, allowedMethodParams, disableContentParam, renderResponseStackTraces, problemDetails, debugMarshalling, eagerInit, lazyChildren, clientVersionHeader, uriAuthority, uriContext, uriRelativity and uriResolution. On a class used as a mixin, the token set additionally includes serializers, parsers, encoders, converters, responseProcessors, restOpArgs, guards, partSerializer, partParser and messages, and blocks the host-to-mixin inheritance walk for that property. The noInherit attribute itself is never inherited.

@RestOp is the general form. The verb annotations fix the HTTP method and therefore do not have a method attribute. Their value attribute is a path-only shorthand, whereas @RestOp(value) takes the combined "METHOD /path" form. Example // All equivalent: @RestOp(method="PUT", path="/{propertyName}") @RestOp("PUT /{propertyName}") @RestPut("/{propertyName}") @RestPut(path="/{propertyName}")

@RestOp, @RestGet, @RestPut, @RestPost, @RestDelete, @RestPatch and @RestOptions all provide: Attribute Type Description value String Shorthand: "METHOD /path" on @RestOp, path only on the verb annotations. path String[] Path pattern(s). See Path Patterns. clientVersion String Client version range (e.g. "[0,1.0)", "1.0") matched against @Rest(clientVersionHeader). guards Class<? extends RestGuard>[] Guards for this operation. roleGuard String Role expression for this operation. rolesDeclared String Declared roles. encoders Class<? extends Encoder>[] Compression encoders. defaultAccept String Default Accept header. defaultCharset String Default character encoding. defaultRequestAttributes String[] Default request attributes. defaultRequestHeaders String[] Default request headers. defaultResponseHeaders String[] Default response headers. allowedSerializerOptions String[] Allowed serializer session option keys. allowedParserOptions String[] Allowed parser session option keys. noInherit String[] Properties not inherited from @Rest. On operations the accepted values are allowedSerializerOptions, allowedParserOptions, problemDetails and debugMarshalling. problemDetails String Tri-state override of @Rest(problemDetails). debugMarshalling String Tri-state override of @Rest(debugMarshalling). observability String Tri-state override of @Rest(observability). asyncCompletionExecutor String Executor bean name for async completion. description String[] Swagger operation description. swagger OpSwagger Swagger operation metadata. matchers Class<? extends RestMatcher>[] RestMatcher classes that let several Java methods share a method and path. See Matchers. summary String Swagger operation summary. defaultRequestQueryData String[] Default query parameters used when not sent by the client. metricName, metricTags String Name and tags for the metrics recorded for this operation.
documents.s: Attributes available on every operation annotation

documents.t: A Y means the attribute is declared on that annotation (derived directly from the annotation sources). Attribute @RestOp @RestGet @RestPut @RestPost @RestDelete @RestPatch @RestOptions method Y - - - - - - serializers Y Y Y Y - Y Y converters Y Y Y Y - Y Y produces Y Y Y Y - Y Y parsers Y - Y Y - Y - consumes Y - Y Y - Y - maxInput Y - Y Y - Y - defaultContentType Y - Y Y - Y - defaultRequestFormData Y - Y Y - Y - virtualThreads Y - - - - - - asyncTimeoutMillis Y - - - - - - Reading the matrix: body-consuming attributes (parsers, consumes, maxInput, defaultContentType, defaultRequestFormData) are not available on @RestGet, @RestDelete or @RestOptions; response-shaping attributes (serializers, converters, produces) are not available on @RestDelete. virtualThreads and asyncTimeoutMillis can currently only be set per-operation on the general @RestOp annotation (both can also be set resource-wide on @Rest).

Attribute Description method The HTTP method name. Besides the standard names: "*" matches any method (use @Method or RestRequest.getMethod() to tell them apart); "" auto-detects from the Java method name (defaulting to GET); "RRPC" marks a remote-proxy interface method; any other value is an overloaded method selected with the &method= URL parameter (on a safe request, only when read=true). See Inferred HTTP Methods and Paths and Overloading HTTP Methods. read Declares that a custom method only reads, so an override on a safe request (GET ?method=VIEW) may reach it. Accepted only on custom methods: POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, CONNECT, "*", "RRPC" or @Mutating fail at startup. See Overloading HTTP Methods. virtualThreads Tri-state override of @Rest(virtualThreads). asyncTimeoutMillis Override of @Rest(asyncTimeoutMillis).

@Mixin is used only inside @Rest(mixinDefs=...). It names a mixin class and lets the host override selected @Rest-level settings for that mixin's endpoints without editing the mixin class. Example @Rest( mixinDefs=@Mixin(type=FooMixin.class, guards=AdminGuard.class) ) public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet { ... } Attribute Type Description type Class<?> Required. The mixin class to compose into the host. mergeIntoHost boolean Opt-in (default false): additionally append the mixin's own list-shaped @Rest attributes to the host's chains, so the host's own operations see them too. path String Host-chosen mount prefix for the mixin's endpoints. paths String[] Host-chosen multiple mount prefixes. noInherit String[] Inheritance-cutoff list for this mixin's sub-context (same tokens as @Rest(noInherit)). Authoritative over the override slots. Override slots mirroring @Rest attributes of the same name: Shape Attributes Semantics List-shaped guards, converters, encoders, serializers, parsers, responseProcessors, restOpArgs, defaultRequestHeaders, defaultResponseHeaders, defaultRequestAttributes, produces, consumes Appended after the host chain the mixin inherits. Replace-shaped partSerializer, partParser, defaultAccept, defaultContentType, defaultCharset, maxInput, roleGuard, rolesDeclared, messages The host override wins when set. Host-only attributes (path, paths, children) are never folded into the host by mergeIntoHost. See Mixin Sub-Contexts for the full inheritance semantics and Mixins and Multi-Mount Paths for composition examples.

The following annotations are documented elsewhere but are often used alongside the ones above: @Mutating - declares that an operation changes state; see Overloading HTTP Methods. Lifecycle annotations (@RestInit, @RestPreCall, ...); see Lifecycle Hooks. Parameter annotations (@Path, @Query, @Header, @Content, @Attr, @Method, ...); see Java Method Parameters.

Add the Juneau transport module and Apache HttpClient 4.5 to your project: <!-- Juneau transport adapter --> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-client-apache-httpclient-45</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <!-- Apache HttpClient 4.5 (transitive from the adapter, pinned here for clarity) --> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.httpcomponents</groupId> <artifactId>httpclient</artifactId> <version>4.5.14</version> </dependency> The Juneau adapter module declares httpclient:4.5.14 as a dependency, so the second block can be omitted if you are happy with the version the adapter brings in.

juneau-rest-client-apache-httpclient-45 provides an HttpTransport implementation backed by Apache HttpClient 4.5.x (org.apache.httpcomponents:httpclient). Consider it when: Your project already pulls in Apache HttpClient 4.5 and you want a single shared client instance across the application. You need mature, battle-tested connection pooling, proxy support, cookie management, or NTLM / Kerberos authentication built into HC 4.5. You are migrating an existing HC 4.5 integration to the Juneau REST client API incrementally. The transport is auto-discovered via ServiceLoader when the module is on the classpath. An explicit .transport(...) call always wins over auto-discovery.

import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json5.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.apachehttpclient45.*; RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .transport(ApacheHc45Transport.create()) // wraps HttpClients.createDefault() .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build(); try (var resp = client.get("/users/123").run()) { var user = resp.body().as(User.class); } client.close(); ApacheHc45Transport.create() is shorthand for ApacheHc45Transport.builder().build(). It creates a default CloseableHttpClient via HttpClients.createDefault().

Simply add the module to the classpath and omit the .transport(...) call: // The ApacheHc45TransportProvider registered via ServiceLoader takes over automatically. RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build();

Use ApacheHc45TransportBuilder.httpClient(CloseableHttpClient) to supply your own pre-configured CloseableHttpClient. The transport takes ownership of the client and closes it when RestClient.close() is called. import org.apache.http.impl.client.*; import org.apache.http.impl.conn.*; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json5.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.apachehttpclient45.*; CloseableHttpClient apacheClient = HttpClients.custom() .setConnectionManager(new PoolingHttpClientConnectionManager()) .setMaxConnPerRoute(20) .setMaxConnTotal(100) .build(); RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .transport(ApacheHc45Transport.builder() .httpClient(apacheClient) .build()) .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build();

Apache HttpClient 4.5 ships PoolingHttpClientConnectionManager, which reuses TCP connections across requests. Tune it to match your workload: import org.apache.http.impl.conn.*; var cm = new PoolingHttpClientConnectionManager(); cm.setMaxTotal(200); // total connections in the pool cm.setDefaultMaxPerRoute(20); // max connections per host:port pair CloseableHttpClient poolingClient = HttpClients.custom() .setConnectionManager(cm) .build();

Pass a custom SSLContext or SSLConnectionSocketFactory when building the CloseableHttpClient: import javax.net.ssl.*; import org.apache.http.ssl.*; import org.apache.http.impl.client.*; SSLContext sslContext = SSLContexts.custom() .loadTrustMaterial(trustStore, null) .build(); CloseableHttpClient tlsClient = HttpClients.custom() .setSSLContext(sslContext) .build();

Configure connect and socket timeouts via RequestConfig: import org.apache.http.client.config.*; import org.apache.http.impl.client.*; RequestConfig config = RequestConfig.custom() .setConnectTimeout(5_000) // ms to establish a connection .setSocketTimeout(30_000) // ms waiting for data .setConnectionRequestTimeout(2_000) // ms to lease a connection from the pool .build(); CloseableHttpClient timedClient = HttpClients.custom() .setDefaultRequestConfig(config) .build();

The RestClient lifecycle maps directly to the underlying CloseableHttpClient: // Build once at application startup RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .transport(ApacheHc45Transport.builder().httpClient(myClient).build()) .build(); // Use throughout the application lifetime; wrap each response in try-with-resources try (var resp = client.get("/items").run()) { return resp.body().as(ItemList.class); } // At application shutdown — closes the CloseableHttpClient client.close();

<!-- Juneau transport adapter --> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-client-apache-httpclient-50</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <!-- Apache HttpClient 5 (transitive from the adapter, pinned here for clarity) --> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.httpcomponents.client5</groupId> <artifactId>httpclient5</artifactId> <version>5.6.1</version> </dependency>

juneau-rest-client-apache-httpclient-50 provides an HttpTransport implementation backed by Apache HttpClient 5.x (org.apache.httpcomponents.client5:httpclient5). Consider it when: You are starting a new project and want the latest Apache HttpComponents API. You need HTTP/2 support within the Apache HC ecosystem. You are migrating an existing HC 5 integration to the Juneau REST client API. The transport uses the classic (synchronous) CloseableHttpClient execution path from HC 5. Async-only HC 5 features (e.g., CloseableHttpAsyncClient) are not exposed; route calls through the transport interface as usual. The transport is auto-discovered via ServiceLoader when the module is on the classpath. An explicit .transport(...) call always wins over auto-discovery.

import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json5.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.apachehttpclient50.*; RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .transport(ApacheHc5Transport.create()) // wraps HttpClients.createDefault() .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build(); try (var resp = client.get("/users/123").run()) { var user = resp.body().as(User.class); } client.close(); ApacheHc5Transport.create() is shorthand for ApacheHc5Transport.builder().build(). It creates a default CloseableHttpClient via org.apache.hc.client5.http.impl.classic.HttpClients.createDefault().

Add the module to the classpath and omit the .transport(...) call: RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build();

Use ApacheHc5TransportBuilder.httpClient(CloseableHttpClient) to supply your own CloseableHttpClient. The transport takes ownership of the client and closes it when RestClient.close() is called. import org.apache.hc.client5.http.impl.classic.*; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json5.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.apachehttpclient50.*; CloseableHttpClient apacheClient = HttpClients.createDefault(); RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .transport(ApacheHc5Transport.builder() .httpClient(apacheClient) .build()) .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build();

Apache HttpClient 5 ships PoolingHttpClientConnectionManagerBuilder for pooled connection management: import org.apache.hc.client5.http.impl.classic.*; import org.apache.hc.client5.http.impl.io.*; var cm = PoolingHttpClientConnectionManagerBuilder.create() .setMaxConnTotal(200) .setMaxConnPerRoute(20) .build(); CloseableHttpClient poolingClient = HttpClients.custom() .setConnectionManager(cm) .build();

import javax.net.ssl.*; import org.apache.hc.client5.http.ssl.*; import org.apache.hc.client5.http.impl.classic.*; import org.apache.hc.client5.http.impl.io.*; SSLContext sslContext = SSLContexts.custom() .loadTrustMaterial(trustStore, null) .build(); var cm = PoolingHttpClientConnectionManagerBuilder.create() .setSSLSocketFactory(SSLConnectionSocketFactoryBuilder.create() .setSslContext(sslContext) .build()) .build(); CloseableHttpClient tlsClient = HttpClients.custom() .setConnectionManager(cm) .build();

In HC 5, timeouts are set via RequestConfig: import org.apache.hc.client5.http.config.*; import org.apache.hc.core5.util.*; import org.apache.hc.client5.http.impl.classic.*; RequestConfig config = RequestConfig.custom() .setConnectTimeout(Timeout.ofSeconds(5)) .setResponseTimeout(Timeout.ofSeconds(30)) .setConnectionRequestTimeout(Timeout.ofSeconds(2)) .build(); CloseableHttpClient timedClient = HttpClients.custom() .setDefaultRequestConfig(config) .build();

Concern HC 4.5 (apachehttpclient45) HC 5 (apachehttpclient50) GroupId org.apache.httpcomponents org.apache.httpcomponents.client5 ArtifactId httpclient httpclient5 Transport class ApacheHc45Transport ApacheHc5Transport Builder class ApacheHc45TransportBuilder ApacheHc5TransportBuilder Timeout API RequestConfig.setSocketTimeout(int ms) RequestConfig.setResponseTimeout(Timeout) Connection manager PoolingHttpClientConnectionManager PoolingHttpClientConnectionManagerBuilder

RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .transport(ApacheHc5Transport.builder().httpClient(myClient).build()) .build(); try (var resp = client.get("/items").run()) { return resp.body().as(ItemList.class); } client.close();

<!-- Juneau transport adapter --> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-client-jetty</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <!-- Jetty 12 HTTP Client (transitive from the adapter, pinned here for clarity) --> <dependency> <groupId>org.eclipse.jetty</groupId> <artifactId>jetty-client</artifactId> <version>12.1.9</version> </dependency>

juneau-rest-client-jetty provides an HttpTransport implementation backed by the Jetty 12 HttpClient (org.eclipse.jetty:jetty-client). Consider it when: Your application already embeds a Jetty server (e.g., via juneau-microservice-jetty) and you want to share the same Jetty lifecycle for outbound HTTP calls. You want a Jetty-native HTTP client without pulling in Apache HttpComponents or OkHttp. The request body is streamed via OutputStreamRequestContent on a background thread, so large bodies do not require full in-memory buffering. Response body bytes are made available as an InputStream via Jetty's InputStreamResponseListener. The transport is auto-discovered via ServiceLoader when the module is on the classpath. An explicit .transport(...) call always wins over auto-discovery.

Note JettyHttpTransport.create() and JettyHttpTransportBuilder.build() declare throws Exception because they may need to start the underlying Jetty HttpClient. import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json5.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.jetty.*; RestClient client; try { client = RestClient.builder() .transport(JettyHttpTransport.create()) // starts a new HttpClient internally .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build(); } catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException("Failed to start Jetty transport", e); } try (var resp = client.get("/users/123").run()) { var user = resp.body().as(User.class); } client.close(); JettyHttpTransport.create() is shorthand for JettyHttpTransport.builder().build(). It creates and starts a new HttpClient with default settings and a 30-second response-header timeout.

Add the module to the classpath and omit the .transport(...) call: RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build(); Auto-discovery uses the same throws Exception build path internally; the exception is wrapped in an IllegalStateException if thrown.

Use JettyHttpTransportBuilder to supply a pre-configured HttpClient or to adjust the response-header timeout. import org.eclipse.jetty.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.jetty.*; // Build your own Jetty HttpClient HttpClient jettyClient = new HttpClient(); // ... configure jettyClient ... RestClient client; try { client = RestClient.builder() .transport(JettyHttpTransport.builder() .httpClient(jettyClient) .responseTimeoutMs(15_000) // wait up to 15 s for response headers .build()) .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build(); } catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } If the HttpClient you supply has not been started, JettyHttpTransport starts it automatically.

JettyHttpTransportBuilder.responseTimeoutMs(long) sets the maximum time to wait (in milliseconds) for the HTTP status line and headers after the request has been sent. It does not limit how long the response body takes to stream. Value Behaviour > 0 (default: 30_000) Wait that many milliseconds; throw TransportException on timeout. 0 or negative Wait indefinitely. JettyHttpTransport transport = JettyHttpTransport.builder() .responseTimeoutMs(60_000) // 60 s for slow endpoints .build();

Configure SSL on the HttpClient before passing it to the builder: import org.eclipse.jetty.client.*; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.ssl.*; SslContextFactory.Client sslContextFactory = new SslContextFactory.Client(); sslContextFactory.setKeyStorePath("/path/to/keystore.jks"); sslContextFactory.setKeyStorePassword("secret"); HttpClient tlsClient = new HttpClient(sslContextFactory); JettyHttpTransport transport = JettyHttpTransport.builder() .httpClient(tlsClient) .build();

JettyHttpTransport.close() calls HttpClient.stop(). Map this to RestClient.close(): RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .transport(JettyHttpTransport.builder().build()) .build(); // ... application runs ... // At shutdown — stops the Jetty HttpClient client.close(); When embedding inside a JettyMicroservice, the transport's lifecycle aligns naturally with the server because both use the same Jetty runtime. If you pass your own HttpClient to the adapter, stopping the client via RestClient.close() also stops that shared instance — factor this in if other components depend on it.
HTTP Transport Adapters — overview and adapter comparison Next-Generation REST Client — full guide to the NG client juneau-microservice-jetty — embedding Juneau with Jetty

The following methods provide logging of requests and responses: RestClient.Builderlogger(Logger)logToConsole()logRequests(DetailLevel,Level,BiPredicate) The following example shows the results of logging all requests that end with /bean. Examples // A simple bean we're going to round-trip. MyBean bean = new MyBean(); bean = RestClient .create() .json5() .logRequests(DetailLevel.FULL, Level.SEVERE, (req,res)->req.getUri().endsWith("/bean")) .logToConsole() .build() .post("http://localhost/bean", bean) .run() .getContent().as(MyBean.class); This produces the following console output: === HTTP Call (outgoing) ====================================================== === REQUEST === POST http://localhost/bean ---request headers--- Accept: application/json5 ---request entity--- Content-Type: application/json5 ---request content--- {f:1} === RESPONSE === HTTP/1.1 200 ---response headers--- Content-Type: application/json ---response content--- {f:1} === END =======================================================================", It should be noted that if you enable request logging detail level DetailLevel.FULL, response bodies will be cached by default which may introduce a performance penalty. Additionally, the following method is also provided for enabling debug mode: RestClient.Builderdebug() Enabling debug mode has the following effects: RestClient.Builder.logToConsole() is called. Classic REST client logging/debug APIs are unchanged and remain available through the classic builder: org.apache.juneau.rest.client.classic.RestClient.Builderlogger(Logger)logToConsole()logRequests(DetailLevel,Level,BiPredicate)debug()

The next-generation client (org.apache.juneau.rest.client.RestClient) uses JUL-level-driven debug logging through RichLogger. org.apache.juneau.rest.client.RestClient.BuilderdebugLoggerName(String)debugFormatter(RestClientDebugFormatter)RestClientDebugFormatterBasicRestClientDebugFormatter Default logger name: RestClient.class.getName(). Debug detail is controlled solely by the resolved JUL logger level: INFO: basic summary line. FINE: basic + request/response headers. FINEST: basic + headers + bounded request/response body capture — only if body dumping has been explicitly opted in via the JUNEAU_REST_DEBUG_ALLOW_DUMP_BODIES environment variable (see Secure by default below); otherwise FINEST emits a suppression placeholder instead of body content. Exactly one LogRecord is emitted per request/error, always at JUL INFO — the resolved tier controls message detail only, so FINE/FINEST-selected detail still travels through INFO sinks. This applies uniformly to both places the pipeline emits from: the normal request-completion path and the transport-exception (synthetic error response) path.

BasicRestClientDebugFormatter mirrors the NG REST server's BasicRestDebugFormatter secret-hardening design (see REST server Logging/Debugging » Secure by default): raising a client's debug logger to FINE/FINEST can never, by itself, turn the log stream into a plaintext-credential dump or a log-forging channel.

Request/response bodies are never dumped by default — not at FINEST, not for any content type. Dumping is a deliberate operator opt-in behind the same environment-variable master gate the server uses: export JUNEAU_REST_DEBUG_ALLOW_DUMP_BODIES=true Semantics are byte-identical to the server's gate: environment variable only (no system-property fallback), read once per JVM and cached, trim-then-parse truthy (any non-empty trimmed value enables except case-insensitive false/0). With the gate unset, formatBody emits a suppression placeholder naming the environment variable plus the captured byte count and content-type — never body bytes in any representation (plaintext, hex, or otherwise), even if a scrubber is configured. With the gate set, bodies render only when the content is renderable (see below); non-renderable/binary content, or a non-identity Content-Encoding (e.g. gzip), yields a distinct "not rendered" placeholder instead. danger Setting JUNEAU_REST_DEBUG_ALLOW_DUMP_BODIES re-enables plaintext request/response body logging at FINEST for both the client and the server. Treat FINEST client logs as sensitive, and supply a bodyScrubber(...) if any secret-bearing bodies (tokens, PII, card data) are possible. Prefer leaving the gate unset in production. isBodyRenderable(String contentType) (on the RestClientDebugFormatter SPI) decides whether a body is text worth logging, using the same predicate as the server's RestDebugFormatter.isBodyRenderable: renderable for text/*, application/json, application/xml, any +json/+xml suffix type, and application/x-www-form-urlencoded; non-renderable for everything else, including multipart/form-data, absent, or blank content types. The decision is made independently per side — the request's own Content-Type governs the request body, the response's own governs the response body.
documents.s: No body dumps without an explicit opt-in

documents.t: When body dumping is opted in, transform body text before it's logged via the RestDebugBodyScrubber SPI, registered with bodyScrubber(...): new BasicRestClientDebugFormatter().bodyScrubber((contentType, body) -> body.replaceAll("\"password\":\"[^\"]*\"", "\"password\":\"***\"")); Gate-subordinate: the scrubber runs only after the master gate has already permitted dumping; it merely chooses scrubbed-vs-raw text and never causes a body to be emitted while the gate is unset. Fail-closed: if scrub(...) throws or returns null, the formatter emits a suppression placeholder instead of the body — it never falls back to the raw, unscrubbed body. Non-null output is still sanitized (control characters escaped) and length-capped before it reaches the log. No default scrubber ships: with the gate set and no scrubber, the raw body is dumped (sanitized + capped).

At the headers tier (FINE-or-finer), header values are masked with [REDACTED] against a widened, formatter-local set — a superset of the shared RedactedHeaders.DEFAULT (Authorization, Cookie, Set-Cookie, Proxy-Authorization, X-API-Key) plus X-Auth-Token, X-Authorization, WWW-Authenticate, Referer, and Location. Matching is separator-normalized: it case-folds and strips -/_, so X-Auth-Token, X_Auth_Token, and XAuthToken all match. The shared RedactedHeaders.DEFAULT itself is left unchanged; this widened set is client-formatter-local, matching the server's own decision to keep its widened set formatter-local rather than merged into the shared default. Configure the masked set with redactedHeaders(Collection<String>) (replaces the masked set).

The request method and URI, header names and values, and body text (raw or scrubber-produced) are passed through a sanitizer that escapes CR/LF and other control characters to visible, inert forms (\r, \n, \uXXXX). A remote server therefore cannot inject a newline into a response header/body to forge a second physical log line. The order applied to every emitted string is mask → escape → cap.

Captured body bytes are bounded at capture time by bodyCap(int) (default 8 KB), then …[truncated N bytes] marks what was omitted; a second character-level cap (bodyCap() * 6) is applied after sanitization so a scrubber that returns an oversized string is still bounded. Unlike the server's formatter, the client does not add separate header-count/header-scan/field-length/URI-length bounding knobs — the client's header source is already a finite, bounded list rather than an adversarial unbounded input stream, so those extra knobs have no client-side analog.

RestClient automatically participates in end-to-end request correlation. By default, every outgoing request carries an X-Request-Id header so a call can be traced through the server logs (which honor that inbound id — see REST server » Always-on request correlation): Auto-send / mint. If the request has no X-Request-Id header, the client mints a fresh time-ordered Uuid7 and sends it. A header the caller already set (globally on the builder or per-request) is honored, never overwritten. Pre-call setter. RestRequest.requestId(String) sets the id for a single call fluently; getRequestId() reads the id that was (or will be) sent. Echo capture. The client captures the X-Request-Id the server echoes on the response, exposed via RestResponse.getRequestId(). When correlating logs, the client uses the echoed id when present and falls back to the sent id otherwise (the effective id). Opt-out. RestClient.Builder.sendRequestId(false) disables auto-sending entirely; an explicitly caller-supplied X-Request-Id header still travels. The effective id flows into debug logging: RestClientDebugPipeline stamps each emitted LogRecord with a structured requestId field (via LogRecordContext.attachIfAbsent(...)), and BasicRestClientDebugFormatter prepends a human-readable [requestId=<id>] marker to the rendered message — mirroring the server's statusLine prefix so a single request reads identically on both sides. try (var client = RestClient.builder().build(); var res = client.get("http://localhost/widgets/123").run()) { // Server-honored, echoed back: var id = res.getRequestId(); } // Explicit per-call id (honored, not overwritten): client.get("/widgets/123").requestId("order-9f2c").run(); // Opt out of auto-sending entirely: var quiet = RestClient.builder().sendRequestId(false).build(); For tests, capture emitted records directly via RichLogger.captureEvents(...): var logger = RichLogger.getLogger("my.client.debug"); logger.setLevel(Level.FINEST); try (var capture = logger.captureEvents(Level.FINEST); var client = RestClient.builder() .debugLoggerName("my.client.debug") .debugFormatter(new BasicRestClientDebugFormatter().bodyCap(8 * 1024)) .build(); var res = client.post("http://localhost/bean").bodyString("{\"x\":1}").run()) { res.body().asString(); var record = capture.last(); // assert on record.getLevel() and record.getMessage() }

<!-- Juneau transport adapter --> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-client-okhttp</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <!-- OkHttp 5 (transitive from the adapter, pinned here for clarity) --> <dependency> <groupId>com.squareup.okhttp3</groupId> <artifactId>okhttp-jvm</artifactId> <version>5.3.2</version> </dependency> OkHttp 5 artifact name The adapter targets OkHttp 5.x, whose Maven artifact is okhttp-jvm (not the older okhttp artifact used by OkHttp 4.x). Make sure your dependency manager resolves the correct artifact.

juneau-rest-client-okhttp provides an HttpTransport implementation backed by OkHttp 5.x (com.squareup.okhttp3:okhttp-jvm). Consider it when: You want transparent HTTP/2 with automatic HTTP/1.1 fallback. You are developing for Android, where OkHttp is the de-facto HTTP client. You want efficient request/response body streaming with minimal in-memory buffering (OkHttp streams the request body directly to the socket when the content length is known). You rely on OkHttp-native interceptors, authenticators, or cookie jars elsewhere in your application and want to share the same OkHttpClient instance. The transport is auto-discovered via ServiceLoader when the module is on the classpath. An explicit .transport(...) call always wins over auto-discovery.

import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json5.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.okhttp.*; RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .transport(OkHttpTransport.create()) // wraps new OkHttpClient() .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build(); try (var resp = client.get("/users/123").run()) { var user = resp.body().as(User.class); } client.close(); OkHttpTransport.create() is shorthand for OkHttpTransport.builder().build(). It creates a new OkHttpClient with default settings.

Add the module to the classpath and omit the .transport(...) call: RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build();

Use OkHttpTransportBuilder.httpClient(OkHttpClient) to supply your own OkHttpClient. The transport will call dispatcher().executorService().shutdown() and connectionPool().evictAll() on it when RestClient.close() is called. import okhttp3.*; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json5.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.okhttp.*; OkHttpClient okClient = new OkHttpClient.Builder() .connectTimeout(java.time.Duration.ofSeconds(5)) .readTimeout(java.time.Duration.ofSeconds(30)) .build(); RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .transport(OkHttpTransport.builder() .httpClient(okClient) .build()) .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build();

OkHttp's documentation strongly recommends sharing a single OkHttpClient instance across the application so that its connection pool and thread pool are reused. Pass the same instance to each adapter: OkHttpClient shared = new OkHttpClient(); RestClient users = RestClient.builder() .transport(OkHttpTransport.builder().httpClient(shared).build()) .rootUrl("https://users.example.com") .build(); RestClient orders = RestClient.builder() .transport(OkHttpTransport.builder().httpClient(shared).build()) .rootUrl("https://orders.example.com") .build(); When sharing, managing the OkHttpClient lifecycle (shutdown) is the caller's responsibility.
documents.s: Sharing One OkHttpClient Across Multiple RestClients

documents.t: OkHttp manages its connection pool internally. You can tune it via ConnectionPool: import okhttp3.*; OkHttpClient pooled = new OkHttpClient.Builder() .connectionPool(new ConnectionPool( 20, // max idle connections 5, java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.MINUTES)) // keep-alive duration .build();

import javax.net.ssl.*; import okhttp3.*; SSLContext sslContext = SSLContext.getInstance("TLS"); sslContext.init(keyManagers, trustManagers, null); OkHttpClient tlsClient = new OkHttpClient.Builder() .sslSocketFactory(sslContext.getSocketFactory(), (X509TrustManager) trustManagers[0]) .build();

OkHttp-native interceptors can be wired through the OkHttpClient builder and are transparent to Juneau's own interceptor chain: OkHttpClient intercepted = new OkHttpClient.Builder() .addInterceptor(chain -> { Request request = chain.request().newBuilder() .addHeader("X-Correlation-Id", UUID.randomUUID().toString()) .build(); return chain.proceed(request); }) .build();

OkHttpTransport.close() drains the connection pool and shuts down the dispatcher's thread pool: // httpClient.dispatcher().executorService().shutdown(); // httpClient.connectionPool().evictAll(); If you supplied a shared OkHttpClient, call close() on the last RestClient to use it, or manage the OkHttpClient lifecycle yourself.
HTTP Transport Adapters — overview and adapter comparison Next-Generation REST Client — full guide to the NG client

Outdated examples (10.0) Examples on this page using RestContext.Builder (constructor injection or @RestInit parameter injection) is pre-10.0 and kept only for historical context. The Builder-injection protocol was removed; migrate to @Rest(...) / @RestOp(...) attributes, @Bean(name="...") bean suppliers, and new RestContext(RestContextInit) for programmatic bootstrap. See the V10 Migration Guide. The RestContext object is the workhorse class for all of the configuration of a single REST resource class. It's by-far the most important class in the REST API. Every class annotated with @Rest ends up with an instance of this object. The object itself is read-only and unchangeable and is initialized from the resource/method annotations plus injected beans in the resource bean store. In 10.0+, configuration is annotation-driven (@Rest(...), @RestOp(...), @RestGet(...), etc.) with optional @Bean(name="...") bean suppliers for programmatic overrides. This class is vast. Combined with RestOpContext (which is the equivalent per-method context), these classes define the entire configuration and workflow of the REST API. For direct programmatic bootstrap, use RestContext.Args with new RestContext(init). This replaces the legacy RestContext.create(...).init(...).build() factory chain. 10.0+ guidance Prefer these configuration surfaces: @Rest(...) for resource-level settings. @RestOp(...) / verb annotations for operation-level settings. @Bean(name="...") bean suppliers for programmatic overrides. note The builders or built objects above can also be defined as injected beans defined in a Spring Configuration if you wish to do all your app configuration Spring-style. This is described in detail in the juneau-rest-server-springboot documentation. The lifecycle methods are still annotation-driven via @RestInit, @RestPreCall, @RestPostCall, @RestStartCall, and @RestDestroy.

As of 10.0.0, the env-driven defaults behind most RestContext.* settings — the values consulted when a @Rest(...) attribute is left unset — are resolved as a single bound object, RestContextProperties, rather than as 15 separate @Value fields. RestContextProperties is declared @ConfigProperties(prefix = "RestContext") (see @ConfigProperties Annotation Basics for how the annotation and its underlying binder work), and it's the framework's own pilot for that feature. Practically, this changes nothing about how you configure these settings — a RestContext.* key is still resolved from the same places it always was: A resource's @Rest(config=...) file, via the config's PropertySource registration in the resource's BeanStore. Environment variables and system properties (relaxed key matching applies, so RestContext.clientVersionHeader, REST_CONTEXT_CLIENT_VERSION_HEADER, and rest.context.client.version.header-style dotted forms are all equivalent). Any other registered PropertySource. What's new is that the bound instance itself is directly accessible — either from the context: RestContextProperties props = ctx.getRestContextProperties(); or from the resource's bean store, since the bind auto-registers it (see Auto-registration in the BeanStore): RestContextProperties props = ctx.getBeanStore().getBean(RestContextProperties.class).orElseThrow(); Every existing public getter on RestContext (isRenderResponseStackTraces(), getClientVersionHeader(), getUriRelativity(), etc.) keeps its exact signature and blending behavior with @Rest-annotation overrides — they're unaffected thin wrappers; only the source of the default half of that computation moved from a private @Value field to RestContextProperties. Two settings are intentionally not part of RestContextProperties: RestContext.uriAuthority and RestContext.uriContext remain standalone @Value("${RestContext.uriAuthority}") / @Value("${RestContext.uriContext}") Optional<String> fields directly on RestContext, because they carry a null-vs-empty distinction that @ConfigProperties' current raw-type-only conversion can't express (see the current limitations of @ConfigProperties). Leniency improvement for present-but-empty booleans Under the pre-10.0.0 @Value boolean fields, a present-but-empty value (e.g. RestContext.eagerInit=) threw BeanCreationException. As of 10.0.0, RestContextProperties carries every boolean setting as a raw string and RestContext parses it leniently, so a present-but-empty value now resolves to false instead of throwing — for all 8 boolean settings (disableContentParam, renderResponseStackTraces, problemDetails, virtualThreads, responseTraceparent, mdcAsyncPropagation, eagerInit, lazyChildren). See the 10.0.0 release notes for details.

REST Java methods are identified on REST servlets using the @RestOp annotation. The annotation allows the framework to identify the available REST methods through reflection. RestOpallowedParserOptions allowedSerializerOptions asyncCompletionExecutor asyncTimeoutMillis clientVersion consumes converters defaultAccept defaultCharset defaultContentType defaultRequestAttributes defaultRequestFormData defaultRequestHeaders defaultRequestQueryData defaultResponseHeaders description encoders guards matchers maxInput metricName metricTags method noInherit observability parsers path problemDetails produces roleGuard rolesDeclared serializers summary swagger value virtualThreads Example @RestOp(method=GET, path="/") public String sayHello() { return "Hello world!"; } The following specialized annotations are also provided for specific HTTP methods: RestGet RestPut RestPost RestPatch RestDelete RestOptions Example @RestGet(path="/") public String sayHello() { return "Hello world!"; }
Refer to the following Javadocs for more information: RestRequestRestResponseRequestContentRequestHeaderListRequestQueryParamListRequestFormParamListRequestPathParamListRequestAttributes

The RestOpContext object is the workhorse class for an individual RestOp-annotated method. Every class annotated with @RestOp ends up with an instance of this object. Similar to RestContext, the object is read-only and unchangeable and is initialized with all of the various annotations pulled from the method. Per-operation configuration is annotation-driven via @RestOp (and its method-specific cousins @RestGet, @RestPut, @RestPost, @RestDelete, @RestPatch, @RestOptions). Programmatic per-operation overrides are supplied via @Bean-named beans (use the methodScope= attribute to scope an override to specific operation methods). Both Builder-injection protocols — per-op @RestInit(RestOpContext.Builder) and class-level @RestInit(RestContext.Builder) — were removed in 10.0; see the V10 Migration Guide for replacement recipes. 10.0+ configuration model RestOpContext is now configured through: @RestOp(...) / @RestGet(...) / @RestPost(...) / @RestPut(...) / @RestPatch(...) / @RestDelete(...) / @RestOptions(...) attributes. @Bean(name="...") bean suppliers (optionally scoped with methodScope=). Resource-level defaults inherited from @Rest(...) (unless blocked by noInherit). See @Rest and @RestOp for every attribute that feeds into the context.

A RestOpContext is created once per @RestOp method when the owning RestContext is initialized, and is shared by all requests to that method. You can get at it in three ways: @RestGet("/info") public String info(RestOpContext opContext, RestRequest req) { // 1. As a Java method parameter (see JavaMethodParameters). // 2. From the request. RestOpContext same = req.getOpContext(); return opContext.getHttpMethod() + " " + opContext.getPathPattern(); } As a method parameter of type RestOpContext (resolved by RestOpContextArgs; see Java Method Parameters). The same resolver also supplies JsonSchemaGenerator, ParserSet and SerializerSet parameters taken from the operation context. RestRequest.getOpContext(). RestOpSession.getContext(). The owning resource-level context is available through RestOpContext.getContext(), which returns the RestContext (see RestContext).
The context exposes the effective, fully-resolved settings for the operation, i.e. the @RestOp value with anything unset inherited from @Rest.

Method Description getJavaMethod() The java.lang.reflect.Method implementing the operation. getHttpMethod() The resolved HTTP method (explicit, inferred from the Java method name, or *). getPathPattern() The first path pattern as a string. getPathMatchers() All UrlPathMatcher objects for the operation. getRequiredMatchers() / getOptionalMatchers() The RestMatcher objects that must / may match for the operation to be chosen. getRestOpAnnotations() The @RestOp-group annotations applied to the method.

Method Description getSerializers() / getParsers() The SerializerSet / ParserSet for the operation. getEncoders() The EncoderSet. getMarshallingContext() The MarshallingContext. getPartSerializer() / getPartParser() The HttpPartSerializer / HttpPartParser. getJsonSchemaGenerator() The JsonSchemaGenerator. getSupportedAcceptTypes() / getSupportedContentTypes() The MediaType lists derived from the serializers/parsers (or produces/consumes). getAllowedParserOptions() / getAllowedSerializerOptions() Session option keys clients may set. getMaxInput() Maximum number of input bytes. getResponseMeta(), getResponseBeanMeta(Object), getResponseHeaderMeta(Object) Response metadata for the return type / a given object.

Method Description getDefaultCharset() Default character set. getDefaultRequestHeaders() HttpHeaderList applied when the client does not send the header. getDefaultRequestAttributes() NamedAttributeMap of default request attributes. getDefaultRequestQueryData() / getDefaultRequestFormData() HttpPartList of default query / form-data values. getDefaultResponseHeaders() HttpHeaderList of default response headers.

Method Description isProblemDetails() Whether RFC 7807 problem-details responses are enabled; inherited from @Rest(problemDetails) when unset. isDebugMarshalling() Whether REST-driven marshalling debug is enabled. isVirtualThreadsEnabled() Whether per-request virtual-thread dispatch is enabled (Java 21+). isObservabilityEnabled() Whether observability is enabled for the operation. getMetricName() / getMetricTags() Metric name and tags from @RestOp(metricName, metricTags). getAsyncTimeoutMillis() / getAsyncCompletionExecutor() Timeout and completion executor for CompletableFuture-returning handlers. getLogger() The per-operation RichLogger. RestOpContext implements Comparable<RestOpContext>, which is what orders operations when a request is matched against them.

RestContext - the resource-level equivalent. Inferred HTTP Methods and Paths - how getHttpMethod() and getPathPattern() are derived when not stated. Overloading HTTP Methods - @Mutating reads getHttpMethod().

One of the most powerful features of the REST client class is the ability to turn a plain Java interface into a fully-working client for a 3rd-party REST resource. See the guide: Call an existing REST API with a typed proxy You describe the API with a Java interface and a handful of annotations — the HTTP method, the path, which arguments become headers, query parameters, form data, or the request body, and what the response should be parsed into. RestClient then hands you back a dynamic proxy that implements the interface, translating every method call into an HTTP request and every response back into a Java return value. The methods used to retrieve remote interfaces are: RestClientgetRemote(Class)getRemote(Class,Object)getRemote(Class,Object,Serializer,Parser)

Define an interface, annotate it, and get a proxy from a RestClient: Example @Remote(path="/petstore") public interface PetStore { @RemotePost("/pets") Pet addPet( @Content CreatePet createPet, @Header("E-Tag") UUID etag, @Query("debug") boolean debug ); @RemoteGet("/pets/{petId}") Pet getPet(@Path("petId") int petId); } // Use a RestClient with default JSON 5 support. RestClient client = RestClient.create().json5().build(); // Instantiate our proxy interface. PetStore store = client.getRemote(PetStore.class, "http://localhost:10000"); // Use it to create a pet... CreatePet createPet = new CreatePet("Fluffy", 9.99); Pet pet = store.addPet(createPet, UUID.randomUUID(), true); // ...and fetch it back. Pet sameCat = store.getPet(pet.getId()); The addPet(...) call above translates to a real HTTP request under the hood: POST http://localhost:10000/petstore/pets HTTP/1.1 Accept: application/json Content-Type: application/json E-Tag: 475588d4-0b27-4f56-9296-cc683251d314 { name: 'Fluffy', price: 9.99 } No hand-written URL building, serialization, or response parsing required — the interface is the contract. See Also The @RemoteOp annotation (and its method/path) can often be skipped entirely if your Java method names follow a simple naming convention. See @RemoteOp for the inference rules.

Method behavior is driven entirely by annotations on the interface, its methods, and their parameters: Annotation Applies to Purpose @Remote Interface Marks the interface as a REST proxy; sets the base path, common headers, and client versioning. @RemoteOp (and @RemoteGet/@RemotePost/@RemotePut/@RemotePatch/@RemoteDelete) Method Maps a method to an HTTP verb + path. Often optional if the method name implies the verb. @Path Parameter URL path variables ({petId}-style placeholders). @Query Parameter Query-string parameters. @Header Parameter HTTP request headers — including dynamic, multi-value forms. @FormData Parameter application/x-www-form-urlencoded body parameters. @Content Parameter The HTTP request body. @Request Parameter or class Bundles multiple parts (content/headers/query/etc.) behind a single request bean. @Response Return type Bundles content/headers/status behind a single response bean. Every one of these supports both single-value forms (@Query("limit") int limit) and dynamic, multi-value forms (@Query Map<String,Object> params) — see the dynamic headers example below for the pattern in detail.
The sections below are short teasers of what's possible. Each links to a deep-dive page with the full set of supported types and edge cases.

Path variables (@Path) fill in {placeholders} in the URL: @RemoteGet("/pets/{petId}") Pet getPet(@Path("petId") int petId); Query parameters (@Query) — and the equivalent for @FormData form posts: @RemoteGet("/pets") Pet[] findPets(@Query("species") String species, @Query("limit") int limit); Dynamic and multiple headers​ @Header (and @Query/@FormData/@Path) isn't limited to one header per parameter. Leave the name off (or use the explicit wildcard "*") and pass a Map, a HeaderList, or a bean — every entry or property is expanded into its own header: @Remote(path="/petstore") public interface PetStore { // Every map entry becomes its own header. @RemoteGet("/pets") Pet[] getPets(@Header("*") Map<String,Object> headers); // Same idea via a pre-built HeaderList... @RemoteGet("/pets") Pet[] getPetsViaHeaderList(@Header HeaderList headers); // ...or a bean whose properties become individual headers. @RemoteGet("/pets") Pet[] getPetsViaBean(@Header PetHeaders headers); } Map<String,Object> headers = JsonMap.of("X-Client-Id", "acme", "X-Trace-Id", UUID.randomUUID()); Pet[] pets = store.getPets(headers); This is a great way to forward a variable, caller-supplied set of headers (correlation IDs, feature flags, tenant context, etc.) without adding a new interface parameter every time one shows up. See @Header for the full list of supported dynamic forms. Request bodies (@Content) accept any serializable POJO, or raw Reader/InputStream: @RemotePost("/pets") Pet addPet(@Content CreatePet pet); Request beans (@Request) bundle several of the above behind one argument, so callers pass a single object instead of a long parameter list: @RemotePost String postPet(CreatePetRequest bean); @Request public class CreatePetRequest { @Content public CreatePet getContent() { ... } @Query public Map<String,Object> getQueryParams() { ... } @Header("E-Tag") public UUID getUUID() { ... } }

Return types are flexible — parsed POJOs, raw streams, async wrappers, or just the status code: @Remote(path="/petstore") public interface PetStore { @RemoteGet("/pets") Pet[] getPets(); // Parsed POJO @RemoteGet(path="/pets", returns=STATUS) int getPetsStatus(); // Just the HTTP status @RemoteGet("/pets") Future<Pet[]> getPetsAsync(); // Async @RemoteGet("/pets/{petId}") InputStream getPetRaw(@Path("petId") int petId); // Raw stream } See @RemoteOp for the complete list of supported return types. Response beans (@Response) do the same thing in reverse — bundle the body, headers, and status code of a response behind one typed object: @RemotePost CreatePetResponse postPet(@Content CreatePet pet); @Response public interface CreatePetResponse { @Content Pet getContent(); @Header("E-Tag") UUID getUUID(); @StatusCode int getStatus(); } Error handling happens automatically through checked exceptions. Declare a throws clause using any of the roughly 60 predefined HTTP response exceptions (or your own), and Juneau throws the matching one when the server returns that status code: @RemoteGet("/pets/{petId}") Pet getPet(@Path("petId") int petId) throws NotFound; try { Pet pet = store.getPet(999); } catch (NotFound e) { // HTTP 404 was returned - Juneau matched the status to the declared exception type. }

Default values let you specify fallbacks for null arguments right on the annotation, so callers don't have to pass every parameter every time: @RemoteGet("/pets") Pet[] getPets( @Header(name="Accept-Language", def="en-US") String language, @Query(name="limit", def="10") Integer limit ); // Uses default language="en-US" and limit=10. Pet[] pets = store.getPets(null, null); def is supported on @Header, @Query, @FormData, @Path, and @Content, at either the parameter or method level (parameter wins when both are set).

The same Java interface can define both the client proxy and the server implementation, so a signature change is caught by the compiler on both sides instead of drifting apart at runtime: @Remote(path="/petstore") public interface PetStore { @RemoteGet("/pet") Collection<Pet> getPets() throws NotAcceptable; } @Rest(path="/petstore") public class PetStoreResource extends BasicRestServlet implements PetStore { @Override @RestOp(method=GET, path="/pet") public Collection<Pet> getPets() throws NotAcceptable { return store.getPets(); } } See Dual-purpose (end-to-end) interfaces for the full walkthrough, including how parameter-level annotations like @Header and @Path are inherited from the interface for free. See Also @Remote - Interface-level configuration: base path, common headers, versioning. @RemoteOp - HTTP method/path mapping, naming-convention inference, return types. @Content - The request body. @FormData - Form post parameters. @Query - Query-string parameters. @Header - Request headers, including dynamic/multi-value forms. @Path - URL path variables. @Request - Bean-style bundling of request parts. @Response - Bean-style bundling of response parts. Dual-purpose (end-to-end) interfaces - Sharing one interface between client and server.

The REST/RPC (RPC over REST) API allows the creation of client-side remote proxy interfaces for calling methods on server-side POJOs using entirely REST. note This is not to be confused with REST Proxies which are entirely client-side driven Java interfaces against arbitrary backend REST interfaces.

The following example shows a remote interface built on the petstore sample's real Pet bean and PetStore service (juneau-petstore). (The petstore samples don't currently expose a remote interface via RRPC; this walkthrough builds one on top of those currently-shipping petstore types purely to illustrate the RRPC mechanism.) @RemoteInterface // Annotation is optional public interface IPetStore { Collection<Pet> getPets(); Pet getPet(long id); Pet createPet(Pet pet); Pet updatePet(Pet pet); void deletePet(long id); } The requirements for a remote interface method are: Must be public. Can be called anything. Can have any number of serializable and parsable parameters. Can return a serializable and parsable value. Can throw any Throwables. Throwables with public no-arg or single-arg-string constructors are automatically recreated on the client side when thrown on the server side.

note REST/RPC is a classic-client-only feature. It is implemented on org.apache.juneau.rest.client.classic.RestClient (the Apache HttpClient 4.5-based client); the next-generation, transport-agnostic NG REST client (org.apache.juneau.rest.client.RestClient) has no getRrpcInterface(...) method and no equivalent. If you're building against the NG client, use standard REST calls with the server-side @RestOp(method=RRPC)/RrpcServlet endpoints instead of a generated proxy. Remote Interface proxies are instantiated on the client side using one of the following methods: RestClientgetRrpcInterface(Class)getRrpcInterface(Class,Object)getRrpcInterface(Class,Object,Serializer,Parser) Since we build upon the existing classic RestClient API, we inherit all of it's features. For example, convenience methods for setting POJO filters and properties to customize the behavior of the serializers and parsers, and the ability to provide your own customized Apache HttpClient for handling various scenarios involving authentication and Internet proxies. Here's an example of the above interface being used: import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.classic.RestClient; // Create a classic RestClient using JSON for serialization, and point to the server-side remote interface servlet. RestClient client = RestClient.create() .json() .rootUrl("http://localhost:10000/remote") .build(); // Create a proxy interface. IPetStore petStore = client.getRrpcInterface(IPetStore.class); // Invoke a method on the server side and get the returned result. Pet pet = petStore.createPet( new Pet() .setName("Fluffy") .setSpecies(Species.CAT) .setPrice(200f) .setStatus(PetStatus.AVAILABLE) ); Under the covers, this method call gets converted to a REST POST. HTTP POST http://localhost:10000/remote/IPetStore/createPet(org.apache.juneau.petstore.dto.Pet) Accept: application/json Content-Type: application/json [ { "name":"Fluffy", "species":"CAT", "price":200.0, "status":"AVAILABLE" } ] Note that the body of the request is an array. This array contains the serialized arguments of the method. The object returned by the method is then serialized as the body of the response.

There are two ways to expose remote interfaces on the server side: Extending from RrpcServlet. Using a @RestOp(method=RRPC) annotation on a Java method. In either case, the proxy communications layer is pure REST. Therefore, in cases where the interface classes are not available on the client side, the same method calls can be made through pure REST calls. This can also aid significantly in debugging, since calls to the remote interface service can be made directly from a browser with no coding involved.

The RrpcServlet class is a simple specialized servlet with an abstract getServiceMap() method to define the server-side POJOs. Note that getServiceMap() maps each interface Class to a POJO instance that implements it — since the petstore's real PetStore service doesn't itself implement IPetStore, a small anonymous adapter delegates each IPetStore method to the underlying store: @Rest( path="/remote" ) public class SamplePetStoreRrpcServlet extends RrpcServlet { // Our server-side POJO. private final transient PetStore store = new PetStore(); @Override /* RrpcServlet */ protected Map<Class<?>,Object> getServiceMap() throws Exception { Map<Class<?>,Object> map = new LinkedHashMap<>(); // In this simplified example, we expose the same underlying store under two different interfaces. // One is IPetStore which only exposes methods defined on that interface, and // the other is PetStore itself which exposes all public methods defined on the class itself (dangerous!). map.put(IPetStore.class, new IPetStore() { @Override public Collection<Pet> getPets() { return store.getPets(); } @Override public Pet getPet(long id) { return store.getPet(id); } @Override public Pet createPet(Pet pet) { return store.createPet(pet); } @Override public Pet updatePet(Pet pet) { return store.updatePet(pet); } @Override public void deletePet(long id) { store.deletePet(id); } }); map.put(PetStore.class, store); return map; } }

The @RestOp(method=RRPC) approach is easier if you only have a single interface you want to expose. You simply define a Java method whose return type is an interface, and return the implementation of that interface: // Our exposed interface. @RestOp(method=RRPC, path="/petstoreproxy/*") public IPetStore getProxy() { return new IPetStore() { @Override public Collection<Pet> getPets() { return store.getPets(); } @Override public Pet getPet(long id) { return store.getPet(id); } @Override public Pet createPet(Pet pet) { return store.createPet(pet); } @Override public Pet updatePet(Pet pet) { return store.updatePet(pet); } @Override public void deletePet(long id) { store.deletePet(id); } }; }

If you point your browser to the servlet above, you get a list of available interfaces: http://localhost:10000/remote Clicking the hyperlinks on each shows you the list of methods that can be invoked on that service. Note that the IPetStore link shows that you can only invoke methods defined on that interface, whereas the PetStore link shows ALL public methods defined on that class.
http://localhost:10000/remote/IPetStore Only the five methods declared on the IPetStore interface are listed here.

http://localhost:10000/remote/PetStore Since this second entry maps the concrete PetStore class directly, every public method declared on PetStore — not just the five on IPetStore — is listed and invocable, including getOrders(), createOrder(Order), getUsers(), and the rest of the petstore service surface. This is why exposing a concrete class this way is dangerous in a real application; prefer exposing a narrow interface like IPetStore instead. Let's see how we can interact with this interface through nothing more than REST calls to get a better idea on how this works. We'll use the same method call as in the introduction. First, we need to create the serialized form of the arguments: Object[] args = new Object[] { new Pet() .setName("Fluffy") .setSpecies(Species.CAT) .setPrice(200f) .setStatus(PetStatus.AVAILABLE) }; String asJson = Json5Serializer.DEFAULT_READABLE.write(args); System.err.println(asJson); That produces the following JSON output: [ { name: 'Fluffy', species: 'CAT', price: 200.0, status: 'AVAILABLE' } ] Note that in this example we're using JSON. However, various other content types can also be used such as XML, URL-Encoding, UON, or HTML. In practice however, JSON will preferred since it is often the most efficient. Next, we can use a tool such as Poster to make the REST call. Methods are invoked by POSTing the serialized object array to the URI of the interface method. In this case, we want to POST our JSON to the following URL: http://localhost:10000/remote/IPetStore/createPet(org.apache.juneau.petstore.dto.Pet) Make sure that we specify the Content-Type of the body as text/json. We also want the results to be returned as JSON, so we set the Accept header to text/json as well. When we execute the POST, we should see the following successful response whose body contains the returned Pet bean serialized to JSON: From there, we could use the following code snippet to reconstruct the response object from JSON: String response = "output from above"; Pet pet = JsonParser.DEFAULT.read(response, Pet.class); RRPC methods are invoked with POST only. A browser link can't call them: GET .../getPets?method=POST is refused with 405, because the router never lets an override turn a GET into a POST. Use a client that can send a POST, for example curl: curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: text/json' -H 'Accept: text/json' -d '[]' http://localhost:10000/remote/IPetStore/getPets curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: text/json' -H 'Accept: text/json' -d '[3]' 'http://localhost:10000/remote/IPetStore/getPet(long)' The body is the JSON array of method arguments. The hyperlinks on the method names above lead you to a simple form-entry page where you can test passing parameters in UON notation as URL-encoded form posts.

Denial of service attacks can be alleviated through the maxInput() setting. Arbitrarily-large input will trigger an exception before causing out-of-memory errors. The default value for this setting is 100MB. Since the parsers do not use intermediate DOMs and instead parse directly into Java objects, deeply nested data structures will almost always trigger stack overflow errors long before memory consumption becomes an issue. However, this is NOT true of the RDF parsers, which build an intermediate DOM. If parsing RDF, you may want to consider lowering the max-input value above.

Juneau ships two request boundaries in org.apache.juneau.rest.server.filter. Both decide whether a state-changing request came from a page your application served (or from a non-browser client) and refuse it when it came from some other site's page. Neither one authenticates the caller, and neither proves the user meant the action; those need their own mechanisms. Boundary Use it when LoopbackBoundary The app is bound to the loopback interface and is reached under one pinned Host (for example 127.0.0.1:8790) over plain HTTP. It pins that single origin and is the stricter of the two. CsrfBoundary Everything else: an app reached under a real host name, over HTTPS, behind a proxy, or under more than one name. Nothing is pinned; the request's own scheme and host are the expected origin. Both are applied by RequestBoundaryFilter. A rejected request is answered directly with a JSON body, a Cache-Control: no-store header, and an X-Request-Boundary header naming the reason (for example ORIGIN_MISMATCH or CSRF_TOKEN_MISSING). The request never reaches application code. Even without a boundary, the router refuses an override of a safe method (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE) to an unsafe one with 405. A boundary still judges any custom-method claim as a write, including one declared @RestOp(read=true).

On every state-changing request (the method is judged after any ?method= or X-Method, X-HTTP-Method-Override, X-HTTP-Method or X-Method-Override override, so an override cannot carry a write past the checks): Origin, with Sec-Fetch-Site as a fallback, must match the request's own scheme, host and port. A literal null origin is refused. A browser request must also carry a synchronizer token in a request header (X-Csrf-Token by default). The token is read from that header and nowhere else: never a query parameter, never a form field. Origins are compared as normalized scheme, host and port. Default ports are equated (https://app.example.com and https://app.example.com:443 match). IPv6 literals are compared in bracketed form exactly as sent, and nothing else is re-canonicalized, so two spellings of the same address do not match each other. That is deliberate: it fails closed.

CsrfBoundary boundary = CsrfBoundary.create() .allowedHosts("app.example.com") .build(); servletContext.addFilter("csrf", new RequestBoundaryFilter(boundary)) .addMappingForUrlPatterns(EnumSet.of(DispatcherType.REQUEST), false, "/*"); Map the filter at /* so nothing can be reached around it. Register it for REQUEST dispatches only. An ERROR dispatch of a refused write can arrive without the token header and be refused in turn, replacing the error page with a 403, and a FORWARD to an HTML view looks like a page load and can create a session. The default registration in a servlet container, and Spring Boot's FilterRegistrationBean, is already REQUEST only. Register it ahead of any filter that acts on the request on the application's behalf. The one exception is described under proxies below. By default the filter creates an HTTP session on a safe request that looks like a page load, so that the page it serves can carry a session-scoped token. Turn that off with createSessions(false).

By default (OriginSource.HOST_HEADER) the request's own origin is request.getScheme() plus the Host header. X-Forwarded-* and Forwarded are never read, so a client cannot spoof them past the boundary. HTTP/2 has no Host header: the :authority pseudo-header plays that part, and servlet containers surface it only as getServerName() and getServerPort(). A request with no Host whose protocol is exactly HTTP/2.0 is therefore judged on its server name and port in Host's place, under both OriginSources and allowedHosts. A request without Host on any other protocol is still refused with HOST_MISSING. HOST_HEADER is consequently protocol-dependent: it reads the raw Host on HTTP/1.1 and the container's server name on HTTP/2, and the server name is what a container's forwarded-header support rewrites (Tomcat's RemoteIpValve with a host header, Spring's ForwardedHeaderFilter, Jetty's ForwardedRequestCustomizer). On HTTP/2 an X-Forwarded-Host that such support honors is therefore trusted under HOST_HEADER too. Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, the scheme the app sees is http while the browser's Origin is https. Use OriginSource.CONTAINER and configure the container's own forwarded-header support, so the container rewrites the request before the boundary sees it: Stack Setting Jetty Add a ForwardedRequestCustomizer to the connector's HttpConfiguration. Tomcat Add a RemoteIpValve. Spring Boot server.forward-headers-strategy=native rewrites before any filter runs, so filter order does not matter. Spring Boot server.forward-headers-strategy=framework registers ForwardedHeaderFilter at Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE. Register the boundary's filter strictly later, never at HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE itself. nginx proxy_set_header Host $host; and proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; The boundary cannot see its own filter order. A misordered or misconfigured deployment shows up as ORIGIN_MISMATCH refusals and a one-time warning in the log naming the likely cause (scheme-only or port-only mismatch). Enable a forwarded-header customizer only behind a proxy that overwrites, rather than appends to, X-Forwarded-*. A browser cannot send those headers, but anything that can reach the connector directly can, and the container then trusts the forwarded host.

A WebSocket upgrade is a GET, so the filter lets it through; the bus WebSocket endpoint applies the boundary to the handshake itself. BusWebSockets.register accepts a bus whose BusPolicy boundary is a LoopbackBoundary or a CsrfBoundary, and refuses to register for any other boundary type (it fails closed). Under a CsrfBoundary: No token can be sent on a handshake, so the control is Origin plus Sec-Fetch-Site. The container's checkOrigin hook runs first. A missing, blank or null Origin, or one that is not a well-formed http or https origin, is refused with HTTP 403 before the upgrade. A well-formed Origin that is cross-site, or does not match the handshake's own origin, is refused after the upgrade: the connection is closed with code 4403 before any frame is sent and before any bus session is touched. The handshake has no server name, so the check judges the raw Host header plus the scheme of the handshake's request URI, whatever OriginSource is set to. ws counts as http and wss as https. A WebSocket over HTTP/2 (RFC 8441, an extended CONNECT) has no Host. When a handshake carries neither Host nor Sec-WebSocket-Key or Upgrade (which mark an RFC 6455 request, and which the container enforces), the authority of its request URI, which is the :authority, stands in for Host. Jetty advertises RFC 8441 by default whenever HTTP/2 is enabled; Tomcat does not support it, so on Tomcat there is no HTTP/2 handshake to judge.
