Chrome templates that did not use <@console> A chrome template containing <@console> A <@page> whose chrome renders no <@console> fails the render. <@card type="js">, type="json", type="calendar" type="html" (body, template= or same-origin src=), type="datatables", or a type registered with JuneauConsole.registerCard The valid built-in types are html (the default) and datatables. A removed type fails the render. The calendar runtime is still available as the opt-in "calendar" toolkit pack. PageDef, Tab, Subtab, PageTable, CardGridTable, ViewCardBody and juneau-pages.js (org.apache.juneau.console.views) <@console> pages with <@navigation> nodes and <@card> directives ViewTable, RegionDef and RegionTable are kept. ViewSlot, RibbonAction (org.apache.juneau.console.views) Region and ribbon JSON handled by juneau-regions.js and juneau-views.js Deleted together with the deprecated Java view emitters. CalendarLayout, SavedViewsMixin, SavedViewStore, InMemorySavedViewStore, SavedViewQuotaException n/a CalendarLayout duplicated juneau-calendar.js. Keep saved views in your own endpoints, or use the browser-side localStorage persistence provider. ThemePack, ThemeSettings, ThemePackSettings, ConsoleChromeMixin.Builder.pack(...) / pageBackgroundImage(...) <@theme> / <@token> in the template (value= for leaves, alias= for live var() references); ConsoleChromeMixin.create().theme("<stock-name>") for the served chrome.css Theming is FTL-only. /juneau-console/assets/logo and /juneau-console/assets/page-bg endpoints The logo is a static chrome.css constant; the page background is the --jc-page-bg token Those paths now return 404 because no route exists. juneau-rest-server-theme-packs module <@theme name="..."> stock themes Remove the dependency. Top-level version key in the #juneau-page contract; PageContractAssert.hasVersion(String) contractVersion; hasContractVersion(String) Only affects code written against an earlier 10.0 snapshot. The value is unchanged ("1"). There is no fallback: the schema forbids version, and assertPage(...) throws if a contract still carries it. Server-rendered nav, header, footer and card wrappers in the HTML body window.JuneauConsole and PageContractAssert Tests that matched that HTML should parse the contract instead. // Before: assert against server-rendered chrome markup. assertTrue(body.contains("<nav")); // After: assert against the page contract. assertPage(body) .isValid() .hasActiveNav("releases") .hasCard("releases", "datatables") .hasFooterText("Apache Juneau Release Manager"); PageContractAssert lives in org.apache.juneau.console.test (module juneau-console). Template failures are reported as HTTP 500 with a message naming the directive and the fix; in the browser, an unusable contract shows a .jc-console-error banner and logs [juneau-console] ... instead of rendering a blank page. See Admin-Console Chrome for the contract schema, the authoring directives and ConsoleTemplateValidator.

The datatable View Settings dialog has these breaking changes. See Datatable View Settings for the new behavior. columnSearchToggle ribbon type removed. Delete { type: 'columnSearchToggle' } from ribbonFront/ribbon lists and templates (an unknown type is ignored silently, so the button just disappears). Per-column search is the search icon in each header cell. Delete any CSS that targets .juneau-view-columnsearch-*. schemaVersion is 2; readViewSettings returns {settings, reset}. Code that called NS.config.readViewSettings(...) and used the result directly must read .settings and may check .reset. Stored blobs at version 1, or with the old string-array sort, are discarded with a one-time notice; saved-view blobs at version 1 are rejected. NS.config.defaultSortMembership removed. Sort is an ordered list of {column, direction} entries. Options gains autoRefreshMs. Old blobs read as Off (0). Code that builds an Options object by hand should include it. isPollSuspended is also true while the dialog is open. A view with pausePollingWhileEditing now pauses polling while the View Settings dialog is open.

The following guide can be used to help migrate your code to v9.0. Note that you can also refer to the Release Notes for changes as well. Old New @RestMethod annotation. Has been replaced with RestOp, RestGet, RestPut, RestPost, RestDelete, RestOptions @RemoteMethod annotation. Has been replaced with RemoteOp, RemoteGet, RemotePut, RemotePost, RemoteDelete. BasicRestServletJena, BasicRestServletJenaGroup classes. These have been removed in 9.0 due to the removal of the Jena packages (due to security issues). Replace with BasicRestServlet and BasicRestServletGroup. @Body annotation. Has been renamed to @Content (to better match HTTP naming conventions such as Content-Type/Content-Encoding headers). @Query(_default), @FormData(_default). Has been renamed to Query.def / FormData.def. Note however that @RestOp-annotated parameters now also support use of Optional parameters which simplifies the coding of default values. @Rest(reqHeaders). Has been renamed to Rest.defaultRequestHeaders and added Rest.defaultResponseHeaders. @Rest(staticFiles). Changed from a string array to a Class<? extends StaticFiles>. If you're extending from BasicRestServlet/BasicRestResource, the getHtdoc() is already implemented for you (via the mixed-in HtdocMixin) to provide static files under the sub-URI /htdocs/. The newer StaticFilesMixin shares the same resolution logic under a configurable prefix (default /static/). The default implementation for finding static files is BasicStaticFiles which provides basic out-of-the-box functionality, so you can usually just remove the previous @Rest(staticFiles) value.

The @Value annotation (introduced in 10.0.0, package org.apache.juneau.commons.inject) is a declarative way to inject configuration values into beans created by BeanInstantiator — constructor parameters, setter parameters, and fields. It complements @Inject: @Inject requests a bean from the bean store by type. @Value requests a configuration value from Settings via the VarResolver.DEFAULT resolver. The two are mutually exclusive on the same injection site — applying both raises BeanCreationException.

Inside a @Value expression (or anywhere you can write SVL), ${key} is shorthand for ${P:key} — the PropertyVar that looks up a unified property by name from Settings. The shortcut also accepts a Spring-style default after a colon: ${some.key} — required key, missing → empty string ${some.key:fallback} — default-when-missing ${section/sub.key} — nested property names (Config sections, etc.) ${a.b:${other:none}} — nested expansion (defaults composed) This is purely surface syntax — the tokenizer rewrites ${...} to ${P:...} before resolution. Everything ${P:...} does (recursive resolution, default values, env-var fallback through chained sources) works identically with ${...}. See Simple Variable Language Basics and Variable Basics for the underlying mechanics.

For most @Value sites, resolution goes through the process-wide Settings.get(name) chain: Settings walks every registered PropertySource in reverse insertion order — the most-recently-added source wins. The default chain (built up at startup) looks like: PropertySourceProvider SPI sources added at process startup (e.g. classpath juneau.cfg via ConfigPropertySourceProvider). These register first and therefore sit at the bottom of the priority list. Per-microservice Config — org.apache.juneau.microservice.Microservice installs a ConfigPropertySource for its own Config in its constructor. Spring Environment bridge — when juneau-rest-server-springboot's SpringBeanStore is constructed, it installs a SpringEnvironmentPropertySource so ${spring.app.key} resolves against application.yaml, env vars, command-line args, and any custom Spring PropertySource. Built-in Settings sources — system properties, environment variables, .env file, argument list, JAR manifest entries. When the @Value site is on a bean that the REST runtime instantiates (resource bean fields, constructor parameters, request-scoped bean fields), the resolution order grows one tier — the resource's @Rest(config=...) Config participates between the Settings override layer and the chain above. Because all sources are checked, the same @Value expression resolves identically under a microservice, a Spring Boot app, or a bare REST resource — the origin of the value changes, the expression doesn't.

import org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.Value; public class MyResource { @Value("${myapp.title:Untitled}") private String title; @Value("${myapp.maxPageSize:50}") private int maxPageSize; } Settings.toType(...) coerces the resolved string to the target type. Coercion supports: Primitives and their boxed wrappers. java.time types (Instant, Duration, Period, LocalDate, etc.) — any type with a parse(CharSequence) or parse(String) static method. Optional<T> — Optional.empty() is injected when the key resolves to null or the empty string; otherwise Optional.of(coerced). Any type with a single-string-argument constructor.

@Value works on constructor parameters and on setter (and any method) parameters: public class JwtValidator { private final Duration ttl; public JwtValidator(@Value("${jwt.cache.ttl:PT5M}") Duration ttl) { this.ttl = ttl; } @Inject public void setKeyResolver(KeyResolver keys) { ... } // @Inject path — bean lookup public void setMaxClock(@Value("${jwt.clock.skew:PT30S}") Duration skew) { ... } }

Declaring a @Value field as Supplier<String> instead of String makes the SVL expression re-evaluate on every .get() call against a fresh VarResolverSession. No annotation flag is required — the field type IS the opt-in signal. public class JwtValidator { // String field: resolves ONCE at bean construction. Captures whatever Settings/PropertyVar // returned at injection time and holds that value for the bean's lifetime. @Value("${jwt.cache.ttl:PT5M}") String ttl; // Supplier<String> field: re-evaluates on every .get() call against a fresh session. // Picks up live Settings.set(...) updates, file-watch reloads, Spring env changes, etc. @Value("${jwt.cache.ttl:PT5M}") Supplier<String> liveTtl; } The returned Supplier is threadsafe — each .get() opens its own VarResolverSession, so it can be cached on shared fields or handed across threads. (Internally this delegates to VarTemplate.asSupplierWithFreshSessions(...).) Literal-only expressions (no variables) take a constant-folding fast path: the resolved string is captured once at compile time and every .get() returns the same cached value with no session overhead.

Combining the Supplier<String> field type with the #{...} function catalog produces concise live-factory patterns: // Request-ID factory — fresh UUID per request. @Value("#{uuid()}") Supplier<String> requestId; // Idempotency key for a downstream API — random per call. @Value("#{concat(ord-, #{randomString(12)})}") Supplier<String> idempotencyKey; // Jittered retry delay (ISO 8601 duration with 100–500ms jitter). @Value("PT0.#{randomInt(100, 500)}S") Supplier<String> retryDelayIso; // Live ISO timestamp on every call. @Value("#{now()}") Supplier<String> nowIso; // Hot-reload config — picks up Settings.set(...) without bean re-creation. @Value("${myapp.cache.policy:write-through}") Supplier<String> cachePolicy; See Simple Variable Language — the VarTemplate compiled-template API, which describes how VarResolver.resolveSupplier(...) pairs with @Value Supplier<String> fields for live-reload.

For consumers migrating from Spring Boot, org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value is detected by fully-qualified name (JsrSupport.SPRING_VALUE) — juneau-commons doesn't declare a compile-time dependency on Spring. The same resolution chain applies, so the following two beans are functionally identical inside a Juneau bean store: public class A { @org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.Value("${jwt.cache.ttl:PT5M}") Duration ttl; } public class B { @org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value("${jwt.cache.ttl:PT5M}") Duration ttl; }

Inside a Spring Boot application, SpringBeanStore automatically installs a SpringEnvironmentPropertySource the first time it's constructed (typically by SpringRestServlet.createBeanStore(...)). This means application.yaml keys are reachable from a Juneau @Value: # application.yaml myapp: title: My Awesome App cache: ttl: PT10M @Rest public class MyResource extends BasicSpringRestServlet { @Value("${myapp.title:Untitled}") private String title; @Value("${myapp.cache.ttl:PT5M}") private Duration cacheTtl; } The bridge is removed when SpringBeanStore.clear() is called — important for tests that build many transient Spring contexts in the same JVM.

When a REST resource declares @Rest(config="my.cfg"), the resolved Config is wired into the resource's BeanStore as a PropertySource bean named "rest.config". Any @Value("${some-key}") site on the resource bean (or on a request-scoped bean whose BeanStore parent-walks to the resource's) consults this scoped PropertySource between the Settings local/global overrides and the global Settings sources chain.

Settings.setLocal(...) / Settings.setGlobal(...) overrides — still win. The test override contract is preserved (overrides beat resource Configs). The resource's @Rest(config=...) Config(s) — via the per-BeanStore PropertySource bean. The process-wide Settings.get(name) chain — reverse-walks the registered sources from the resolution-order section above. The @Value default branch — the ${key:default} literal.

api.cfg on the classpath / cwd: api.key = secret-A api.url = https://a.example.org/ [section] nested = nested-value @Rest(config="api.cfg") public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet { @Value("${api.key}") // → "secret-A" String apiKey; @Value("${section/nested}") // → "nested-value" String nested; @Value("${unknown:fallback}") // → "fallback" (key absent, default used) String fallback; @Value("${java.home}") // → System property (falls through to Settings) String javaHome; }

Each RestContext carries its own BeanStore with its own "rest.config" bean. Resource A's @Value("${foo}") resolves against A.cfg, Resource B's @Value("${foo}") resolves against B.cfg — the two never see each other's Config. The same isolation extends to MockRestClient's static RestContext cache and to long-lived Spring Boot contexts because the registration lives on the per-resource BeanStore, not on the process-wide singleton.

When @Rest(config="parent.cfg") on ParentResource and @Rest(config="child.cfg") on ChildResource extends ParentResource declare different config names, the child's keys win on collision and the parent's keys fill the gaps: # parent.cfg parent.only = parent-value shared = parent-shared # child.cfg child.only = child-value shared = child-shared @Rest(config="parent.cfg") public class ParentResource extends BasicRestServlet { @Value("${parent.only}") String parentOnly; @Value("${shared}") String shared; } @Rest(config="child.cfg") public class ChildResource extends ParentResource {} A ChildResource instance sees child-value for child.only, parent-value for parent.only (child's Config doesn't define it — parent fills the gap), and child-shared for shared (child wins on collision).

The resource-scoped Config is consulted after the Settings override stores, so existing test fixtures that call Settings.get().setGlobal("api.key", "from-test") continue to take precedence over api.cfg — matching the established override contract.

@Value Supplier<String> field types compose with the resource-scoped chain: the BeanStore reference is captured (by-reference, not snapshotted) by the supplier, so every .get() call re-evaluates against the current state of the resource's PropertySources. This means hot- reload of the resource Config (or Settings.set(...) of an override key) takes effect on the next .get() call without rebuilding the resource bean.
documents.s: Supplier<String> re-evaluates against the scoped BeanStore

documents.t: The juneau-config module ships a META-INF/services entry for ConfigPropertySourceProvider. At startup, Settings.useServiceLoader() discovers the provider and registers a lazy bridge to Config.getSystemDefault(). The resolution is deferred to the first lookup so it can't trigger class-init cycles, and the bridge is silent when no classpath default juneau.cfg exists. This means a plain juneau.cfg on the classpath transparently feeds @Value("${section/key}") without any explicit wiring.

@Value and @Inject on the same field, parameter, or setter is an error: @Inject @Value("${some.key}") // BeanCreationException at injection time private String value; The exception message identifies the offending site to make the conflict easy to fix.

Simple Variable Language Basics — the full SVL surface, the #{...} function catalog, and the VarTemplate compiled-template API. SVL Variables — list of built-in ${X:...} resolvers. Variable Basics — how variables work inside a Config. org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.Value org.apache.juneau.commons.settings.Settings org.apache.juneau.commons.svl.vars.PropertyVar org.apache.juneau.commons.svl.VarTemplate org.apache.juneau.rest.server.springboot.SpringEnvironmentPropertySource

This page documents the framework-internal sites that read configuration through the @Value seam (introduced in 10.0.0). It is a reference for users who: Used to import the deleted CallLogger.SP_xxx constants directly. Want to know which framework defaults are now @Value-driven (and therefore overridable through the standard Settings precedence chain — system properties, environment variables, registered PropertySources, and Settings.setGlobal(...)).

In 10.0.0, the following framework-internal config readers were rewritten on top of the @Value annotation and BeanInstantiator: Class Field / Property Inline expression RestContext env-driven defaults for uriAuthority, uriContext (Optional<String>-typed; null-vs-empty preserved) ${RestContext.uriAuthority} / ${RestContext.uriContext} RestOpContext env-driven defaults for defaultCharset, maxInput ${RestContext.defaultCharset:UTF-8} / ${RestContext.maxInput:100000000} VersionProvider.Builder javaVersionDefault ${java.version:Unknown} Microservice.Builder juneau.workingDir ${juneau.workingDir} (via @Inject initializer) JettyServerComponent availablePort, juneau.serverPort ${availablePort} / ${juneau.serverPort} (Optional<String> fields) JwtTokenValidator.Builder jwksCacheTtl ${juneau.jwt.jwksCacheTtl:PT5M} JwtTokenValidator.Builder jwksEagerRefreshOnKidMiss ${juneau.jwt.jwksEagerRefreshOnKidMiss:true} JwtTokenValidator.Builder jwksEagerRefreshCooldown ${juneau.jwt.jwksEagerRefreshCooldown:PT10S} BctConfiguration.Defaults sortMaps, sortCollections concat-form: ${" + BCT_SORT_MAPS + ":false} / ${" + BCT_SORT_COLLECTIONS + ":false} Every one of these sites used to call env(...) or System.getProperty(...) directly. The new flow routes through BeanInstantiator and inherits the standard Settings lookup chain documented in @Value Annotation Basics. 10.0.0 update — most RestContext.* sites moved to @ConfigProperties The 14 other RestContext.*-prefixed sites (allowedHeaderParams, allowedMethodHeaders, allowedMethodParams, disableContentParam, renderResponseStackTraces, problemDetails, virtualThreads, responseTraceparent, mdcAsyncPropagation, eagerInit, lazyChildren, clientVersionHeader, uriRelativity, uriResolution) were collapsed in 10.0.0 into a single @ConfigProperties-bound bean, RestContextProperties — see @ConfigProperties Annotation Basics and the RestContext topic page. Only uriAuthority and uriContext (the table rows above) remain plain @Value fields on RestContext. (The REST debug/logging redesign separately removed RestContext.debugDefault entirely — see Logging / Debugging — so it is no longer one of these sites at all.)

The four builders that did not previously flow through BeanInstantiator now do, via a small static factory that hands the builder off to BeanInstantiator.of(Builder.class).run(): public static Builder create(BeanStore beanStore) { return BeanInstantiator.of(Builder.class, beanStore).run(); } Builders affected: VersionProvider, Microservice, JwtTokenValidator, plus the static-utility nested class BctConfiguration.Defaults. The BctConfiguration.BCT_SORT_MAPS and BCT_SORT_COLLECTIONS constants on that class were kept — they are part of the public BCT API and have external production consumers; they're now referenced from @Value annotations via concat form. For classes that are not constructed through BeanInstantiator (because they're built by the framework — RestContext, RestOpContext, JettyServerComponent), the constructor / lifecycle hook calls ClassInfo.of(this).inject(this, beanStore) after the bean store is populated, which performs the same @Value field injection on the existing instance.

The mergeReplacedStringAttribute precedence inside RestContext — where @Rest annotation values from the resource hierarchy override the env-driven default if non-blank — is unchanged. The DefaultConfig class (whose @Rest(...) defaults pull from ${S:j.<name>: ${E:J_<NAME>:<fallback>}} SVL chains) still wins over the new @Value field for properties whose DefaultConfig fallback is non-blank. The @Value-driven default only takes effect in the same situations the previous env(...) default did.

The Microservice API incorporates the Simple Variable Language API. For the default resolver and its built-in variables, see VarResolver.DEFAULT. The variable resolver can be augmented through the following methods: Microservice.Buildervars(Class...)varBean(Class,Object) A typical usage pattern is shown below: // $A used in variable resolver. VarResolver varResolver = Microservice.getInstance().getVarResolver(); System.out.println(varResolver.resolve("Main class is set to ${MF:Main-Class: unknown}")); The variable resolver becomes much more powerful when used in REST resource annotations which will be described later in juneau-microservice-jetty. It supports the variables listed in VarResolver.DEFAULT plus ${C:key[:default]} (ConfigVar) for the microservice configuration. note Juneau 10.0.0 removed the 11 transformation/conditional $Var{...}-style variables (the pre-10.0 syntax) that previously lived here (IfVar, SwitchVar, CoalesceVar, PatternMatchVar, PatternReplaceVar, PatternExtractVar, UpperCaseVar, LowerCaseVar, NotEmptyVar, LenVar, SubstringVar) and replaced them with the #{name(args...)} function-call syntax — see #{...} Function-call Syntax for the current equivalents (e.g. #{if(...)}, #{switch(...)}, #{upper(...)}, #{lower(...)}).
VarResolver.DEFAULT Simple Variable Language

The main class for performing variable resolution is VarResolver. A resolver holds a set of Var classes and context objects, and replaces each ${X:key} in a string with the value its variable produces.

Use your own VarResolver when you need variables beyond the defaults, or variables that depend on application objects such as a Config. For plain ${S:...} and ${E:...} lookups, the shared VarResolver.DEFAULT is enough. Resolvers are immutable; to add variables, copy an existing one with copy() and build the copy.

import org.apache.juneau.commons.svl.*; public class VarResolverExample { // A bean that a variable can look up through the session. public static class Greeting { public String text = "Hello"; } // The ${G:name} variable reads the Greeting bean from the session. public static class GreetingVar extends SimpleVar { public GreetingVar() { super("G"); } @Override public String resolve(VarResolverSession session, String key) { return session.getBean(Greeting.class).map(g -> g.text).orElse("Hi") + ", " + key; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { // Copy the default resolver (which has $S and $E), add $G, and register the bean for all sessions. VarResolver resolver = VarResolver.DEFAULT .copy() .vars(GreetingVar.class) .bean(Greeting.class, new Greeting()) .build(); System.out.println(resolver.resolve("${G:World}! Java is ${S:java.specification.version}.")); // A session can override a bean for one resolution only. Greeting formal = new Greeting(); formal.text = "Good day"; System.out.println(resolver.createSession().bean(Greeting.class, formal).resolve("${G:World}")); } } Two methods are provided for resolving variables: VarResolverresolve(String)resolveTo(String,Writer)

Var resolvers can rely on the existence of other objects. For example, ConfigVar relies on the existence of a Config. This is accomplished through the following methods: VarResolver.Builderbean(Class<T>, T) - Specify a bean for all sessions.VarResolverSessionbean(Class<T>, T) - Specify a bean for this session. Beans are accessible through the following method: VarResolverSession.getBean(Class) Builder method Effect defaultVars() Add the default variables ($S, $E and the others). VarResolver.DEFAULT already has them. vars(Class...) / vars(Var...) Add variable classes or instances. functions(...) / defaultFunctions() Add #{...} functions; see Simple Variable Language. bean(Class, T) Register a bean that variables read through the session. build() Create the resolver. Var resolvers can be cloned and extended by using the VarResolver.copy() method. Cloning a resolver will copy it's Var class names and context objects.
Marshall Simple Variable Language SVL Variables VarResolver.DEFAULT Simple Variable Language

Config files can contain variables that get resolved dynamically using the previously-described VarResolver API. See the guide: Externalize config with INI/YAML and variables Example #-------------------------- # My section #-------------------------- [MySection] # A system property locale = ${S:java.locale: en_US} # An environment variable path = ${E:PATH: unknown} # Another value in this config file anotherLocale = ${C:MySection/locale} # Look for system property, or env var if that doesn't exist, or a default value if that doesn't exist. nested = ${S:mySystemProperty:${E:MY_ENV_VAR:${C:MySection/anotherLocale}}} # A POJO with embedded variables aBean = {foo:'${S:foo}',baz:${C:MySection/anInt}} Config config = Config.create().build(); Locale locale = config.get("MySection/locale").as(Locale.class).orElse(null); String path = config.get("MySection/path").asString().orElse(null); String anotherLocale = config.get("MySection/anotherLocale").asString().orElse(null); ABean bean = config.get("MySection/aBean").as(ABean.class).orElse(null); By default, Configs use the VarResolver.DEFAULT variable resolver which provides support for the following variables and constructs: SystemPropertiesVar - ${S:key[:default]}EnvVariablesVar - ${E:key[:default]}ConfigVar - ${C:key[:default]} The variable resolver is controlled via the following setting: Config.BuildervarResolver(VarResolver) Additionally, the following method can be used to retrieve a Config with a different variable resolver: Configresolving(VarResolverSession)

View-based projection lets you define named views — property subsets — on a bean and choose which view is active per serialize/parse call. Only the properties belonging to the active view are emitted on serialization; on parsing, out-of-view properties are silently discarded (or rejected, depending on your unknown-property policy). This is the Juneau equivalent of Jackson's @JsonView / MapperFeature.DEFAULT_VIEW_INCLUSION.

Use the @MarshalledProp(view) member to tag a property with one or more string view names: public class Person { // Untagged — visible in every view (default policy). public String id; // Visible only when the "summary" view is active. @MarshalledProp(view = "summary") public String name; // Visible only when the "detail" view is active. @MarshalledProp(view = "detail") public String description; // Visible in EITHER "summary" OR "detail" (union semantics). @MarshalledProp(view = {"summary", "detail"}) public String email; } View names are plain strings. No marker-class hierarchy is required.

Call activeView(String) on any serializer or parser builder to set a context-level default: // Serialize with the "summary" view. var s = Json5Serializer.DEFAULT.copy().activeView("summary").build(); s.write(new Person()); // → {id:'1',name:'Alice',email:'alice@example.com'} To override the view for a single call without rebuilding the serializer, use activeView(String) on a session: var session = serializer.createSession().activeView("detail").build(); session.write(new Person()); // → {description:'A person',email:'alice@example.com',id:'1'} Passing null clears the active view for that session, making all view-tagged properties visible again.
documents.s: Activating a view on a serializer or parser

documents.t: When an active view is set, untagged properties are included by default — this matches Jackson's MapperFeature.DEFAULT_VIEW_INCLUSION default and the principle of least surprise: only explicitly-tagged properties become view-restricted. To flip the policy so that only tagged properties are visible, call disableDefaultViewInclusion(): // Strict mode: only tagged properties appear. var s = Json5Serializer.DEFAULT.copy() .activeView("summary") .disableDefaultViewInclusion() .build(); s.write(new Person()); // → {email:'alice@example.com',name:'Alice'} (id omitted — it was untagged)

Flat string names. No class-hierarchy inheritance; a view named "summary" has no relationship to any other view. Union membership. A property tagged {A, B} is visible whenever the active view is A or B. There is no intersection requirement. No active view = all properties visible. If no activeView() is set (or it is set to null), the feature is off and every property is serialized as normal.

If you cannot annotate a class directly (third-party, generated, or sealed), apply view membership via the @MarshalledPropApply *Config mechanism: // Config annotation — does not require modifying ThirdPartyBean. @MarshalledPropApply(on = "ThirdPartyBean.name", value = @MarshalledProp(view = "summary")) @MarshalledPropApply(on = "ThirdPartyBean.description", value = @MarshalledProp(view = "detail")) public static class ThirdPartyBeanViewConfig {} // Apply the config when building the serializer. var s = Json5Serializer.DEFAULT.copy() .applyAnnotations(ThirdPartyBeanViewConfig.class) .activeView("summary") .build();

When parsing, properties that are not in the active view are treated as unknown properties. By default Juneau silently discards unknown properties, so out-of-view input is quietly ignored: var p = Json5Parser.DEFAULT.copy().activeView("summary").build(); // description is not in the "summary" view → ignored (default behavior). Person person = p.read("{id:'1',name:'Alice',description:'ignored'}", Person.class); To make out-of-view input throw an exception, disable the unknown-property tolerance with ignoreUnknownBeanProperties(false): var p = Json5Parser.DEFAULT.copy() .activeView("summary") .ignoreUnknownBeanProperties(false) // strict: out-of-view input throws .build(); p.read("{id:'1',description:'oops'}", Person.class); // throws ParseException

When multiple property-control mechanisms interact, the precedence is: @MarshalledIgnore / @BeanIgnore — hard exclude (wins over everything). readOnly / writeOnly — direction filter. Active view — membership filter. beanProperties / beanPropertiesExcludes — further narrowing. Swaps / value-level inclusion knobs — applied to surviving properties. Views and beanProperties* compose by intersection: a property must pass both filters to appear.

View selection lives in MarshallingContext / BeanPropertyMeta — the bean model layer — not in any format-specific serializer. The same activeView() call produces consistent projection across JSON, XML, HTML, MsgPack, YAML, and every other Juneau format.

Jackson Juneau @JsonView(MyView.class) on a property @MarshalledProp(view = "MyView") @JsonView({A.class, B.class}) @MarshalledProp(view = {"A", "B"}) objectMapper.writerWithView(MyView.class).writeValue(...) serializer.createSession().activeView("MyView").build().write(...) objectMapper.readerWithView(MyView.class).readValue(...) parser.createSession().activeView("MyView").build().read(...) MapperFeature.DEFAULT_VIEW_INCLUSION = true (default) default — untagged properties included MapperFeature.DEFAULT_VIEW_INCLUSION = false serializer.copy().activeView(...).disableDefaultViewInclusion().build() Marker-class view tokens (class SummaryView {}) Not needed — Juneau uses plain strings View inheritance (class DetailView extends SummaryView) No equivalent — Juneau views are flat names; list both: view = {"summary", "detail"}

By default, interface proxies are enabled, which allows the Juneau parsers to parse content into virtual beans (bean interfaces without implementation classes). Calling MarshallingContext.Builder.disableInterfaceProxies() turns this behavior off. For example, the following code creates an instance of the specified unimplemented interface: // Our unimplemented interface public interface Address { String getStreet(); void setStreet(String value); String getCity(); void setCity(String value); StateEnum getState(); void setState(StateEnum value); int getZip(); void setZip(int value); } // Our code Address address = Json.to( "{street:'123 Main St', city:'Anywhere', state:'PR', zip:12345}", Address.class ); int zip = address.getZip(); address.setState(StateEnum.NY); Getter and setter values can be any parsable values, even other virtual beans. Under-the-covers, a virtual bean is simply a proxy interface on top of an existing BeanMap instance. From a programmatic point-of-view, they're indistinguishable from real beans, and can be manipulated and serialized like any other bean. Virtual beans can also be created programmatically using the MarshallingContext class: Address address = MarshallingContext.DEFAULT.createSession().build().newBean(Address.class);

Apache Juneau™ combines a marshalling core with no required external dependencies, REST servers and clients that share one set of annotations, and in-process testing. Here's why developers choose Juneau over alternatives.

The juneau-marshall core needs only juneau-commons. A REST service adds the Jetty microservice bundle. Import the BOM once and leave versions off; see Install Juneau, and Framework Comparisons for how this compares. Juneau: <dependencyManagement> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-bom</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> <type>pom</type> <scope>import</scope> </dependency> </dependencies> </dependencyManagement> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-microservice-jetty-bundle</artifactId> <type>pom</type> </dependency> </dependencies> Alternative (Spring Boot + Jackson + Swagger): <dependency> <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId> <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId> <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId> <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui</artifactId> </dependency> <!-- Plus many more dependencies -->

Juneau provides a single, consistent API for serializing to multiple formats: // One API, multiple formats Person person = new Person("John", 30); // JSON String json = Json.of(person); // XML String xml = Xml.of(person); // HTML String html = Html.of(person); // URL-Encoding String urlEnc = UrlEncoding.of(person); // ...and the rest of the 38 formats With alternatives, you need different libraries and APIs for each format.

Juneau automatically generates Swagger documentation from your POJOs and annotations: @Rest(title="User API", description="User management service") public class UserResource extends BasicRestServlet { @RestGet("/users/{id}") public User getUser(@Path("id") String id) { return userService.findById(id); } @RestPost("/users") public User createUser(@Content User user) { return userService.create(user); } } Result: Swagger UI at /swagger with full API documentation, request/response schemas, and interactive testing. The Swagger v2 document is at /api and OpenAPI 3.1 at /openapi.

Create type-safe client interfaces that feel like local method calls: // juneau-rest-client (org.apache.juneau.rest.client.RestClient) @Remote("http://api.example.com") public interface UserService { @RemoteGet("/users/{id}") User getUser(@Path("id") String id); @RemotePost("/users") User createUser(@Content User user); } // Use like a regular Java interface UserService service = RestClient.builder().build().remote(UserService.class); User user = service.getUser("123"); No more manual HTTP client code, JSON parsing, or error handling. This uses juneau-rest-client, the recommended REST client. The Apache HttpClient-based juneau-rest-client-classic stays supported for existing users; see Choosing a REST Client.

Test REST APIs without starting servers or containers: @Test public void testUserAPI() throws Exception { try (MockRestClient mock = MockRestClient.create(UserResource.class); var resp = mock.get("/users/123").run()) { resp.assertThat().isOk().body().contains("John"); } } Fast, reliable tests with no server or network.

Juneau 10 introduces a low-level streaming API for processing large datasets without buffering the entire document: // Stream a large JSON5L (JSON5 Lines) file record-by-record — O(1) memory try (RecordReader r = Json5l.DEFAULT.readRecords(inputStream)) { while (r.canRead()) process(r.read(Person.class)); } // Fine-grained structural token cursor (JSON, CBOR, MsgPack) try (TokenReader r = Json.DEFAULT.readTokens(inputStream)) { while (r.next() != TokenType.END_OF_STREAM) { switch (r.getCurrentToken()) { case FIELD_NAME -> System.out.print(r.getFieldName() + " = "); case VALUE_STRING -> System.out.println(r.getString()); default -> { /* structural token, e.g. START_OBJECT/END_OBJECT */ } } } } RecordReader/RecordWriter work across every Juneau format; TokenReader/TokenWriter add fine-grained structural events for token-shaped formats (JSON family, CBOR, MsgPack). Both are first-class @RestOp parameter types, so REST endpoints can stream large responses directly to the client without intermediate buffering. With alternatives, large-dataset streaming requires format-specific libraries and manual integration.

Each point links to the matching section of Framework Comparisons, which states the evidence. Formats. 38 formats (26 in juneau-marshall, 12 RDF in juneau-marshall-rdf) through one API: JSON, XML, HTML, YAML, CSV, MessagePack, MarkdownDoc and more. juneau-marshall covers the core formats and juneau-marshall-rdf the RDF ones, where Jackson adds a jackson-dataformat-* module per format. See Juneau vs Jackson. REST and API docs built in. Jackson is a data-binding library, not a REST framework. Spring Boot adds OpenAPI through an add-on such as SpringDoc, and JAX-RS through a separate library such as MicroProfile OpenAPI; Juneau generates it from @Rest and @RestOp. See Spring Boot and JAX-RS. Content negotiation from one method. One Juneau method answers JSON, XML, HTML and the other registered formats based on Accept. Spring needs separate methods or HttpMessageConverter configuration per format; JAX-RS supports it through @Produces/@Consumes, with format-specific handling done by hand. See Spring Boot and JAX-RS. Testing without a server. MockRestClient calls a resource in-process. Spring uses @SpringBootTest/@WebMvcTest or embedded containers; for JAX-RS it depends on the implementation and its test tooling. See Spring Boot. Annotations, not a container. Juneau and Spring are both annotation-based. JAX-RS is a specification that needs an implementation such as Jersey or RESTEasy. Juneau resources can also run inside Spring Boot. See JAX-RS.

Consistent APIs: Same patterns across serialization, REST services, and testing Built-in Documentation: Automatic Swagger generation reduces documentation maintenance Content Security Policy: First-class CSP header support with per-request nonce injection (10.0+), protecting the HTML UI and Swagger UI against XSS with a single opt-in setting
Flexible Deployment: Works with any Jakarta Servlet 6.1 container, embedded Jetty, or embedded Tomcat Easy Testing: MockRestClient enables comprehensive testing without external services

Rapid Prototyping: A running REST API in about 10 minutes: see Getting Started Automatic Documentation: Swagger UI generated automatically from your code Content Negotiation: Support multiple formats with no per-format setup Type Safety: Compile-time checking for REST client interfaces MCP Support: juneau-rest-server-mcp (revision-neutral core) plus the juneau-rest-server-mcp-v20260728 (current) and juneau-rest-server-mcp-v20250618 adapters expose any @Rest resource as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint, enabling LLM tool-calling with no additional framework — client-side MCP support (juneau-rest-client-mcp and its revision adapters) is also available
This is guidance, not a measurement; for the feature-by-feature comparison see Framework Comparisons.

Multi-format APIs: When you need to support JSON, XML, HTML, and other formats Rapid Development: When you want to build APIs quickly without complex configuration Microservices: When you need lightweight services on embedded Jetty or Tomcat Testing: When you want comprehensive testing without external dependencies Documentation: When you need automatic API documentation generation Learning: When you want to understand REST APIs without framework complexity

Heavy Spring Ecosystem: You're already deeply invested in Spring Boot's ecosystem Complex Enterprise Features: You need advanced enterprise features like distributed transactions Large Team: Your team has extensive experience with other frameworks Legacy Integration: You need to integrate with existing Spring-based systems
Getting Started builds and runs a REST app in about 10 minutes.

Documentation: Comprehensive guides and examples at juneau.apache.org Examples: Working code examples in the juneau-examples repository Community: Join discussions on the Apache Juneau mailing list Issues: Report bugs and request features on GitHub Issues

Juneau offers an alternative to assembling several libraries. It provides a unified API for serialization, REST services, and testing, on a marshalling core with no required dependencies, so developers can focus on business logic rather than framework configuration. Still not convinced? Check out our Framework Comparisons page for detailed technical comparisons, or explore our comprehensive examples to see Juneau in action.

The @Marshalled(typeName) annotation can be used to override the Juneau default name on bean elements. Types names serve two distinct purposes: To override the element name. To serve as a class identifier so that the bean class can be inferred during parsing if it cannot automatically be inferred through reflection. Example Data type JSON example Without annotation With annotation @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { public String a; public int b; } { a: 'foo', b: 123 } foo 123 On bean properties, a _type attribute will be added if a type name is present and the bean class cannot be inferred through reflection. In the following example, a type attribute is used on property 'b' but not property 'a' since 'b' is of type Object and therefore the bean class cannot be inferred. Example Java Without annotation With annotation class MyBean { public BeanX a = new BeanX(); public Object b = new BeanX(); } @Marshalled(typeName="X") class BeanX { public String fx = "foo"; } info string, number, boolean, object, array, and null are reserved keywords that cannot be used as type names. Beans with type names are often used in conjunction with the @Marshalled(dictionary) and @MarshalledProp(dictionary) annotations so that the beans can be resolved at parse time. These annotations are not necessary during serialization but are needed during parsing in order to resolve the bean types. The following examples show how type names are used under various circumstances. Pay special attention to when _type attributes are and are not used. Example Java XML @Marshalled(dictionary={BeanX.class}) class BeanWithArrayPropertiesWithTypeNames { public BeanX[] b1 = new BeanX[]{ new BeanX() }; public Object[] b2 = new BeanX[]{ new BeanX() }; public Object[] b3 = new Object[]{ new BeanX() }; } @Marshalled(dictionary={BeanX.class}) class BeanWith2dArrayPropertiesWithTypeNames { public BeanX[][] b1 = new BeanX[][]{{ new BeanX() }}; public Object[][] b2 = new BeanX[][]{{ new BeanX() }}; public Object[][] b3 = new Object[][]{{ new BeanX() }}; } @Marshalled(dictionary={BeanX.class}) class BeanWithMapPropertiesWithTypeNames { public Map b1 = new HashMap<>() {{ put("k1", new BeanX()); }}; public Map b2 = new HashMap<>() {{ put("k2", new BeanX()); }}; } Bean type names are also used for resolution when abstract fields are used. The following examples show how they are used in a variety of circumstances. Example Java XML @Marshalled(dictionary={A.class}) class BeanWithAbstractFields { public A a = new A(); public IA ia = new A(); public AA aa = new A(); public Object o = new A(); } interface IA {} abstract class AA implements IA {} @Marshalled(typeName="A") class A extends AA { public String fa = "foo"; } @Marshalled(dictionary={A.class}) class BeanWithAbstractArrayFields { public A[] a = new A[]{new A()}; public IA[] ia1 = new A[]{new A()}; public IA[] ia2 = new IA[]{new A()}; public AA[] aa1 = new A[]{new A()}; public AA[] aa2 = new AA[]{new A()}; public Object[] o1 = new A[]{new A()}; public Object[] o2 = new Object[]{new A()}; } @Marshalled(dictionary={A.class}) class BeanWithAbstractMapFields { public Map a = new HashMap<>() {{ put("k1", new A()); }}; public Map b = new HashMap<>() {{ put("k2", new A()); }}; public Map c = new HashMap<>() {{ put("k3", new A()); }}; } @Marshalled(dictionary={A.class}) class BeanWithAbstractMapArrayFields { public Map a = new LinkedHashMap<>() {{ put("a1", new A[]{new A()}); }}; public Map ia = new LinkedHashMap<>() {{ put("ia1", new A[]{new A()}); put("ia2", new IA[]{new A()}); }}; public Map aa = new LinkedHashMap<>() {{ put("aa1", new A[]{new A()}); put("aa2", new AA[]{new A()}); }}; public Map o = new LinkedHashMap<>() {{ put("o1", new A[]{new A()}); put("o2", new AA[]{new A()}); }}; } On a side note, characters that cannot be represented in XML 1.0 are encoded using a simple encoding. Note in the examples below, some characters such as ' ', ' ', and ' ' can be represented as XML entities when used in text but not in element names. Other characters such as ' ' and ' ' cannot be encoded in XML 1.0 at all without inventing our own notation. Whitespace characters in element names are encoded as well as whitespace end characters in text. Example Java XML class BeanWithSpecialCharacters { public String a = " "; } @Marshalled(typeName=" ") class BeanWithNamesWithSpecialCharacters { @MarshalledProp(name=" ") public String a = " "; } <_x0020__x0020__x0008__x000C__x000A__x0009__x000D__x0020__x0020_> <_x0020__x0020__x0008__x000C__x000A__x0009__x000D__x0020__x0020_> _x0020_ _x0008__x000C_ _x0020_ While it's true that these characters CAN be represented in XML 1.1, it's impossible to parse XML 1.1 text in Java without the XML containing an XML declaration. Unfortunately, this, and the uselessness of the XMLInputFactory.IS_REPLACING_ENTITY_REFERENCES setting in Java forced us to make some hard design decisions that may not be the most elegant.

The @Xml(format) annotation tweaks how a POJO is rendered in XML. Its value is one of the enum constants defined in XmlFormat, and it can be applied to both bean classes and individual bean properties. At the class level, a format changes the default treatment of every property on the bean (for example, rendering all properties as attributes). At the property level, a format changes the treatment of that one property (for example, promoting a single property to an XML attribute or flattening a collection into the parent element). Property-level formats override class-level defaults, so the two levels can be combined.

The table below summarizes every XmlFormat value and where each is documented in detail. Because the formats fall into a handful of related families, the worked examples are organized by family across the pages listed in the last column. Value Applies to Summary Documented in DEFAULT Class & property Normal formatting. On a class it behaves like FREEFORM; on a property it behaves like ELEMENT. This is the behavior when no @Xml(format) is specified. — ATTR Property Render a property as an XML attribute instead of a child element. Attribute Formats ATTRS Class & property On a class, render all properties as attributes; on a Map property, render arbitrary attributes from the map entries. Attribute Formats ELEMENT Property Render a property as a child element, overriding an ATTRS default set on the class. Attribute Formats COLLAPSED Property Serialize the members of an array/collection directly inside the bean element, without an enclosing wrapper. Collapsed Format FREEFORM Property Serialize free-form child elements. All other properties on the bean must be attributes. Element & Mixed Formats MIXED Property Like FREEFORM, but element names are stripped from primitive values to produce mixed content. Element & Mixed Formats MIXED_PWS Property Same as MIXED, but whitespace in text nodes is preserved during parsing. Element & Mixed Formats TEXT Property Render a single value as the text content of the element. Text Formats TEXT_PWS Property Same as TEXT, but whitespace in the text node is preserved during parsing. Text Formats XMLTEXT Property Like TEXT, but the string is treated as fully-formed XML and serialized as-is. Text Formats VOID Class Marks an element that never contains content (e.g. HTML
). Affects how empty elements are collapsed by the HTML serializer. —

The remaining @Xml(format) pages document each family with worked before/after examples: Attribute Formats — ATTR, ATTRS, and ELEMENT for moving values between attributes and elements. Collapsed Format — COLLAPSED for flattening arrays and collections into the bean element. Element & Mixed Formats — FREEFORM, MIXED, and MIXED_PWS for free-form and mixed content. Text Formats — TEXT, TEXT_PWS, and XMLTEXT for text-node and raw-XML content. Whitespace Handling — how empty strings and whitespace are preserved (or lost) across the MIXED and TEXT families.

The attribute-oriented XmlFormat values move bean-property values between XML attributes and child elements: XmlFormat.ATTR promotes a single property to an attribute. XmlFormat.ATTRS makes a whole bean render its properties as attributes, or lets a single Map property contribute arbitrary attributes. XmlFormat.ELEMENT forces a property back to a child element, overriding an ATTRS default applied to the class.

The XmlFormat.ATTR format can be applied to bean properties to serialize them as XML attributes instead of elements. Note that this only supports properties of simple types (e.g. strings, numbers, booleans). Data type JSON example Without annotation With annotation class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.ATTR) public String a; } { a: 'foo' }
documents.s: Rendering a property as an attribute — ATTR

documents.t: The XmlFormat.ATTRS format can be applied to bean classes to force all bean properties to be serialized as XML attributes instead of child elements. Data type JSON example Without annotation With annotation @Xml(format=XmlFormat.ATTRS) class MyBean { public String a; public int b; } { a: 'foo', b: 123 }
documents.s: Rendering all properties as attributes — ATTRS

documents.t: The XmlFormat.ELEMENT format can be applied to bean properties to override the XmlFormat.ATTRS format applied on the bean class. Data type JSON example Without annotation With annotation @Xml(format=XmlFormat.ATTRS) class MyBean { public String a; @Xml(format=XmlFormat.ELEMENT) public int b; } { a: 'foo', b: 123 }

The XmlFormat.ATTRS format can also be applied to a single bean property of type Map to denote arbitrary XML attribute values on the element. These can be mixed with other XmlFormat.ATTR annotated properties but there must not be an overlap in bean property names and map keys. Data type JSON example Without annotation With annotation class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.ATTRS) public Map a; @Xml(format=XmlFormat.ATTR) public int b; } { a: { k1: 'foo', k2: 123 }, b: 456 }
documents.s: Arbitrary attributes from a Map — ATTRS

documents.t: @Xml(format) Annotation for the full list of XmlFormat values. Collapsed Format for flattening arrays and collections.

The XmlFormat.COLLAPSED format can be applied to bean properties of type array/Collection. This causes the child objects to be serialized directly inside the bean element. This format must be used in conjunction with @Xml(childName) to differentiate which collection the values came from if you plan on parsing the output back into beans. Note that child names must not conflict with other property names. Data type JSON example Without annotation With annotation class MyBean { @Xml(childName="A",format=XmlFormat.COLLAPSED) public String[] a; @Xml(childName="B",format=XmlFormat.COLLAPSED) public int[] b; } { a: ['foo','bar'], b: [123,456] }
@Xml(format) Annotation for the full list of XmlFormat values. @Xml(childName) Annotation for naming the collapsed child elements. Element & Mixed Formats for other ways to render collections.

The element-oriented XmlFormat values let a single property produce free-form or mixed child content: XmlFormat.FREEFORM emits child elements for the property value. XmlFormat.MIXED and XmlFormat.MIXED_PWS produce mixed content by stripping element names from primitive values.

The XmlFormat.FREEFORM format can be applied to a single bean property of either a simple type or array/Collection. It allows free-form child elements to be formed. All other properties on the bean MUST be serialized as attributes. Data type JSON example With annotation class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.ATTR) public String a; @Xml(format=XmlFormat.FREEFORM) public String b; } { a: 'foo', b: 'bar' } <object a='foo'> bar </object> class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.ATTR) public String a; @Xml(format=XmlFormat.FREEFORM) public Object[] b; } { a: 'foo', b: ['bar', 'baz', 123, true, null] } <object a='foo'> bar baz 123 true </object>

The XmlFormat.MIXED format is similar to XmlFormat.FREEFORM except elements names on primitive types (string/number/boolean/null) are stripped from the output. This format particularly useful when combined with bean dictionaries to produce mixed content. The bean dictionary isn't used during serialization, but it is needed during parsing to resolve bean types. The XmlFormat.MIXED_PWS format identical to XmlFormat.MIXED except whitespace characters are preserved in the output. Data type JSON example Without annotations With annotations class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.MIXED) @MarshalledProp(dictionary={MyBeanX.class, MyBeanY.class}) public Object[] a; } @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBeanX { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.ATTR) public String b; } @Marshalled(typeName="Y") class MyBeanY { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.ATTR) public String c; } { a: [ 'foo', { _type:'X', b:'bar' }, 'baz', { _type:'Y', c:'qux' }, 'quux' ] } It should be noted that when using MIXED, you are not guaranteed to parse back the exact same content since side-by-side strings in the content will end up concatenated when parsed. For a detailed treatment of how empty strings and whitespace are preserved (or lost) in MIXED and MIXED_PWS output, see Whitespace Handling.
@Xml(format) Annotation for the full list of XmlFormat values. Text Formats for TEXT, TEXT_PWS, and XMLTEXT. Whitespace Handling for the whitespace rules that apply to mixed content.

The text-oriented XmlFormat values render a single property value directly as the character content of the element: XmlFormat.TEXT and XmlFormat.TEXT_PWS serialize any string-convertible value as a text node. XmlFormat.XMLTEXT serializes a string that is itself fully-formed XML as-is.

The XmlFormat.TEXT format is similar to XmlFormat.MIXED except it's meant for solitary objects that get serialized as simple child text nodes. Any object that can be serialize to a String can be used. The XmlFormat.TEXT_PWS is the same except whitespace is preserved in the output. Data type JSON example Without annotations With annotations class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.TEXT) public String a; } { a: 'foo' }

The XmlFormat.XMLTEXT format is similar to XmlFormat.TEXT except it's meant for strings containing XML that should be serialized as-is to the document. Any object that can be serialize to a String can be used. During parsing, the element content gets parsed with the rest of the document and then re-serialized to XML before being set as the property value. This process may not be perfect (e.g. double quotes may be replaced by single quotes, etc...). Data type JSON example With TEXT annotation With XMLTEXT annotation class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.XMLTEXT) public String a; } { a: 'Some XML text' }

@Xml(format) Annotation for the full list of XmlFormat values. Element & Mixed Formats for FREEFORM, MIXED, and MIXED_PWS. Whitespace Handling for how empty strings and whitespace are preserved in TEXT output.

The XmlFormat.MIXED, XmlFormat.MIXED_PWS, XmlFormat.TEXT, and XmlFormat.TEXT_PWS formats all serialize values directly as element content, which raises the question of how empty strings and leading/trailing whitespace survive a round trip. This page collects the whitespace rules that apply to those formats. Whitespace (tabs and newlines) are not added to MIXED child nodes in readable-output mode. This helps ensures strings in the serialized output can be losslessly parsed back into their original forms when they contain whitespace characters. If the XMLInputFactory.IS_REPLACING_ENTITY_REFERENCES setting was not useless in Java, we could support lossless readable XML for MIXED content. But as of Java 8, it still does not work. XML suffers from other deficiencies as well that affect MIXED content. For example, <X/> and <X></X> are equivalent in XML and indistinguishable by the Java XML parsers. This makes it impossible to differentiate between an empty element and an element containing an empty string. This causes empty strings to get lost in translation. To alleviate this, we use the constructs "xE000" to represent an empty string, and "x0020" to represent leading and trailing spaces. The examples below show how whitespace is handled under various circumstances: Data type XML @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.TEXT) public String a = null; } <X/> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.TEXT) public String a = ""; } <X>_xE000_</X> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.TEXT) public String a = " "; } <X>_x0020_</X> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.TEXT) public String a = " "; } <X>_x0020__x0020_</X> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.TEXT) public String a = " foobar "; } <X>_x0020_ foobar _x0020_</X> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.TEXT_PWS) public String a = null; } <X/> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.TEXT_PWS) public String a = ""; } <X>_xE000_</X> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.TEXT_PWS) public String a = " "; } <X> </X> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.TEXT_PWS) public String a = " "; } <X> </X> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.TEXT_PWS) public String a = " foobar "; } <X> foobar </X> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.MIXED) public String[] a = null; } <X/> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.MIXED) public String[] a = {""}; } <X>_xE000_</X> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.MIXED) public String[] a = {" "}; } <X>_x0020_</X> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.MIXED) public String[] a = {" "}; } <X>_x0020__x0020_</X> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.MIXED) public String[] a = {" foobar "}; } <X>_x0020_ foobar _x0020_</X> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.MIXED_PWS) public String[] a = null; } <X/> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.MIXED_PWS) public String[] a = {""}; } <X>_xE000_</X> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.MIXED_PWS) public String[] a = {" "}; } <X> </X> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.MIXED_PWS) public String[] a = {" "}; } <X> </X> @Marshalled(typeName="X") class MyBean { @Xml(format=XmlFormat.MIXED_PWS) public String[] a = {" foobar "}; } <X> foobar </X>

This page describes how the different POJO datatypes are represented in XML. The representations mirror how the same data structures are represented in JSON: Simple values (strings, numbers, booleans, nulls) render as elements named after their datatype (<string>, <number>, <boolean>, <null/>) when loose (not a direct bean property value). Maps and beans render inside <object> elements. Collections and arrays render inside <array> elements. The examples below show one representative case per category. For the complete set of data-type representations (all Map, array, Collection, and bean shapes), see the reference tables on the XML Serializers page.

The representation of loose (not a direct bean property value) simple types are shown below: Data type JSON example XML string 'foo' <string>foo</string> boolean true <boolean>true</boolean> integer 123 <number>123</number> float 1.23 <number>1.23</number> null null <null/>
Loose maps and beans use the element

Loose collections and arrays use the element <array> for encapsulation. Collections (e.g. List, Set) serialize identically to their array equivalents. The following representative example shows a mixed-type Object[]: Data type JSON example XML Object[] ['foo', 123, 1.23, true, null] <array> <string>foo</string> <number>123</number> <number>1.23</number> <boolean>true</boolean> <null/> </array>
Let's go back to the example of our original Person bean class but add some namespace annotations:

@Xml(prefix="per") @Marshalled(typeName="person") public class Person { // Bean properties public String name; @MarshalledProp(calendarFormat=CalendarFormat.ISO_INSTANT) public Calendar birthDate; public List addresses; // Getters/setters omitted } @Xml(prefix="addr") @Marshalled(typeName="address") public class Address { // Bean properties @Xml(prefix="mail") public String street, city; @Xml(prefix="mail") public StateEnum state; @Xml(prefix="mail") public int zip; public boolean isCurrent; // Getters/setters omitted } The namespace URLs can either be defined as part of the @Xml annotation, or can be defined at the package level with the @XmlSchema annotation. Below shows it defined at the package level:

@XmlSchema( prefix="ab", // Default namespace xmlNs={ @XmlNs(prefix="ab", namespaceURI="http://www.apache.org/addressBook/"), @XmlNs(prefix="per", namespaceURI="http://www.apache.org/person/"), @XmlNs(prefix="addr", namespaceURI="http://www.apache.org/address/"), @XmlNs(prefix="mail", namespaceURI="http://www.apache.org/mail/") } )

Person person = new Person() .name("John Smith") .birthDate("1946-08-12T00:00:00Z") .addresses( new Address() .street("100 Main Street") .city("Anywhereville") .state(NY) .zip(12345) .isCurrent(true) ); // Create a new serializer with readable output, this time with namespaces enabled. // Note that this is identical to XmlSerializer.DEFAULT_NS_SQ_READABLE. XmlSerializer serializer = XmlSerializer.create().ns().ws().sq().build(); String xml = serializer.write(person); Now when we run this code, we'll see namespaces added to our output: <per:person> <per:name>John Smith</per:name> <per:birthDate>1946-08-12T04:00:00Z</per:birthDate> <per:addresses> <addr:address> <mail:street>100 Main Street</mail:street> <mail:city>Anywhereville</mail:city> <mail:state>NY</mail:state> <mail:zip>12345</mail:zip> <addr:isCurrent>true</addr:isCurrent> </addr:address> </per:addresses> </per:person> Enabling the XmlSerializer.Builder.addNamespaceUrisToRoot() setting results in the namespace URLs being added to the root node: <per:person xmlns='http://www.apache.org/2013/Juneau' xmlns:per='http://www.apache.org/person/' xmlns:addr='http://www.apache.org/address/' xmlns:mail='http://www.apache.org/mail/' > <per:name>John Smith</per:name> <per:birthDate>1946-08-12T04:00:00Z</per:birthDate> <per:addresses> <addr:address> <mail:street>100 Main Street</mail:street> <mail:city>Anywhereville</mail:city> <mail:state>NY</mail:state> <mail:zip>12345</mail:zip> <addr:isCurrent>true</addr:isCurrent> </addr:address> </per:addresses> </per:person> We can simplify the output by setting the default namespace on the serializer so that all the elements do not need to be prefixed: // Create a new serializer with readable output, this time with namespaces enabled. XmlSerializer serializer = XmlSerializer.create().ws().sq().ns() .defaultNamespace(Namespace.of("per", "http://www.apache.org/person/")) .build(); This produces the following equivalent where the elements don't need prefixes since they're already in the default document namespace: <person xmlns:juneau='http://www.apache.org/2013/Juneau' xmlns='http://www.apache.org/person/' xmlns:addr='http://www.apache.org/address/' xmlns:mail='http://www.apache.org/mail/' > <name>John Smith</name> <birthDate>1946-08-12T04:00:00Z</birthDate> <addresses> <addr:address> <mail:street>100 Main Street</mail:street> <mail:city>Anywhereville</mail:city> <mail:state>NY</mail:state> <mail:zip>12345</mail:zip> <addr:isCurrent>true</addr:isCurrent> </addr:address> </addresses> </person> By default, the XML serializer class will make a first-pass over the data structure to look for namespaces defined on classes and bean properties. In high-performance environments, you may want to consider disabling auto-detection and providing your own explicit list of namespaces to the serializer to avoid this scanning step using XmlSerializer.Builder.disableAutoDetectNamespaces(). The following code will produce the same output as before but will perform slightly better since it avoids this pre-scan step. // Create a new serializer with readable output, this time with namespaces enabled. XmlSerializer serializer = XmlSerializer.create() .ns() .ws() .sq() .disableAutoDetectNamespaces() .namespaces(Namespace.of("per", "http://www.apache.org/person/")) .build();
The XmlParser class is used to parse XML into POJOs.

Use XmlParser to read XML produced by XmlSerializer, or XML in the same element conventions, back into beans, collections and maps. For XML with a different shape, such as an arbitrary third-party schema, map the elements with the @Xml annotation or parse into a generic JsonMap. The parser reads through a StAX reader; the secure-XML library (commons-secure-xml) must be on the classpath.

import java.util.*; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.xml.*; public class XmlParserExample { public static class Person { public String name; public int age; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String xml = "<object><name>John Smith</name><age>45</age></object>"; // Parse into a bean with the default parser. Person person = XmlParser.DEFAULT.read(xml, Person.class); // Parse a list; the second class is the element type. List<Integer> numbers = XmlParser.DEFAULT.read( "<array><number>1</number><number>2</number></array>", List.class, Integer.class); System.out.println(person.name + " " + person.age + " " + numbers); } } Parsers are immutable and thread-safe, so build one once and reuse it.

The following pre-configured parsers are provided for convenience: Instance Accepts XmlParser.DEFAULT XML with the default settings. For anything else, start from the builder's create() method. The settings readers reach for first: Builder method Effect preserveRootElement() Keep the root element name when parsing into a map, so it can be serialized back unchanged. validating() Validate the XML against its DTD while parsing. reporter(...) Set the XMLReporter that receives parse warnings. resolver(...) Set the XMLResolver used to resolve external entities. eventAllocator(...) Set the StAX XMLEventAllocator used to create events. trimStrings() Trim whitespace from parsed string values. beanDictionary(Class...) Classes the parser may instantiate from type-name attributes. swaps(Class...) Object swaps that convert parsed values into other types. The class hierarchy for the builder of this parser is below. Refer to the builder javadocs for the full set of configurable settings. Context.BuilderMarshallingContextable.BuilderParser.BuilderReaderParser.BuilderXmlParser.Builder

The XmlSerializer class is used to serialize POJOs into XML. The XmlDocSerializer class is the same but serializes a <?xml?> header at the top of the file. The class hierarchy for the builder of this serializer is: Context.BuilderMarshallingContextable.BuilderMarshallingTraverseContext.BuilderSerializer.BuilderWriterSerializer.BuilderXmlSerializer.Builder Refer to the builder javadocs for configurable settings. The following pre-configured serializers are provided for convenience: XmlSerializerDEFAULT DEFAULT_JUNEAU_NAMESPACE DEFAULT_NS DEFAULT_NS_SQ DEFAULT_NS_SQ_READABLE DEFAULT_SQ DEFAULT_SQ_READABLE

The following tables are the complete reference for how each POJO datatype is rendered by XmlSerializer. They mirror how the same data structures are represented in JSON. See XML Methodology for a conceptual overview of the mapping rules.

Loose maps and beans use the element <object> for encapsulation. _type attributes are added to bean properties or map entries if the type cannot be inferred through reflection (e.g. an Object or superclass/interface value type). Data type JSON example XML Map { k1: 'v1', k2: null } <object> <k1>v1</k1> <k2 _type='null'/> </object> Map { k1: 123, k2: 1.23, k3: null } <object> <k1>123</k1> <k2>1.23</k2> <k3 _type='null'/> </object> Map { k1: 'v1', k2: 123, k3: 1.23, k4: true, k5: null } <object> <k1>v1</k1> <k2 _type='number'>123</k2> <k3 _type='number'>1.23</k3> <k4 _type='boolean'>true</k4> <k5 _type='null'/> </object>

Loose collections and arrays use the element <array> for encapsulation. Collections (e.g. List, Set) serialize identically to their array equivalents. Juneau supports converting arbitrary POJOs to and from XML using ultra-efficient serializers and parsers. The XML serializer converts POJOs directly to XML without the need for intermediate DOM objects. Likewise, the XML parser uses a STaX parser and creates POJOs directly without intermediate DOM objects. Unlike frameworks such as JAXB, Juneau does not require POJO classes to be annotated to produce and consume XML. However, several XML annotations are provided for handling namespaces and fine-tuning the format of the XML produced. The following example shows XML for a typical bean:

@Marshalled(typeName="person") public class Person { // Bean properties public String name; @MarshalledProp(calendarFormat=CalendarFormat.ISO_INSTANT) public Calendar birthDate; public List addresses; // Getters/setters omitted } @Marshalled(typeName="address") public class Address { // Bean properties public String street, city; public StateEnum state; public int zip; public boolean isCurrent; // Getters/setters omitted }

Person person = new Person() .name("John Smith") .birthDate("1946-08-12T00:00:00Z") .addresses( new Address() .street("100 Main Street") .city("Anywhereville") .state(NY) .zip(12345) .isCurrent(true) );

<person> <name>John Smith</name> <birthDate>1946-08-12T04:00:00Z</birthDate> <addresses> <address> <street>100 Main Street</street> <city>Anywhereville</city> <state>NY</state> <zip>12345</zip> <isCurrent>true</isCurrent> </address> </addresses> </person> Juneau produces JSON-equivalent XML, meaning any valid JSON document can be losslessly converted into an XML equivalent. In fact, all of the Juneau serializers and parsers are built upon this JSON-equivalence.

The @Xml(childName) annotation can be used to specify the name of XML child elements for bean properties of type collection or array. Example Data type JSON example Without annotation With annotation class MyBean { @Xml(childName="X") public String[] a; @Xml(childName="Y") public int[] b; } { a: ['foo','bar'], b: [123,456] } class MyBean { @Xml(childName="child") public int[] a; } { a: [123,456] }

The @YamlConfig annotation is used to apply YAML serializer and parser configuration annotations to REST resources, methods, and other contexts.

Use @YamlConfig to set YAML options once on a class, method or REST resource, instead of calling builder methods on every serializer. In a plain program you apply it by passing the annotated class to a builder's applyAnnotations; in a REST resource Juneau applies it for you.

import org.apache.juneau.marshall.*; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.yaml.*; public class YamlAnnotationExample { @Marshalled(typeName="person") public static class Person { public String name = "John Smith"; } public static class Holder { public Object item = new Person(); } // The annotation turns on _type properties for any serializer that applies this class. @YamlConfig(addBeanTypes="true") public static class Config {} public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { YamlSerializer plain = YamlSerializer.create() .beanDictionary(Person.class) .build(); YamlSerializer typed = YamlSerializer.create() .beanDictionary(Person.class) .applyAnnotations(Config.class) .build(); System.out.println(plain.write(new Holder())); System.out.println(typed.write(new Holder())); } } The first serializer writes name: John Smith under item; the second adds _type: person there, because the declared type Object hides the runtime type.

Element Effect addBeanTypes Add _type properties to beans whose runtime type differs from the declared type. A true or false string, resolved through SVL. rank Overrides the default ordering when several config annotations apply to the same target.

YAML support can be added to REST resources using the BasicYamlConfig interface or by including the YAML serializer and parser in BasicUniversalConfig: // YAML-only REST resource @Rest class MyYamlResource extends RestServlet implements BasicYamlConfig { @RestGet("/person/{id}") public Person getPerson(@Path int id) { return findPerson(id); } } // Universal resource supporting JSON, XML, HTML, UON, and YAML @Rest class MyUniversalResource extends RestServlet implements BasicUniversalConfig { @RestGet("/person/{id}") public Person getPerson(@Path int id) { return findPerson(id); } }

You can configure the YAML serializer and parser through annotation or programmatic builders: @Rest( serializers = YamlSerializer.class, parsers = YamlParser.class, defaultAccept = "application/yaml" ) class MyResource extends RestServlet { // ... }

juneau-config supports YAML config files as an alternative to INI/CFG files. See the guide: Externalize config with INI/YAML and variables
Use YAML when the config is nested or shared with tools that already read YAML. INI remains the default format.

A .yml or .yaml config name auto-selects the YAML format. import org.apache.juneau.config.*; import org.apache.juneau.config.store.*; public class YamlConfigExample { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { // Put a YAML file in an in-memory store so the example is self-contained. MemoryStore store = MemoryStore.create().build(); store.update("MyConfig.yaml", "foo:
 bar:
 baz:
 k1: v1
"); // A .yaml name auto-selects the YAML format. Config config = Config.create().name("MyConfig.yaml").store(store).build(); System.out.println(config.getString("foo/bar/baz/k1")); } }
Setting Effect name("MyConfig.yaml") Picks YAML from the file extension yaml() Forces YAML for any name, for example MyConfig.cfg Config c = Config.create() .name("MyConfig.cfg") .yaml() .build();
INI section paths map directly to nested YAML maps: [foo/bar/baz] k1 = v1 foo: bar: baz: k1: v1 A config lookup like config.getString("foo/bar/baz/k1") works the same for either format.
INI remains the default format. FileStore now searches cfg,yml,yaml by default. Existing value modifiers and SVL variable resolution continue to work unchanged.
